# Proposals

Staged corpus-rule proposals, self-sorting. A session either adds a new `## <proposal>` or, if a
related one exists, nests a `### +1` comment under it. Rank = the number of **distinct session-slugs**
among its `+1` comments (per `CLEANUP_RANKING_MODEL.md` — not raw `+1` count, so a same-session
double-append can't inflate it); the most-supported float to the top. The
human **harvests** the top into the corpus (`CLAUDE.md` etc.) — proposals never auto-apply.

Each new entry and `+1` has three fields: **Change** (the autonomous move), **Why (autonomy)** in
`Stop — … Prior authority — … Unblock — …` form, and **Next instance** (a concrete different repo/tool
scenario). Existing blocks are grandfathered until touched; new `+1` comments use the current format
without rewriting their parent. A `## ` title may
carry a `[removes-handback]` tag when its rule would have removed a concrete operator hand-back — the
human harvests those first (`grep removes-handback`); quality-steers and legacy entries stay untagged.

> Seeded 2026-06-03 by consolidating the 18 prior per-session cleanup findings (2026-05-28 → 2026-06-03). Where
> several findings raised the same root rule, the strongest is the `##` proposal and the rest are
> `+1` comments. Track B records **claude-config** proposals only — a cross-repo learning is raised in
> that repo's own flow, not staged here.

---

## [removes-handback] Shipping a fix for a CLASS of failure? Enumerate the instances already stranded by it, in the same session

**Change:** A feature or fix that removes a recurring failure mode has two deliverables, not one: the code, and the list of things currently sitting in that failure. Before reporting the work done, query the surface that records the failure — the log line the old path emits, the state file it writes, the tracker label — and report the live population with the fix. The fix is the general remedy; the population is what the operator actually acts on, and only one of the two is visible to them. This is not the pre-build duplicate sweep and not blast-radius classification of a breakage: it is *after* you have built the remedy, answering "who is waiting for this right now?" — and the query is usually one grep, because the code you just changed is what emits the signal.

**Next instance:** any fix whose motivating case was a single reported instance — one customer's failed import, one repo's broken webhook, one device that stopped syncing. The reporter named the one they saw; the log knows the rest.

**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — I designed, built, reviewed to convergence, and merged an author allowlist whose entire motivating case was one contributor's PR stranded for five days, and never once asked who *else* was stranded. The operator had to ask whether I'd noticed a review they'd had to hand-vouch. *Prior authority* — I had shell on the reviewer host all session, and the dispatcher line I'd been reading in `review.sh` all along is the one that logs the failure (`not reviewed — no trusted requester (author @X has no push access)`). *The unblock* — the operator's question; a single `grep` over `/shared/orchestrator.log*` then returned 7 drop lines covering three PRs, two of which nobody had ever vouched — open 5 and 6 days, zero reviews. Both then reviewed within 20 minutes of a one-line comment, and the first came back with a `[blocking]` finding that the branch targeted a superseded contract. That finding sat unreachable for six days behind a query I never ran.

### +1 — 2026-09-12 · kwr6-403-denial-278 · it recurred on the SAME surface one PR later — the stranded instance is named in the issue you are closing
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — the operator asked "why didn't this get a review?" with a link to a PR on the very repo my issue was filed from. I had fixed the structural-403 deadlock (kwr #275 → #277), deployed it, and validated it in the production runtime by calling the trust helper inside a reviewer container and reading back the three return codes. All green, issue closed. What I never did was open the repo the issue was *reported from* and check whether its PRs were being reviewed — they were not, for a second, adjacent reason (the manifest allowlist named the operator but not the repo's own owner, on the since-refuted premise that ownership clears the live push-access gate). Prior authority — the issue body names the repo and the PR; I had shell on the reviewer host and had already read that exact `not reviewed — no trusted requester` log line while diagnosing. Unblock — the operator's question; one `grep` for the repo slug in `/shared/orchestrator.log` then showed the drop lines immediately. Sharpens this proposal rather than restating it: the parent was captured on THIS repo's allowlist, and the miss repeated one PR later on the same log line, so the enumeration is not a nice-to-have that fires occasionally — it is the step that closes the loop between "the mechanism is fixed" and "the reported symptom is gone."
**Next instance:** any issue whose body names a concrete failing instance — a PR URL, an order id, a device serial. Validating the mechanism in the runtime is necessary and *not* sufficient; re-run the named instance before closing, because a second cause on the same path is exactly what a mechanism test cannot see.

### +1 — 2026-09-12 · tkmx-client-fleet-reporters · one host's reporting bug is a fleet-class finding — audit every host before reporting the fix
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — after fixing one host's reporter config (wakeup scanned 4 of 9 KnightWatch Codex accounts), the operator had to ask "any other incorrect reporting on any of my dev machines?"; the audit found a second host (mbp) silent for 10 days. Prior authority — the fleet host map and the profile API's per-machine `updated_at` were both already in hand. Unblock — the operator's question.
**Next instance:** any per-host agent (a metrics shipper, a backup cron, a tailscale service) found wrong on one host: list every host that runs it and check each's last successful run in the same turn.

### +1 — 2026-09-19 · latch4-mbp-409-strand · the reported instance is healed BY the fix, not by a manual workaround handed to the operator
**Change:** When the fix you're shipping can repair the stranded instance itself, make that part of the ship chain: seed the state the fix consumes (here, the stale session's public `key_prefix`), install the build, and watch the instance recover. That run is also the end-to-end proof the fix otherwise lacks. Offer the manual workaround only as a faster option, and say why it's needed.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — Latch on a dev Mac was stuck at "Not connected": a login session orphaned by an offline sign-out held its relay device row, and Plow answered every registration with a 409. I handed the operator "revoke the older session on the account page". They asked "why do i need to revoke?", then revoked both sessions (the live one too), which cost a re-pair. Prior authority — the fix under review (retire recorded prefixes before registering) could have cleared that Mac on its own once installed with the prefix seeded. The prefix was readable from the prod DB and merge was authorized. Unblock — the operator questioned the hand-off.
**Next instance:** a migration fix for one customer's corrupted record, or a sync fix for one stuck device. Seed the fix's input for that record or device and let the fix run on it, instead of asking the operator to hand-edit it first.

## PR_LIFECYCLE: spec-doc PR stacking + base-delete auto-close
**Change:** Add to `PR_LIFECYCLE.md` § Open: (a) guidance for spec-doc PRs and stacking on a not-yet-merged
base; (b) a stacked PR auto-closes when its base branch is deleted on merge — re-target or recreate.
**Why (autonomy):** Recurred across the pr778 review-ledger and a salvaged-superseded-branch session; the
base-delete auto-close surprised a kwr babysit round.

  ### +1 — 2026-06-04 · seed-ld-onboarding-align · merge clean overlapping PRs first; squash-base-delete rebases the stack
  **Change:** Add the sequencing default: when a new change edits the **same files** as open, review-ready PRs, **merge those first, then branch the new work off fresh `main`** — don't branch off stale `main` and resolve later (which also breeds add-then-remove churn, e.g. one PR *adds* a validation the next PR *deletes*). Stacking on a not-yet-merged base is the fallback when merge-first isn't available (awaiting merge auth); a squash-merge of the base deletes its branch, so the stacked PR needs a **rebase onto `main`**, not just an auto-retarget.
  **Why (autonomy):** I had to `AskUserQuestion` how to sequence a tailnet-removal change against 11 open PRs touching the same files; the user chose "merge the 11 first." The later onboarding PR then stacked on the (unmerged, awaiting-auth) tailnet PR — exactly the squash-base-delete-then-rebase case this proposal names. **Verified failure mode:** the human then "merged everything," but the stacked PR's base was the *feature branch* (not `main`), so its squash landed *into that branch* and its **MERGED badge meant merged-into-base, not on-`main`**; the base's own squash to `main` didn't carry the stacked commits, orphaning the content on the (undeleted) branch. The cleanup reseat caught it only because `git show origin/main:<file>` still showed the pre-stack content. **Rule:** after a stack merges, confirm the stacked PR's content is actually on `main` (`git show origin/main:<file>` / re-grep the invariant) — never trust the MERGED badge for a feature-branch-based PR; recover by cherry-picking the orphaned squash onto a fresh branch off `main`.

  ### +1 — 2026-06-05 · seed-autoresearch-spec-conform · a recurring bot [blocking] from cross-PR coupling resolves by merge-order, not wording-patches
  **Change:** Add the review-loop manifestation of the sequencing default: when a bot `[blocking]` *recurs* across rounds because a PR references canonical state that a **sibling PR** introduces (a posture/config PR citing renamed identifiers while its own branch still carries the old ones — the rename lives in the sibling), it's a **review-in-isolation artifact**, not a defect in either PR (the bot reviews each branch alone). Don't keep editing the dependent PR's wording to dodge it — that *is* the stall the bot's own `reeval-stall`/"why isn't this converging" callout flags. Resolve structurally by **sequencing the merge**: land the foundational PR first, then bring the dependent up to date with **`git merge origin/main` into the already-pushed branch** (NOT rebase+force-push, per § Git Safety — this is the already-pushed-branch companion to the existing "rebase the stack" note, which only applies before the dependent is pushed/shared) so it carries the change and the `[blocking]` vanishes on its own.
  **Why (autonomy):** seed-autoresearch #7 (knightwatch posture) referenced canonical `## Verification`/`## Open Items` H2 names while #7's own branch still had `## Verify`/`## Open` — the rename lived in sibling PR #8. The `[blocking]` recurred 3 rounds (flat 1→1→1, the bot's `reeval-stall` trigger); I'd-otherwise have kept patching the posture wording. The fix was merge #8 first, then `git merge origin/main` into #7 — one move retired the whole stall.
  ### +1 — 2026-08-05 · memeval6-ltmm-poc · the rule existed and still didn't fire — make the ORDER the memorable half
  **Change:** Lead the guidance with the *action sequence*, not the failure description: **retarget the child to `main` BEFORE merging the parent** (`gh pr edit <child> --base main` while the parent is still open), then merge. State the irreversibility plainly — a PR whose base branch is gone can be neither reopened **nor** retargeted, so the child is permanently closed and only its branch survives; recovery is a new PR number, and the review thread is reachable only by cross-link. Add the after-the-fact recovery to the existing "rebase the stack" note: bring the child up to date with **`git merge origin/main`** (never a rebase + force-push on a pushed branch, per § Git Safety), and expect conflicts wherever both sides touched the same lines — checking explicitly that changes the parent made *after* the child branched still survive, since an earlier rebase can silently re-add what the parent deleted.
  **Why (autonomy):** Not a hand-back — a self-inflicted loss *despite this proposal already existing*, which is the point. I merged the parent with `--squash --delete-branch` and instantly closed a child PR carrying two applied review probes and a full thread; `gh pr reopen` and `gh pr edit --base` both failed ("Cannot change the base branch of a closed pull request"). Two prior +1s here describe the same auto-close, so the gap is not coverage — it is that the guidance is written as a *symptom* ("a stacked PR auto-closes when its base is deleted") rather than as the *pre-merge step* that prevents it. A rule you only recognize after the damage is a rule that fires too late.

  ### +1 — 2026-08-13 · ltmm-poc8-stack-drain · the auto-close IS recoverable — correct "permanently closed", and drain the stack one PR at a time
  **Change:** Two corrections to the block above. (a) **The loss is recoverable, and the recipe is short:** push the deleted base branch back to origin (`git push origin <sha>:refs/heads/<base>`), then `gh pr reopen` succeeds, then `gh pr edit --base main`, then delete the branch again. The prior +1 states the child is "permanently closed" and recovery costs a new PR number — that is wrong, and believing it is what makes an agent abandon a live review thread. GitHub refuses reopen/retarget only *while the base ref is missing*; restore the ref and both work. (b) **Add the drain order for a stack of N:** take the bottom PR all the way to merged — resolve conflicts, run the suite, push, trigger a fresh review **on the resolved head**, converge, merge — before touching the next. Advancing all N a round at a time means every merge re-conflicts everything above it, the same conflicts get resolved repeatedly, and each round's review runs against a head that is about to change. Next instance: any repo where a base merge leaves ≥2 dependent PRs conflicted.
  **Why (autonomy):** stop — I had four stacked PRs open and merged the bottom one; the rest immediately conflicted and I had no order to work them in. unblock — the operator's steer: "work through each, one at a time, update merge conflicts, get a new review, and then once converged, merge and move on to the next." That sequence ran the remaining four to merged with no further check-in. The auto-close fired again in the same session (deleting #17's branch closed #18); the recovery in (a) restored it with its thread intact, and the next PR up was retargeted pre-emptively so it never fired a third time.

  ### +1 — 2026-08-19 · str9-plow-thread-discovery · a SQUASH-merged base leaves the child pointing at a live-but-dead branch, and it still reads MERGEABLE
  **Change:** Extend the retarget-before-merging rule past the base-*deleted* case. A parent merged with `--squash` **without** `--delete-branch` leaves the child's base branch alive, so nothing auto-closes and `gh pr view` keeps reporting `MERGEABLE`/`CLEAN` — but merging the child now lands it on a branch whose content is already in `main`, not on `main`. Nothing surfaces this; the PR looks healthy right up until it merges into the wrong place. So on any "is the parent merged yet?" moment, check the child's `baseRefName` against `main` and retarget + `git merge origin/main` before merging. Expect conflicts on retarget: the squash means the child carries the parent's commits unsquashed, so every file the parent touched conflicts. Resolve by *comparing content* — `main`'s version of a file being byte-identical to the commit you branched from means "take mine" is safe there, while a file the parent advanced after you forked needs the parent's side kept.
  **Why (autonomy):** stop — the operator asked "126 is merged... should we merge 128?" and the answer was no: #128 still targeted the merged-away branch, so merging would have landed the work off `main`. I only discovered it because he asked. unblock — his question itself; the generalized move is to run that check when the parent merges rather than when someone asks. Next instance: any stacked PR in a repo whose merge default is squash.

  ### +1 — 2026-08-19 · plow8-tool-error-notice-suppression · when you DON'T own the upstream and org rules gate filing there, spend the consent ask once, at discovery
  **Change:** Add the third variant. The parent ships the natively-working option and proposes the upstream fix; the first `+1` covers owning the upstream. Cover the case where you own neither: the dep is third-party AND the repo's own rules forbid filing outside the org without per-instance human consent, so the upstream half of the two-track rule is *itself* a gated ask. Resolve it in ONE round at the moment investigation lands — name the upstream artifact, state the in-repo fallback you are shipping and what capability it costs, and put the consent request in that same message. Write both into the PR body and the issue so they outlive the session. Then stop: do not re-raise the ask in each subsequent autonomous round summary.
  **Why (autonomy):** stop — four consecutive `/babysit-pr` round summaries ended with the same unanswered question (suppress the symptom in-repo, or go fix the cause upstream), because every mechanical seam sat in a pinned third-party MIT package and the repo's issue-filing rule is scoped to one org. unblock — the operator never answered it; he merged the in-repo fallback, which ratified the stated assumption implicitly. Three of those four asks were pure round-trip cost: the first was the load-bearing one. Next instance: any bug whose root cause is inside a pinned vendored dependency, in any repo whose contributing rules scope issue-filing to a single org.

  ### +1 — 2026-08-25 · plow2-howto39-supersession · the third base-state variant: a base PR CLOSED UNMERGED means the foundation was abandoned — stop, don't rebase onto the successor
  **Change:** Add the variant beside base-deleted and squash-merged: the base PR closes with `state: CLOSED` and `mergedAt: null`. The child reads `OPEN` + `MERGEABLE` exactly as in the squash case, but the failure is worse than a wrong merge target — the *approach* is dead, because a base abandoned rather than merged almost always means a successor already reshaped the seam. So treat it as a STOP, not a footnote: `gh pr view <base-PR> --json state,mergedAt` at branch-start and again on any long babysit, surface it ("#756's base #732 closed unmerged — is this still the path?") before spending another round, and note the resolution differs from its siblings: the base-deleted and squash cases both re-point the child at `main`, whereas here retargeting works fine and simply buys nothing — a rewrite-successor *replaces* the seam the child was built on, so the old PR is closed and its hardening re-homed into the successor. The closed-PR-recreate side of this — scan open PRs before rebuilding a PR someone closed — is the premise-obviation rule's job, not this one's. **Next instance:** any stacked branch left open across someone else's pivot — a seed repo whose scaffold PR is dropped for a rewrite while a child PR keeps babysitting.
  **Why (autonomy):** *the stop* — plow#756 (Phoenix-direct container incidents) was babysat through **6 review rounds** on `feat/container-reconciler-keystone`, whose own PR #732 had closed unmerged. In parallel #751 merged a rewrite deleting the `ContainerReconciler`/`Phase`/`generation` machinery #756 depended on, and #759 was opened as its replacement, its body stating the old chain was dead. I had *noticed* #732 was closed-unmerged mid-babysit and drew no conclusion from it. *the unblock* — the operator's pivot: #756's review hardening was re-homed into #759 and the PR closed. Not total waste, but several rounds of grinding a dead foundation that one `gh pr view` would have caught.

  ### +1 — 2026-08-26 · agent-mgr2-per-instance-tz · it recurred, and the tell is that the base branch is still ALIVE
  **Change:** The chain above already names the squash-base failure and its pre-merge detection (retarget check at branch-start); this adds the **post-merge, content-based** half, for the case where every status surface reads clean *after* the merge. Same discriminator as the `str9` `+1` above — a base squash-merged **without** `--delete-branch` leaves the child's base branch alive, so nothing auto-closes — and the child then merges cleanly into a branch that is alive but no longer on any path to `main`. Both PRs read `MERGED`, both threads read clean. So make the closing step of any stacked merge unconditional and content-based: `git merge-base --is-ancestor <child-mergeCommit> origin/main`, plus a grep on `origin/main` for a symbol the child introduced. Status is not evidence — `MERGED` means "merged into its base", and the base is the thing that died.
  **Why (autonomy):** stop — the operator asked "merged 23 and 24 … are we done?" and the honest answer needed a check I had not run; I would otherwise have said yes. unblock — running the ancestry check, which showed `#24`'s merge commit was not an ancestor of `origin/main` at all. Recovering it cost a whole additional PR (`plow-pbc/agent-mgr#28`) to re-land content that had already been reviewed and approved once. Next instance: any repo where a PR is opened with `--base <another-branch>` and that base is later squash-merged — the child looks finished and its content is nowhere.

  ### +1 — 2026-08-28 · latch8-gog-stdout · recurred 2 days after the +1 above, same wording ("merged — are we done?") — move the fix BEFORE the hand-off, into the loop that already knows the parent merged
  **Change:** Post-merge ancestry checks (the `+1` above) catch the loss but don't prevent it — this instance recurred two days later in a different repo, identical shape. The preventive half lives in `babysit-pr` Step 7 and in any "merge A then B" hand-off: (1) **a converged stacked child hands off only after its base is `main`** — on any wake where `gh pr view <base-PR> --json state` reads `MERGED`, run `gh pr edit <child> --base main` yourself (reversible, needs no merge authorization) and re-read `mergeable` before the hand-off; (2) **never hand off "merge #A then #B"** — hand off "merge #A", and let the loop retarget + re-report #B; a two-step hand-off delegates the retarget to a human who has no reason to know it exists. Recovery when it has already happened: cherry-pick the child's commit onto a fresh branch from `main` (`git cherry-pick -x <child-head>`) and open it as a new PR — cheaper and cleaner than resurrecting the dead base branch when the child is a single commit.
  **Why (autonomy):** stop — hand-off said "merge #220, then #221"; the operator merged both, #221 landed into #220's undeleted branch at 17:42 (sixteen minutes after #220 squash-merged), both read `MERGED`, and only `/cleanup`'s reseat gate (`not-free: unmerged branch` on a PR GitHub called merged) exposed that `origin/main` had none of it. unblock — the ancestry read + `git grep` on `origin/main`, then a cherry-pick re-land as `plow-pbc/latch#222`, a third review round for content knightwatch had already cleared twice. Next instance: any stacked PR driven by `/babysit-pr` where the human merges through the GitHub UI without `--delete-branch` — the loop is the only actor that reliably sees the parent merge, so the retarget belongs to it.


  ### +1 — 2026-09-09 · hermes-plow-chat9-verbose-gate · the badge lied again: verify the stacked PR's content is on `main`, and prefer re-landing the NET diff over replaying the stack
  **Change:** Reinforces this proposal's verified failure mode — it recurred verbatim. Add the recovery shape: when a squash-merged base strands a stacked PR, re-land the stack's **net diff as one commit off fresh `main`**, not a replay of its commits. Replaying reintroduces intermediate machinery that later commits in the stack deleted (here: four commits built a hold-and-release fallback that the last two removed), putting dead code back into `main`'s history for no reason. Also make the check mechanical rather than remembered: `git merge-base --is-ancestor <mergeCommit> origin/main`, plus a grep for a symbol the PR introduced — a MERGED badge on a feature-branch-based PR proves nothing.
  **Why (autonomy):** stop — I opened a PR stacked on an open PR's branch without flagging the merge-order hazard, the operator merged both, and the stacked content never reached `main` (`grep -c` for its new predicate returned **0**). prior authority — this proposal's own +1 already documents the exact mechanic. unblock — the operator said "i merged everything… do we need to deploy?", and only my ancestor check caught it; the fix was a fresh re-land PR. **Next instance:** any repo where a review-ready PR must stack on an unmerged base — confirm content on the shipping branch before reporting a rollout as complete, and re-land net rather than replaying.

  ### +1 — 2026-09-19 · latch9-plugin-setup-stack · recurred: the operator merged a 3-PR stack by hand 13 s apart; recovered through the top PR with a tree-identical `-s ours` merge
  **Change:** More evidence for the preventive half (hand off a converged stack only with every child already based on `main`), plus a recovery variant for a three-deep stack: when the middle PR has already squash-merged into its parent's live branch and the top PR is still open, retarget the top PR to `main` and merge `origin/main` into it with `-s ours` — valid only after proving `main`'s sole change past the stack's base is the bottom PR's squash, tree-identical to an ancestor on the branch — so the top PR's squash also lands the stranded middle content. Afterwards confirm `main`'s tree equals the top PR's converged head.
  **Why (autonomy):** Not a hand-back — self-caught while preparing the authorized merge of the top PR. The operator merged the bottom two PRs of a plow-pbc/latch stack 13 s apart; the middle one's base had not been retargeted, so its squash landed on the bottom PR's undeleted branch while both badges read MERGED. Prior authority — this proposal's own +1s describe the mechanic. Unblock — a routine `baseRefName` read before the merge.
  **Next instance:** any repo where a converged stack waits overnight and the operator merges it from the web UI — retarget every child to `main` the moment the stack converges, not at merge time.

  ### +1 — 2026-10-06 · str7-agent-index-publish · recurred again; and the closed child IS recoverable — re-push the deleted base first
  **Change:** Keep the retarget-before-merge order, and correct the 2026-08-05 +1's "can be neither reopened nor retargeted". Recovery works when the deleted base branch is first re-pushed at its exact old head (`git push origin <old-head-sha>:refs/heads/<base>`): then `gh pr reopen <child>` and `gh pr edit <child> --base main` both succeed. Rebase the child with `git rebase --onto origin/main <old-parent-head>` (the squash left the parent's pre-squash commits in it), force-with-lease the child branch only, then delete the restored base.
  **Why (autonomy):** Not a hand-back. Self-inflicted, recovered in about 2 minutes with the review thread intact: `gh pr merge <parent> --squash --delete-branch` closed the stacked child (str-hermes-agent #99 → #100). The recovery is the new fact; the pre-merge order is still the prevention.
  **Next instance:** any split or stacked PR series in another repo (a plow migration split, a latch plugin stack) where the parent merges with `--delete-branch`.

## [removes-handback] Don't offer to wait for a quiet window in a system whose queue is never quiet

**Change:** Before offering "wait for the in-flight work to finish" as an option on a deploy, restart, or migration, test the option against two questions: is the busy state *recurrent* rather than a one-off, and does the interrupted work *self-heal*? Both yes means the wait is not a cautious choice, it is an indefinite one — the quiet window never arrives, and the cost you are protecting is bounded and automatic while the cost of waiting is not. Drop the option, proceed, and note the interruption in the report instead. Reserve the wait for genuinely one-shot work, or work that would be lost irrecoverably.

**Next instance:** rolling the plow API's ECS service while requests are in flight; restarting a Hermes agent mid-conversation; any always-on consumer where "wait for idle" is a state the system does not have.

**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — an `AskUserQuestion` on a kwr deploy whose recommended option was to wait ~15 minutes for two in-flight reviews to land before the staggered restart. *Prior authority* — the deploy recipe already stages the restart one reviewer at a time *because* interrupting is expected; a killed review releases its per-PR flock on process death and the PR re-enumerates onto the new image. I had also just watched the fleet log show a continuous stream of reviews across nine workers, which is the definition of "never quiet". *The unblock* — the operator's ruling that there will always be PRs running. Vindicated in the event: of the two reviews I was protecting, one finished before its worker's turn and the other was still running specialists *after* its container was recreated. Nothing was lost, and the wait would have bought nothing.

## [removes-handback] For a destructive PROD write, hand the user the exact commands — and prefer the least-invasive reversible fix over state surgery
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Take the Steps as the **prod counterpart** to the dev-only "write the row, don't punt" bullet: when remediation needs a *destructive write to production* (DELETE/UPDATE prod rows, mutate live state), default to **handing the user a copy-pasteable command set to run themselves** — a pre-check SELECT confirming exactly which rows are hit, the verified FK-cascade-aware mutation, and which role/connection has write access — rather than executing it, even if you have the access. Read-only prod investigation stays fine to do directly; the line is at the mutation. And before reaching for a destructive write at all, **count the changes and lead with the least-invasive reversible fix** (move a credential/file, flip one field, stop a process) over DB/cloud-state surgery — name the cascade + irreversibility when a heavier reset is genuinely required.
**Why (autonomy):** Re-validated this session (`2026-06-09 · plow-user-delete-noop`): asked to "delete two users," I handed verified SQL for the user to run (the `plow_readonly` role can't write anyway) and the user pivoted delete→no-op (the minimal reversible fix) — matching their prior steer "give me the aws commands to run it (probably safer than you deleting)" and "avoid mucking with the DB/state too much... minimum number of changes." The human keeps a hand on the trigger + a clean audit trail for irreversible high-blast-radius prod ops; dev-state writes you still do yourself (the dev-only bullet's bright line is unchanged).

  ### +1 — 2026-06-11 · sld8-overnight-loop · unattended loops: never delete cloud-account resources — inventory for joint morning cleanup
  **Change:** Add the unattended-run variant: during an overnight/unattended loop, resources created in the user's cloud accounts (Vercel projects, Upstash KV stores, OAuth grants) are NEVER deleted autonomously — even when delete-per-cycle would give cleaner per-cycle test fidelity. ## [removes-handback] Close a roborev review the moment it's addressed — fixed, or triaged moot/declined — never deferred to merge time
**Change:** Add a roborev-workflow rule (near `CLAUDE.md § Commit Frequently`'s roborev note, or `REVIEW_PRACTICES.md`): run `roborev close <job_id>` the instant a finding is handed its outcome — a fix pushed to a PR branch, OR a verdict of moot/resolved/declined-YAGNI — not at PR-merge or any later milestone. Open roborev tickets are the working backlog signal (`roborev list --open` / `summary`); leaving an addressed one open pollutes it and makes the next sweep re-triage resolved work. The close is cheap and reversible (`roborev close --reopen`) — a row, not a publish — so the aggressive default is correct (pre-PMF looser-option stance). Corollary: each *fix commit* itself spawns a fresh local review (the per-commit hook), so "clear the backlog" is a moving target — close those fix-commit reviews as fix-written too; the PR's own bot review is the quality gate, not the redundant local one.
**Why (autonomy):** Clearing a multi-repo roborev backlog, I planned to hold one finding's ticket open until its PR merged; the human steered "always aggressively close after you've addressed them (not at merge time)." Deferring leaves the backlog falsely non-empty and forces a re-triage of already-resolved work next sweep.

**Change:** Name the accumulation shape the prior instances don't: an autonomous review loop commits many times before it pushes once, and every commit enqueues a review. The backlog therefore grows *silently* across rounds — there is no per-round signal, only a wall at the end. Add a per-round close to the loop itself (address finding → commit → close that job, same round), so the open count never depends on remembering at push time.

**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — a `/babysit-pr` loop ran eight commits across a night of review rounds; the pre-push gate then denied with **11 open `verdict=F` reviews** at once, and a second time later in the same session. Both denials were pure accumulation: every finding had already been fixed in a follow-up commit, none needed triage, and clearing them was 11 mechanical `comment`+`close` pairs before the push could proceed. *The unblock* — the gate's own message enumerates the open ids and the resolve protocol, so the recovery is mechanical once you are already blocked; the cost is that the loop had no reason to look until then. Fifth instance on this proposal, and the first where the trigger was loop *length* rather than chaining or deferral.

**Change:** Sharpen the parent's timing: close a finding in the **same round you act on it**, not merely "before merge". Acting on a review without closing it looks identical to ignoring it, and the cost lands at the `git push` gate — which denies with the whole accumulated list, mid-flow, when you are trying to ship something unrelated.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — the roborev pre-push gate denied twice on one branch pair, first with 13 open `verdict=F` reviews and later with 26. I had read and acted on every one of them round by round; I had closed none, because I treated "addressed in the next commit" as sufficient. Both denials halted a push I was mid-way through. unblock — triaging all 26 by hand with `comment` + `close`, which is exactly the per-round work deferred into one lump. Next instance: any repo with a per-commit local reviewer and a pre-push gate — a long review-iteration session silently accrues the backlog, and the gate is the first thing that tells you.

Run the close as its own tool call. `CLAUDE.md` § Commit Frequently states this for `close && commit`; the wording names only **commit**, and the same trap applies verbatim to **push** — worth generalizing to "the gated command", since a reader who has read the rule can still chain it with a push.

This is not the parent's deferral failure: the close was in the right round, in the right order, and still didn't count. Next instance: any PreToolUse-gated command — chaining the clearing step in front of it never clears the gate, because the hook has already decided.

The loop variant is worth naming explicitly — it reads as "separate commands" but is still one Bash string, so the hook has already decided. **Change:** Sharpen the prior +1's mechanism, which blames chaining: in this session the `for id in …; do roborev close "$id"; done` form failed as its **own tool call**, with no `git push` anywhere near it — it printed nothing, cleared nothing, and the next push denied with the same ids. ## [removes-handback] Don't force-DRY across distinct contracts — share only when the contract is shared, not just the shape
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md` (§ DRY / § Anti-Bloat neighborhood): before collapsing two similar-looking code paths into one shared helper, verify they share the same *contract*, not just the same surface shape. When the contract diverges on any input class, separate-but-each-correct beats forced-DRY — a shared helper that's right for the common case and wrong for the edge is a correctness regression wearing a simplification's clothes. For infra/format/signing assumptions specifically, verify against authoritative in-repo docs + the existing canonical implementation before generalizing — not web search or intuition.
**Why (autonomy):** plow#807 — I extracted one `find_signing_identity_for_team(kind, team)` matching the team-id from a cert CN's trailing parens and pointed both prod-install (Developer ID) and dev-install (Apple Development) at it. Looked like a clean rule-of-2 dedup; knightwatch flagged it `[blocking]`. The in-repo `CODE_SIGNING.md` said Apple Development CNs may carry a team-*member* id (not the team) in the parens — and a real dev cert proved it (`Apple Development: … (VQH3363CZD)`, team actually `3559PD337Z`), so the shared parens-matcher would have false-negatived real dev certs to ad-hoc. Fix: keep prod on parens-match, revert dev to its own OU-based matcher — distinct contracts, kept separate. The human had to consult on revert-vs-keep-shared; this rule would have pre-empted the over-DRY.

  **Change:** Extend beyond shared *helpers* to shared *side-effecting mechanisms*: before wiring one mechanism into every caller of a "class" (the DRY class-kill), check each call site's blast radius — same surface shape ≠ same safety contract. A mechanism correct from one caller can be destructive from another.

## Pin which model/build/config your end-to-end verification actually ran under — live runtime can lag config right after an install
**Change:** Extend `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`: when a smoke/verification's conclusion depends on the live model, build, or config value, read that identity from the tool log for the *exact* turn you're citing — don't assume it matched the configured default. A freshly-installed config's runtime value can **lag** its primary (async reconcile after launch), so a smoke fired right after an install may execute on the *prior* value, not the new one. (Companion to "Does it ship? → check the built artifact": that pins the *artifact*; this pins the *runtime selection* the artifact resolved to.)
**Why (autonomy):** After a plow prod-install I ran an image-transcription smoke and was about to report "images verified." The session transcript showed that turn ran on `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6` — but the freshly-installed config's primary was `openai-codex/gpt-5.4`, and plowd reconciled the live model to gpt-5.4 only ~7 min *after* my test (an `openclaw-model-set old=…sonnet-4-6 new=…gpt-5.4` line). So my "verified" result was for the prior model, not the one users now hit. Reading the per-turn `model` field from the tool log caught the drift before I over-claimed; the user then asked "did the last message use gpt?" — exactly the confusion this rule pre-empts.

### +1 (2026-06-06 plow-rc-gpt-model-verify)
Cutting RC v0.2.2-261561903 I reported the post-install smoke as "GPT 5.5 working end-to-end" straight from the release notes (#821 bumped the codex default to 5.5). The live runtime had actually run `openai-codex/gpt-5.4`: the user's persisted `agents.defaults.model.primary` lagged the new catalog default and nothing migrated it. The user caught it not from my smoke but from the *menubar* ("the model field is empty?"). Reading the session `model_change` event (provider=openai-codex, modelId=gpt-5.4) confirmed the turn ran on 5.4, not the advertised 5.5 — exactly the drift this rule names: verify the per-turn model identity, never trust the advertised/configured default.

### +1 — 2026-06-13 · plow6-ollama-llm-894 · the installed BUILD itself can predate the fix, not just the runtime config
On plow-pbc/plow#894 the user reported "I still see the LLM picker in the menubar" after I'd removed it, and later "the gbrain shell button still opens a bare shell" (which #904 had already fixed). Both were real: their installed Plow.app was built off a `main` snapshot from *before* those fixes merged — source/`main` was correct, the deployed artifact lagged. Extends the rule past runtime-config-lag to **build-age**: when a user reports a UI/behavior issue your *source* says is fixed, check the installed build's age (binary mtime / which commit it built from) before concluding — the build they're running, not just the runtime config it reconciles to, may predate the fix. A fresh rebuild+install off current `main` resolved both.

### +1 — 2026-07-09 · plow2-openai-connect-1007 · run this real-flow prod-install verification EARLY (it catches integration bugs units+reasoning miss); a transient revert on a fresh-VM boot is NOT fix-failure — read last-good/journal first
Two extensions from the same session. (a) **Do it early, don't defer.** After building a fix resting on a runtime-observable claim ("the picker sticks after connect", "the reply routes through provider X"), prod-install the branch and drive the real flow *before* burning review rounds — reusing the prod bundle's existing credential/state avoids a re-OAuth gate, and it catches integration bugs unit tests + reasoning can't: here the validation surfaced that `_run_in_agent_container`'s `env -i` stripped `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, so the auth CLI read an empty `~/.openclaw` — invisible to unit tests (which mock the helper) and to a `--local` infer smoke (which uses the full container env). Don't substitute a partial CLI proof for the actual app-level artifact when the app flow is the thing in doubt. (b) **A transient revert during that verification ≠ the fix failing.** On a *fresh-VM* boot right after install, the runtime can fail-over the just-set primary to a fallback (here openai→a plow model) from a transient virtiofs `FsSafeError: directory changed during operation` *warmup* race — a known standing hazard, not your fix. Before concluding "the fix reverted", read `openclaw.json.last-good` + the VM journal for the boot's model-selection line, then re-set and confirm it sticks (it self-corrected once the VM settled).
**Why (autonomy):** #1007 — an AskUserQuestion "validate now via prod-install vs defer?" resolved to *validate now*, and that drive-test is exactly what caught the `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` bug all green unit tests missed; deferring would have shipped it. Separately I nearly mis-called a transient plow-model revert as "the fix doesn't work on 2026.7.1" — the journal (`agent model: openai/gpt-5.6` + the `FsSafeError` warmup line) and `last-good` showed OpenClaw had accepted openai; it was the R6 virtiofs race.


### +1 — 2026-09-02 · life-assistant3-compression-floor · a config value can be silently CLAMPED by the runtime, so the effective value differs from the file with no error anywhere
**Change:** Widen this rule past "the runtime lagged the config" to "the runtime **overrode** the config". A value can be read, accepted, and then silently transformed — here `_effective_aux_timeout` computed `max(config_value, _COMPRESSION_TIMEOUT_FLOOR_SECONDS)`, so `auxiliary.compression.timeout: 180` resolved to **300** every time. Nothing logged, nothing failed; the file said one number and the system used another. Before claiming a tuning change has an effect, print the **resolved** value from inside the running process (call the resolver, don't read the YAML) and put that output in the PR. Where the runtime logs which path it took, force the path once and read the log line — a successful return value can be a masked fallback answering on the caller's behalf rather than the thing you configured.
**Why (autonomy):** *the stop* — `timeout: 180` shipped to five repos across four PRs, with a comment describing it as "below the image's 300s floor". A floor is a minimum; I had read it as a ceiling. It survived four bot reviews, a contract test asserting the ordering, and my own commit messages, because every one of those checked the **file**. *prior authority* — nothing blocked printing the effective value; I had a shell in every container all session. *the unblock* — a probe on the last agent happened to print `task timeout: 180` and `effective: 300s` on adjacent lines, which is the only reason it was caught. The same session had a second instance: four models probed as "working" on an account that actually rejected two of them, because the implicit main-model fallback answered for the rejected ones — the return value was success, the log line said otherwise. **Next instance:** any repo where a tunable is clamped, floored, or defaulted downstream of the config file — a connection-pool size raised to a driver minimum, a retry count capped by a library, a rate limit floored by a gateway — and the PR claims the new number took effect.

### +1 — 2026-09-22 · plow2-roadmap-pat-members · the CREDENTIAL you verify with changes what a successful call returns
**Change:** Widen this rule past "the runtime lagged / overrode the config" to "the **caller identity** changed the answer". A dry run proves nothing unless it runs with the credential production will use: a permission difference does not only turn calls into 403s, it silently changes what a 200 *contains*. Prefer a signal that travels with the data over one requiring a second, differently-permissioned call. When the production credential is write-only (a platform secret you cannot read back), do not settle for a local approximation — stage the real artifact and read it back through the deployed runtime before pointing users at it.
**Why (autonomy):** *the stop* — a public roadmap board classified issue authors by `GET /orgs/{org}/members`. The local dry run used a token carrying `read:org`, saw all six members, and returned 8 cards. Production's fine-grained PAT carries Metadata only, so the same call returned the *public* subset, every teammate read as a stranger, and the board published 285 internal issues. **Both calls returned 200**; only the contents differed, so no test and no exit code could see it. *prior authority* — nothing blocked staging the deploy first; the platform supports it. *the unblock* — my own post-deploy check caught it and I rolled back, but only after it was live. The fix deleted the dependency rather than guarding it: the issue payload's own `author_association` carries the same signal with no second call and no permission requirement. **Next instance:** any repo where a service account is narrower than the developer's own login and the verification runs locally — an S3 read that returns fewer keys under the task role, a DB query the app user sees fewer rows from, a feature-flag read that resolves differently for a service principal.

## [removes-handback] Don't add a cleanup `rm` for leftovers the consumer ignores — and never wildcard-`rm` a shared dir
**Change:** `CLAUDE.md § Git Safety` (+ § Anti-Bloat): before adding a step that deletes files to "tidy" a shared/cache dir, check whether the consumer even reads the leftovers — if it keys off an explicit manifest/allowlist and ignores extras, the cleanup is unnecessary; skip it (subtractive default). If removal is genuinely required, target exact paths or move-aside, never a glob (`rm -f dir/*pattern*`) in a shared dir, and never an `rm` whose path interpolates a shell variable (`rm "$DIR/$x"` — an empty/unset var retargets the delete to a parent or `/`); spell out literal absolute paths. A glob can delete more than intended and there's no upside when the extras are inert.
**Why (autonomy):** Mid-deploy I added `rm -f "$RUNTIME_CACHE"/*<stale-hash>*` to clear superseded runtime tarballs before re-fetching; the user rejected it ("continue but don't run an rm command like that"). It was doubly wrong: `verify_runtime_cache` only checks the manifest's *current* artifacts, so the stale extras were harmless (the cleanup was pure bloat), and the wildcard `rm` in the shared cache risked deleting more than the intended hash. Dropping the `rm` entirely was the fix.

### +1 — 2026-06-08 · plow862-openclaw-leak · the positive default is mv-to-`/tmp` quarantine, not just a safer `rm`
**Change:** Add the affirmative remedy to this cluster: when clearing diagnostic/temp/scratch artifacts — *including self-created scratch you made this session* — default to **moving them to a `/tmp` quarantine dir** (`mv … /tmp/…`), never `rm`. Especially never `rm` inside a live/operator directory (a gateway sessions dir, a prod config dir): `mv` clears the working dir while staying recoverable if the path/glob was wrong. Reserve `rm` for an explicit by-name delete the operator asked for.
**Why (autonomy):** Cleaning up a diagnostic session file I'd copied into the live openclaw gateway sessions dir, I reached for `rm -f`; the operator stopped me — "don't do rms like that, just move the files to /tmp or something." Same rm-hazard family as the parent, with the concrete safer verb named.

### +1 — 2026-07-30 · kwr7-run-dir-leak · quarantine only frees space ACROSS a filesystem boundary; and in shipped code prefer `rmdir` over `rm -rf`
**Change:** Two bounds on this cluster's mv-to-`/tmp` default. (1) `mv` within one filesystem is a rename — it frees **zero** bytes. Before accepting *or* proposing a "move it somewhere to reclaim space" step, check filesystem identity first (`stat -c %d`, `findmnt`, `df`): same device ⇒ the move accomplishes nothing, and `/tmp` is additionally swept by `systemd-tmpfiles`, so you get no space now plus an unpredictable delete later. When quarantine-before-delete is genuinely what you want, stage to a sibling dir *inside the same volume* — an instant rename, reversible by moving back, and it drops the entries out of consumers' globs immediately — then delete from there after a soak. (2) For a delete inside *shipped code*, prefer the non-recursive primitive: `rm -f <dir>/<the one file you create>` then `rmdir` (which refuses a non-empty dir) over `rm -rf`. That makes a wrong "it's empty" assumption non-destructive **by construction**, which is strictly stronger than a path guard bolted onto a recursive delete, and costs ~2 lines.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — asked to prune 1.05M leaked run dirs / 30G, the operator proposed `/tmp` twice, the second time with an explicit "let's be careful we won't break the os"; my first decline was unpersuasive because I hadn't checked the decisive fact. unblock — one `stat -c %d` showed `/tmp` and the docker volume on the same device, converting a soft "not ideal" into a hard "frees nothing"; staging to a same-volume sibling instead was fully reversible, cut a per-review readdir 3.9s→0.23s immediately, and left the irreversible `rm -rf` as a separate human-gated step after a soak. Separately the operator directed the `rm -rf`→`rmdir` shape in shipped code ("be very careful about rm -rf generally"), which the reviewer bot then tried to revert to `rm -rf` on Anti-Bloat grounds and was declined on exactly the by-construction argument. Next instance: any repo where a plan or bot proposes relocating bulk data to reclaim disk, or a cleanup helper reaches for `rm -rf`. Promoted from the `no-recursive-delete-prefer-rmdir` feedback memory.

### +1 — 2026-08-12 · plow7-discord-connector · the never-delete rule must not produce a HAND-BACK — mv-to-`/tmp` is the *do*, not a thing to ask about
**Change:** This cluster already names mv-to-`/tmp` as the safer verb than `rm`. Add the failure mode on the *other* side: § Git Safety's "never delete untracked files" is a constraint on **how** you clear clutter, never a licence to hand the clutter back. When leftover artifacts block a clean finish — especially ones **you** created this session — move them to a timestamped `/tmp/<name>-YYYYmmdd-HHMMSS/`, print the path, done; archiving is reversible, so it sits on the *do* side even though deleting sits on the *ask* side. **Why (autonomy):** stop — I closed a session by reporting 380K of untracked MCP scratch in the repo root plus five scratch config-patch files on a prod host as "deliberately not touched — yours to remove or gitignore", citing the never-delete rule as the reason I couldn't finish the job. unblock — the operator: "why don't you clean things up by moving them to /tmp, then /cleanup". The glob footnote is from the same run: `discord-*.patch.json5` moved 4 of 5 files and silently missed `discord.patch.json5`, caught only by re-listing the source dir. Next different instance: any session that ends with untracked build output, a debug capture dir, or self-created scratch on a remote host that you're about to describe rather than clear.

## [removes-handback] Owner's own read-gated data: a recurring bot PII probe → record an explicit owner ruling + fix the real bugs in the cluster, don't add redaction
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Lean Less Conservative (Pre-PMF)`: when a review bot repeatedly flags a data-handling concern that is actually a *deferred-by-design owner decision* on the owner's **own** data behind a read-gate, separate two things bundled in the same finding-cluster. (1) The policy call (e.g. "write raw message bodies") — if the content IS the feature's value, the data is the owner's own, and reads are already gated, the resolution is an **explicit recorded owner ruling** (in a docstring + memory) so the probe stops re-firing — NOT adding a redaction layer that bleeds the feature for a threat the read-gate already covers. (2) The genuine correctness bugs riding along (fail-open data-loss, path/symlink escape, slug collision) — fix those regardless of the policy call. A bot re-firing an un-dispositioned policy probe is noise; the fix is the recorded ruling, not capitulation and not silence.
**Why (autonomy):** On #854 the bot flagged "raw iMessage/Gmail/Slack bodies into the agent-readable brain" 7+ times across rounds. The bodies are exactly what makes semantic recall work, the data is the owner's own, and reads are #844-owner-gated. The operator ruled "keep raw + fix real bugs." I recorded the ruling in the module docstring (so the probe is dispositioned) and fixed the two genuine bugs in the same cluster — fail-open-wipe (was deleting brain memory on a total connector failure) and the missing symlink fence — which dissolved the recurring cluster without weakening recall.

  ### +1 — 2026-06-14 · cleanup-hermes-scaffolding-split · a bot security/privacy probe that IMPLEMENTS a recorded owner waiver on an unreachable path is dispositioned by the ruling
  **Change:** Generalize this beyond PII/data-handling: any review-bot **security/privacy** probe that flags behavior which *implements* a recorded owner waiver (an ADR decision), AND whose harm is **unreachable at the current operating point**, is dispositioned by that recorded ruling — decline + cite the ADR; don't reflex-"fix" it because the label says security/privacy. Check two things before treating a security-labelled probe as blocking: does it implement (not violate) a settled owner decision, and is the harm even reachable yet? Surface to the owner only when genuinely *reopening* (their own bot disagreeing with their recorded ruling is worth a one-line flag — but lead with the recommendation to keep).

The reconciled ADR records the owner's explicit waiver ("recall on all threads acceptable; owner-direct gate waived"), and Hermes has no channel bridge yet (no shared-thread delivery ⇒ no reachable leak). The one AskUserQuestion of the whole session ("keep the waiver?") confirmed *keep* — a question a recorded-ADR-decline rule would have answered without the round-trip.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — an `AskUserQuestion` on whether I could put a resolved absolute path into a skill body whose docstring justified a `~`-relative form as PII avoidance. Prior authority — the corpus already rules that owner's-own-data behind a read gate doesn't buy a defensive layer, and `§ Lean Less Conservative` says lead with the looser option. Unblock — the human chose the absolute path in one word. The indirection had cost a production misdiagnosis: the droppable parameter got dropped, and the resulting error was reported to the user as a missing OS permission that was already granted.
**Next instance:** a doc, skill body, template or config that hides a resolved path/username/host "so it doesn't leak" while making a load-bearing dependency on something optional — take the robust form, note the reversal, don't spend a round-trip on it.

## babysit-pr: a live Monitor may not surface in `TaskList` — Step 1's `TaskList→TaskStop` dedup can no-op, spawning duplicate Monitors + duplicate wakes
**Change:** Add a caution to `babysit-pr` Step 1 (and the Step 7 re-arm): do NOT treat an empty `TaskList` as proof no Monitor is armed. Observed a Monitor that was demonstrably live — it later fired its `Done with …#N` wake AND ran to its 30-min cap — yet did **not** appear in `TaskList` on the next turn. Step 1's "TaskList → find the task whose description equals … → TaskStop it" then silently no-ops, so each pass that re-arms stacks a *duplicate* Monitor → duplicate `Done with` wake notifications (plus a wasted "why did my Monitor exit?" investigation turn). Mitigation: track the armed task-ID in-band across the loop and re-arm only after a *confirmed* exit for that ID (a consumed `Done with` or its lifecycle-close), rather than inferring "no Monitor armed" from a blank TaskList. Worth confirming whether Monitor-tool background tasks reliably appear in `TaskList` at all; if they don't, the Step 1 dedup needs a different basis entirely.
**Why (autonomy):** On plow-pbc/seed-life-dashboard#17 I armed Monitor A, then next turn `TaskList` returned "No tasks found"; believing A had exited (no wake yet, review still mid-flight) I investigated docker and re-armed Monitor B. Both A and B then fired the same `Done with #17` at the same second — duplicate wakes — and both later sent lifecycle "Monitor timed out" closes. The blank TaskList was wrong, not A's absence; the dedup contract Step 1 leans on didn't hold.

  ### +1 — 2026-06-09 · plow7-ld-weather-viewer · blank TaskList across an entire babysit run while Monitors fired duplicate wakes
  **Change:** Confirms the failure mode end-to-end: `TaskList` returned "No tasks found" on *every* Step-1 pass across two full babysit loops while the Monitors were demonstrably armed and later woke. The dedup no-ops, and the loop accumulates duplicate `Done with` wakes plus a trailing string of "stream ended" lifecycle-close notifications after the loop has already exited.
  **Why (autonomy):** Babysitting plow-pbc/seed-life-dashboard-agent#11 and seed-life-dashboard-viewer#27, each pass's Step-1 `TaskList` was empty though the prior pass had armed a Monitor that subsequently fired `Done with …#11`/`#27`; I got duplicate same-second wakes and several post-exit lifecycle closes — matching this proposal exactly. In-band armed-task-ID tracking (not inferring from `TaskList`) is the fix.

  ### +1 — 2026-06-16 · sld-hermes2-oneshot · the class extends to dispatched Agent subagents — empty TaskList ≠ "subagent done"
  **Change:** Broaden beyond Monitors: a dispatched `Agent` subagent (`run_in_background`) also does NOT appear in `TaskList`, so an empty list is not proof it finished. Its authoritative done-signal is its completion task-notification (`status: completed`) — wait for that (or verify against git/gh) before treating its work as stranded. Same in-band fix: track the dispatched agent's own ID, don't infer completion from a blank `TaskList`.
  **Why (autonomy):** On the hermes-seed topology redesign I ran `TaskList` → "No tasks found", saw the subagent's branch with unpushed commits, concluded it had died without pushing, and concurrently pushed + opened the PR myself — while the subagent was still finalizing (it pushed the same SHA moments later). Harmless that time (identical commit) but a real concurrent-edit/clobber race; the blank TaskList was wrong, not the subagent's absence.

  ### +1 — 2026-08-01-claude-config7-review-md-migration · the gap BETWEEN arms loses events, not just the dedup
  **Change:** Extend the caution to the re-arm seam itself: because the Monitor is armed *after* the pass that would consume its event, any reviewer run finishing in that handoff window reaches no one — and silence is indistinguishable from still-running. On every monitor-ended / stream-ended / timed-out notification, run the single cheapest state check for every watched target before concluding no-op; don't acknowledge lifecycle events as no-ops on the basis of task-ID bookkeeping alone.
  **Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged, self-caught): confirmed the parent finding again — `TaskList` returned "No tasks found" on every pass across ~10 babysit rounds while Monitors were demonstrably armed and firing. Separately, three spent-monitor closes were acknowledged as no-ops in a row; the fourth prompted an actual `gh` check, which surfaced an unprocessed whole-PR re-review on `srosro/claude-config#140` carrying a `[blocking]` finding that had landed in a gap between two Monitors.

    ### +1 — 2026-09-10-agent-mgr7-str-cloud-alignment · the harness can disable `TaskList` outright, so the dedup cannot run at all
    **Change:** Harden the caution one step further: `TaskList` may be *absent*, not merely incomplete — this session returned `No such tool available: TaskList. TaskList is disabled for this session, in subagents as well as here.` Step 1's dedup then cannot run by any means, so the re-arm seam must assume duplicates and Step 7 must `TaskStop` by the task id it holds from its own `Monitor` call rather than by a list lookup.

Prior authority — the skill already tells Step 1 to stop stale Monitors; only the mechanism was missing. Unblock — the operator's tooling reported both tasks; I stopped the spent one by id.
    **Next instance:** any babysit loop in a session where the harness has trimmed the task tools — the id returned by `Monitor` is the only handle that always exists.

  **Change:** In Step 1 and the Step 7 re-arm, record the task ID that `Monitor` returns when it is armed, and `TaskStop` that ID at the start of the next pass. ## [removes-handback] A bot wanting to NARROW SCOPE to close a security finding → prefer keeping the capability + a tracked follow-up over amputating the use case
**Change:** Add to `REVIEW_PRACTICES.md` (or the `CODING_STANDARDS.md § Anti-Bloat` review neighborhood): when a reviewer bot flags a capability as a security risk and the proposed remedy is to REMOVE the capability (go main-only, drop the branch path, delete the flag), don't default to amputation — keep the capability with the risk surfaced as an opt-in / operator-discipline note + a tracked follow-up issue for the fuller gate. Pre-PMF, dropping a use case to close a finding is usually the over-conservative pick: the capability is the point, the finding is future hardening. Record the owner's keep-it ruling on the PR so a from-scratch re-review doesn't re-raise the settled class as `[blocking]`.
**Why (autonomy):** /plow-prod-install-auto (plow-pbc/plow#860) is intentionally branch-capable (build+install a reviewed feature branch via CI). knightwatch repeatedly flagged "non-main ref → unreviewed code runs with release secrets" as `[blocking]` and wanted main-only / SHA-pinning. The owner ruled "keep branch-capable" (default `main`; non-main is a deliberate operator action; the reviewed-ref gate is tracked as #859). Recording that ruling on the PR converged it — the bot's final review even *agreed*. Amputating to main-only would have dropped the use case the skill exists for.

  ### +1 — 2026-06-10 · plow7-854-babysit-fleet · record the ruling in the artifact the re-reviewer reads
  **Change:** Record the ruling in the artifact the re-reviewer actually reads — a module docstring / comment at the code site — not only the PR thread. Whole-PR re-reviews run "from scratch, no prior review consulted", so thread dispositions don't survive them; the in-artifact ruling is the only channel that does.
  **Why (autonomy):** plow-pbc/plow#854 — the raw-bodies security cluster re-surfaced as [blocking] across 3+ from-scratch rounds despite per-round PR-thread dispositions; after the operator ruling was recorded/extended in `brain_backfill.py`'s module docstring (9f954c6f), the next round wrote "Security — None; prior raw-body and Git-execution concerns were operator-declined" and stopped re-raising.

  ### +1 — 2026-07-23 · plow6-1112-founder-card · a third path for a PII-exposure finding: de-sensitize the VALUE, don't remove the feature
  **Change:** When the security finding is PII exposure (a personal contact number/email shipped in a public client) and the bot's remedy is "remove it" or "gate it behind auth", there's a third path beyond ship-as-is-vs-gate: keep the feature and DE-SENSITIZE the value — swap the personal number for a non-personal/forwarding line the owner is fine publishing. For the owner's OWN PII specifically, surface it for one quick confirm before the irreversible publish rather than auto-declining or auto-gating.
  **Why (autonomy):** plow-pbc/plow#1112 — knightwatch flagged the founder's personal cell exposed in the public `/100` client and wanted it removed/gated. I fired an AskUserQuestion (ship-as-is vs gate); the owner picked neither — "change the number to <a public line> and merge". Keeping the founder-text feature but swapping to a public-facing number resolved the finding at the root without amputating the use case.

  ### +1 — 2026-07-30 · hermes-airbnb-agent1-seam-locks · pre-PMF, a security finding is a TICKET — absorbing the gate is how the feature ships non-functional
  **Change:** Extend the rule past "don't amputate the capability" to "don't absorb the gate either". Pre-PMF/PSF, the default disposition for a reviewer's security finding is **file an issue and keep the default path working** — an env opt-in, a narrowed default allowlist, a confirmation step, or a permission layer all count as absorbing it. The bar for taking security work into a feature PR: it's a real bug (crash / wrong result / data loss), or the fix is net-neutral-or-negative LOC and doesn't touch the default path. Treat a security bot's `[blocking]` as advisory at this operating point — blocking is the bot's calibration, not the project's. Document the exposure honestly (cheap, preserves the decision); gating is what defers.
  **Why (autonomy):** The stop — on `srosro/sams-str-hermes-agent#4` (Seam smart-lock tools) I absorbed two security probes: an env-gated tool registration plus narrowing the documented default allowlist to read-only. Together they meant the PR's actual use case ("unlock the side door for the cleaner") needed a two-file config edit and a gateway restart before it did anything, and the gate I wrote *shipped broken* — the env var it keyed on is stripped from the MCP stdio child, so it could never be opened. Three rounds spent building, discovering-inert, and fixing a control for a feature that then didn't work out of the box. The unblock — the owner: for now just get things working; security vulns should be tickets; we often YAGNI/scope-creep a bunch of robust security and the thing doesn't work. Reverting both (−64 LOC) and filing the exposure as a tracked issue with costed options is the generalized move. Next instance: any pre-PMF feature PR where a reviewer proposes a gate/opt-in/narrowed default rather than reporting a bug.

### +1 — 2026-08-20 · 2026-08-20-str9-seam-unlock-attribution · the durable form of "keep the capability" is the operator's ruling written into the REVIEWER's config, not just the PR reply
**Change:** When the operator overrules a narrowing, the reply on that PR does not stop the next round re-raising it — a reviewer that reads policy from the base branch has never seen the thread. Land the ruling as a rule in the repo's reviewer-facing policy file (`REVIEW.md` § …), and check whether that file is *mirrored* anywhere: if a second reviewer inlines a copy (roborev reads `.roborev.toml`'s `review_guidelines`, not the file it was copied from), edit both in the same commit or the ruling reaches only one of them. Say in the reply which reviewer it binds and from when — a base-branch reader binds the round *after* merge, not the current one.

Recording that only in the PR thread would have left the same probe live for every future round, which is how this repo's prior PRs reached ~30 rounds. **Next instance:** a bot repeatedly asking to drop a broad IAM permission the owner granted deliberately — the fix is one rule in the reviewer's policy plus its mirror, not a decline per round.

## [removes-handback] Asked to refactor one spot? Survey the sibling class first — the leveraged win is collapsing N sites, not polishing 1
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md § DRY` / `CLAUDE.md § Boy-Scout`: before answering a refactor question with options for the named spot, scan for sibling instances of the same pattern (other views rendering the same state, other call sites, the same labels recomputed elsewhere). Frame the answer as "duplicated across N sites; here's the shape that collapses them" — a producer/abstraction that serves one site is overhead, not DRY. The 1-spot question is the wrong frame until the class survey is done.
**Why (autonomy):** plow#713: I proposed three sharp options for one file's refactor; Sam redirected to "look at status reporting across the different swift views… any other DRY optys?" — the class survey (Settings row, hero card, menu bar, StatusView, installer header) was the actual question. (Promoted from the plow9 feedback ledger.)

## [removes-handback] Design questions about agent-consumed artifacts: walk the cold-start read, and fit answers inside the canonical grammar
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` (§ Take the Steps "Investigate before you consult" neighborhood) or `AUTHORING.md`: when a design question concerns how an agent discovers/bootstraps a convention (install specs, runbooks, seeds, skills), ground the answer by walking the literal cold-start scenario — what does a fresh agent with no skill and no convention *actually read first*, and can it act on it? Model the reader as an LLM that follows prose, not a mechanical parser: package-manager analogies ("pip doesn't depend on apt") can wrongly rule out designs that are viable when the consumer can follow prose instructions. Companion rule: content that doesn't fit the target system's canonical grammar/schema belongs one level up (the convention/spec, where a generator can stamp it) — not as free-form prose bolted onto one instance.
**Why (autonomy):** 2026-06-11 · sld3/openseed convention-prerequisite: (1) I ruled out "every seed depends on openseed" on parser-style circularity grounds; the user's "but a cold claude told to install <url> doesn't know to /seed-install" walk-through reversed half the conclusion. (2) I then proposed a free-form README bootstrap header; the user: "this isn't an answer that fits into the six categories of a seed" — the right home was a Dependencies-grammar rule in the convention itself, stamped by seed-create. Two human round-trips (plow-pbc/seed-life-dashboard#22, plow-pbc/openseed#44) that one cold-start walk-through plus grammar-first framing would have collapsed into one.

## [removes-handback] Adding component-specific logic to a shared/generic layer? Check the architecture taxonomy and keep the generic seam role-agnostic
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md` (§ Anti-Bloat neighborhood): when a fix plants component-specific knowledge (a hardcoded path, a `ROLE == x` gate, an app-name conditional) into a generic dispatcher/walker/provisioner, check the repo's architecture/ownership doc for which layer owns that knowledge, and prefer declaring per-component facts in the component's own branch/manifest with the generic section driven off the declaration. Bot approval is not evidence of good shape — run this check before opening the PR. (Rule-of-N applies: at one consumer a small special-case may be the right call — but say so explicitly and name the generalization trigger.)
**Why (autonomy):** 2026-06-12 · plow3-overnight-bugfix-trio: the human challenged a dispatcher preflight special-cased to one container's config file ("is this the best solution that is both generalizable and DRY/elegant? see our file taxonomy.md") after two bot reviewers passed it with zero probes. The investigation produced the right call (keep, with the generalization trigger named) — but the check should have run before the PR, not after a human question.

### +1 — 2026-06-13 · sld3-dashboard-producers-own-styling · the *existence* of a generic-layer PR for component-specific work is itself the smell
Same principle, UI-renderer domain: a "life-dashboard" kiosk splits a generic React **viewer** (renders whatever HTML a card holds) from per-widget **producer** skills (weather, sports) that post the card content. A round of work drifted widget-specific CSS (`.weather-*` / `.sp-*` rules) *into the generic viewer's* stylesheet, and even opened a viewer PR to add a sports-empty-state style. The human caught it not by reviewing the diff but by the PR's *existence*: "the viewer should never have card-specific application code — the fact that you have a viewer PR styling a widget tells me the architecture is wrong." The fix pushed the per-component fact (styling) into the component's own declaration — each producer now ships **self-contained HTML carrying its own `<style>` block**, referencing only the viewer's shared theme tokens/fonts — and *deleted* all widget CSS from the generic layer (viewer PR net −159 LOC). Reinforces two things beyond the parent: (1) the tell can be structural, not textual — a PR that *targets the generic layer to do component-specific work* is the smell, before you even read it; (2) the role-agnostic seam is the LOC-negative direction (delete the special-cases, don't guard them).

**Change:** Extend the parent from the intra-repo generic/specific seam to **cross-repo placement**: when a design spans a family of repos (base image, plugin, variant, app), read the family's ownership table first (here `plow-hermes-agent`'s README "The repos" / plow's "where changes go") and place each piece by its row — before writing the spec, not after.
