### +1 — 2026-09-16 · plow2-durable-smoke-host-side · placement by the ownership row isn't enough — split base-owned files by DELIVERY: the base pin carries image-baked files, never host-side compose.yml
**Change:** After the ownership table says a file is base-owned, split base-owned files by how they reach consumers. **Image-baked** files (Dockerfile-copied, runtime templates) DO reach existing forks/variants through the `FROM …base-<sha>` pin bump. **Host-side** files — `compose.yml` above all — do NOT: they're run by `docker compose` on the host, never in the image, so a variant's copy changes only via a hand-written "take the base" edit. For a host-side base change the base PR is necessary but NOT sufficient: land it in the base (canonical + covers new forks) AND in each fork that needs it now. Never close the variant change assuming the base pin will propagate it.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — on plow#1995's durable smoke I put the compose credential override in the life-assistant variant, the operator asked "surprised you changed the variant vs upstream," so I moved it to the base (plow-hermes-agent#113) and closed the variant PR (#215) — then knightwatch flagged (correctly) that the variant's host-side compose can't inherit it via the image pin, and the operator had to have me reopen #215. Prior authority — the base README already spelled out the two delivery paths (image vs the host-side compose the exe.dev path never reads). Unblock — the reviewer + operator surfaced the host-side gap.
**Next instance:** any change to a base-owned file in a template-and-forks family (base image + variants, a cookiecutter/scaffold + generated repos) — before choosing base-only, ask whether that file rides the artifact the consumers pin (propagates) or is a host-side/scaffold copy they own (doesn't), and cover both when it's the latter.

## [removes-handback] A concurrently-working instance refutes a "broken everywhere" root cause — diff broken-vs-working state (and trace the divergent state's provenance) before asserting the fix
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` (sibling to "Root-cause writeup that exonerates a prior mechanism: date-check every historical occurrence"): before asserting a root cause — or that a code change is even needed — when a known-working peer exists (another machine / deployment / env running the ostensibly-same build), diff broken-vs-working *state* first. A root cause that implies "broken everywhere" is falsified by one working instance, so a working peer is the cheapest, sharpest test of the hypothesis. Especially watch **accreted/persisted state drift** (allowlists, caches, auth profiles, feature flags that only-add-never-remove): identical code + identical version can diverge on state alone. And when the working peer makes the *user* doubt the fix is needed, prove necessity by **tracing provenance** — establish who/what wrote the divergent state on the working instance, and show the broken instance has no current path to reach it without the change (a `git log -S` / grep that no code seeds it turns "fix needed" from assertion into proof). Distinct blade from the date-check sibling: that reconciles historical occurrences against an activation window; this diffs against a *concurrently-working* peer.
**Why (autonomy):** plow-pbc/plow#909 — "Connect OpenAI" failed on one Mac (mbp); my first framing blamed the OpenClaw runtime broadly. The user pushed back twice with a working peer ("my other Mac on the identical build + same OpenClaw works fine — are you positive this is needed?"). Diffing the two gateway configs surfaced the real cause: the working Mac had `openai` grandfathered into its allowlist under the *prior* runtime (accreted, survived the upgrade); the broken one never did. `git log -S'"openai"'` then proved plowd never seeds it and no code path adds it — so the working peer's entry came from a now-blocked old-runtime login, and the fix was genuinely required. The working-peer diff + provenance trace would have pre-empted both pushbacks (~2 correction round-trips).

### +1 — 2026-06-15 · cc1-tmux-scroll-stale-server · the working peer can be the session you're operating FROM — reconcile your own host/session identity against the user's pasted context first
Mouse-scroll dead in Claude Code on the mba (swipe sent Up/Down arrows = alternate-scroll mode). I spent two rounds diagnosing the tmux server I was *running in* (`cc1-mbp`, on the mbp) and reported its `mouse on` as the answer — but that was the working peer; the broken target was `plow1-mba0` on the mba. The tell sat in the user's first paste (status bar `[plow1-mba0` ≠ my actual session `cc1-mbp`), but I only reconciled identity in round 3, after the user volunteered the mba-vs-mbp split. Diffing the two servers then made provenance instant: the mba's tmux server was up since May 14, predating the ~Jun 14 `set -g mouse on` rollout (off cached in-memory); the mbp's started after (on). A round-1 identity check (`hostname` / `tmux display -p '#{session_name}'` vs the pasted prompt/status-bar) plus the working-peer diff would have aimed at the right target before any diagnosis.

### +1 — 2026-06-26 · plow1-gbrain-embeddings-ledger · a *causal/historical* premise ("version regression", "earlier build provisioned it") is itself a claim — verify the premise exists before it cascades into an issue + memory + code change
**Change:** Extend this rule to the *historical-premise* case: before writing "it's a version regression / provisioned by an earlier build / they changed the API" into a diagnosis, **check the premise is even true** (`git log`/`-S` on the pin or config, the changelog, the real history) — a plausible mechanism is not a verified one. And when a working reference instance exists, **read its actual config/state FIRST** — it holds the proven mechanism and the discriminator. The failure mode this prevents is a *cascade*: one unchecked premise becomes a confident bug report, a saved memory, and a built fix, all resting on nothing. Prefer "I can't yet explain why X works and Y doesn't" over inventing a cause.
**Why (autonomy):** Promoted from the plow1 feedback ledger (origin e843ad52, gbrain embeddings). I wrote (to the user and in a bug report) that an embedding failure was a "version regression — the dev box was provisioned by an earlier gbrain version"; the user pushed back ("haven't we only ever pinned one build?") and one `git log` showed exactly one pin, ever — the premise was fabricated. I'd already built a fix and filed an issue **without ever reading the working dev-box brain's `.gbrain/config.json`**, which showed the supposedly-impossible config and rewrote the whole diagnosis. Reinforced this session: diagnosing the Plow morning-cron failure, I declined to assert a single cause for "why did the next message succeed" (gave two grounded mechanisms) and re-verified a `grep -l` hit before asserting an exchange existed locally — it was a false positive on onboarding boilerplate.

### +1 — 2026-09-22 · the-plow-times8-hosted-print-credential · you may never LOOK for the peer — and a peer diff read on the wrong surface produces a false match, which is worse than no diff

**Change (extends):** Two failure modes upstream of diffing. First, **searching for the peer at all**: the existing entries all assume one is in hand. Make "where does this work?" the first question on any works-here-not-there bug, and find the peer **by artifact, not by name** — list containers/images/units per host; a display name can be a shared persona (five owners' agents were all called "Alder"), so a name search returns nothing and reads as "no working peer exists". Second, **the surface**: a parent's environment is not evidence about its children's. Where a runtime *injects* env per tool invocation (reading a dotenv or an s6 `container_environment` dir itself, then handing values to each subprocess), the value is absent from `docker exec env` and from `/proc/<parent-pid>/environ` while the child still receives it — so a diff on the parent's environ shows "both lack it" and *confirms the wrong hypothesis*. Note the mechanism, because it bounds the claim: file-backed config is **not** automatically inherited, so the value's presence in a child is evidence about that application's injection, not a general rule. Check the surface the application actually loads (the home's dotenv, `/run/s6/container_environment/`, a unit's `EnvironmentFile`) **and** the child's real invocation — or, cheapest, a behavioural probe: a script that already `require()`s the variable and demonstrably succeeded proves it was set for that child, with no config read at all.

**Compare presence, never values** (`CLAUDE.md § Secrets`): the set of key *names*, whether a given key is non-empty, byte counts. Compare names as names — an ad-hoc regex over dotenv lines is its own bug surface (a too-narrow class truncates `S3_BUCKET`; an `export ` prefix reads as the key), and two configs that differ can then compare identical, which is the failure this bullet exists to prevent. Never `diff` two credential files or print a value — a working *production* peer is the likeliest place to leak one, and the diff needs only the shape.

**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — a hosted install could not print. I traced the failing path from both ends, reproduced the error byte-for-byte, filed four issues and carried a PR through five review rounds, all while a working install sat on another host whose `.env` had exactly the two keys the broken one lacked. I never asked where it worked. *Prior authority* — `systematic-debugging` Phase 2 already says find the working example; the peer was on a host in the standing host map. *The unblock* — the operator: my Mac is connected, I'm using this actively, and it prints — check my container. Worse, I had twice read the wrong surface and reported a variable absent when it was present, which nearly made me contradict them. The working-peer diff then produced the diagnosis in one step and showed my proposed fix targeted the wrong layer entirely: I had blamed the platform's provisioning, and the real fix was one line in our own repo.

**Next instance:** a cron that fires on one Pi but not its sibling, or an API call that works for one tenant — get on the working host, diff its unit `EnvironmentFile` / dotenv against the broken one, and do not conclude "absent" from `systemctl show` alone.

### +1 — 2026-08-25 · plow9-vip-thread-shape · N working peers make a single differing *attribute* look like a mechanism — check the peers underwent the same OPERATION, not just that they share the feature
**Change:** Extend this rule to the one-broken-vs-many-working shape, where the peer diff is most tempting and most misleading. With 1 failure and N successes, the attribute that only the failure has reads as decisive by sheer arithmetic — but a shared attribute is not a shared *history*. Before asserting it: (a) hunt the refuting case deliberately (a working instance that also has the attribute, or a broken one without it) rather than waiting for the user to supply one, and (b) check whether the working peers were produced by the same **operation** as the broken one — created-new vs adopted-existing, cold vs warm, first-run vs repeat. State "correlation, mechanism unproven" until one of those closes. The cost of skipping it isn't a slow diagnosis, it's a *wrong gate*: the fix that follows from a fabricated mechanism usually breaks the working peers it was derived from.
**Why (autonomy):** A VIP group thread was created and reported "Done" while no group existed on any device — sends returned 200 with a provider `message.sent` and were never delivered. That VIP's number was the only one of 15 with no iMessage history, and all 14 working threads had one, so I named non-iMessage as the root cause and proposed gating setup on the provider's `service` field. The user refuted it in one message with a working VIP thread on a non-iMessage number. The real discriminator was the operation: every working thread's group either predated the VIP setup or was created for an iMessage-capable peer; the broken one was the only *new-create* against a non-iMessage number — and it started working the moment the user built the group by hand, which the provider reconciled onto the same chat id. Had I shipped the guess, `plow-pbc/plow#1368` would have rejected a VIP thread that is working in prod today. It shipped as diagnostic logging plus `#1369` instead, with "do not gate on `service`" written into the issue. One correction round-trip, and a wrong fix avoided only because the user happened to have a counterexample on hand.

### +1 — 2026-08-25 · plow7-costco-bot-block · the working peer can be another CLIENT on the SAME host — that is what separates "the network blocks us" from "the browser is detected"
**Change (extends):** Widen "working peer" past another machine/deployment to **another client on the same host**. When a diagnosis is about to blame the environment — the IP, the network, rate limiting, a firewall — the cheapest refuting case is the same request from a different client on that same box, because it holds the network constant and varies only the client. Run it before writing the environmental cause down, not after; the parent's newest `+1` says hunt the refuting case rather than wait for the user, and this is the specific instrument for the environment-blames-us shape.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer, but it had already reached an artifact. A Costco sign-in returned 429 from our Camoufox on a profile with no history and again after a full profile wipe, so I reported the block as "almost certainly your IP plus server-side scoring" and recommended closing the PR on that basis. The operator refuted it in one line — Safari and Chrome sign in from the same machine, same IP, same account — which moves the cause off the network entirely and onto our browser being detected. Same host, different client: it holds the network fixed, and it was available the whole time for the cost of one manual login. The filed issue would otherwise have pointed a future reader at egress instead of at the fingerprint, and `_abck`'s verdict segment sitting at `-1` across three sessions and two resets was the corroborating evidence I already had in hand.

## [removes-handback] babysit-pr: stand down (sync read-only, don't clobber) when the PR head moved to a commit you didn't author
**Change:** In `babysit-pr` — and any loop where you push to a branch — before each push compare the live `headRefOid` to the last commit YOU pushed. If it moved to a commit you didn't author (`git show <sha> --format='%an'`), a human or another session has taken hold of the branch: **stand down from pushing** — `git pull --ff-only` to sync read-only, do NOT commit your in-flight (stale-base) edits, and surface the situation + confirm the division of labor (reviews-only / hand off / resume) before continuing. One driver per PR.
**Why (autonomy):** 2026-06-16 · seed-life-dashboard-install. A human (and an "overeager eng") pushed 4 commits onto a PR I was babysitting while I was mid-triage; the § Git Safety HEAD==remote check caught it before I committed my round's fixes — which would have clobbered all 4. Without an explicit babysit stand-down rule I had to ad-hoc the "you're co-driving, how do we split this?" consult; a rule makes it a reflex (sync read-only, surface once, then await direction).

  ### +1 — 2026-07-08 · plow3-gbrain-toggle · the verbal form: an explicit "I'll babysit it" is the same stand-down signal
  **Change (extends):** The stand-down trigger includes the human's *explicit* takeover — "I'll babysit it separately" / "no need to babysit" / "I'll handle the PR from here" — as a scoped per-PR override of the post-push auto-`/babysit-pr`: skip the auto-invoke for that PR for the rest of the session (say so in one line); a *different* PR in the same session keeps the default. One driver per PR, whether detected by head-authorship or declared verbally.
  **Why (autonomy):** Duplicate drivers (their babysit + my auto-spawned loop) burn a slot and double every notification; once they've volunteered, their channel is the source of truth. Promoted from the plow3 feedback memory `skip_babysit_when_user_takes_over` (captured on a 2026-06 session where the auto-invoke default needed the override).

  ### +1 — 2026-07-10 · plow6-gpt5.6-enablement · the trigger is a PARALLEL agent/session, NOT the operator's own commit
  **Change (refines):** Scope the stand-down trigger to a *parallel agent/session* taking the branch — NOT the operator committing to their own PR. When the head moves to a commit the OPERATOR (the human owner) authored (`git show <sha> --format='%an'`), that's participation, not a takeover: keep babysitting, treat their commit as authoritative (build on / incorporate it), keep processing review rounds. Only a genuine parallel *agent/session* actively replying+committing warrants the sync-read-only stand-down; absent an explicit verbal "I'll take it" (the plow3 +1 above), the operator's own commit does NOT hand off the loop.
  **Why (autonomy):** stop — Sam committed one review fix + triggered a re-review on a PR I was babysitting; I read "head moved to a commit I didn't author" as a co-driver signal and PAUSED, asking "who's driving?". unblock — Sam: that was "a moment where you should've auto-babysat" — his own commit wasn't a second driver. The over-broad trigger cost a hand-back; scoping it to parallel *agents* keeps the loop running through the operator's own edits.

  ### +1 — 2026-08-13 · ltmm-poc-pr22 · after standing down, DIFF their work against your round and usually discard yours
  **Change (extends):** The stand-down says what not to push; it should also say what to do with the round you already built. Diff their implementation against yours before deciding. When theirs is equivalent-or-better — the common case, since they had the same review and shipped first — **discard your round**: preserve the commits on a clearly-named local branch, push nothing, and rebase nothing. A divergent duplicate of already-landed work is strictly worse than no work; it re-opens a settled question and costs another review round. Reserve carrying anything forward for a concrete gap you can name in their version, and then send it as its own small PR rather than as a competing head.
  **Why (autonomy):** A full apply round (verify probes → edit → test → roborev drain) ran hours of wall-clock, during which a second driver landed the same two fixes. The parent's pre-push `headRefOid` check plus the in-flight push gate caught it exactly as designed. The diff then showed theirs was better on two axes mine got wrong: `samefile` over comparing resolved paths (catches a case-insensitive volume, where `--out .../Facts.db` resolves to a different *string* than the file it would destroy, and hardlinks), and qualifying the shared `ORDER BY` fragment while aliasing the callers `FROM fact f`, so one fragment serves all three sites — where I had left the view separate to dodge an alias-binding trap. Discarding was the cheap correct move; the reflex to salvage a finished round is what this refinement is aimed at. Timing note for the parent's "before each push": a clean check at Step 1 *expires* — re-run it immediately before the push, not only at pass start.

  ### +1 — 2026-08-26 · agent-mgr4-mvp-followon · the trigger fires BEFORE the first push, on a PR you were never babysitting
  **Change (extends):** The parent detects a second driver at push time (`headRefOid` moved to a commit you didn't author). That check cannot fire in the shape that actually bit: a **survey** turn that finds prerequisite work sitting in someone else's open PR, and slides from *recommending* it into *editing* it — no push yet, no babysit loop, head never moved. Add the earlier gate: **before editing any branch you did not open this session, check for signs another actor owns it** (recent commits you can't account for, an open review round, the operator saying so) and ask first. The blocking-ness of the fix is not authorization to take the wheel; it is a reason to *say* it's blocking. Back out with `git merge --abort` on an in-progress merge and verify the remote head is unchanged.
  **Why (autonomy):** stop — handed a 4-item work list whose item 1 was "fold the 6 commits production runs but PR #8 lacks", I checked out that PR's branch and began merging; the operator **rejected the `git checkout` tool call**. unblock — "wait, don't work on #8 … someone else is already handling #8. just wait until it is converged with knightwatch, merge it, and then do your work as follow-on PRs." That sequence — wait for convergence, merge, then land your own work as follow-ons against `main` — is the move to generalize, and it also produced the cleaner result: the other driver took #8 through seven review rounds that reshaped the very files my port touched, so every line I'd have written would have been thrown away. Next instance: any repo where the thing blocking your task lives in a teammate's or another agent's in-flight PR and the mechanical fix looks free.


## [removes-handback] Root-cause writeup that exonerates a prior mechanism: date-check every historical occurrence against the activation window first
**Change:** Add to CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done: before publishing a root-cause that overturns prior fixes ("X was never involved", "all N prior issues mis-modeled the mechanism"), pull the filed/observed dates of every prior occurrence in the bug class and reconcile each against the new mechanism's activation window; scope falsification claims to what was actually reproduced, and state which historical occurrences are proven vs merely plausible.
**Why (autonomy):** plow-pbc/plow#887 — the writeup claimed the whole #740/#744/#887 exit-120 class was one mechanism and called the old mitigations "demonstrably dead"; the human had to paste an external reviewer's critique ("the May 27 history doesn't fit the activation story") before the date check happened. The check (gh issue view: #740 filed May 27, not "pre-May 27" as #887's own table said) took one query and *tightened* the story — done proactively it would have removed the whole correction round-trip.

### +1 — 2026-06-13 · cleanup-chronic-vs-regression · a "chronic treadmill" that was really a one-time migration regression
plow-pbc/knightwatch-reviewer — plow's `just test` failing in the reviewer looked like a chronic "image keeps missing test deps" treadmill, and I'd scoped a runtime `.knightwatch/test-deps` manifest mechanism (trust-gated, base-ref-sourced). The human's steer — "I'm surprised this broke, tests passed recently, I don't remember adding these deps" — triggered git-blame + a time-sort of the reviewer's own run logs: the failure was present from the very first retained log, dating to the May-28 containerization (#103) + host-reviewer retirement (#119) that replaced the host's *ambient* toolchain (ffmpeg/compose/sqlite3 — all still installed on the host) with a minimal image. A bounded one-time migration regression, not a treadmill — the elaborate mechanism collapsed to one apt line (ffmpeg), source-of-truth = the repo's own CI. Same root as the parent: the failure timeline (git-blame/log) is the authoritative check before any "chronic mechanism" narrative, and "I'm surprised it broke / it worked recently" is the tell to run it.

### +1 — 2026-08-04 · install-ordering-rca · a bug found *during* an investigation is not automatically the symptom's cause
**Change:** Widen the parent past "exonerating a prior mechanism" to any causal attribution: before writing "Y was stale/broken **because** of bug X", confirm X's code path actually *executed* during the failure window — the job's own log directory is the cheapest possible disproof — and that X's effect matches the symptom's magnitude. Tell to watch for in your own draft: a hedge like "benign this time only by luck" or "all instances happened to be equivalent". That hedge IS the refutation; follow it through rather than keeping the causal framing around it.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — I found a real tie-break bug in the prod installer and framed a machine's 11-day-stale app as caused by it, carrying that framing into a filed issue and into a PR description that then merged. unblock — the human's "I actually think this was because the machine was offline… are you sure of your RCA?", which took one `ls` of the install cron's log dir to settle: 88 consecutive daily logs, then a 10-day gap, and the last run had installed the newest build *correctly*. The bug could not have produced the symptom, by two independent arguments (the cron never ran at all; every candidate build was the same commit anyway). I had even written the "benign this time only by luck" hedge myself and kept the causal story. Next instance: any repo where a real bug surfaces while chasing a reported symptom — prove the path ran before claiming cause, else label it latent and describe when it *would* bite.

### +1 — 2026-09-04 · life-assistant5-elm-attribution · the attributed cause was an ACTOR, and timing correlation was the only link
**Change:** Widen the parent from a causal *mechanism* to a causal **actor** — which session, process, job, or person did the thing. Before writing "<named actor> did X", state the evidence link out loud; if the only link is "its start time falls inside the window", the honest answer is "I can't identify the actor" — complete as written, and strictly better than a guessed name the operator will act on. Cheap discriminators, in order: process parentage (the `PPid` chain from `/proc/<pid>/status`, `docker inspect --format '{{.State.Pid}}'`), a command in that actor's own scrollback (`tmux capture-pane`), or a log line naming it. Amplifier to avoid: never park a named actor in the closing "what I need from you" slot — placement asserts relevance even when the prose hedges ("nothing to unblock X, but…"), so the operator reads a dependency you never meant to claim and goes off to interrupt it.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — asked why a containerized agent had gone unresponsive, I correctly traced a redeploy that destroyed and recreated it, then named a specific parallel Claude session as "the session that did this migration" purely because its tmux start time fell inside the deploy window — and put that in the closing ask. unblock — the operator pushed back that they had already cleared that session's prompt, and asked how it could possibly affect an agent running in a container; two commands settled it: capturing the pane showed a session that had just opened and run nothing, and the container's `PPid` chain showed it parented by `containerd-shim` → `systemd`, structurally independent of every session. Prior authority — I had already captured that same pane once earlier in the turn and had full read access to both surfaces; nothing was blocking either check.
**Next instance:** any repo or host where a shared resource changed while several agents / cron jobs / CI runs were active in the same window — name the actor only from parentage, scrollback, or a log line that says so, and when asked whether A affects B, prove independence structurally (lifecycle owner, restart policy) instead of asserting it.

## [removes-handback] First localhost/preview/dev server of a session binds tailnet-reachable, not 127.0.0.1
**Change:** When spinning up any short-lived localhost server for the user to look at (superpowers:brainstorming visual companion, vite/Storybook/Playwright UI, plowd dashboards), bind it tailnet-reachable from the *first* launch — `--host 0.0.0.0` plus the framework's URL-host flag set to this Mac's short Tailscale name (look it up live via `tailscale status`, don't hardcode) — and print the URL with that hostname so it's clickable from whichever device the user is on. Don't accept a tool's 127.0.0.1 default just because it's the default; a loopback URL forces a mid-session server restart. Trusted tailnet only — don't bind `0.0.0.0` on an untrusted shared network. The proactive complement to "Hand the user a URL only after verifying it from THEIR vantage, not localhost" — bind it right so the URL works, *then* verify.
**Why (autonomy):** 2026-06-16 · plow-api-deploy · promoted from a captured steer. The user works across multiple Tailscale devices (mbp/mba/rpi5/<kiosk-host>) and routinely views a server running on one machine from another; a 127.0.0.1-bound preview URL breaks that flow and forces a restart they have to ask for.

### +1 — 2026-09-17 · plow8-plowco-latch-dedup · a Linux fleet host and a plain `http.server` are the same case; bind to the tailnet IP and print both URL forms
**Change:** Widen the parent past "this Mac" and framework dev servers: it applies to any fleet host (`wakeup` included) and to a bare `python3 -m http.server`, whose `--bind` defaults to every interface but which gets pointed at loopback the moment you think "it's just for me". Run `hostname` first so the URL names the right host, bind to that host's tailnet IP from `tailscale ip -4` — not `0.0.0.0`, which reaches no further on a tailnet-only need and exposes the port on every other interface — and hand over **both** forms in the message that offers the preview: `http://<tailnet-ip>:<port>/…` and `http://<host>.<magicdns-suffix>:<port>/…`, since MagicDNS search domains may not be set on the viewing device.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — offered a design preview as `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/…` from a session on `wakeup`; the operator was on another fleet host, reported it didn't load, then had to ask for the tailscale URL — two messages for a URL that should have been right the first time. Prior authority — `hostname` had already been run this session, and the `tailscale-ssh` skill documents that the operator works across fleet hosts routinely. Unblock — the operator asked for the tailnet URL, which cost one rebind and one `tailscale ip -4`.
**Next instance:** Standing up a reproduction server or a docs preview in a different repo — bind it to the tailnet IP and print both URL forms in the same message that first offers the preview, rather than after it fails to load.

## Before resolving conflicts to merge an old PR, check whether an intervening base merge obviated its premise — if so, close (don't merge, don't redo)
**Change:** When asked to "resolve the merge conflicts and merge" an older PR, treat a non-mechanical (semantic) conflict as a prompt to re-verify the PR's *premise* against current `main` — not just reconcile the text. If an intervening merge to the base eliminated the very problem the PR solves, recommend **closing** it: abort the in-progress merge (`git merge --abort` — safe, drops only the uncommitted resolution, leaves committed work intact), present the evidence (base `file:line` / the obviating PR#), and confirm before the outward-facing close. Distinct from *mechanical* staleness (a PR many commits behind main, conflicting → close + redo fresh, work still wanted); this is *semantic obviation* — the work is no longer wanted at all (don't redo). A clean babysit/convergence against the base-at-open-time does not survive the base moving.
**Why (autonomy):** 2026-06-16 · seed-life-dashboard-hermes #11. #11 added an exec-ability fail-fast gate motivated by "an arm64 scaffold under qemu on an x86_64 Docker host can't `docker compose exec`." While it sat in review, #12 moved the scaffold to a co-located **native-arm64 Pi** and main's `SEED.md` now states that failure mode "does not arise." Mechanically honoring the literal "merge it" would have re-introduced a YAGNI guard for an impossible case AND contradicted main's own prose. I caught it during conflict resolution, surfaced it with evidence, and the human confirmed close — but a standing "does the base still *need* this PR?" check would flag it *before* I start resolving, not mid-merge.

  ### +1 — 2026-07-06 · plow-968-durable-log-reshape · premise obviated by a SIBLING investigation (not just a base merge); bot convergence ≠ should-exist
  **Change:** The premise-obviation check fires at *build/review* time too, not only when merging an old PR — and the obviating event can be your OWN sibling deliverable's investigation, not a base merge. A converged/approved bot review is NOT evidence the PR should *exist*: the bot reviews the diff, never whether the need is still real. When one deliverable's investigation shows another deliverable's justification is already satisfied, re-question scope and close/reship — don't let convergence + an approval carry a now-pointless PR to merge.
  **Why (autonomy):** plow-pbc/plow#968 — I built a durable-logging pipeline (new plowd endpoint + bespoke HTTP client + 305 test LOC; 469 total) for silent-drop diagnosis and carried it through 4 knightwatch rounds to converged + coworker-approved + merge-ready. But deliverable #1 (the root-cause investigation) had already found the abort is durably recorded in the VM systemd journal — making the whole pipeline redundant. The bot never flagged it. Only the operator's "470 loc sounds like a ton for logging" steer surfaced it; closed #968, reshipped as a +14-LOC doc recipe (#970). A standing "does this still need to EXIST?" premise-check — sibling-investigation as trigger, not just a base merge — catches it before the review rounds.

  ### +1 — 2026-07-10 · plow-957-ollama-ctx-fork · PARTIAL obviation (base merged a *different* solution to the same problem) → keep canonical wholesale, add only the irreducible delta
  **Change:** Complement the obviation→close case: when the intervening base merge landed a *different solution to the same problem* but your PR still carries an irreducible contribution (not *fully* obviated), resolve the conflict by keeping the just-merged canonical code **wholesale** and reducing your PR to the single minimal delta on top — then rewrite the now-stale PR title/body to match. Lead with this fewest-concepts resolution as the recommendation, not a neutral menu; re-deriving canonical in the PR's older/larger shape is the reinvention, even when that shape was "more correct" in the abstract. A bounded fix on canonical usually beats an unbounded-on-main bug plus a heavyweight rewrite that regresses the common case.
  **Why (autonomy):** plow#957 (plowd ollama contextWindow) hit a *semantic* merge conflict after #955 merged a `model_info` arch-max derivation for the same value; the open PR carried a larger served-`num_ctx` + fail-loud rewrite. Mechanically reconciling toward the PR's original shape would have re-derived #955's canonical code in a ~288-LOC parallel form. The steer was to keep ALL of #955's just-merged reviewed code and add #957's one irreducible contribution as a single `min(…, CAP)` clamp — collapsing the rewrite to +30/−10, then dropping the PR's now-redundant apparatus (extra branches, namedtuples, fail-loud guards).

  ### +1 — 2026-08-25 · plow2-howto39-supersession · the obviating sibling can still be IN FLIGHT — scan open PRs before RECREATING a closed one, not just before merging an old one
  **Change:** Both cases here fire on something that already landed — a base merge, a finished sibling investigation. Extend the premise-check to an obviating sibling that is still **open**, where main has not moved at all and your PR reads `OPEN` + `MERGEABLE`, so every main-side and self-side signal is green. Concretely: **before recreating a closed PR, scan open PRs in the same subsystem** — not just "did my dependencies merge?" A PR is more often closed because a larger restructuring obsoletes its whole approach than because a dependency wasn't ready, and that restructuring is usually still in review rather than landed. Same reviewer blind spot the sibling-investigation `+1` names: convergence grades the diff, never whether the diff should exist. The base-PR side of this — a base PR that closed unmerged, so the foundation itself was abandoned — is the base-state stacking rule's job, not this one's. **Next instance:** any repo where sibling sessions open PRs minutes apart — a docs site where one PR restructures the shared asset another PR is still editing inline.
  **Why (autonomy):** *the stop* — plow#749 was recreated as #761 after confirming its dependencies (#748/#750/#753) had merged; #758 — open, mergeable, opened ~7 minutes earlier — was the real group-messaging reshape, collapsing the send surface to a single `thread_handle` and already carrying the exact two files #761 touched. #761's content documented the very model #758 obsoletes. *the unblock* — the operator's pivot, not my loop: the duplicate was closed and the contribution folded into the successor.   **Change:** Two additions. Recommended close with evidence; the property walk found participant-bound redemption already covered on main and one benign residual (no server-side existing-user eligibility gate) filed as plow-pbc/plow#1575 with a ~15 LOC sketch. The operator's only touches were the original question and a one-line confirm of the outward-facing close.
  **Next instance:** any repo where parallel agent sessions race similar features to main — the older PR's "should this still exist?" gets answered by property-diffing the merged sibling, with residuals landing as issues.

  **Change:** Before opening a pin, revision, or version-bump PR, run `gh pr list --state open --search "<pin file or key>"` (or `-- <path>` on the file) in the target repo and read what's already moving that pin. ## [removes-handback] A user file under a macOS TCC-protected dir (~/Desktop, ~/Documents, ~/Downloads) EPERMs for the agent shell — ask for a cp to /tmp up front, don't burn calls discovering it
**Change:** When the user points at a file under a macOS TCC-protected location (`~/Desktop`, `~/Documents`, `~/Downloads`, iCloud Drive), the agent's shell usually can't read it — `Read` returns `EPERM: operation not permitted`, and a fallback `cp`/`ls` fails the same way because the *whole directory* is blocked, not just the file. Recognize the protected-dir prefix on sight (or on the first EPERM) and immediately ask the user to copy the file somewhere readable (`cp "~/Desktop/X" /tmp/`) or re-save it under `/tmp` — don't spend a Read→cp→ls discovery loop re-confirming what the path prefix already tells you. (One-time alternative the user can do instead: grant the controlling terminal / Claude Code **Full Disk Access** in System Settings → Privacy & Security.)
**Why (autonomy):** stop — debugging a "not connected" report hinged on seeing a screenshot the user referenced under `~/Desktop/`; `Read` EPERM'd, a fallback `cp` to `/tmp` failed ("No such file or directory" — the dir itself is unreadable), and `ls ~/Desktop` returned "Operation not permitted", so I was hard-blocked and had to surface it. unblock — the user manually `cp`'d the file to `/tmp/`, which the shell could then read. Generalized: the protected-dir prefix is the signal — ask for the `/tmp` copy at first sight instead of running the discovery loop.

### +1 (sld-hermes9)
**Change:** Add iCloud Drive's real path prefix — `~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/` (users say "iCloud" but the path isn't obvious) — to the recognize-on-sight set, and add the discriminator: the block persists **even with the agent sandbox explicitly disabled**, so it's macOS TCC, *not* the Claude sandbox — a sandbox-off retry is wasted. Go straight to the `! cp <icloud-path> ~/Desktop/` (or `/tmp`) hand-off, or the one-time Full Disk Access grant.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — RCA'ing a white-on-white dashboard bug hinged on a camera screenshot the user referenced under `~/Library/Mobile Documents/.../Screenshots/`; `Read` EPERM'd, and `cp`/`ls` failed "Operation not permitted" both normally AND under `dangerouslyDisableSandbox`, so I burned ~5 calls before handing back a `! cp` one-liner. unblock — the user copied it to `~/`. Reinforces the parent: iCloud Drive is the same TCC class as `~/Desktop`; recognize the `Mobile Documents` prefix immediately and don't waste a sandbox-off retry.

### +1 — 2026-06-26 · plow1-gbrain-embeddings-ledger · once you can't read the artifact, DON'T narrate a code-derived guess as the diagnosis — get it (the `/tmp` cp / FDA) or query the live system's ground truth first
**Change:** Add the diagnostic-discipline layer beyond the access mechanics: when a user points at a screenshot/log/artifact to show a bug and you can't see it, do **not** reason from the code about what it "must" show and present that as the diagnosis — the user shares a concrete artifact precisely because it carries information your mental model doesn't, so a code-based guess about *which* surface/message/state is involved is often wrong about the specific thing they're looking at (and wastes a fix on the wrong bug). Two unblocks, in order: (1) get the artifact via the `/tmp` cp / Full Disk Access hand-off above, or (2) go to the live system's **ground truth** instead — often *better* than the screenshot for "why did it fail" (query the running status endpoint / grep the daemon log). Only then diagnose; if still blocked, say "I can't see it yet" and ask — never narrate a guess as if it's what they're seeing.
**Why (autonomy):** Promoted from the plow1 feedback ledger (origin e843ad52, gbrain embeddings live test). The user shared an iCloud screenshot of "two conflicting warm-up messages"; blocked from reading it, I inferred the two messages from the SwiftUI code (a phase-text mismatch), wrote a confident diagnosis, and **applied a fix** — the user corrected me: the screenshot actually showed **"Warm-up failed"**, a different and more important bug. Querying the box's `/status` for the warm-up phase + grepping plowd logs would have been ground truth. This session applied the rule correctly: rather than guess at the pasted cron message, I drove to the real data (session trajectories, token-usage records, the model config) before diagnosing.

### +1 — 2026-08-27 · latch2-activation-fda · over SSH the FDA grant target is sshd (`sshd-keygen-wrapper`), and it takes effect immediately — no tmux-server restart
**Change:** Add the SSH facet to the recognize-on-sight set: when the session runs over SSH (SSH_CONNECTION set, or the user says "I'm sshed in"), a terminal-app Full Disk Access grant is irrelevant — the TCC identity is **sshd**, which appears in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Full Disk Access as `sshd-keygen-wrapper` (equivalently: System Settings → General → Sharing → Remote Login → ⓘ → "Allow full disk access for remote users"). Name that target in the first hand-off instead of the generic "grant your terminal FDA". Two observed refinements: (1) TCC-protected *databases* (`~/Library/Messages/chat.db`) fail as sqlite "authorization denied", not EPERM — same class, recognize it; (2) the grant took effect **immediately** in an existing tmux-hosted shell — don't preemptively require `tmux kill-server` (the folklore that the tmux server's stale TCC attribution blocks it did not hold; killing the server would also kill the Claude session, so warn only if a post-grant retry still fails).
**Why (autonomy):** stop — asked to confirm a Plow activation SMS in Messages, `sqlite3 ~/Library/Messages/chat.db` returned "authorization denied" over SSH+tmux and I handed back a two-option checklist (grant FDA / run it yourself with `!`), including a probably-unnecessary tmux-restart warning. unblock — the user asked "how about sshd-keygen-wrapper?" and enabled it; the very next query succeeded with no restart. Knowing the sshd target and the immediate-effect behavior would have made the hand-off one precise line — or zero, on a Mac where it's pre-granted.

## [removes-handback] An async user + a genuinely human-gated decision in an autonomous loop → file detailed tracked issues (bug w/ repro + design ticket), don't park on an AskUserQuestion picker
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps` (companion to "don't menu at a long autonomous loop's convergence"): when an autonomous loop (e.g. `/babysit-pr`) reaches decisions that are genuinely the human's to make AND the human is async/asleep, default to capturing each blocker as a **thorough, self-contained GitHub issue** — a bug with full reproduction (version, exec seam, exact command sequence, impact) and a design ticket with before/after + acceptance criteria, cross-linked to the PR and to each other — then stop the loop with a clean summary. A synchronous `AskUserQuestion` A/B/C picker forces a live decision and leaves a thin record; a detailed issue is durable, actionable on the human's own schedule, and preserves the investigation. Also: don't keep re-spinning the review bot once the only open items are human-gated (it just re-flags the deferred probe). The quick picker stays right when the user is *present* for a fast live choice; this fires when they're **away** and the decision carries enough context to deserve a tracked artifact.
**Why (autonomy):** Promoted from the plow1 feedback ledger (origin e843ad52). stop — I surfaced a live two-question `AskUserQuestion` picker (a blocking pin decision + a reshape-scope decision) to an async user. unblock — the user declined the picker and asked me to "create a bug with extensive detail + how to reproduce" and "a ticket for the reshape in more detail." Defaulting to detailed issues + stopping the loop (instead of the picker) would have removed the hand-back entirely. Relates to [[land-minimal-fix-ship-plan-redesign-parallel]] (defer the bigger structural work to a follow-up) and the see-the-artifact discipline (ground the bug in reality before writing it up).

## Classify a prod breakage's blast radius (machine-local vs affects-other-users) before remediating — global cause → PR + /babysit-pr, not a one-host hand-patch
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` (workflow / remediation guidance): when a prod issue surfaces, FIRST classify whether its cause is **host-specific infra** (a self-hosted service left disabled on one box, a GPU/driver module missing for a freshly-upgraded kernel, local config drift) or lives in **shipped code / shared config / a provisioning recipe every install consumes**. Host-specific → a local repair on that box is legitimate, but state explicitly *why* it's local (name whose config/code owns the failing path). In-codebase / shared-config → the deliverable is a code/config PR driven through `/babysit-pr`, **not** a manual patch to the machine in front of you — a one-host patch leaves every other user broken and isn't durable (it vanishes on the next reinstall/reimage). Verify the global-vs-local call against evidence (the failing path's actual owner), don't assume; "it's only local" carries the same burden of proof as any claim.
**Why (autonomy):** not a hard stop — a `/goal` directive set the policy up front on a prod-Plow LLM outage ("if it broke in a way that's global / other users affected, open a PR and /babysit-pr; avoid patching this machine"), so it's untagged. The outage proved **machine-local** (only this user routes its primary chat + embeddings model to a self-hosted ollama-on-`wakeup`; the model id + `:11434` provider endpoint live solely in this user's local `openclaw.json` — every other install runs the cloud model and never touches that host), so the on-host repair was correct and no PR was warranted. The reusable rule is the *classification discipline* it encodes: the scope check (+ stating why a fix is local) is the step that decides whether the right output is a host fix or a PR. Evidence: this session (ollama disabled + NVIDIA module missing for the new kernel on `wakeup`); project memory `feedback-global-breakage-fix-via-pr-not-machine-patch`, `project_prod_plow_llm_is_ollama_on_wakeup`.

## Latest review/reply on a PR → `gh api --paginate`; the bare list endpoint returns only page 1, so `| last` is silently stale past ~30 comments
**Change:** Add to `PR_LIFECYCLE.md` / babysit-pr: when fetching the NEWEST review or reply on a PR/issue, always `gh api --paginate repos/<o>/<r>/issues/<n>/comments` (or sort/select on `created_at`) — the unpaginated endpoint caps at the first 30, so `… | last` yields page-1's last, not the actual newest. Same trap on `pulls/<n>/comments` (inline threads) and any GitHub list endpoint. Tell: a review's `git diff <a>..<b>` banner naming a range *behind* your current head means you're reading a stale/cached review — re-fetch paginated for the one whose range ends at the real head.
**Why (autonomy):** Promoted from the plow1 feedback ledger (origin e843ad52). Real bug-class fence: on a 30+-comment PR I read the "latest review" via the bare endpoint + `last`, got an hours-old review, and replied to it as if current — twice — misreading resolved probes as re-raised and missing the genuinely-newest review's new probes, until I switched to `--paginate`. Wasted a babysit round and produced misleading replies.

### +1 — 2026-09-24 · plow6-watson-upstream · the same trap inside a Monitor's seed, where it manufactures phantom events
**Change (extends):** The parent fences the *read*; extend it to any **watcher** that seeds a `since=` cursor from the same endpoint. A Monitor that seeds `last=$(gh api …/comments --jq 'last.created_at')` without `--paginate` anchors on page-1's last comment, so every poll re-reports comments already handled as if new. The symptom is not a stale read — it is a watcher that fires on your own posts, which reads as reviewer activity and costs a fetch-and-triage round each time. Seed and re-seed with `--paginate`, and filter the event on the review body's own shape (`contains("**Overview**")`) rather than on "a comment appeared".
**Why (autonomy):** Self-caught, no hand-back — recorded as a bug-class fence rather than a handback. A babysit Monitor on a PR that had grown past 30 comments kept emitting events for my own replies; the seed was page-1's last (16:45) while the real last was 13 minutes later. Two spurious wake-and-check rounds before I looked at why.
**Next instance:** any poll loop keyed on `created_at`/`updated_at` from a GitHub list endpoint — issue comments, PR reviews, check runs — in a repo with enough history to paginate.

A multi-purpose check name can fail on a step unrelated to its name (an "API" job failing on its `cli` lint step). Third instance, and a **new failure mode with no error signal at all**: the collision can happen between *concurrent subagents dispatched from one brief template*, not just across sessions. Three agents were given the same hardcoded `/tmp/rv.md` scratch path in their briefs; running in parallel they interleaved read/edit/write on it, and one pushed a *different repo's* policy file into its target — wrong title, wrong payload, wrong script names. Every individual step reported success: no Write error fired, and the API `sha` precondition guarded only against a concurrent *remote* write, not a corrupted local staging file. ### +1 — 2026-08-26 · claude-config6-slot-lane-rules · the two commands this proposal offers are NOT interchangeable — `--is-ancestor` is a false negative on a squash-merged branch

(b) Sibling failure of clause (2): a pass *framed* as "trim narration from comments" netted +9 because two watchpoint comment blocks I added outweighed the −5 trims, and I reported the raw +19/−10 without flagging the sign had flipped on a reduction-framed pass; the human caught it ("i think your DRY attempt actually increased LOC?"). Generalizes the proposal: comments count as LOC in the ledger, and a reduction-framed pass must be sign-checked (additions compressed to minimum-viable) before commit — not just reported.

### +1 — 2026-07-23 · tkmx-watchmepivot-sparkline-107 · replacing a framework component to gain ONE capability is its own net-positive class
**Change:** Extend clause (1) with a distinct high-cost shape: when the fix *replaces a framework-provided component* to gain one capability the framework can't express, the ledger must name the **takeover cost** — everything the framework did for free that you now own (container + lifecycle, positioning, show/hide, and the content it already rendered). State that in the PR body up front, together with the cheaper in-framework alternative and why it was rejected. Refines clause (2) at its boundary: explanatory comments earn their LOC, but a comment written to *answer a reviewer's probe* duplicates the reply thread — answer in-thread (or in the filed issue) and keep the file to ~1 line + pointer.
**Why (autonomy):** Restoring a lost hourly sparkline on a Chart.js daily chart landed at +100 net for what intuitively felt like a ~30-line feature, and the human asked why it needed so much more code. Honest decomposition: only ~12 LOC + ~15 CSS were the sparkline itself — Chart.js tooltips are text-only, so drawing bars forced `enabled:false` + a hand-rolled external tooltip, taking over the shell/positioning/rows/total the built-in had provided (~35 of the additions merely replaced the 35 deleted lines of tooltip config). The cheap in-framework route (a unicode-block sparkline inside the built-in tooltip) had already been tried and rejected in the legacy code for glyph-baseline drift — worth citing up front rather than on request. Separately, an inline timezone-contract comment ballooned to 8 lines answering a roborev probe that the reply thread + filed issue already answered.

### +1 — 2026-08-20 · ltmm-poc2-date-facts-40 · the same probe-answering prose at 12× scale, plus the two tells that separate explanation from churn
**Change:** Give the tkmx `+1`'s boundary clause a detection rule — "answer in-thread, keep the file to ~1 line + pointer" only helps once you notice you have stopped explaining. Two tells that prose has crossed from intent-explaining (worth its LOC, per clause 2) into churn: (a) **the code diff is frozen while findings keep landing in comments** — successive rounds change no executable line; (b) **the reviewer asks to add a clause one round and cut it a later round**. Either one means stop writing and push. This accrues fastest *before* a PR exists, where no LOC ledger is running yet.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — on srosro/ltmm-poc#40 a ~32-line executable change carried a 136-line `src/` diff. Eleven doc-only commits (+20, +50, +28, +19 and seven pure-wording ones) each closed a local review probe by writing the justification into the file; the last four rounds landed entirely inside three docstring paragraphs, with the reviewer asking to add a positional aside one round and cut it two rounds later. I asked the operator twice whether to trim and got no answer — a hand-back offered for a decision `CLAUDE.md § Default to the Simplifying Option` and the repo's own `prefer=cut-loc-over-add` operating point had already settled. unblock — knightwatch's own LOC-growth callout naming the stall; the trim then took `src/` from +136 to +73 with every load-bearing contract kept. Next instance: any repo with a per-commit reviewer where two consecutive rounds change no executable line.

### +1 — 2026-08-26 · domo-desktop7-reap-blocked-exec-176 · when the growth IS the fix, split it by commit before answering the size question

**Change:** Extends the ltmm `+1` past "stop writing and push" to the case where the executable diff keeps moving and the total still overshoots. When a reviewer's LOC-growth callout fires (or your own ledger breaches), run `git log --stat --no-merges "origin/$BASE..HEAD"` and split the additions into **seam-correction** (the round that found the real seam — those lines are the fix) and **accretion** (defensive contracts the loop pushed in). Answer the callout with that split, naming which half you keep and which you delete, rather than trimming indiscriminately or handing the size decision back. A capability-adding fix whose growth is concentrated in ONE seam being corrected is not the pathology this rule exists to catch; a growth spread across defensive layers is.

**Why (autonomy):** stop — on plow-pbc/latch#176 a "~100 line" reaper shipped at +647 net, and I offered the operator the same trim/split/ship hand-back three times across three turns with no answer, exactly as the ltmm `+1` describes. unblock — none came from the human; what actually resolved it was the reviewer's own re-eval callout, answered by tracing the growth: 251 additions were the fix, ~420 were one lifecycle seam being corrected (settling a run on its command's `exit` rather than on `close`, which *was* the bug's shape), and only the callback-isolation contract on top was accretion — deleted on the reviewer's own probe, ~70 LOC back. The split is what made the size question answerable; without it the only moves available are trim-blind or ask-again. Next instance: any repo where a per-commit reviewer and a PR reviewer disagree about whether a growing diff is the fix or the bloat.

### +1 — 2026-09-04 · kwr7-pipeline-dag-254 · a hard operator LOC ceiling turned clause (2) into an active hazard: the implementer trimmed its own comments to fit

**Change:** Add the ceiling case. When the operator sets a *quantitative* merge gate ("no more than +30% from here"), clause (2) stops being advice and becomes a fence the loop will actively push against — an implementer one line over budget will compress explanatory prose to land under it, because prose is the cheapest thing to cut. State in the dispatch brief that the ceiling applies to logic and that comments are out of scope for trimming, and require the agent to *say it cannot fit* rather than quietly buying room from the comments. On review, read what was cut before accepting a suspiciously exact landing.

**Why (autonomy):** stop — none; caught in review, so this is a near-miss rather than a hand-back. On plow-pbc/knightwatch-reviewer#254 the operator authorized merge under a +30% LOC ceiling. A review round landed 8 net lines *over* it; the implementer trimmed 16 net lines of its own comment prose to get under, and disclosed it. Inspection showed genuine compression with every load-bearing fact surviving, so it stood — but the shape is exactly what this proposal warns about, and it was the ceiling that produced it. Prior authority — clause (2) already says explanatory comments are not the bloat to cut; nothing carried that into the dispatch. **Next instance:** any repo where an operator grants conditional merge authority with a numeric size cap, and a fix round lands marginally over it.

### +1 — 2026-09-16 · latch6-plugins-tab-412 · the babysit size ledger reported the overshoot every round but never converted it into a trim offer

Reporting `actual +N · declared: none` each round is not enough; the crossing is a wrong-shape signal the loop acts on, not a number it prints and waits.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — the operator had to ask "this was more loc than i was expecting… any YAGNI? or dead code?" on plow-pbc/latch#412 after the loop watched it grow +937→+1383 across rounds. ## [removes-handback] For an auth/credential failure, read the executing engine's request-time error before theorizing from config/credential inventory
**Change:** Add to the debugging guidance (`CLAUDE.md` § Verify Before Claiming Done family): on any "missing API key" / "provider not configured" / auth failure, the first move is locating the actual failing request's error in the engine's own logs (which provider, which store, what fallback state) — not enumerating which stored credential looks expired or absent. A credential's state is a *candidate*, not the cause, until the failing request is shown to actually reach it; generic user-facing auth errors deliberately omit the provider, only the engine's internal error names it.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — debugging Plow's "Missing API key for the selected provider," I spent two turns building a theory around an expired `openai-codex` OAuth sitting in the credential store (a compelling red herring). The unblock — the steer to pull the runtime error: the VM journal's request-time line named a *different provider and mechanism entirely* (no key for `ollama`; an empty per-agent auth store after an engine upgrade). Reading the engine's own error first would have skipped the wrong-theory turns without any human redirect.

### +1 — 2026-08-20 · plow3-desktop-launch-page · read WHICH credential the client offered, not just what the error said — and a remedy unchanged across N sessions is wrong, not deferred
**Change:** Two sharpenings. (1) The request-time error names *what* failed but often not *whose* credential was used; get the identity before designing any remedy. For git-over-SSH that is two cheap reads — `ssh -T git@<host>` prints the authenticated identity (a **repo** name means a deploy key, a user name means a user key), and `ssh-keygen -lf <key>.pub` prints the comment the key was provisioned with. Compare against a host known to work; a purpose-scoped credential doing exactly its job reads identically to a broken one at the error line. (2) When a finding recurs across many sessions with an unchanged recorded remedy, treat the **remedy** as the suspect, not the operator's responsiveness — an ask nobody has acted on for six sessions is usually an ask that was never the fix.
**Why (autonomy):** hard stop — I handed back "grant a write-capable credential for the repo", which is what the five previous sessions had also concluded and recorded. It was wrong: the host had no personal SSH key at all, only a read-only deploy key, so nothing needed granting. The unblock was the user refusing the hand-off — asking why an ssh login on another machine had working credentials and saying something wasn't right — which forced the key-identity comparison nobody had run. The real fix needed no grant: a global `url."https://github.com/".insteadOf` rewrite onto a token that already carried the scope, verified on the write path (a push dry-run failing non-fast-forward instead of permission-denied). Six sessions of stranded corpus commits traced to it. Next instance: any recurring auth failure whose recorded remedy is "someone needs to grant X" — verify X is actually absent before repeating the ask. (Session: 2026-08-20 · plow3-desktop-launch-page)

### +1 — 2026-08-28 · life-assistant8-plow-gog · read which credential STORE the executing context hits — and a provably-superseded stale credential entry is junk to delete, not a decision to hand back
**Change:** Third sharpening. When the same CLI authenticates from your shell but not from a daemon/LaunchAgent/cron, the discriminator is the credential *store* each context reaches (macOS Keychain vs a file store, per-user vs system env), not the daemon's health or a restart. Compare the stores' write times (`security find-generic-password … | grep mdat` vs the file's mtime); the stale one shadowing the fresh one is the bug. And once a credential artifact is provably expired *and* superseded by a fresh copy, deleting it is a routine repair under § Lean Less Conservative / § Take the Steps — do it and verify with a real job, don't ask.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — roborev's claude-code jobs on the mba died with "OAuth session expired" while `claude -p` worked from every shell; the daemon reported healthy, its agent probe passed, and a restart changed nothing (three false-greens). I found the stale Keychain item (Aug 18) shadowing the fresh `~/.claude/.credentials.json` (Aug 27), then fired "delete it, or you re-login on the GUI — which?" The unblock — "you do you": the delete was the obvious reversible repair (a login recreates it), and the first real review job after it completed end-to-end. The question cost a round trip that § Dev/staging state is mutable already licenses.

### +1 — 2026-09-01 · plow6-willow-cwd-drop · before reporting a remote BLOCKED, actually attempt the connection — from every host that might already hold access
**Change:** Fourth sharpening, and the bluntest: the rule says read the *failing request's* error — which presupposes you made the request. Extend it to the case where no request was ever made. Before declaring a host/service unreachable or credential-blocked, **attempt the operation at least once**, and attempt it from each host that plausibly already has access (the fleet host map is the enumeration) — not just the box you happen to be on. Credential inventory is a candidate, never the cause: "no key in my `~/.ssh`" plus "IAM denies me the stored secret" are two facts about *one* access path and say nothing about the others. Report blocked only with the attempts and their real errors attached.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — asked to ssh into a cloud-agent tenant VM, I posted a red BLOCKED banner and a two-option hand-off checklist (register a key / paste a key path). Prior authority — the user had just asked me to ssh in, the fleet host map was available, and I was *already running on the fleet host that had the key*; I never ran `ssh` once. Unblock — the human pasted a terminal transcript of the connection succeeding with no setup at all. The whole hand-back was manufactured by inferring blockage from a credential inventory on the wrong access path.
**Next instance:** any "I can't reach X" conclusion — a staging box, a customer VM, a registry, an internal endpoint — where the evidence so far is missing-credential *inventory* rather than a real attempt's error. Try it, and try it from the other hosts, before it becomes an ask.

### +1 — 2026-09-03 · hermes-plow-chat8-elm-email-line · fifth sharpening: before RE-handing an admin-console step, isolate the layer and sweep every store — then report the negative as a table

**Change:** Two sharpenings for the case where the remedy is a GUI/console edit the operator must make. (1) A *repeat* hand-off of the same console step is evidence the diagnosis is wrong, not that the operator is unresponsive — before asking a second time, isolate which layer actually fails (did the credential load? was the request well-formed? did the provider answer?) and name the single variable that changed since it last worked. (2) Before declaring the measurement impossible, sweep every credential store the operator actually has — the deploy secret, each fleet host's dotfiles, the password manager — and report the negative as an auditable table of stores checked, so "I can't measure this" is a finding rather than an assumption.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — I handed back a Google Workspace domain-wide-delegation edit the operator had already performed three times, and separately declared an API token unobtainable after checking two paths. Prior authority — the failing request's own error was reachable, and the operator's stores were enumerable from the fleet host map. Unblock — "i've done this like 3 times... are you sure this is the last time?" and "can't you find an api token somewhere on one of my machines?" The first forced a control-matrix probe that found the real scope mismatch; the second found a working production credential sitting in every agent container's own dotenv. Late in the same session the sweep ran *first* and correctly returned empty (IAM denies the secret, absent from both hosts, only a LOGIN item in the vault) — which turned "blocked" from a guess into a table.

**Next instance:** any remedy that routes to a console, dashboard, or another person's action — a DNS record, an OAuth consent screen, a billing seat, an IAM grant. Isolate the layer and sweep the stores before the ask, and always before the *second* ask.

### +1 — 2026-09-16 · hermes-agent4-elm-latch-smoke · sixth arrival: a state FILE read right after a restart is mid-init — attempt the live op before declaring a device unpaired/blocked
**Change:** Sixth sharpening, on the READ side of the same rule. A device/service state file (an app's `settings.json`, a pairing or credential store) read seconds after you restarted that app can catch it mid-initialization — an empty field then means "not done booting", not "unpaired/absent". Before reporting a device blocked on an operator action, confirm the negative against the live authoritative surface — an established relay/websocket socket, or a real device-status probe — not the static file. And when the first live attempt fails, read the executing surface's OWN log before blaming the device: the failure is frequently your own input.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — I posted a red SMOKE BLOCKED banner asking the operator to re-pair the QA Latch and rotate tokens, from a `settings.json` read taken ~1s after I restarted the app (empty `relayCredential`). Prior authority — the live relay socket and a device-status probe were both available on the host I was already on. Unblock — the operator's "what do you need? latch is installed" nudge; on re-check the device was paired with a live socket, and the real, self-fixable failure was my probe wording tripping the app's adversarial-review guard, visible in the app's own audit log. The whole hand-back was inferred from a mid-restart static read.
**Next instance:** any "device X is unpaired / offline / not configured" conclusion drawn from a config or state FILE — a menubar app's settings, a daemon's state dir, a pairing store — especially one read right after a restart. ## [removes-handback] CI flake diagnosis → hunt the durable de-flake fix before recommending re-run
**Change:** When you diagnose a CI failure as a transient/known flake, don't end at "it's a flake — re-run CI." First trace the existing retry/guard path for that test/area and `git log -i --grep` for prior de-flake fixes, identify the precise gap (e.g. the retry covered transport timeouts but not the proxy's transient 502 — and distinguish *which* sibling flake a recent PR actually fixed), then offer/implement the targeted extension. "Re-run" is the fallback only when no durable seam exists.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — I closed a scenario-test failure (upstream 502) as "flake, recommend re-run," handing the loop back to the operator. The unblock — the user's "I thought we fixed this in a recent PR," which restarted the trace; the prior fix covered a sibling failure mode, and naming the gap produced the real de-flake PR. (Promoted from a plow4 feedback memory, origin session 64b8173b.)

### +1 — 2026-08-04 · install-ordering-rca · re-ran a live-LLM flake without hunting the durable seam
**Change:** No change to the parent — recording recurrence. One shape worth naming: a *live upstream call* whose output length is nondeterministic (an LLM completion truncated at a token cap) is the flake class where "re-run" is most tempting and least durable, and the seam lives in the owning subsystem (the cap, or the judge's tolerance), not in the PR that tripped it.
**Why (autonomy):** No operator steer this round — logging recurrence, which is the parent's whole point. A red API check on a shell-only PR diff-scoped cleanly to `test_llm.py::test_coaching_reply_quality — LLM completion truncated at 1024 tokens`; I re-ran it, it went green, and I handed off. I never traced that test's retry/guard path or `git log -i --grep`'d for prior de-flake work on it, which is exactly the parent's ask. Next instance: the same red-check triage in any repo — diff-scoping proves the failure isn't yours, but that is the *start* of the durable-fix hunt, not permission to stop at re-run.

### +1 — 2026-08-11 · plow8-hdiutil-attach-leak · the discriminator that turns "flake" into a located bug: error text only one branch could emit
**Change:** Name the cheap discriminator the parent's "trace the retry/guard path" step needs a starting point for — **read the failure's exact text and ask which code could have emitted it**. A flake's message usually localizes the bug better than its stack: if the text can only come from one branch, the flake is a *reachability proof* for that branch, and re-running just hides it. Concretely, compare against what the blamed component actually prints (run it against a bad input to see) — a mismatch means you are blaming the wrong layer. Corollary for the durable fix: once located, check whether the working sibling path already solves it (`CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps`'s DRY-with-prior-art bullet), so the de-flake conforms to an existing seam instead of inventing a parallel one.
**Why (autonomy):** No operator steer — the rule fired correctly and is recorded as evidence, like the `cc6-track-a-owning-file` +1 elsewhere in this file. A macOS CI job failed on a DMG test the PR's diff didn't touch, and a rerun of the same commit went green — textbook "flake, move on." Instead: the captured stderr *ended with the DMG path*, but a real `hdiutil` failure prints `hdiutil: attach failed - <reason>` with no path (verified by running it against a non-DMG). That mismatch proved the only reachable emitter was the script's own `failed to mount` branch, which requires `hdiutil attach` to have returned **0 with no mount point** — a real bug: the transient was never retried, and because every caller's cleanup trap keys on the mount path, the attached device was never released (the orphan `diskimages-helper` in the job's cleanup). Durable fix shipped as `plow-pbc/plow#1203`. Next instance: any "known flake" whose message you have not actually attributed to an emitter — a green re-run is not evidence the code is sound.

### +1 — 2026-08-13 · plow2-main-flake-sweep · when the durable fix looks like a threshold, read that constant's history first
**Change:** Two sharpenings. (1) When the seam you land on is a **threshold** — a token cap, a timeout, a retry count, a buffer size — read that constant's own git history before tuning it. A value already raised N times is not the seam; the seam is whatever leaves the quantity *unbounded*, and the next raise loses the same race. (2) One `main`-level flake is a prompt to sweep the branch's whole CI-failure history for the class, not just to fix the one blocking today's PR — `gh run list --branch main --status failure` costs one call and turns a single re-run into a complete ledger.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — I re-ran the failed job on a docs-only PR and handed off with "want me to file an issue, or raise the cap / retry on `length`?", the *same* shape the `install-ordering-rca` +1 above already recorded for this *same* test. Third recurrence of the parent's exact failure mode. The unblock — the operator's "use systematic-debugging to understand the reason tests are failing and if needed, open a pr to fix and get the pr to convergence… retry is fine, or changing the model call to something more predictable," which reframed the goal from *dispositioning today's red* to *removing the flake*. Evidence for (1): the cap had already gone 300 → 600 → 1024 across prior PRs and truncated at every value; bounding the generation instead (a length-only system message, ~150 tokens against the unchanged 1024 budget) made the cap stop mattering — `plow-pbc/plow#1225`. Evidence for (2): the same sweep surfaced six `main` reds in three weeks, yielding a second merged de-flake (`#1230`) and a third filed with a repro (`#1227`). Next instance: any flake whose proposed remedy is "raise the timeout / bump the retry / grow the buffer" — if that constant has moved before, it is the wrong lever.

### +1 — 2026-09-17 · latch8-413-flake-fix-smoke · the de-flake fix's ship sequel is the flake's own measurement, re-run on merged main — name it in the hand-off so the merge wake runs it unasked
**Change:** Two sharpenings. (1) A flake fix is verified by the *measurement the issue reported failing* — the full suite N× on merged `main`, unloaded and under CPU contention — not by one green CI run. Name that re-run as the merge-conditional ship sequel in the PR hand-off, so `babysit-pr`'s MERGED wake runs it and reports the pass ledger without the operator asking. (2) Confirm an issue's RCA before planning from it: plow-pbc/latch#413 named the right *class* (real timers racing real I/O) but the wrong *mechanism* for the headline test (a 20ms window; widening it to 2000ms still failed 3/3 — the true cause was nondeterministic queue arrival order) and the wrong *line* for the second — a plan built on the issue's text would have "fixed" the wrong thing and shipped the flake.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — after the operator merged plow-pbc/latch#430 they had to come back and ask for a smoke test. Prior authority — the PR body I wrote already spelled out the verification recipe (each file 5× alone + 3× under ten CPU hogs), `CLAUDE.md` § Take the Steps chains smoke into the ship flow, and `babysit-pr` § Step 1 already runs a merge-conditional sequel when the hand-off names one; I named none. Unblock — "merged 430... can you smoke test", which produced an 8/8 full-suite ledger on `main` @ de23ede3 that should have been the MERGED wake's own report.
**Next instance:** a `plow` CI flake fixed in `api/tests/` and merged — the sequel is `just test` N× on merged `main` under load, reported as a pass ledger by the babysit MERGED wake, not a re-run the operator requests; and any issue whose RCA a planner inherits — reproduce the named mechanism deterministically first (force the suspected ordering, widen the suspected window) before a plan argues from it.

## A terse user statement contradicting system-recorded identity state (hostname, host map) → ask, don't rewrite your model
**Change:** Add near `CLAUDE.md` § Which machine you're on: `hostname` is authoritative for "which machine am I on"; the checked-in host map for name→host resolution. A one-line user statement that *contradicts* them is more likely a typo than a correction to settled state — respond "hostname says X; confirming before I adjust," not by rewriting your world model (or a just-written memory) around the contradiction. Corollary: a feedback memory written immediately after one correction can encode the wrong lesson; when a second correction reverses the first, revisit the memory too.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — during a multi-host deploy, a terse "mbp is this local machine" (contradicting `hostname` = mba) got trusted over the system record; I rewrote my model and a fresh memory around it, and the human had to spend a *second* correction ("mba is this machine") reversing both. The unblock was the system record all along: one confirm-against-hostname reply would have collapsed two correction round-trips into zero.

The resolution is two cheap reads: `hostname`, then the `<user>@<host>` pair from `lib/fleet.sh`'s `_fleet_hosts()`.

Same discriminator as the parent, arrived at from self-reference rather than contradiction.

  **Change:** Extend to indirect naming with a supplied identifier: when a task names a machine indirectly ("the other machine with more RAM", "my other MacBook Pro") AND supplies a concrete identifier — a tailnet IP, a shell transcript, an ssh prompt — bind the host by probing that identifier (`ssh <user>@<ip> hostname`, `tailscale status | grep <ip>`) BEFORE any install, config write, or cron registration. ## "Validate then fetch" as two probes with split fail semantics → collapse to one fail-loud call
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md` § Fail-Fast (sibling of the owned-seam fail-loud rule harvested there 2026-07-09 — different shape: redundant-probe collapse, not guard placement): when a flow calls the same service twice with split fail semantics — call A fail-loud as a validation gate, call B fail-soft as the data source — check whether one call can both validate and return the data, and collapse to it failing loud (deleting the redundant pass is usually net-negative LOC). Fail-soft on the call whose result drives the feature's core decision silently ships a degraded config while reporting success. Verify the single call accepts the same inputs the old gate did with a real run before deleting the old path.
