## A merged change isn't live on a route served by a rewrite/proxy to a separate deploy pipeline — trace the serving path before implying merge ships it

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Verify Before Claiming Done (next to the executing-context "an integration works only when the runtime that owns it produced the user-visible artifact" bullet): before telling the user a merged change is (or will be) live on a URL, trace how that *exact route* is served. A path can be a rewrite/proxy to a different host, or a separately-built SPA staged into another service — which deploys from its **own** trigger, so the merge that ships the main site never touches it. When the route deploys from a different pipeline, say so explicitly and name the deploy step ("merged, but /X needs the API deploy to go live"), then verify the deployed page rather than asserting live-ness from the merge.

**Why (autonomy):** plow-pbc/plow #1079 + #1093 — I handed off two merged PRs implying "merge → live," and the user came back reporting `plow.co/100` still showed the old content. Investigating surfaced that `/100` is a `vercel.json` rewrite to `api.plow.co` — an SPA built + shipped only by a separate prod API deploy (`cd api && just deploy`), never by the plow.co static-site deploy the merge triggers. Tracing the serving path of the specific route before claiming live-ness would have replaced the user's "why isn't this updated?" round-trip with an upfront "note: /100 deploys separately." Promoted from feedback memory `feedback-verify-serving-pipeline-before-claiming-live`.

### +1 — 2026-09-04 · life-assistant1-elm-reminders-rca · the serving path can be a REVISION PIN in another repo — and bumping it is pre-authorized

**Change (extends):** The parent traces a proxy/rewrite route. The same gap opens when the delivery mechanism is a **version pin another repo holds**: the fix merges, the pin still names the old revision, and the runtime that needed it keeps running the broken code. Trace the pin the same way you'd trace a route, and treat the bump as part of shipping rather than a follow-up. The operator has since made this standing: pin-bump PRs are created **and merged** without asking, the one class exempt from per-PR merge consent.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — I merged the fix for a producer that had never worked, verified it on `main`, and reported it done; the cloud variant's pin still pointed at a pre-fix revision, so every affected tenant kept failing on a five-minute timer. Prior authority — I had myself written in the PR body that the pin *is* the delivery mechanism, so the gap was named and then not acted on. Unblock — the operator said to always create and merge new pins; the bump, its CI build, and a pull-and-inspect of the published image took about fifteen minutes.
**Next instance:** any repo whose artifact is consumed by a manifest elsewhere — a base image SHA, a skill-bundle ref, a lockfile entry — where merging the fix and stopping leaves the consumer on the old bytes.

## [removes-handback] Stalling race/isolation probe loop → move the resource OFF the shared substrate and delete the guard machinery
**Change:** When a bot-review loop keeps surfacing the same class of race/security finding (TOCTOU, symlink-follow, ownership-transfer) on operations against a resource living on a shared / adversary-mutable substrate, the structural fix is relocating the resource off that substrate (a non-shared, correctly-owned path), then deleting the accumulated guard machinery — not hardening the next filesystem op. Every path-based guard on a concurrently-mutable path has a fresh TOCTOU window; leaf patches never converge. Before patching probe N+1, ask "why is this resource on the shared substrate at all?" and trace whether the real consumer needs it there. Prefer the move even when it abandons accumulated hardening LOC. Surface it as the recommendation at the stall point (the bot's own stall callout is the trigger). Next instance: any repo where a shared volume/dir/cache draws repeated race-class probes on a helper that keeps growing.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — kwr PR #165: a cache-reclaim helper grew 23→137 LOC over 4 rounds, blocking count flat, all one symlink/race class, because the cache sat on a dind-shared volume a PR-controlled process could mutate; the loop stalled until knightwatch fired its REEVAL trigger and the decision went to the human. unblock — Sam chose the substrate move: redirect caches to the unprivileged user's own HOME and delete the helper + its smoke (~−90 LOC), making the race class disappear. Recommending that pivot myself at the stall point removes the operator round-trip. (Promoted from the plow5 feedback ledger; concrete substrate-level form of the simpler-seam and vestigial-shape rules.)

### +1 — 2026-08-20 · kwr232-bind-the-pause-file · second kwr instance, one level up: the substrate was a writable DIRECTORY bind, and the move was to bind a FILE

**Change:** Add the earliest, cheapest tell to the existing rule: **a writable DIRECTORY mounted across a trust boundary is itself the finding** — don't wait for the stall. Anything reachable *inside* a shared directory is plantable by the other side, and when that side is root, no mode closes it (`CAP_FOWNER` bypasses both the directory bits and a sticky bit). Binding a single **file** removes the class topologically: a bind-mount target cannot be unlinked (EBUSY), so the inode is pinned and there are no siblings to create. Corollary once bound: a file bind is inode-pinned, so writes must be **in place under `flock`** — temp+rename strands the other side on the old inode — and the lock must live on the bound file itself, since a sidecar `.lock` falls outside the bind and serializes nothing across the boundary.

**Why (autonomy):** *the stop* — `plow-pbc/knightwatch-reviewer#231` mounted the host's throttle **directory** into every reviewer to unify a rate-limit pause, then spent **14 local review rounds** guarding what could be planted in it: cross-UID modes and their self-heal, a `gh_pause_path_sane` predicate, a `gh_pause_clear_plant` repair, planted symlink/FIFO/directory matrices on two paths, an unopenable lock, an unbounded `flock`. Two of those rounds were the reviewer *churning* — asked to add a sticky bit one round, asked to remove it the next once it broke `rename(2)` for the non-owner. The PR reached +820 net against a declared <150, and I handed the scope call back to the operator rather than acting on it. *the unblock* — the operator reacted to the size (“wow 845 loc??!”); the replacement, built on the reviewer's own probe, landed at **+222 net** and the entire 433-line hardening surface was deleted rather than fixed, because with a file bind it has nothing to defend. **Next instance:** any agent/CI container handed a writable host *directory* for one piece of shared state — bind the file.

### +1 — 2026-08-26 · agent-mgr6-two-layer-fleet-cli · the substrate can be SEMANTIC: an argv grammar you don't own, where every miss fails OPEN

**Change (extends):** The existing rule moves a resource off a shared *physical* substrate. The same move applies when the shared substrate is a **grammar** — a guard that decides safety by parsing another tool's argv/config is re-implementing a parser you neither own nor version, and **every spelling it fails to recognize is a false accept**. Two checks turn the stall into a decision: (1) **count the misses, not the fixes** — two wrong readings of one inference in one review round is the signal, do not ship the third patch; (2) **name the failure direction** — fail-open ⇒ delete the inference or move it to a seam that holds the real answer; fail-closed ⇒ patching one more spelling is survivable. Grep for real callers first: a convenience with zero callers never justifies a parser that fails open.

**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer, untagged (bot-caught). A guard proved `docker compose pull` safe by finding `--ignore-buildable` in the argv. It was wrong three ways in one round, each **measured**: presence is not the value (a later `--ignore-buildable=false` overrides an earlier bare one); past `--` the word is a service name; and `pull --policy --ignore-buildable` has `--policy` swallow the word as its value, so Compose never sees the flag and pulls. Each fix recognized one more spelling; the third arrived after the second shipped. The property was not in the argv at all — whether a fetch can substitute anything depends on whether the *resolved* service is buildable, which another seam already read. Refusing the subcommand outright was net-negative LOC and ended the class. Deleting it also cascaded: it moved an ownership check ahead of the refusal, whose remedies ("rename", "unregister") are doors that do not open for a refused subcommand — so re-derive the neighbours after a deletion, and look for the prior art (a sibling rule already pre-checked at the dispatch) before inventing machinery.

## [removes-handback] "PR converged / merge-ready" is a claim about THREE surfaces — sweep `gh pr checks` + `mergeable` too, not just the review bot
**Change:** Add to babysit-pr Step 7 / `PR_LIFECYCLE.md` (convergence report): before a wrap-up report calls a PR "converged and clean / ready to merge," verify all THREE merge-gating surfaces, not just the review bot's convergence — (1) review convergence (knightwatch `Probes: None`, no open findings), (2) `gh pr checks <PR#>` for any non-green *required* check (diff-scope a red one per `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` before assuming it's yours), (3) `gh pr view <PR#> --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus` for `CONFLICTING`/`DIRTY`. Read the states: `mergeStateStatus: BLOCKED` on `MERGEABLE` is just the standing review gate (fine to report as "needs human approval"); `CONFLICTING` is a conflict to resolve in-loop (`PR_LIFECYCLE.md` § Merge conflicts). Act on red checks + conflicts in the same turn, then report — don't emit a "ready for your merge decision" the human has to bounce. Each dissolved in one command (`gh pr checks`, `gh pr view --json mergeable`). Sweeping all three surfaces at the convergence report removes both hand-backs. Distinct from the "Red required CI check → read the log first" proposal (that triages an *already-known* red check; this is about looking at the checks/mergeability surfaces *at all* before claiming merge-ready). ## Incident evidence of an event class ≠ evidence it hits the guarded window — recompute the coincidence before citing it
**Change:** When defending or attacking a guard for a narrow failure window, evidence that the event class occurs is NOT evidence it intersects the window. Before citing observed incidents in a probabilistic argument (yours or a bot's), check the timing overlap: an abort observed minutes into a stream cannot support "aborts land in the few-ms write at stream end" — those incidents provably missed the window. Downgrade to base-rate reasoning (window duration / exposure × event rate) and argue the guard's cost-benefit on the honest number. Next instance: any review debate over keeping/removing a shield, retry, or lock where "we've seen X happen" is doing the load-bearing work.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged): defending PR plow-pbc/plow#1096's cancellation shield I cited the outage's observed ~150s client aborts as "mid-write cancellations are observed"; Sam's one-line "is it a few milliseconds or 150s?" exposed the conflation — the cited aborts died minutes before the write existed. On recount the ruling flipped from hold-the-shield to coin-flip-leaning-removal. (Session: 2026-07-22-plow5-outage-fix)

## [removes-handback] No fallback paths — present the canonical path as THE path, don't build/bless/advertise a degraded secondary
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Default to the Simplifying Option` / § Anti-Bloat family: when a capability already has a canonical path (e.g. a CI-based deploy), do NOT build, bless, or advertise a secondary "fallback" — a degraded local path, an alternate mechanism, a Rosetta/OS-workaround convenience. One sanctioned way. If a shared implementation must physically exist (CI invokes `deploy.sh`), frame it as *the implementation the canonical path runs*, not a blessed local alternative: drop "fallback" wording and "you can also run this locally" affordances from docs/help/comments, and don't leave a machine in a special-cased state to prop up a fallback (revert it). A fallback is a second contract that drifts and invites people off the blessed path — bloat unless explicitly requested. Next instance: any repo where a canonical path exists and I'm tempted to add a degraded secondary mechanism "for convenience."
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged): I repeatedly offered a "local fallback" (Rosetta as a documented local-deploy convenience *alongside* the canonical CI deploy); the operator corrected with "no fallbacks — so revert mbp rosetta." I'd have shipped the extra surface (a second path + a machine left in a special state); the steer collapses it to the single canonical contract. Promoted from the `no-fallback-paths` feedback memory.

### +1 — 2026-08-14 · 2026-08-14-plow1-ocr-billing-fallback · the rule extends to a RUNTIME fallback across billing accounts, and there it is a hard stop, not a quality steer
**Why (autonomy):** stop — plow-pbc/plow#1260. OCR was pinned to a Plow-metered model regardless of the operator's selected LLM, so a direct-provider account still spent Plow credits and 402'd once the balance hit zero. Removing the pin was NOT sufficient: the engine then appends every other authed provider as an automatic fallback, so the charge still landed on the account the operator hadn't chosen. I treated "keep the fallback vs fail loudly" as a product fork and handed it to the operator, stalling the PR on a decision I'd framed as unanswerable. unblock — the operator ruled flatly: there should never be a fallback; a model without OCR should just fail. Applying THIS proposal would have made that my own call — a degraded secondary path is exactly what the canonical-path rule forbids, and the billing case is the sharpest instance of it because the degradation is invisible until a bill or a 402 arrives. Generalization worth carrying: check what the framework does when the setting is ABSENT, not only when it's set — "I removed the hardcoded fallback" and "there is no fallback" are different claims.

## [removes-handback] Required bot reviewer blocked for days (quota/outage) → merge on the resolved-last-review + independent-local-reviewer-clean signal, don't stall
**Change:** When a merge is gated on a bot review that's externally blocked for days (`⏸ paused` on a multi-day quota reset, reviewer outage) and the fresh pass genuinely can't land, don't stall the launch for days AND don't silently merge. Treat the fresh re-review as satisfied when ALL hold: (a) the last COMPLETED review's only finding is resolved by a minimal, targeted change; (b) an independent local reviewer (roborev) cleared the EXACT merge commit; (c) the delta since the reviewed head can't introduce a new class of issue (a trivial string/value change). Then surface the deviation + the external blocker in one quick confirm (deploy is an irreversible prod publish), lead with "merge + deploy now" as the recommendation, and proceed on the go-ahead. Next instance: any repo whose merge gate depends on a rate-limited/outage-prone bot reviewer while the change under review is already independently vetted.
**Why (autonomy):** plow-pbc/plow#1112 — I triggered a fresh `/srosro-review` of the final head, then knightwatch hit its codex quota (`⏸ paused`, reset ~5 days out), so the "after a knightwatch review, merge" gate couldn't get a fresh pass that day. The last completed review's sole probe (a personal-cell exposure) was already resolved by a 1-line number swap, and roborev independently cleared the exact merge commit. I fired an AskUserQuestion (proceed-now vs wait-~5-days); the owner chose merge+deploy now. Waiting days for a phone-number-string delta would have defeated the same-day launch. Promoted from the `proceed-on-strong-signal-when-bot-reviewer-quota-blocked` feedback memory.

## A self-healing enforcer on "wrong-looking" state means intentional — and intentional means find what keeps breaking
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` (or § Take the Steps): before recommending "restore to canonical / make it match the reference" for a diverged install or config, grep for machinery that actively *enforces* the current state — cron/scheduled jobs, systemd/launchd units, provisioning hooks, reconcile loops — especially ones whose name references the thing you're about to change. Found → the divergence is deliberate: surface the enforcer and offer embrace-it vs retire-it (disable the enforcer too), never a silent restore that the enforcer will revert overnight. Corollary: intentional ≠ correct — an enforcer is evidence something *keeps breaking*; trace the recurring symptom it compensates for, because the durable fix is usually in the product, not the per-machine band-aid. Next instance: any repo/infra where a "drifted" file, symlink, or unit differs from a reference machine and a reconciler owns it.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged): reconciling a family member's prod install against the reference, I recommended (and the operator picked) "restore canonical" for a skills symlink — then found a daily `restore-skills-symlink` cron that would have auto-destroyed that fix the next morning; the divergence was the design. The rule would have surfaced the enforcer before the wrong recommendation shipped. Promoted from the `check-enforcing-machinery-before-restore-canonical` feedback memory. (Session: 2026-07-23-plow9-gpt56-reply-drop)

## [removes-handback] A duplicate/race across a MULTI-ACTOR pipeline usually has contributors on BOTH producer and requester — audit each, and enforce an in-flight latch at a mechanism (hook/lock), not prose
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` (debugging): when diagnosing a duplicate / race / thrash in a system with more than one actor (a producer that emits work + a requester that also triggers it), don't stop after fixing the first plausible root — explicitly enumerate the OTHER actors touching the same resource/lifecycle and check whether each also contributes and whether its guard is actually enforced. For a latch meant to hold during an in-flight operation, verify ALL the ways an actor can perturb it are covered by the same MECHANISM enforcement (a PreToolUse hook, a flock), not prose the agent is merely asked to follow — prose latches get skipped in exactly the race window they exist for. Next instance: any producer/consumer or orchestrator/worker system (a queue + its enqueuers, a build + its triggers) where the same symptom can originate on either side.
**Why (autonomy):** removed a hand-back: after I root-caused + fixed the orchestrator side of knightwatch's duplicate reviews (plow #1102, PR #182), the owner had to prompt "isn't there also something in /babysit-pr about not requesting a review while one's in progress?" to surface the second, independent contributor (the babysit posting a trigger while a review ran). The enforcement hook then turned out to gate `git push` but not the trigger comment — a prose-only latch on the trigger path, gapped in the race window. Auditing both actors up front would have removed the owner's nudge. Promoted from `feedback_check_every_actor_in_a_race`. (Session: 2026-07-23-plow8-knightwatch-dup-reviews)

## [removes-handback] Visual/layout work isn't done until you RENDER it yourself — serve it locally, measure the constrained axis, screenshot; never ask where it's hosted
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`: for any edit to markup/CSS/layout/copy inside a size-constrained container, a successful string edit is not evidence — overflow, wrapping and clipping are invisible to both the source diff and to reasoning about the CSS. Serve the artifact yourself (`python3 -m http.server` on a scratch port + the `playwright` skill renders any local file; `file:` is blocked by the MCP server, so the throwaway server IS the path) and assert the specific constraint the edit stresses via `browser_evaluate`: `scrollWidth` vs client width for horizontal overflow, content `scrollHeight` vs container height for vertical fit. Prototype candidate fix values live in the page before baking them into the file, then re-render to confirm. Screenshot as the report's evidence. Never end a turn asking the operator where the thing is served in order to check it visually — standing up the render is a one-minute self-service step.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — after editing a fixed-width HTML banner I reported the change applied and handed back a question asking where the file gets served so I could verify it visually. unblock — the operator's "use playwright to preview it — do you see any issues?" restarted it; the very first render exposed two defects I had already called done: an appended URL clipped by `overflow:hidden` on a `nowrap` line (334px of text in 309px), and a tagline pushed to two lines with zero vertical slack. Next instance: any generated artifact whose correctness is visual — a chart PR, a PDF export, a README table, a dashboard tile — inspect the rendered form, not the source. (Source: tkmx-server feedback memory `render-ui-work-in-a-browser-before-calling-it-done`, 2026-07-27.)

### +1 — 2026-08-11 · awu-join-community-nav · the parent's two named metrics BOTH lie — assert per-element geometry, and diff against `origin/main` to place the blame
**Change:** Sharpen the parent's measurement advice, which names `scrollWidth` vs client width for horizontal overflow. That metric has two blind spots that each hid a real defect in one session: (1) an ancestor `overflow-x: hidden` clips the overhang *and* clamps page `scrollWidth`, so the check returns clean while content sits off-screen — and an element's own `scrollWidth` is equally unreliable when its `overflow` is `visible`; (2) a grid/flex container under width pressure often does not overflow **at all** — it compresses an `auto` track instead, so every overflow-based check passes while a logo silently collapses from 101px to 0px wide. Assert **per-element geometry** instead: each element's `getBoundingClientRect()` right/left against the viewport, plus rendered-vs-intrinsic size for images (`height × naturalWidth/naturalHeight - width > 2` catches squash). Two riders: sweep breakpoint edges (N and N+1), not just one phone and one desktop width — and load the page in an offscreen same-origin **iframe** per width, since iframes get their own viewport for media queries, so one `browser_evaluate` covers a whole sweep instead of one resize round-trip each. When a reviewer predicts a layout defect, run the same metrics against `git show origin/main:<file>` before accepting or declining — that comparison is what distinguishes a regression you introduced from a pre-existing bug, and it can invert the verdict.
**Why (autonomy):** not a hard stop — the parent rule fired correctly (I rendered and swept locally without being asked), so this is a quality sharpening of its specifics rather than a removed round-trip. Adding one nav link to a 3-column grid header produced two regressions invisible to both named metrics: the homepage lockup collapsed to 0–6px wide across 561–760px (no overflow anywhere — the grid ate an `auto` track), and on two sibling pages `body{overflow-x:hidden}` masked a 34px overhang that `scrollWidth` reported as clean. A reviewer separately predicted overflow at 320/360px; measuring per-element geometry against `origin/main` showed the opposite — the branch *removed* a pre-existing 34px overhang — which turned a "mirror this fix onto two more files" instruction into a documented decline. Next instance: any responsive/constrained-container change in any repo — a dashboard tile, an email template, a PDF export — where the obvious overflow metric can be silenced by a clipping ancestor or absorbed by a flexible track. (Source: aiworthusing project memory `verify-layout-with-element-geometry`, plow-pbc/aiworthusing#10.)

## [removes-handback] A reviewer recommending a SPLIT on a converging PR is advice, not a gate — keep driving to mergeable
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps` (companion to "don't menu at a long autonomous loop's convergence"): when a review bot recommends closing and resubmitting as stacked PRs, and the loop is otherwise converging (blockers trending to zero, every remaining finding scoped and understood), treat the recommendation as advice — record it in the PR thread as considered-and-declined, then continue to a mergeable state. Do NOT park the loop on an `AskUserQuestion` about split-vs-push-through. The split call is the author's, but by the time a loop has surfaced, verified and scoped every remaining finding, the expensive thinking is already done and stopping converts a finishable task into a round-trip. Stop only for the genuinely-human things: an irreversible action, a credential you don't hold, or a change to user-visible behaviour they already approved. "Mergeable" still stops short of `gh pr merge` unless authorized.
**Why (autonomy):** Promoted from the youtube-live-count-chime feedback ledger. stop — with two reviewers and the plan's own LOC tripwire all recommending a split, I fixed the blocking CI failure, verified the four remaining probes, then parked the loop and asked split-vs-push-through. unblock — the operator answered with a directive to babysit it to a mergeable state, i.e. the question itself was the only thing blocking. Recording the recommendation and continuing would have removed the round-trip entirely. Relates to [[async-user-human-gated-decision-file-issues]] — that one fires when the human is *away* and the decision is genuinely theirs; this one fires when the decision is *already effectively made* by the loop's own convergence.

After it is written, tested, and passing, the argument has to be stronger than diff size: real coupling risk, an unreviewable mix, or a piece that genuinely should not ship yet. **Change:** When asked to assess a PR that "won't converge", pull `mergeStateStatus`, `reviewDecision`, `statusCheckRollup`, head stability, and the actual findings — not the round count. ## On an "expose this data" ask, inventory the existing public API before adding a route — and classify the real obstacle (availability vs access vs shape)
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps` (sibling to the DRY-with-prior-art bullet): when a request arrives as "someone wants to query X", curl/grep the live API for a route that already carries the data before writing one. Then name which obstacle actually blocks the consumer — availability (the data isn't served), access (CORS/auth), or merely shape (aggregation the caller can do in a few lines). Only availability justifies a new endpoint by default; access is fixed at the middleware, and shape is answered with the existing URL plus a snippet. A new endpoint is permanent surface (route, db helper, OpenAPI entry, tests, plus a proxy rewrite before a separate frontend repo can even see it). Evidence you generated yourself earlier in the same session is the strongest signal the data is already reachable — notice it.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — I started building a `GET /api/tools` route one turn after personally aggregating that exact list out of the already-public `/api/users` with curl; the operator caught it. unblock — his redirect to the existing endpoint also surfaced the true blocker for a third-party browser consumer, which was that the server sends no CORS headers at all — something the new endpoint would not have fixed. Next instance: any "make X queryable" ask on a service with an existing public read API. (Source: tkmx-server feedback memory `check-existing-endpoint-before-adding-one`, 2026-07-24.)

### +1 — 2026-08-26 · agent-mgr2-per-instance-tz · auto-claim must take the atomic claim, not a "looks free" glance — and slots can be reserved
**Change:** Two conditions on the auto-claim this proposal asks for. (a) **Use the atomic claim** (`tc claim`, the same lock the subagent path takes), never a hand-rolled read of branch + `git status`: the read is a TOCTOU window, and a parallel session that starts working between your check and your `checkout` loses its work with no trace. Do not rely on a chained `checkout && reset --hard` failing safely — it only protects when the *checkout* is the step that trips, and a slot already on the base branch with dirty files lets the checkout succeed and the reset destroy them. (b) **Free-looking is not unclaimed:** the operator may reserve specific slots for specific agents, which no dirty-count reveals — so announce the slot you took and treat a correction as authoritative, and prefer a slot the operator has assigned you over the lowest free one.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — I took `agent-mgr3` (a peer's active branch, three dirty files; only a `&&` short-circuit saved it) and then `agent-mgr4`, where a peer began working concurrently. unblock — the operator's steer naming a reserved lane for me and telling me not to use the other. Next instance: any numbered slot pool shared by parallel agents, in any repo — the auto-claim is right, but "lowest free" has to mean "lowest atomically claimed", not "lowest that looked idle a second ago".

## [removes-handback] A bot's blocking finding on code you rewrote → run the flagged property against `main`'s version; regression → fix here, identical on main → run it through `babysit-pr` Step 5's intent fence
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` (sibling of the released-vs-merged bullet, and of the "check origin/main for the already-landed fix" proposal above — that one asks *is the fix already on main*, this one asks *is the hole already on main*): before applying OR declining a security/correctness finding on a function you rewrote, extract the property under test and exercise it against `main`'s version (`git show origin/main:<file>`, or a 5-line scratch script driving the old primitive). Prefer *executing* it to reading it — inherited guarantees are often syscall-level and invisible in the source. Then: **regression ⇒ fix it here** regardless of how peripheral it feels (not regressing is always in intent); **identical on main ⇒ run it through `babysit-pr` Step 5's intent fence — within intent, apply (counter-propose the LOC-negative or branch-negative version if the remedy trips Anti-Bloat); not within intent, file the issue and decline**, and write "identical on `main` at `<file:line>`" in the reply — a fact the bot can't re-litigate, unlike a scope opinion it will re-probe next round. A rewrite silently inherits *and* silently drops properties of the code it replaces, and neither shows up in the diff as a deletion. When the bot critiques your *deferral remedy* rather than the deferral, that's a correction to the issue, not grounds to absorb the work.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — on `plow-pbc/knightwatch-reviewer#191` I fired an `AskUserQuestion` asking how to handle a `[blocking]` probe demanding +15-20 LOC of `dir_fd` anchoring, because I couldn't tell from my own reasoning whether the hole was mine. unblock — the operator's "hold the line + trim" ruling; generalized, the deciding fact was mechanical and I could have established it myself. I had judged two probes on the same rewritten function from memory of what the old code "gave" and was wrong in **opposite directions**: probe A (re-plant race) I had filed as deferred hardening, but the old `_relink`'s `symlink_to()` → `symlink(2)` fails `EEXIST`, so the old code was race-safe for free and my `write_bytes()` was strictly weaker — a regression, fix here; probe B (directory-level redirect) looked structural and blocking, but `main`'s `_relink` does the identical `link.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` before writing — byte-for-byte the same exposure; run through the fence it landed not within intent, filed as an issue. Both settled in seconds by a check I hadn't run. Cost of getting it wrong is asymmetric and two-sided: a shipped regression, or LOC absorbed to fix something `main` already ships. Next instance: a Copilot/Vercel-agent review flags a missing auth check on a plow route you refactored — diff the route against `main` before either absorbing the guard or declining it. (Source: knightwatch-reviewer9 feedback memory `diff-against-main-to-settle-regression-vs-preexisting`, 2026-07-27.)

## [removes-handback] Deliverable outgrowing the ask → say "you asked for X, this is N× X" IN CHAT; a size note in a PR body is not surfacing
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Concise Code` (beside the LOC-target bullet): when a diff passes roughly 2× the size the request implied, stop and present a breakdown **by purpose, in chat** — which lines serve the thing they described versus which serve an enabling mechanism they never asked about — and name the ratio out loud with a recommendation and the option to cut. Recording it in a PR description, a review reply, or a scope note does NOT count: the requester is carrying a mental model of the work's size and will keep approving incremental rounds against it, because each round looks small and the total is never presented. Watch the test-to-production ratio as its own trigger (`§ Tests` flags >2×).
**Why (autonomy):** Promoted from the youtube-live-count-chime feedback ledger. stop — a "notify me when the count rises, ideally with the name" request shipped as ~2,850 changed lines; the size was noted in the PR body and several review replies and the split question asked once, but never in the plain form "you asked for X, this is 6× X". The operator found the total themselves and reacted with alarm, which then forced a live scope `AskUserQuestion` I had to fire. unblock — presented a by-purpose breakdown (73% of production existed to guess a name, 100% of the setup burden and nearly every blocking bug lived there) and they chose to split. Presenting that ratio unprompted at 2× would have removed both the alarm and the picker. Sibling of [[fix-shaped-small-landing-net-positive-is-a-wrong-shape-smell]] — that one checks the ledger yourself, this one is about telling the human.

## [removes-handback] Request's domain noun ≠ the model's noun → reconcile BEFORE designing, don't build on the literal word

## [removes-handback] Unblock a tooling trust-gate with a one-off manual run, never by widening the durable permission
**Change:** When a tool refuses to act because a contributor/principal is "untrusted" (a reviewer bot's push-access gate, a CI trust check, an IAM/sudoers/API-scope gate), do NOT propose granting the broad durable permission (repo write, an IAM role, sudoers) to satisfy it. Lead with — and by default just do — the one-off/narrow unblock: run the gated action via the non-gated path, a scoped bypass, or the operator's own credentials. Surface the permission-widening option only as a named, non-recommended alternative, if at all. Reserve a confirm for a genuinely irreversible/prod effect; a dev-side reversible manual run just proceeds. Next instance: any repo/tool where an untrusted-principal gate blocks a wanted action (a bot's collaborator check, a CI trust gate, an IAM role).
**Why (autonomy):** stop — kwr8: knightwatch's container gate skips read-only-collaborator PRs (erans/drodio on srosro/tkmx-client), leaving their PRs unreviewed; I fired an `AskUserQuestion` offering grant-write / one-off-manual-run / leave-it. unblock — the operator picked "one-off manual run, no permission change." A standing rule (tooling trust-gate → manual/narrow unblock, never widen the durable grant) removes that picker: repo write is a broad, long-lived security grant that outlives the one task, and "trusted enough to review their PR" ≠ "trusted to push." (Session: 2026-07-29-kwr8-pr194-roborev-scope-creep) [promoted from the dont-widen-repo-permissions-for-tooling-gates feedback memory]

## [removes-handback] At the altitude check, classify the diff — if most of it is generated, the split is code-in/data-out, not smaller feature PRs

**Change:** Before `gh pr create`, don't just measure the diff against the >20-files / >600-additions bar — classify it. Machine-generated artifacts (LLM-authored prose, manifests, exported bundles, lockfile-scale state) never belong in a feature PR alongside the code that produces them: ship the pipeline and let the pipeline's own run commit its output. When a review loop stops converging, check the diff's *composition* before concluding the reviewer is churning or the architecture is wrong.

**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — a PR reached 6,940 additions of which 5,543 (80%) was generated vault content plus a 505-line design doc; only ~890 lines was engineered code. It ran roughly 30 review rounds without converging, because a reviewer reading generated prose always finds something and that is not a defect class review can close. I kept babysitting it and handed back a non-converging PR. *The unblock* — the operator stopped me and asked whether to split, cut scope, drop the docs, or move the facts to their own PR. Reshaped to 1,033 additions of pipeline only, the same reviewer converged in three rounds. The existing altitude rule fired on size and I still misread the remedy as "smaller feature PRs"; the actual remedy was a different axis entirely.

**Next instance:** any repo where a job writes artifacts into the tree it lives in — a codegen'd client, a compiled schema, a scraped dataset, a docs site build — where the instinct is to include the output "so reviewers can see it works".

### +1 — the code/data split is ORDERED, and a reviewer demanding the data in-PR is answered by the repo's own promote gate

**Change:** Extends the parent with sequencing and a decline script. The split is not just *which PR* but *what order*: the generator's contract must merge and **deploy** before the regeneration runs, because the run has to execute under the new contract from the deployed clone — so "regenerate and commit it here" is not merely bigger, it is impossible to do correctly pre-merge. When a reviewer escalates to `[blocking]` on "the migration is incomplete, commit the regenerated output in this PR", decline by citing the repo's own promote gate (the line saying generated content reaches the default branch only in a PR the operator opens), not by arguing size. State plainly what the PR does and does not deliver — a contract change is not a delivered user outcome — rather than letting the title imply the whole migration.

**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — knightwatch escalated a data-integrity probe to `[blocking]` demanding a full-corpus regeneration and ~26 regenerated pages be committed inside a ~30-line policy PR; I could not resolve merge-vs-expand on my own and fired an AskUserQuestion. *The unblock* — the operator ruled merge-the-contract, vault-PR-follows, which is what the repo's own `REVIEW.md` already said; I had the citation and still treated the scope call as his rather than reading the gate as dispositive. The probe's *diagnosis* was right and worth recording (the PR was inert without the regen) — only its remedy was misrouted. (Session: 2026-08-03-str9-vault-access-contract)

**Next instance:** any repo where a committed artifact is produced by a job that reads its own contract — a codegen'd client after an IDL change, a docs site after a template change, a fixture corpus after a schema change.

**Change:** Two gaps in cleanup's own ranking machinery, both surfaced by reviews of cleanup commits rather than by the corpus itself. (b) `tests/test-corpus-format.sh` should gain a `PROPOSALS.md`-scoped assertion — parse `## ` blocks plus their nested `### +1` session-slugs and assert distinct-slug rank is non-increasing top to bottom (see the **Also amends gap (b):** clause on the `plow1271-transparent-flatten` `+1`: the one-slot nudge op cannot produce that ordering, so this has to pair with a stable re-sort on append, or move the narrow just-moved-block check into cleanup's own Track B post-append step, which knows which block it moved) — so Track B's self-sort is enforced instead of re-caught by hand.
**Why (autonomy):** Not a hard stop — no operator round-trip — but a recurring reviewer cost: a `/cleanup` run nudged a bullet in § Verify Before Claiming Done and deliberately skipped the available section swap (§ Verify above § Top Rules, which would demote a pointer index below a detail section). The reviewer agreed the judgment was right and still flagged it, because no rule sanctions it. Separately the same review noted rank inversions persisting in `PROPOSALS.md` across three consecutive rounds, each caught manually. Both fixes convert a judgment the reviewer has to re-litigate every round into a rule or a test. Recorded rather than applied because cleanup may not auto-edit rule content or ship test changes.
