By the time the revert was attempted a second session had nudged the same housekeeping bullet up *again* (4th → 3rd → 2nd in one day), so reverting would have undone another session's work and added another flip; the demotion stands in `main` because the only safe remedy is the model change, not a fifth reorder. Same run, same review: the § Git Safety *section* completed a zero-information flip-flop (above → below → above across three commits), which is the damper this proposal's siblings already ask for. Next instance: any ranked corpus where a rule's value is measured by how often it is cited, and the highest-stakes rules are the ones you hope never to need.


## [removes-handback] "X isn't anywhere" — search the whole surface and VALIDATE the candidate before reporting a credential/artifact absent
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` (beside the existing negative-claim bullet): a search-backed absence claim needs *breadth* and *candidate validation*, not just a grep that returned nothing. Breadth — search the **variable name**, the **assignment shapes** (`NAME=`, `"NAME":`), the vendor's **API hostname**, and directory/repo names; scope by exclusion (`.git`, `node_modules`, caches), never by hand-picking a few directories; include shell history, credential stores, and the repo list. Long scans go to the background rather than getting narrowed to fit a timeout. Validation — before believing a candidate hit, print its **surrounding context** (masked) to check the match's boundaries, and exercise it against the **live service**. Also discount self-referential hits: N mentions of a variable name may be a *previous agent session grepping for the same thing*. When it genuinely isn't there, list what was searched so the negative is auditable, and offer the likely explanation.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — I reported "no Seam API key on this machine, on wakeup, or in any 1Password vault" after grepping four hand-picked directories with a guessed key prefix. The owner pushed back — he'd run a related app from that host and remembered part of its name — which restarted the search. The unblock generalized: the broadened pass (whole home, assignment shapes, history, `gh repo list`) reached the *same* conclusion, but only then was it evidence rather than a guess, and it surfaced two things the narrow pass had produced: a `seam_`-prefixed 83-char string that looked exactly like a key but was a coincidental substring inside another service's opaque blob (proved by masked context + a live 401), and ~1000 hits on the variable name that were a prior agent session running my own search. It also found the real answer — the remembered app integrated a *different vendor* entirely. A narrow search that finds nothing is indistinguishable from a thorough one that finds nothing, and only one is worth acting on. Next instance: any "is credential/config/artifact X present anywhere?" question on any host or repo.


  ### +1 — 2026-08-19 · str9-plow-thread-discovery · validate the INSTRUMENT, not just the search surface — a probe that can't see a positive proves nothing
  **Change:** Extend breadth-and-candidate-validation to the measuring instrument itself. Before reporting that a periodic or short-lived event is *not happening*, prove the probe could have caught it: (1) the tool exists in the environment being probed, not just on the host — a missing binary makes every sample empty and reads exactly like silence; (2) the sampling interval is well under the event's expected duration, so estimate that duration first; (3) the signal you're waiting for actually forms in this system. When a negative survives all three it is a finding; otherwise report the probe inconclusive and fix the probe, and corroborate a surprising result with a second, differently-shaped measurement.
  **Why (autonomy):** Self-recovered, so untagged — but it reached the operator, which is the cost. I reported "the poll loop may be dead — investigate" about a healthy production loop, off a sampler built on `ss`, which is not installed in that container; it had compared empty strings for 130 seconds. Two further probes failed differently: 3-second sampling against a ~550 ms connection, then waiting on a TIME_WAIT that never forms because the socket closes immediately. The valid probe found it at 1 Hz and confirmed at 20 Hz. Next instance: any "the cron/daemon/poller isn't running" claim based on sampling.


  ### +1 — 2026-09-05 · code-config2-exclamation-miner · "did we write a PR / is there an issue for X" is an absence question too — enumerate the tracker namespace, don't grep for it
  **Change:** Extend the rule from credentials/artifacts to tracker objects. When asked whether a PR, issue, or branch already exists for an idea, the authoritative surface is the *listing* — `gh pr list --state open`, `git branch -r`, `gh issue list` — scanned by title, then grep. A `gh … --search` query carrying punctuation (`"!"`) or a `git log --grep` over merged history returns empty for structural reasons, not because the thing is absent.
  **Why (autonomy):** Stop — asked "did we write a PR to look for `!` in cleanups?", I answered "No, nothing in this repo looks for it" off a `git log --grep` and a `gh pr list --search '"!"…'` that can't match punctuation; `srosro/code-config#213` had been open for five hours with exactly that title. Prior authority — the open-PR list was one call away, and `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`'s negative-claim bullet already required the surface that owns the event class. Unblock — the operator's "there's no PR?", one wasted round-trip plus a retraction.
  **Next instance:** "do we have a ticket for the flaky CI test?" in a repo tracked on Linear or GitHub Issues → list open issues by recency and read titles; never conclude "no" from a keyword search of commit messages or a search API with special characters in the query.

  ### +1 — 2026-09-17 · hermes-plugin-plow6-founder-agent-locate · a candidate that surfaces under a DIFFERENT provider/label than the one you searched for is a hit to resolve, not a non-match
  **Change:** Extend candidate validation to *shape mismatches*: when the search for X-as-a-cloud-VM returns X-as-a-self-hosted-row (or X-as-a-cron-job returns a systemd timer, X-as-a-package returns a vendored copy), that row IS the thing — resolve it to its runtime (host, container, process) before answering, and read the operator's locator ("on exe.dev") as naming the class loosely ("in the cloud"), not as a filter that excludes the hit.
  **Why (autonomy):** Stop — asked whether the founders-agent was running, I reported "no founders-agent of yours on exe.dev" and offered to provision one; the operator came back with a screenshot of the live chat. Prior authority — the prod DB row for the operator's agent on that line (provider `self_hosted`, session last-seen minutes earlier) and ten local checkouts of the founder-agent repo were already in the transcript when I wrote the negative. Unblock — the correction; one `grep -qF <session key prefix>` across `~/services/*/plow-credentials` on the Linux box located the docker-compose container in a single call.
  **Next instance:** "is my backup running on the NAS?" — `crontab -l` is empty but `systemctl list-timers` shows a differently-named timer → that timer is the backup; resolve and report it, never "no backup job".

## Un-wiring `Closes #N` from a PR body doesn't stop a squash-merge — the keyword also rides in the commit messages
**Change:** Add to `PR_LIFECYCLE.md` / `CLAUDE.md § Branch Workflow`: when a PR references an issue it must **not** close (the PR fixes one part; the issue tracks more), rewriting the PR body from `Closes #N` to `Refs #N` is necessary but not sufficient. Also grep the branch's commit messages — `git log origin/main..HEAD --format=%B | grep -nEi '(close[sd]?|fix(e[sd])?|resolve[sd]?) #<N>'` — because `gh pr merge --squash` concatenates the branch's commit bodies into the squash commit, so a closing keyword in *any* commit message reaches the default branch and closes the issue regardless of the PR body. Fix by rewording that commit or editing the squash body at merge time. Verify the body edit took with `gh pr view <PR> --json closingIssuesReferences` (it lags an edit by seconds — re-query before trusting an unchanged reading), and re-check issue state right after merging; if it closed anyway, `gh issue reopen` and record why on the issue.
**Why (autonomy):** self-recovered (untagged, per the tag bar): on `plow-pbc/knightwatch-reviewer#197` I deliberately rewrote the body from `Closes #189` to `Refs #189` and confirmed `closingIssuesReferences` had gone empty, specifically so the issue's still-outstanding third part — a 16G reclaim awaiting a soak — would survive the merge. The squash closed #189 anyway: `git log origin/main -1 --format=%b | grep -n "Closes #189"` → line 42, inherited from an early commit message on the branch. Caught only because I re-checked issue state immediately after merging; the silent failure mode is that the tracking issue vanishes and the remaining work goes with it. Next instance: any multi-part tracking issue where one PR fixes only a subset.


  ### +1 — 2026-08-20 · domo6-click-timeout · ordinary prose forms the keyword too — "Filed rather than fixed: #N" closed two deliberate follow-ups

  **Change:** Widen the pre-merge check from "did I write a closing keyword" to "does the body *contain* one, however it got there". GitHub matches `fixed: #N` with the colon, so the phrase `Filed rather than fixed: #95` — written to say the opposite — is a closing reference. Any of close/closes/closed/fix/fixes/fixed/resolve/resolves/resolved before a `#N`, with or without a colon, counts. So the `gh pr view <PR> --json closingIssuesReferences` step this proposal already prescribes is the whole fence: run it on *every* PR that mentions an issue number, not only ones where you deliberately wrote a keyword, because the failure mode here is that you never wrote one. Safe phrasings for the file-and-decline route: "Filed rather than fixed here — see #N", "Not in scope; tracked in #N", "Refs #N".

  **Why (autonomy):** Self-recovered, untagged — no hand-back, but the cost is exactly what the file-and-decline route exists to prevent. Two PRs each carried a "Filed rather than fixed: #N" line naming a follow-up deliberately left out of scope, and each merge silently closed the issue it named, `stateReason: COMPLETED`, two seconds after the merge, with no work done. Both were the *only* durable record of a deferral — the reason to file rather than absorb. Caught here at `/cleanup` because §3.7 re-reads tracker state; nothing in the babysit loop looks at issue state after a merge, and the PR thread shows nothing wrong. Next instance: any repo where a review round declines a finding as out-of-intent and the reply names the tracking issue in the PR body — the prose that best explains "I did not fix this" is the prose most likely to close it.

### +1 — 2026-08-21 · plow4-drop-browser-container · the inverse failure: a comma-list `Closes #A, #B, #C` closes ONLY #A, and the other ten stay silently open

**Change:** Add the other direction of the same mechanism, because it fails silently in the opposite way and the existing remedy already catches it: GitHub honors a closing keyword per *reference*, not per *list*. `Closes #1103, #1053, #979, …` in a squash-commit body closes **#1103 and nothing else** — every subsequent number is parsed as a bare cross-reference. The keyword has to be repeated (`Closes #1103, closes #1053, closes #979, …`) for each one. Concretely: a squash merge whose body named eleven issues closed exactly one; the remaining ten stayed open, and the PR read as though the whole backlog had been reconciled. The tell is cheap and is already this proposal's remedy — **re-check issue state right after merging** — so state it as bidirectional: verify both that nothing closed which shouldn't have, and that everything you claimed would close actually did. **Next instance:** any PR that retires a subsystem and sweeps a backlog of related issues in one merge — a dependency removal, a feature deletion, a deprecation.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged) — self-caught during the same session's `/cleanup` issue-reconciliation pass, and no operator round-trip was spent. Recorded because the silent failure is the expensive half: had the reconciliation pass not run, ten issues describing deleted code would have stayed open indefinitely, each one still reading as live work against a subsystem that no longer exists — the mirror image of this proposal's original "the tracking issue vanishes and the remaining work goes with it".


## Impact established near-zero → offer only subtractive options, never the additive "correct in every state" fix
**Change:** Once investigation establishes a defect's real-world effect is ~0 (nothing reads the artifact, no consumer, it self-heals), the only options that belong on the table are **remove the unused surface** or **leave it**. Don't rank an additive remedy — extra state, a restore branch, a guard — alongside them, and specifically don't justify one on "it preserves an operator affordance": an affordance with zero code readers and zero demonstrated use is the thing to delete, not a capability worth spending branches on. The capability-vs-code-shape carve-out in `CLAUDE.md` § Default to the Simplifying Option protects *real* runtime capability and user-visible reach, not a hypothetical convenience. The tell is catching yourself inventing a plausible user for the thing in order to justify the additive fix. Next instance: any repo where a reviewer/bot finding is triaged as cosmetic — a stale cache key nothing reads, a dead feature flag, an unconsumed log field — and the tempting remedy is to make it correct rather than to delete it. Distinct axis from the *Don't add a cleanup `rm` for leftovers the consumer ignores* proposal, which governs the safety of a delete you've already decided on; this one governs which options make the shortlist at triage time, before any verb is chosen — keep them separate rather than merging on the shared "subtractive default" phrasing.
**Why (autonomy):** Established that a dangling `runs-by-pr/<pr>/latest` symlink had zero code readers anywhere (repo, config corpus, live skills, cron, deploy host) — and then still led with a 5-LOC `PREV_LATEST` restore as the recommendation, on the grounds that it preserved a `tail -f` affordance. The operator redirected: near-zero impact means only complexity-reducing options belong on the table. The actual fix was deleting the symlink outright (plow-pbc/knightwatch-reviewer#197), which also retired the tracked follow-up (#196) with no code of its own, and collapsed a bug class that had eaten four of five review rounds. Pairing "impact is nil" with "so let's add LOC to make it correct in every state" is self-contradictory; naming that at triage time removes the redirect round-trip. Promoted from the `near-zero-impact-only-subtractive-options` feedback memory.

## [removes-handback] Explaining a finding located by a document's internal numbering → name the section and quote the line, never the positional label
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Delivering work` (or the reporting neighborhood): when reporting where a defect lives inside a structured document — a prompt, a YAML workflow, a config file, a spec — never identify it by its positional label (`step d`, `item 3`, `the second bullet`). Those labels are meaningful only to someone who already has the file open at that spot, and they are exactly the thing that renumbers. Instead: name the section, quote the offending line, and state the rule it encodes. The self-check is whether the sentence still locates the problem for a reader who has never opened the file. This composes with the no-step-ordinals lesson on the test side — a positional label is unstable as a *pin* and unusable as an *explanation*, for the same reason. Next instance: explaining why a CI job fails by citing "step 4" of a workflow YAML instead of naming the step and quoting its `run:` line; or citing "rule 2" of a linter config the reader has never seen.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — asked why two PRs' bot reviews lacked specialist/severity tags, I reported the cause as "step d says to skip the per-probe severity enumeration," citing a lettered sub-bullet nested inside one of three output modes in a 216-line prompt. The operator couldn't follow it and had to spend a full turn asking what step d was, adding that they thought there was only one kind of review. The unblock — that question forced me to lay out the three modes as a table and show the numbering collision, which is what made the finding actionable *and* surfaced the real answer (the modes were not DRY; the probe-rendering contract was physically nested inside one of them). The positional citation had actively concealed the structural problem: naming it "step d" made it sound like a line to change, when the finding was that the document had three modes whose numbered lists collided. Landed as plow-pbc/knightwatch-reviewer#199. (Session: 2026-07-30-kwr8-probe-contract-unconditional)

### +1 — 2026-08-27 · 2026-08-27-agent-mgr8-onboarding-runbook · the same failure applies to YOUR OWN report's numbering, not just a document you are describing
**Change:** Extend the rule from documents you cite to lists you write: a positional label is unresolvable across a message boundary too. When a report contains more than one list, never refer back to items by number in a later turn — restate the item. The reader is scanning a rendered transcript, not holding your message open with the numbering in view, and a second list in the same message makes "2–4" ambiguous even in principle.
**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — I closed a turn with a numbered list of three next steps followed by a separate bulleted list of housekeeping items, then offered to "do 2–4". The operator's whole next turn was asking what 2–4 meant. *The unblock* — that question; restating the five items as one labelled table with an owner column resolved it in a line, and that table is what the rest of the session ran on. Same defect as the parent — the label was meaningful only to someone holding the source at that spot — but the source here was my own previous message rather than a file, which is the harder case to notice because I *can* still see the numbering. Next instance: any multi-part status report where a follow-up says "let's do 1 and 3".

## [removes-handback] Merge-readiness leads with review status, not CI — never offer merge before a current-head bot review has landed and been addressed
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Branch Workflow` (beside the never-merge-without-authorization rule): CI-green + mergeable + your own self/subagent review is necessary but NOT sufficient for "merge-ready." Before presenting or recommending a merge, confirm a **current-head** bot review has landed AND its findings are resolved (applied / counter-proposed / declined-with-reason), and lead the readiness summary with that review status rather than with CI. A delayed or quota-blocked bot is not a reason to skip the verification round — when a fix resolves a `[blocking]` finding, the value is the bot verifying *the fix* on the new head; wait, or surface the delay and let the human decide, rather than merging on CI-green plus prior-rounds-addressed. Next instance: any repo with a review bot — a seed repo, plow, openseed — where CI goes green before the bot has run and the PR looks done.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — on a kwr PR I presented "merge now" while no bot review existed at all; the operator had to ask directly whether that PR had outstanding comments. The unblock — that question, which reframed merge-readiness around review status instead of CI. It recurred on the same PR: with the reviewer's own LLM quota exhausted for days, I again offered "merge now because the bot is down," and was overruled with "wait for one more review, then merge." Held correctly this session on plow-pbc/knightwatch-reviewer#199 (waited three review rounds to convergence, then handed the merge decision back rather than taking it), which is what makes the rule worth stating in the corpus rather than only in one project's memory. Promoted from the `dont-offer-merge-before-bot-review-lands` feedback memory. (Session: 2026-07-30-kwr8-probe-contract-unconditional)

## [removes-handback] Never hand-fix a generative pipeline's committed output — fix the generator, or record the defect; and never pin the fix
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` (companion to the altitude-check rule about classifying a generated diff): when a reviewer flags defects in artifacts a generator produced and committed — LLM-extracted pages, codegen output, scraped datasets, recorded fixtures — do **not** edit the artifact. The committed output *is* the measurement of how well the generator works; hand-correcting it makes the system look better than it is and removes the owner's ability to assess it independently. Route each finding to one of three places: (a) the generator's **contract** — prompt, spec, schema — so the next run stops producing it; (b) a **gate** that should have caught it and didn't (fix the validator, let it block); (c) an **issue**, as evaluation data. A finding that *looks* like bad data is often (b): a page publishing a physical key's location is a missing scanner pattern, not a sentence to reword — the extraction was faithful. **And never pin the correction in a test.** A regression row asserting your hand-written phrasing is a ratchet: a faithful regeneration now fails CI, so honest output reads as a regression and the edit is forced to persist — inverting what the test is for. Wiring *around* generated content (manifests, index/nav links, set-relation invariants) is bookkeeping the generator does not author; that stays hand-fixable and is worth testing, because prose rewrites cannot satisfy it.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — over roughly a dozen commits I hand-corrected fact-quality defects a review bot found in 26 LLM-compiled operations pages (contradictory grill fuel, parking capacity, coffee stock, snowshoe counts), and pinned eight of them in a parametrized regression test. Every individual finding was real, which is exactly why the category error was invisible: each fix looked correct. The user interrupted a tool call to stop it — the point being that hand-fixing makes the memory system appear to function better than it actually does, and they wanted to assess its accuracy independently. unblock — reverting all page edits to raw extractor output and deleting the regression rows, then re-routing the same findings: the extraction contract gained merge-before-append and resolve-don't-average rules, the commit-gate scanner gained a physical-key-location pattern, and the rest were filed as issues. The reviewer then explicitly agreed and stopped proposing page edits. Next instance: any repo where a codegen step, scraper, or snapshot fixture writes checked-in artifacts and review flags defects in them — the reflex to "just fix the file" is the same, and so is the damage to the signal. Promoted from the `dont-hand-fix-generated-output` feedback memory.

### +1 — the discriminator is what DETECTING it took, not which category the file is in

**Change:** Sharpens the parent's boundary. The parent splits by category — content is the generator's, wiring/bookkeeping is hand-fixable — which leaves the common middle case unresolved: damage *inside* the content that the generator plainly did not intend. Better test: **did establishing the defect require reading the content and judging meaning?** If no — a citation written into the page body instead of its frontmatter list, a URL retyped with a truncated scheme, a value the raw input carries verbatim — it is mechanical restoration of what the pipeline meant to write, it is provable without judgement, and repairing it is legitimate *provided the generator-side fix lands with it* so the next run doesn't redo the damage. If yes — this conversation doesn't support that claim — it is fact-quality: route it upstream, however small the edit looks. Rider for two-directional invariants: when a bot proposes fixing one side of a both-ways contract (drop the manifest record so it matches the page), doing so re-opens the disagreement the other side was just repaired to close — move both sides or neither.
**Why (autonomy):** operator directive, issued pre-emptively rather than as a stop — asked to babysit two PRs to convergence, with the standing instruction that findings on generated files get fixed via the generator if real, never patched in the artifact. It arrived one round before the reviewer filed a `[blocking]` probe on exactly that seam, and the rule decided the reply: a cited conversation that doesn't support the page's fact required *reading the transcript* to establish, so it was declined and filed upstream as an issue asking the extraction contract for the rule it lacked — a citation is evidence, not attendance. The same session's earlier repair sat on the other side of the same line and was right to: 38 misplaced citations and 392 truncated URL schemes, each provable against the manifest and the raw inputs with no content judgement, landed as a script whose every move was derived rather than authored. Both halves in one session are what produced the discriminator. Next instance: a generated OpenAPI client, protobuf stub, or recorded snapshot where review flags a defect — ask what it took to *find* it before deciding whether the artifact or the spec is where the fix goes. Promoted from the `fix-the-generator-not-the-generated-file` feedback memory. (Session: 2026-08-04-str7-vault-citation-repair)

### +1 — 2026-09-10 · agent-mgr8-course-qa-cloud-alignment · the same rule outside codegen: a wrong file/permission/value on this machine is an issue against whatever WROTE it

**Change:** The parent covers artifacts a generator committed. The producer-not-artifact rule generalizes to anything a tool writes onto a machine — a file's permissions, a dotenv key, a config value, a directory layout. Before offering to repair it, ask what produced it; if a tool did, read that tool's code to confirm the defect is the producer's rather than local environment (a umask, an operator's earlier edit), then file the issue naming the offending code path. Offer the local correction only as an explicit stopgap the operator asks for, and say plainly it does not fix the cause. Reading the producer first is load-bearing in both directions: on this occasion it dissolved the bug entirely — the "world-writable credential" was a symlink, and I had read the link's mode instead of the target's (`stat -c %a` → 777, `stat -Lc %a` → 600).
**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — I offered to `chmod` a credential file in place, treating a fleet tool's output as a local mess to tidy. *Prior authority* — the producing tool's source was on this machine and readable. *The unblock* — the operator: is this a bugfix? let's not chmod but file the issue upstream. A local correction fixes one machine, hides the defect, and the next run of the same tool recreates it everywhere. **Next instance:** any host-hygiene finding — a stray file, a wrong owner, a duplicated dotenv key — where a provisioning tool, installer, or deploy script is the thing that wrote it.

### +1 — 2026-08-01 · str-wiki-regeneration · the PROOF that a generator fix is durable is regenerating from it, not the edited output

**Change:** after fixing the generator, archive (don't delete) the current output, regenerate, and diff old against new; report the fix durable only when the regenerated output is right with no hand-edit.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — a hand-fix of LLM-compiled wiki pages read as a fix that worked while the generator stayed free to reproduce the defect. Prior authority — the fix-the-generator rule above already applied. Unblock — the operator asked for the regeneration; it was the only evidence separating a durable fix from a patch.
**Next instance:** a codegen template (OpenAPI client, ORM models) emits a wrong type: fix the template, regenerate, diff — never hand-patch the emitted file.

## Declare the PR's intent and expected complexity up front, then check the diff against it every review round
**Change:** Add to `babysit-pr` (and `PR_LIFECYCLE.md § Open`): a PR body opens by naming its **business intent and expected complexity** — the operator's phrasing: "We intended to create human-in-the-loop polling & reply logic, expected to write ~100 LOC given it's pre-PMF but requires several conditionals." `/babysit-pr` then re-runs `git diff --stat origin/main...HEAD` against that declared number **every round**, not once at hand-off, and reports the delta in the round's reply. Two specifics that make the check bite: count **prose** — README, docstrings, inline comments — and tests, not just executable code, since a review loop inflates prose specifically (the cheapest way to close a probe is to write the justification into the artifact rather than the reply); and treat a single doc section larger than the code it documents, or a prose:code ratio above ~0.5:1 in a source file, as the tell. Answer probes **in the PR thread**, which is the durable record and costs the reader nothing. Next instance: any repo where the user names a size ("just logging", "~100 lines") and the PR then enters a bot-review loop.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — on the str3 Hostex poller the operator interrupted with surprise at the PR reading +917 when the actual program was 88 lines, right at the size he expected. The unblock — that interruption, which forced a re-scope: one README section had reached 242 lines (larger than the program it documented, 3.5x the next-biggest section in the file), the script carried 130 lines of comment for 88 of code, and tests hit 4.3x prod against a 2x red flag. Every addition answered a real review probe and was individually defensible; nobody was tracking the total across ~25 rounds. Untagged rather than [removes-handback]: the PR would have landed either way — the operator's interjection changed its size, not whether it shipped — but a declared expectation makes the overshoot visible at the round it happens instead of at hand-off, and turns the target into a commitment a reviewer can check rather than something only the author holds. Requested explicitly by the operator to be raised at cleanup. Promoted from the `babysit-pr-should-track-diff-vs-declared-intent` and `loc-ledger-counts-prose-not-just-code` memories. (Session: 2026-07-31-str3-hostex-poller)
### +1 — 2026-08-01 · 2026-08-01-str9-owners-group-approval · answer "is scope increasing?" with a code/tests/docs SPLIT, not a total
**Change:** Sharpen the reporting half: when the human challenges size, the useful artifact is the **three-way split** (code / tests / docs), not the total — because it is the only form that separates "scope grew" from "one contract is restated in many documents". State the split *up front* on any change to a stated contract, where the prose share is structurally dominant rather than incidentally so.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — mid-PR the operator asked "why is this pr increasing loc? is scope increasing?" on `srosro/sams-str-hermes-agent#62`. The unblock — computing the split: net +110 = **+21 code, +14 tests, +75 docs**, which answered the real question (scope had not grown; the approval rule is restated in ~8 places, three of them functional copies the runtime reads and cannot be collapsed). A bare "+110" could not have answered it either way. Same repo and same week as the parent's str3 instance, arrived at independently — this class recurs here because the repo deliberately states its contracts in many voices. Untagged for the same reason the parent is: the PR would have landed regardless; declaring the split up front removes the round-trip, not the merge.

## An unknown about a system you don't own is a MEASUREMENT request, not a case to tolerate — one read-only probe beats machinery correct under either answer
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` (as the companion to the load-bearing-assumption bullet): when a finding or design turns on how a system you don't own actually behaves — a dependency's parser, a base image's env loader, a CLI flag's semantics — settle it with one read-only probe against the real thing *before* the next commit. Do **not** encode a hedge that stays correct under either answer, and do not write the uncertainty into prose. The probe is nearly always cheap and safe: a throwaway container, a temp fixture, a scratch repo — never a mutation of live config. If a probe is genuinely impossible, state the assumption in one line and pick a side; do not build the fork. Two tells you are already in the failure mode: (a) you are adding a verdict/branch/state that exists *only* because you don't know something, and (b) you are arguing in a review reply about what is *likely* true of someone else's code. Next instance: any repo, any dependency — "does this library strip X?", "does this flag do Y?", "does the runtime reload Z?"
**Why (autonomy):** self-recovered (so untagged, per the tag-bar rule), but the most expensive single pattern measured in this repo. On `srosro/sams-str-hermes-agent#43`, **13 of 20 commits** built an `AMBIGUOUS` machinery — a dual-reading parser, culprit discovery, a key-list invariant, an internal-error arm — whose entire purpose was to stay correct whether or not the gateway's dotenv loader stripped inline comments. All 13 were deleted in the final commit (script 85→33 lines, tests 144→65). The local reviewer had **named the exact probe two rounds before I started building** ("verify once against the deployed gateway"); I classified the question as unknowable instead of unmeasured and never ran it. Running it during the retro took ~20 seconds and returned an answer that was *neither* branch I had hedged: the loader strips `KEY=v  # c` but keeps `KEY=v#c` — which also refuted a later review finding that a `#` anywhere could only be a comment. The same error recurred inside the retro itself: I described a tool's behavior from its config comment and the operator's question ("how does it decide when to run a review if it's not per commit?") forced the measurement, which showed the mode changed review *scope* but not *frequency* — the opposite of the recommendation I had just given. Promoted from the `measure-external-behavior-dont-hedge-it` feedback memory.

### +1 — the unmeasured quantity can be a RATE, not a behavior, and the system can be one you own

**Change:** Extends the parent's trigger. There the unknown was *how a system you don't own behaves*; here the behavior was fully known and correctly reasoned, and the unmeasured quantity was *how often it actually happens*. Same tell — machinery that exists only because you never ran a query — and the same remedy: before adding a guard, test, or fence for a failure mode, query whatever production record exists for its real frequency. "The mechanism is real" is a different claim from "this happens", and only the second one sizes the fix. Two riders: separate the populations before quoting a rate (how often the bad value reaches a *decision* vs how often it is *written at all* are different numbers, and a fix living in the second isn't justified by the first), and price the fix separately from the fence — closing the source is often one line where fencing it is dozens.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — handed back two merge-ready PRs totalling +88 LOC (a one-line prompt constraint plus two self-testing regression fences across two repos) for a phantom severity value in a generated file. unblock — the operator asked whether it was a real issue, whether we could just live with it, and whether fixing it was over-engineering. One query against the reviewer's own 53,973-run store answered all three: the bad value had appeared once in ~190,000 severity emissions and had never reached a verdict. The fences came out and the pair shipped at 4 lines. The data sat on a host I own the entire time; several review rounds all tightening *the same guard* was the tell I kept misreading as progress. (Session: 2026-08-03-claude-config-150-medium-verdict-drift)

### +1 — a probe that measures an adjacent property manufactures false confidence; read the vendor's docs first, since they tell you WHICH property to measure
I did run the probe this proposal asks for, and it is what got me into trouble: needing to know whether an account-level websocket ticket would *deliver* messages for chats the gateway never subscribed to, I confirmed that `POST /v1/ws/ticket` accepted an empty body, that the returned ticket opened a socket, and that the socket stayed up across a 75-second sample. All true, none of it the question. I wrote "delivery unverified" in the PR, shipped it, and deployed — and the socket turned out to deliver a frame carrying no type and no message, so the gateway went deaf on **every** chat including the operator's own DM. The unblock was the operator asking whether one of two linked docs pages answered it; the API reference states the ticket endpoint takes `{"chat_id": …}` and documents no account-level mode at all. So the refinement: before probing an external contract, **read its documentation** — that is what tells you which property is load-bearing, and it is cheaper than the probe. And when you do probe, make it exercise the behaviour you will depend on end to end (a message arriving), not the nearest observable (a connection opening); a handshake succeeding is `200 OK`, not proof of semantics. **Next instance:** confirming a queue's dead-letter behaviour by observing that publishes are accepted — read the broker's redelivery docs and then actually fail a consumer, rather than inferring from the happy path.

## [removes-handback] Trimming defensive machinery can delete the original bug's coverage with it — re-run the first mutation after the cut
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Tests` (companion to "Tests must fail loudly"): when a review loop drives you to *delete* accreted machinery — guards, branches, a fake's state model — the deletion is not done when the suite goes green. Re-run the mutation for the **defect the PR was opened to fix**, not just for the code you removed. Accreted machinery frequently carries the original defect's coverage as a side effect, so cutting it can leave a green suite that no longer catches the bug the PR exists for. Same check applies to the inverse (§ Concise Code's stop-iterating rule tells you *to* cut; this is what "verify" means afterwards). Next instance: any repo where a small fix accretes guards across bot-review rounds and is then trimmed back — re-mutate the first commit's defect before pushing the trim.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — on `srosro/sams-str-hermes-agent#47` I fired an `AskUserQuestion` on scope after a two-bug shell fix grew 48 → 129 lines across four review rounds, all of them flaws in machinery distinguishing cases that do not exist at a one-operator operating point. unblock — the operator picked "trim to the observed bugs", which was right. But the trim silently removed the recorded-invocation capture, so the fake answered every create with a fixed listing: **both original defects — a one-shot schedule and a missing prompt — became unpinned while the suite stayed green.** Caught only by re-running the two mutations from the opening commit. Later rounds hardened the same lesson from the other side: deleting a guard also deleted the only assertion that its user-facing message printed, and four consecutive commits churned one message pair before the fix moved to a table-wide invariant. (Session: 2026-07-31-str3-enable-script-cron-contract)

### +1 — the trim came from a reviewer probe whose premise was true but incomplete, and the green suite was the false comfort
A green suite after the cut is not evidence the coverage survived: the deleted case may never have had a test at all. On `plow-pbc/plow#1176` (audit classifier: recognize a `{"type":"tool_error"}` payload printed to stdout), the bot filed a `[low] [simplification]` — scan only the *last* line, not every line, since the producer logs the payload and exits. Its premise checked out against the producer's own source, I applied it, and **all 48 cases still passed**, because none of them covered the case the trim dropped. The local per-commit reviewer then caught what neither of us had: the producing script is not the last writer to that string — a long-output run gets a truncation footer appended *after* the payload, confirmed on real hook payloads in a captured `audit-events.jsonl`. Under last-line-only the footer is the last line, the parse fails, and a failed call audits as success — the exact defect the PR existed to fix, on the noisiest runs. Reverted, documented the second writer inline, and added the missing case so the trim can't be re-proposed blind. Generalizes the parent rule to *reviewer-driven* trims: when a probe justifies narrowing a check by citing a producer's contract, ask who else writes to the same artifact before accepting it, and treat an unchanged green suite as an untested claim rather than a pass. (Session: 2026-08-04-plow-stranded-roots)


## Never offer an option you haven't verified is possible — the user will pick that one
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps` (the investigate-before-you-consult neighborhood): every option in a recommendation menu must already be verified as *possible* against the real system — not inferred from a plausible-looking config surface, CLI flag, or API. If you can't verify one before writing it up, verify it first or leave it out and say what you'd need to check. Run the command that proves it (`--help`, a sandboxed `set`, a schema check) — and test in a throwaway `HOME=`/config dir so the user's real state is never touched.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged, self-recovered): closed an investigation with two remedies and flagged the second as "the DRYer, fleet-wide one" without checking it existed. The user picked exactly that one. It didn't exist — the tool hard-rejects that key outside a per-repo file — so the turn went to re-investigation instead of execution. Sam reliably picks the DRYest/simplest option in a menu, which makes an unverified entry the *most* likely one to be chosen.

### +1 — a single offered follow-up is a menu of one; verify its premise before floating it, not after they say yes

**Change:** Extends the parent from *menu options* to any offered next step, including a lone "want me to X?" — the offer is a claim that X is possible and sound, so it carries the same verification burden as a recommendation. Applies hardest to changes in a *shared* or *other-repo* surface, where "is this safe here?" also means "is it safe for every other consumer?" Verify before floating it; if you can't, say what you'd need to check rather than offering the unverified shape.

**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged, self-recovered) — closing out a fix, I offered to teach the shared review bot to render exit code 2 as "setup failed", on the unchecked assumption that 2 is a portable setup-failure signal. Sam said "yes that's fine". It isn't portable: `tsc` exits 2 when it emits despite diagnostics (hit in that same session), and make/pytest/argparse use 2 for their own failures — so the change would have relabeled genuine test failures as "tests not run" across every repo the bot reviews. The turn went to retracting an authorized change instead of making it. Same shape as the parent, one rung earlier: the parent's menu entry was unverified, mine was the whole offer. (Session: 2026-07-31-tkmx-client8-test-exit-codes)

## Check whose threat model applies before absorbing a reviewer's security finding
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md § Anti-Bloat` (or the Broken-Glass neighborhood): a security-shaped finding still has to pass the YAGNI test. Name the attacker for *that specific component* before adding the guard; if the answer is "the person running it, on their own machine, against their own commits", there is no attacker and the guard is pure cost. Two reviewers over the same seam can hold genuinely different threat models — apply the guard only where the model holds.
**Why (autonomy):** real bug-class fence. Security findings feel non-declinable, so they slip past the anti-bloat posture that would catch an equivalent defensive guard — and the cost is everything the guard then requires. Absorbing one finding about branch self-modification (real for a reviewer of *other people's* PRs, meaningless for one reviewing your own local commits) manufactured a blocking stale-tracking-ref bug, a second blocking gap in a sibling repo, a manual post-merge step nothing detected, and a cross-repo merge-order dance. Deleting the guard removed all four.

### +1 — 2026-08-04 · memeval-judge-runbook-signet · measure the reachable audience before accepting "this leaks to every clone"
**Change:** Extend "name the attacker" with the cheap measurement that answers it for a *repo-scoped* exposure finding: query the actual reach — `gh api repos/<o>/<r>/collaborators`, `forks_count`, `private` — before accepting a reviewer's framing or escalating the remedy to the human. Reviewers argue from worst-case defaults because they cannot see the access list. When the reachable audience turns out to be the data's own owner, the finding has no audience and the remedy should be weighed against that, not against "every clone". Also weigh whether the prescribed remedy actually closes what it targets: for git history, a rewrite + force-push only cleans future fetches — the host keeps orphaned commits and PR views until support purges them — so a squash-merge with `--delete-branch` can close the same hole with no destructive operation.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — two review rounds framed a tracked-data finding as exposing third parties' contact and medical details "to every clone of the repository", and I fired an `AskUserQuestion` asking how the owner wanted the branch history handled. unblock — the operator picked the non-destructive path, and the fact that settled it was one command away the whole time: the repo had exactly one collaborator (the data's owner) and zero forks, so the disclosure had no audience and the destructive remedy was never warranted. Measuring reach first would have made the call without the round-trip.

### +1 — 2026-08-28 · latch9-adversarial-default · measure the guarded POPULATION before absorbing a migration/compat guard
**Change:** Extend "name the attacker" / "measure the reachable audience" to existing-state guards: when a reviewer proposes a grandfather/migration/compat branch for a hypothesized legacy-state class ("homes whose settings predate field X"), query the authoritative surface for whether that class is inhabited — at fleet scale that is a handful of SSH one-liners reading presence-booleans (`jq 'has("field")'`, never values) — before applying. An empty population makes the guard a Broken-Glass decline with the fleet evidence as the recorded ruling; an inhabited one makes it a real fix. A bot's `[blocking]` severity is a claim about consequence, not evidence the population exists.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer with a real round-trip. On plow-pbc/latch#233 (flip the default approval mode), knightwatch flagged a `[blocking]` consent regression for legacy settings files and I absorbed a grandfather branch + test + probe follow-up (~25 LOC over two review rounds). The PR converged carrying it; the operator's challenge ("100 loc?? are there fallbacks?") triggered the 3-command fleet check that showed every signed-in install already stored the field explicitly — the guard protected nobody, and the revert round + re-review were pure rework. Measuring first would have made it a decline at round 4 with zero added LOC.

## A stated one-sentence goal is a live filter on what to work on next, not context to acknowledge once

    ### +1 — 2026-09-10-agent-mgr7-str-cloud-alignment · promoted from a project `feedback` memory: the rule holds for in-flight mentions too
    **Change:** Confirms the rule's edge: it applies to a PR that is *still open and mid-review*, not only to a finished hand-off. A "still converging" status line the operator may act on carries the raw URL just as a merge report does.
    **Why (autonomy):** Stop — the operator asked for the PR URL after a status update that referenced the PR by number alone. Prior authority — the corpus rule already says every turn-final mention carries the raw URL. Unblock — the operator asking for the link.
    **Next instance:** any multi-round review loop where intermediate rounds get reported — each round's report is turn-final for the operator reading it.

## [removes-handback] A stated one-sentence goal is a live filter on what to work on next, not context to acknowledge once
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps`: when the operator states a short-term goal, re-check each new PR or review round against it *before* starting — name which step of the goal it advances, and say so plainly when the answer is "none directly". A repeated "what is our goal?" is never a quiz; it is the operator observing drift, and the correct response is a one-sentence restatement plus an honest admission, not a status table that buries the goal under progress. Next instance: any multi-day autonomous run where the operator opened with a single-sentence objective.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged, per the tag-bar rule) — the operator opened with "get one real guest message all the way through the loop: drafted from the wiki, texted to Sam, approved by reply, sent to the guest", then watched an entire session go into a configuration-backup PR that was supporting infrastructure. The review loop was locally productive every round, which is exactly what makes this drift invisible from inside. The operator asked "do you see our goal for this project?" and then simply "what is our goal?" — twice, because the first answer was a progress summary rather than an admission. Promoted from the `anchor-work-to-the-stated-goal` feedback memory.

### +1 — 2026-09-10 · agent-mgr8-course-qa-cloud-alignment · every answer restates the goal and hands over steps that stand alone

**Change:** The parent fires when the operator *asks* about the goal. Extend it to the default shape of every answer on a long-running task: open with the goal in one line ("this gets X doing Y"), then separate **what I did** from **what you do**, the operator's part as numbered, copy-pasteable commands with what success looks like. Name files, PR numbers and hosts explicitly — never "the PR" or "that host". An answer written as though the thread is fresh in the reader's head is an answer they must re-read the thread to use. Detail is not the problem; unanchored detail is.
**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — across a multi-hour migration I reported findings and review rounds accurately every turn, and the operator still had to reconstruct what to actually do, and why it mattered, from earlier messages. *Prior authority* — `CLAUDE.md § Answer Shape` already required leading with the result and naming the ask; what was missing was re-anchoring to the goal and rendering the operator's part as steps. *The unblock* — an explicit mid-task format demand: always give concise answers with clear actionable steps followable without looking back through the history, and always tie the steps to the high-level goals. A format demand mid-task is a hand-back: every prior answer had to be re-read to be used. **Next instance:** any multi-session migration or incident where the operator dips in and out between long autonomous stretches — a fleet cutover, a multi-PR refactor, an overnight run they read at breakfast.

## Rank an external best-practice list against your own data before recommending — don't inherit the doc's emphasis order
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`: after researching an authoritative external source (vendor docs, a spec), do not carry its ordering into your recommendation. Measure which of its levers your own data actually supports and lead with that one, even when the source names a different item first. Run the discriminating query before writing the recommendation.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged): recommended a "nit volume cap" as the top fix for PR review churn because the vendor's docs list it first. The user pushed back that nits get fixed and merged, so they can't be what fails to terminate. Measuring the actual findings showed Mediums recurring on the *same file* 20–40 times across rounds, never converging — the cap would have suppressed 107 of 157 findings and left every one that drove the churn. The data was already in hand; the error was ranking by the doc instead of by it.

## A PR that changes the review rules is reviewed under the OLD rules — decline what it exists to prevent
**Change:** Add to `REVIEW_PRACTICES.md` (bot-findings triage): when the change under review is a change to the review system itself — reviewer policy, severity calibration, operating-point config — the reviewers grading it are still running the previous configuration and do not know the goal the PR encodes. Hold the line by default: fix real bugs and contradictions in the new rules (reviewers are good at finding those), but decline scope-increasing findings with a one-line citation of the operating point being installed, and say plainly that the reviewer is running the pre-change config. Watch the diff stat every round — a review-system PR that grows is failing at its own thesis — and prefer merging sooner over chasing a clean round, since the rules only pay off once live.
**Why (autonomy):** explicit operator directive, given preemptively while asking for a babysit run across the migration PRs: the reviewers don't understand the business goal, and that gap is precisely what the change fixes. Without the rule the default is to absorb, which inflates the very PR meant to stop the inflation and delays the fix that would have prevented the round.

## Define an autonomous run's goal by observable end-state plus its proof surface, not by a list of steps

**Change:** When the operator hands off a long autonomous run (overnight, `/goal`, a sleep-time mandate), write the goal as a numbered list of **end-state assertions, each paired with the command or surface that proves it** — "PR merged AND `git show origin/main:<binary>` resolves", "container Up AND started after the restore", "one gateway per home, proven by this `docker inspect | uniq -d` one-liner" — never as the steps to execute. Add three things a step list cannot carry: an explicit NOT-in-scope list, the bounds that must not be crossed, and the stop-and-report conditions. State plainly which criteria cannot be reached autonomously rather than dropping them; a gate reported `unverified` with evidence is correct, reporting the diagnostics around it as success is not.

**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged — no round-trip was lost), promoted from a captured `feedback` memory in this project's store. The operator asked for a handoff goal and specified its shape: focus on the external definition of done, e.g. the container is working and validated with X, the reviewer is converged. Writing it that way is what made a ~5h unattended run auditable — each criterion carried its own proof command, so "done" was checkable by the operator without reading the transcript, and the run could report partial progress precisely (criterion 3 half-done: one PR merged, one in review) instead of as prose. It also did real work during the run: the criterion that named a *real message* as the gate is what stopped four green diagnostics from being reported as a pass, and the one-gateway-per-home criterion shipped as a runnable one-liner caught its own baseline before the deploy touched anything. A step list would have been fully executed and still left the outcome unverified. **Next instance:** any long unattended run in a different repo — a migration, a fleet sweep, a deploy watch — where the operator is away and needs to check the result rather than the process. (Session: 2026-08-26 · agent-mgr3-str-cutover)

  ### +1 — 2026-10-06 · kwr1-status-page · name the artifact's spirit, not just its checks
  **Change (extends):** A definition of done has three parts: the qualities the code must have (converged, DRY, no YAGNI or scope creep, the stated data-model limit), what the delivered artifact shows, and the *spirit* it serves ("a teammate opens it and in 30s knows whether anything needs them"). Keep only hard boundaries and granted authority besides; the plan owns the steps. The spirit is what lets the run judge whether the result is any good, and in this run it decided four review rounds (which reds are noise).
  **Why (autonomy):** Stop — asked for a `/goal` before an overnight run, I drafted a step list; the operator had to come back and ask for outcomes plus spirit. Prior authority — this parent proposal already said end-state, not steps. Unblock — the operator spelling out the code qualities, the URL's contents and its spirit.
  **Next instance:** writing the `/goal` for an overnight migration or deploy in plow or latch, where the artifact is a working endpoint or app rather than a page.

## Fork + "add a PR" usually means the PR belongs ON the fork — that's what routes it to your own reviewer
**Change:** Add to `PR_LIFECYCLE.md` (or `CLAUDE.md § Branch Workflow`): when a task pairs "fork this repo to my account" with "open a PR", open the PR **within the fork** (`<user>/<repo>`, base its own `main`) rather than only upstream. Forking is unnecessary for a one-off patch, so an explicit fork step usually means review routing: the org-scoped review fleet polls whole orgs from its own tracked-org config, so a PR filed against a third-party upstream is invisible to it while the identical branch on the fork gets reviewed. Before asserting which reviewer will or won't see a PR, read that tracked-org/repo config — don't infer from the repo name. When both destinations are plausible, state which reviewer sees which PR instead of silently picking one.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged), but it cost a full round-trip and a duplicate PR. I read "fork it, then add the PR" as staging for an upstream contribution and opened the PR against the third-party upstream, then reported — accurately, after checking the config — that the reviewer would not review it and offered adding the repo to the tracked list as a fix. The unblock was the user pointing out the fork *was* the routing mechanism; opening the same branch as a PR within the fork took one command and needed no config change. The reviewer's coverage list was readable the whole time; I only consulted it to explain the miss, not to choose the destination.

  ### +1 — 2026-09-24 · plow6-watson-upstream · base the fork's staging PR on a mirror of upstream's main, and clean up in dependency order
  **Change (extends):** The parent routes the PR to the fork; extend it to the fork's whole lifecycle when the fork is a **staging ground** for an upstream contribution. (a) Base the staging PR on a branch mirroring `upstream/main` (`git push origin upstream/main:refs/heads/upstream-base`), not the fork's own `main` — against the fork's `main` the diff shows spurious removals of your own earlier additions. (b) Keep the fork's `main` fast-forwarded to upstream's so every branch is upstream-based by construction. (c) Converge on the fork, then push the same head upstream and verify both report identical additions/deletions before un-drafting. (d) Clean up in dependency order: the upstream PR's head branch must survive until it merges or closes, and archiving a fork freezes it and can strand an open upstream PR — archiving also does not make a fork private, since a fork never can be.
  **Why (autonomy):** Stop — I opened an upstream PR from a hand-ported branch no reviewer had seen, and later proposed archiving the fork while its branch was the head of a live upstream PR. Prior authority — the operator had already said to converge locally first and to clean up "without breaking anything". Unblock — the operator's correction that PRs go to the fork first, reviewed, *then* upstream.
  **Next instance:** contributing a fix to any third-party repo through a personal fork — a CLI tool, a plugin, an SDK — where the fork exists only to get the review fleet's eyes on it first.

  ### +1 — 2026-10-01 · plow8-feedback-drain · operator states the fork-first flow as a standing default
  **Change (extends):** Treat fork-first as the default for ANY third-party contribution, not only when the operator says "fork": PR on `srosro/<repo>`, `/babysit-pr` there, and only at convergence `gh pr create -R <owner>/<repo> --head srosro:<branch>`; then close the fork PR with a link so the inactivity re-review doesn't spend quota on it.
  **Why (autonomy):** Stop — I asked for consent to open REVIEW.md PRs on two collaborator repos without a destination plan. Prior authority — the parent proposal and the review fleet's whole-org coverage of `srosro`. Unblock — the operator spelling out "fork first, babysit, then open upstream".
  **Next instance:** a docs fix to an upstream SDK or CLI the operator doesn't own, where the fork PR gets the fleet's review and upstream gets one clean PR.

## [removes-handback] No local toolchain for the repo you're changing → provision one on a fleet build host, don't hand-roll a sync loop per verification
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Which machine you're on`: when a repo's toolchain (Go, Rust, a JDK, a language runtime) is absent from the machine you're on, treat "where does this build?" as a one-time provisioning decision, not a per-command one. Install the toolchain user-level on a beefier fleet host (`~/.local/…`, no sudo), and pin down the sync-and-run loop once — a single `rsync` + `ssh` invocation with the PATH exported — instead of re-deriving it each round. This is the same routing the memory-constrained-host rule already prescribes for heavy loads; the trigger here is *absence* of the toolchain rather than scarcity of RAM, and the answer is the same host map.
**Why (autonomy):** ergonomics, ~10 min/session on any repo outside the usual stack. No Go existed on any fleet host, so verifying a Go PR meant installing a toolchain and then hand-writing the same `rsync --delete … && ssh … 'export PATH=…; go test'` 8 times across review rounds, each one a fresh chance to omit an exclude or a PATH entry. Nothing blocked and the user never had to intervene — the cost was entirely in repeated setup that a named loop would have absorbed. Worth checking whether this belongs as a small skill rather than a bullet: the mechanical half (claim host → install toolchain → sync → run gate → report summary line) is identical every time.

  ### +1 — 2026-08-14 · plow1271-transparent-flatten · the same widening, arriving from the CI-gate side rather than the build side
  **Change:** Extend the parent from "where does this build?" to "where does this **verify**?" — the same one-time host decision, triggered by a *gate lane* you can't run rather than a toolchain you can't compile with. A CI lane that dies locally on a missing tool is not a lane you may report unverified: route it to the fleet host first, and only ticket it (per the proposal titled `A valid finding you can't validate on this host → ticket it, never untested, never dropped`) when no reachable host can run it either. Worth stating because the failure looks different from the parent's: there is no "I need a toolchain" moment to prompt the provisioning decision, just one recipe step erroring mid-run, which reads as a property of the gate rather than of the machine.
  **Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged) — no operator round-trip, which is itself the finding: nobody had to intervene because I never surfaced it as a blocker, I just accepted it. plow-pbc/plow#1271's `just test-fast` died at `_ensure-dbs` with `docker: command not found`, so the `api` lane went unrun and the PR body plus three chat summaries all carried "not run locally; CI covers it." I had SSH-confirmed `wakeup` reachable twice in that same session (arming the babysit Monitor) and still never considered running the gate there. Distinct from the proposal titled `` [removes-handback] Docker daemon down at a test/hook gate → start it and wait, never `--no-verify` ``: you cannot start a daemon that isn't installed, so the remedy is a different host, not a retry. Next instance: any repo whose test gate needs a tool absent from the current machine — a simulator, a GPU, a container runtime.

  ### +1 — 2026-09-19 · latch2-gatekeeper-onboarding · a real-app (Electron) check was about to be handed back as "unverified" while a reachable fleet Mac could run it
  **Change:** Apply the same "where does this verify?" widening to runtime checks. Before a hand-off or PR body lists a real-app or device check as "unverified — needs a test machine", enumerate fleet hosts from the `tailscale-ssh` map that have the runtime (macOS plus Xcode and Electron, for a desktop app). ## [removes-handback] Don't harden a code path that has never executed once — ship the loop, then let real runs name the failures

If it has not, decline the fix, record it as an issue so the deferral is on the record rather than re-litigated each review round, and prioritise getting the thing running. Revisit once real runs produce real failures. The exception is a check that catches *silently broken data* — those stay in scope even on an unexercised path, because they are what makes the first real runs trustworthy.

## Deferring work to a schedule: pick the scheduler by whether the task needs LOCAL reach — cloud routines can't see your fleet
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Which machine you're on: when the user asks to defer or repeat work ("do this at 4am", "check every hour"), choose the scheduler by *where the work has to run*, and say which you picked and why. A **cloud routine** (`/schedule` → `RemoteTrigger`) runs in Anthropic's cloud on a fresh checkout: no SSH, no Tailscale, no local daemons, no `~/.hermes`-style host state — so any task whose steps touch a fleet host, a container, or a private network **cannot** run there, and will fire and fail rather than not fire. A **session-local job** (`CronCreate`) runs inside the current session with its full environment and network reach, but is in-memory and **dies when the session ends** — so it needs the user warned to leave the session open. Neither is a default: cloud for self-contained repo work, session-local for anything host-touching, and state the tradeoff at scheduling time rather than after it silently no-ops.
**Why (autonomy):** self-caught near-miss, untagged (no hand-back — see "The [removes-handback] tag requires a BLOCKED stop"). 2026-08-01 · str7: asked to start a deploy at 4am, I invoked the `/schedule` skill; every step of the task was `ssh <user>@wakeup` + `docker exec`, which a cloud routine cannot do. Caught only because the skill's setup notes spell out that it spawns an isolated cloud session — the trigger phrase ("set an alarm to work at 4am") gives no hint that the two schedulers differ in reach. Switched to `CronCreate` and warned about the session-lifetime caveat; the run fired correctly. The failure mode this prevents is the quiet one: a routine that exists, fires on time, and fails at its first command while the user believes the work is scheduled.

## An installer/check's "X is not on PATH / not found" warning describes ITS OWN shell, not the user's — re-verify in a login shell before reporting a host defect
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` (as the mirror of the existing scheduled-job bullet): when a script you ran over non-interactive `ssh`, in CI, or inside a hook emits an environment finding *about the user's machine* — "not on PATH", "command not found", missing alias, unset var — that finding is scoped to the environment the script ran in, which sourced neither `.zshrc`/`.bashrc` nor `.zprofile`. Before reporting it as a host defect or offering to edit a dotfile, re-check the way the user actually experiences it: `ssh <host> 'zsh -l -i -c "command -v <tool>; echo $PATH"'`. The existing bullet points one way (don't verify a *job* by hand); this points the other (don't report a *non-interactive* result as the user's reality). Next instance: any remote install/bootstrap/doctor script whose output you're relaying — a Homebrew "not in PATH" notice, a `pip install --user` script warning, a `doctor` command run over SSH.

I relayed it as a real gap on that host and closed the turn offering to append a PATH export to their shell rc. The user's correction was a one-line refutation — pasting their own prompt showing the tool running fine. The check had reported on the deploy's own bare-PATH env (`/opt/homebrew/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:…`); the login shell has `~/.local/bin` three times over, and the tool resolved to the symlink that same deploy had just written. Cost: one wasted round-trip, and had they answered "yes" instead of correcting me, a pointless edit to a dotfile that was already correct. Second-order note worth harvesting with it: the *check itself* is misleading for exactly this reason and cries wolf on every remote deploy — the durable fix is to test the rc-sourced PATH, per "A workaround that unblocked THIS session is the durable fix's spec". (Session: 2026-08-01-claude-config8-issue83-deploy, promoted from session friction)

**Change:** When a root-cause claim depends on what an agent or skill actually *did* at runtime — which files a skill read, which branch it took, why a step never fired — close it against the real session transcripts in `~/.claude/projects/<cwd-slug>/*.jsonl` before proposing the fix. Treat "the spec says X, and outcomes correlate with X" as a hypothesis, not a finding: it is the same producer-only gap `CLAUDE.md` § Verify Before Claiming Done names in "close a diagnosis from both ends". Twelve real runs then showed the correlation held but a *second* mechanism existed that no spec read could reveal: a session cited a rule owned by another file, resolved it against the proxy pointer, declared it "not nudge-eligible," and redirected the nudge elsewhere — recorded verbatim in its own reasoning text. Shipping the PR from the static case alone would have fixed one of two causes. The transcripts are two tool calls away and are the only authoritative surface for agent behavior.
