Don't conclude what the model emitted from a correlation; rebuild the exact request through the harness's own request builder (system prompt + active session rows read-only + the tool list as it stood), replay it against the same endpoint with the variable flipped (A/B, a few runs each), and read the raw stream. Check fidelity by comparing reconstructed prompt tokens against the logged count.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — I reported "best guess: the model tried to call a tool that had been removed" with fixes attached, from a tool-list-absent correlation plus billed-but-unparsed completion tokens. Prior authority — the parent rule and `CLAUDE.md` § Verify (close a diagnosis from both ends, runtime half). Unblock — the operator asked to investigate further and get more confident; the replay (3/3 empty without the tools, 0/3 with) showed the call leaked as text and the harness's own stripper erased it, which a correlation could not have named. The same session then stopped again at "the tools were parked" until asked why; the ultimate cause was a plugin forcing a reconnect on a live session.
**Next instance:** a support chatbot that "sometimes answers nothing" on one provider — replay the logged conversation with and without the suspected tool/system-prompt delta and read the raw SSE before blaming the model.

## Convert a CONDITIONAL authorization into a stated numeric line before resuming the loop
**Change:** When an operator grants authority conditionally — "merge unless scope increases quite a bit, in which case I want to look at it", "deploy unless it looks risky" — do not carry the qualitative condition into the loop. State the baseline and an explicit threshold *before* resuming, in the reply and (for a PR) in-thread where the next round can check it: e.g. baseline net +91 / 9 files, escalation line net +110 **or** a 10th file. Report `baseline · actual · line` every round, and on a breach hand back **even when every finding that round was valid and applied**. A new file or newly-touched subsystem is a breach independent of LOC, since that's scope the line alone won't catch.
**Why (autonomy):** A conditional grant delegates the action but retains a veto whose trigger is undefined, so the agent ends up grading its own homework at precisely the moment it holds the authority and has least incentive to escalate — convergence. Naming the number first makes the veto checkable by the operator instead of by the agent, and posting it in-thread means a re-review (which reads the diff from scratch) can see the ruling. Concretely: the line I set was crossed by 2 net lines, mostly comment prose, and honoring it was still right — a gate honored only when convenient isn't a gate. This one *adds* a hand-back by design; its value is that the hand-back is predictable and pre-agreed rather than discovered at merge time.

## Asking which isolated checkout to use? Enumerate the slots first, then recommend the lowest clean one
**Change:** `CLAUDE.md` § Workspace Isolation requires asking which numbered slot to use for interactive work. Ask *with a recommendation*, never as a flat menu of equivalents: first enumerate each slot's branch and dirty-file count, then recommend the lowest-numbered slot that is clean and on `main`, listing the other clean ones as alternates. Still ask (a slot can be reserved for parallel work a dirty-count doesn't reveal), and never silently clone a new slot — the only no-prompt exceptions are `/cleanup` and a dispatched subagent running `tc claim`.
**Why (autonomy):** Quality-steer grade. Asked which of four sibling slots to use; all four were clean and on `main`, and the operator took the lowest one. The enumeration is the part carrying information (which slots hold live parallel work); the choice among verified-clean slots is arbitrary, so an unweighted menu makes the operator do ranking for no gain. Mirrors `/cleanup`'s own claim loop, which auto-claims the lowest unused slot. (Promoted from a cc6 feedback memory.)

## Before committing a guard, revert it and confirm the test goes red — an assertion that can't fail is worse than no test
**Change:** Add to `TESTING.md` (and `CODING_STANDARDS.md § Fail-Fast`'s neighbourhood): a test written to pin a fix is not done when it passes — it is done when it **fails with the fix reverted**. Run that negative control before committing, as its own step, the same way the suite's summary line is read rather than inferred. Three shapes account for most false-green pins, all of which pass while the bug is live: (a) asserting **absence** against a stream the capture discarded (`assert_not_contains "$OUT" …` where `OUT=$(cmd 2>/dev/null)` and the message only goes to stderr); (b) asserting against a **fixture that structurally can't exhibit the property** (a stub writing `.rgval` while the guard protects `.roborev.toml`, so a bypass lands somewhere the assertion never looks); (c) asserting only a **generic verdict** where a neighbouring branch produces the same verdict for a different reason (`FAIL` + `no SKIP`, when an unrelated healthy path also yields `FAIL`) — pin a branch-distinguishing token instead. Next instance: any repo, any language — a Python test for a new validation guard, a shell assertion on a new refusal path, an integration test for a new 403.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer, untagged (bot-caught, no operator hand-back — see "The [removes-handback] tag requires a BLOCKED stop"). 2026-08-02 · plow-pbc/seed-auto-roborev#26: **three separate placebo assertions in one PR, all mine**, each shipped green while the thing it named was broken. (a) `assert_not_contains "$D1" "has no .roborev.toml"` with `D1=$(… 2>/dev/null)` — that message is stderr-only, so the needle could never appear; (b) `assert_eq "x" "$(cat outside.toml)"` for "the symlink target was never written through" — the fake `roborev` wrote `.rgval` and never `.roborev.toml`, so deleting the guard outright left it green; (c) a broken-script fixture asserting only `FAIL` + no `SKIP`, which an unsynced-repo run also satisfies, so the fixture would have stopped testing its branch the moment its `sed` stopped matching. Each cost a review round. What actually caught them, once adopted, was mechanical: copy `ref/` to a temp dir, revert the guard there, re-run, confirm red — cheap enough to do per guard, and it converted "I exercised the branches in a sandbox" (done by hand four times, leaving nothing behind) into a gate. Composes with the existing "a blank grep of a NUL-bearing log is NOT proof of absence" proposal — same root: absence is only evidence when the needle *could* have been present. (Session: 2026-08-02-claude-config8-move-review-guidelines)

### +1 — the same placebo shape, reached through the *verification path* rather than the assertion
Four of seven review rounds on one PR found the defect in **how I checked**, not in the code, and every check ran green: a `--help` invocation "proved" a new `just` recipe worked when a real run died at an optional-dependency import that `--help` returns before reaching; a guard `stat`ed a directory that the very next call creates, so it could never fire; a permissions test asserted the leaked *process umask* instead of the mode of a file the CLI wrote; and a crash-window test passed with its fix reverted because a different code path did the work. Adds two operational rules to the parent: **verify through the entry point a real consumer uses** (a cheap proxy — `--help`, `--dry-run`, a unit call that skips the boundary — returns before the failure lives), and **for a security fix, exercise the attack and show before/after** rather than asserting. The symlink fix that closed the round shipped with a planted victim file: `open("w")` truncated it, `O_NOFOLLOW` refused. Next instance: any repo where a fix is verified by the fastest command that exits cleanly rather than the one a user would run. (Session: 2026-08-04-memeval-mem0-adapter)

### +1 — 2026-08-26 · agent-mgr6-two-layer-fleet-cli · a MALFORMED revert produces a red that proves nothing — size the failure against the guard's blast radius

**Change (extends):** After reverting to confirm red, check *which* tests failed, not just that something did. A revert applied with `sed`/string-surgery can break the file instead of restoring the prior behaviour, and a syntax error fails **everything** — which reads as a very convincing red. The check is one line: **the failure set must be no wider than the guard's blast radius.** A guard on one code path that reddens five unrelated test files did not get reverted; it got broken. Restore from git (`git show <sha>:<path>`) rather than re-deriving the old code by hand, and re-run the suite after restoring to confirm you are back to green.

**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer, untagged (self-caught, no operator hand-back). Reverting a Compose-flag guard to prove a new test discriminated, my python cut at the wrong `esac` and left the shell file unparseable. The suite went red across `test_credentials.py`, `test_install.py` and three others — none of which the guard touches. Had I not looked at the failure *names*, I would have recorded "verified red first" for a test that had never been exercised. The correct revert, applied to the exact arm, reddened exactly one test. Same session, same PR, twice: the second revert (of a dispatch-level hoist) also had to be checked this way.

### +1 — 2026-09-08 · life-assistant8-quiet-group-threads · a fourth placebo shape: the test HELPER was derived by copying the code under test

**Change (extends):** Add the oracle to the list of places a placebo hides. The parent's three shapes are all about the *assertion*; this one is about what the assertion compares against. A test helper written to model "what the code produces" by transcribing the production expression inherits its bugs, so the assertion is comparing a value to itself and cannot fail. Rule: a test's expected value must be derived **independently** of the implementation — spelled out literally, or asserted as a property the implementation does not state. When a helper must mirror production shape, assert the *seam* the helper cannot fake.

**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer, untagged (caught by the local per-commit reviewer, no operator hand-back). Moving a prompt fragment to a single composition seam, I joined it with a bare `+`, dropping the space every rendered prompt needed — the rule arrived glued to the previous sentence. The test could not see it, because the `_rendered` helper I wrote to model a rendered prompt performed the *same* unspaced join, and the assertion only checked membership (`assert RULE in rendered`), which passes against a helper carrying the identical defect. The fix was to model the separator in the helper and assert `f" {RULE}" in rendered` — an assertion that would have failed on the original. Note the failure survived a green full-suite run and a clean bot review; only a reviewer reading the diff for *intent* caught it. **Next instance:** any test whose expected value is built by a helper that re-implements a formatting, serialization, or path-joining expression the production code also performs — a URL builder, a cache-key composer, a prompt assembler.

## [removes-handback] Asked to act on "<person>'s account"? Enumerate the candidate set at a DISCRIMINATING mask level immediately — don't ask which one
**Change:** When the user names a person's record ("disable swag's account", "remove Bob's key") and you hold a small enumerable candidate set, don't reply with a category question ("which system do you mean?") or an enumeration too coarse to discriminate. Print the candidates immediately at the *narrowest mask that actually distinguishes them* — a 2-3 character prefix of the identifying field plus its domain (`sw*********@gmail.com`, `da****@plow.co`) — which is usually enough for you to identify the target yourself, and always enough for the user to answer in one word instead of a paragraph. Mask per `CLAUDE.md § Secrets`; a 2-char prefix is proportionate when the user has explicitly asked you to find a record *by* that field. Then verify the match programmatically (exact field comparison, not eyeballing the prefix) before acting.
**Why (autonomy):** the stop — asked to disable a teammate's codex account among 5 reviewer credentials, I enumerated only domains + local-part *lengths*, which discriminated nothing, then asked the user which system they meant and for the email. The unblock — they replied that it was one of the five; I then printed 2-char-masked local parts and `sw*********@gmail.com` identified it instantly, with no further input. The discriminating enumeration was available on the first turn and *was* the answer — asking for it cost two round-trips. Generalizes past credentials to any "act on X's record" request over an enumerable set (SSH keys, org members, API tokens, DB user rows).

## babysit-pr: a truncated comment fetch is a state check, not a read — and a MERGED/CLOSED PR still owes its final drain

**Change:** Add to `skills/babysit-pr/SKILL.md` (Step 2 / Step 3): when comments are fetched with a truncated or projected body (`.body[0:150]`, a narrow `--jq`) to answer a *state* question, that fetch does not discharge the read. Before concluding anything about content — including "nothing here needs a reply" — re-fetch the full body of every comment not already replied to. Step 1 already requires draining a `MERGED`/`CLOSED` PR; truncation is the practical way that requirement gets skipped, because the bot marker is visible in the first 150 characters and the verdict is not. Next instance: any repo, any PR, any reviewer — the trigger is a projected fetch standing in for a read, the same shape as a `--jq '.state'` check tempting you past an unread review.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — asserted a session was complete while an unreplied bot review sat on the just-merged PR; the operator had to ask whether I had seen it. unblock — reading it took one command and surfaced what the truncation hid: the review's Strengths section endorsed a decision I had already reversed, and reached it by repeating a stale claim from the very repo file that PR series was correcting. A review whose rationale rests on a fact you are currently fixing is not an endorsement — but that is only visible if you read it. (Session: 2026-08-03-claude-config-150-medium-verdict-drift)

## [removes-handback] Don't commit an edit to a file the RUNTIME also writes — the next prod fast-forward aborts on it

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Code Lives in ~/Hacking, Deploys Run from ~/services`: before committing an edit to any tracked file the deployed runtime also writes (a cache, an index, a manifest, a journal, a generated config), stop — the prod clone's copy diverges between deploys, so `git pull --ff-only` there will abort on exactly that path, mid-deploy, and the only ways out are discarding live data or diverging the prod clone. A deploy-clean check that exempts the runtime's writable area will NOT warn you: it is designed to treat that dirt as normal. Fix the generator/contract instead and let the next regeneration rewrite the file. When the stale content must not survive until then, prefer collapsing the line to a back-reference at whatever owns the rule (one small edit, one collision) over rewriting several. When a deploy does hit this, back up the live file outside the repo first, and check whether the at-risk content is already durable elsewhere before recommending a discard.

**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — a deploy aborted at `git pull --ff-only` on a hot-cache file I had hand-edited in the merged PR; the repo's own deploy-clean gate had printed `DEPLOYABLE` seconds earlier because it exempts that directory by design. I could not clear it without discarding a live runtime write, so I fired an AskUserQuestion and the deploy sat half-done. *The unblock* — the operator authorized backing the file up and overwriting it. The edit itself had been well-motivated (the cache is read back as standing guidance by the next job, so a stale rule in it would have re-taught the very thing the PR removed) — which is what makes this worth a rule: the motive is sound and the mechanism still bites.

**Next instance:** any repo where a daemon or scheduled job writes into its own checkout — a scraped dataset, a compiled search index, a rotating credential-free state file — and a PR touches the same path. (Session: 2026-08-03-str9-vault-access-contract)


## [removes-handback] Before dispatching a build/deploy job, check whether a SCHEDULED run already produced the artifact you need

**Change:** When a task needs a built artifact (an installable DMG/image/tarball at some ref), check the repo's *scheduled* producers before triggering a fresh build. Recon is three cheap commands: `grep -ln "schedule:" .github/workflows/*.yml` for self-running workflows, `gh run list --workflow=<wf>` (the `schedule` event rows show which SHA each nightly built), and `gh release list` — scheduled output frequently lands as a **draft** release, invisible on the public Releases page, with the artifact already uploaded to S3/registry. Generalize past nightlies to any pre-existing producer: cron deploys, scheduled image builds, recurring data jobs. The question is always "does the thing I am about to produce already exist at the ref I want?"

**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — I ended a turn offering to run the CI-build install path, which dispatches a workflow and waits ~30–45 min for sign+notarize, to bring a host to latest `main`. *The unblock* — the human's "isn't there a nightly job to build?"; there was, it had run 3 hours earlier, and it had built the exact tip commit. The artifact was already on S3; the whole build half of the job was unnecessary. Checking first also surfaced the *real* systemic gap in that setup, which the build-dispatch framing had hidden: the nightly only ever creates **drafts** and nothing promotes them, so the published artifact can lag head indefinitely while the builds themselves are green.

**Next instance:** any repo with a scheduled producer — needing a container image at `main` to reproduce something, and last night's scheduled build already covers that SHA. Also the inverse tell: if scheduled builds are green but the deployed/installed artifact is stale, suspect a missing *promote* step rather than a broken build.

## [removes-handback] "Not verified on a live install" is your action item, not a caveat to hand over — build it and drive it on a machine you can reach
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`: before writing any "not verified in production / on real hardware / end-to-end" caveat into a hand-off, name which reachable machine could run it — **including the one you are already on**. A CI-built artifact installed on the local host (`/plow-prod-install-auto` and equivalents) turns most of these caveats into a 30-minute unattended step. Only genuinely unavailable substrate (hardware you don't own, another person's device/account) belongs in the hand-off. Two riders: (1) when the shipped build is still installed, reproduce the bug **before** upgrading — a before/after pair on one machine is far stronger than an after-only pass, and it costs nothing while CI builds; (2) a consent question about a *side effect* (a message landing in someone else's thread) is separate from the verification question — get consent for the side effect, don't use it to skip verification you can run against your own install.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — I closed a merged-ready PR summary with "not verified on a live install; that's the gap I'd close before this reaches users," treating it as the operator's problem. unblock — the user asked whether I could just do it on this machine with extra instrumentation, naming the install skill. I could: CI built the branch, the install replaced the local app, and one real agent turn produced a before/after pair (shipped build: restart → SIGTERM → the error notice; branch build: no restart, real reply, in-session refresh). It also caught a **false PASS in my own harness** — a restart check that sampled `head -1` of two matching units and reported "not restarted" for a run whose journal showed SIGTERM — which no amount of unit testing would have surfaced. Driving the real thing is where the findings are. (Session: 2026-08-04-plow3-1157-runtime-bounce)

## [removes-handback] roborev backlog sweep: the helper prints `reviews.id`, but `close`/`comment` take `job_id` — map before acting, and verify in the DB

**Change:** Fix the sweep recipe in the `roborev` skill (and anything that cites it): the machine-wide helper `roborev-list-all.py` selects `reviews.id AS id`, while `roborev close <id>` / `roborev comment <id>` resolve their argument as a **`job_id`**. The two namespaces overlap numerically, and the CLI accepts a mismatched id **silently** — reporting `Job N closed` while closing an unrelated review in another repo. Before any bulk sweep, translate ids once:

```sql
select r.id as helper_id, r.job_id, p.name, j.branch, r.closed
from reviews r join review_jobs j on j.id = r.job_id join repos p on p.id = j.repo_id
where r.id in (<ids from the helper>);
```

Act on `job_id`, sanity-check that each row's repo/branch matches the branch you meant, then verify the result in the DB (`select sum(closed=1), count(*) …`) rather than trusting the command's success line. Also note `roborev comment` silently no-ops for some job_ids — a printed success is not proof, so confirm via the `responses` table.

**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — a `/cleanup` backlog sweep closed 23 findings on branches confirmed merged, and every command reported success, yet the backlog count did not move. *The unblock* — querying `~/.roborev/reviews.db` directly, which showed the closes had landed on **plow7 / plow2 / plow3 / claude-config** reviews I had never looked at (mostly already-closed or PASS rows, so no review signal was lost), and left 24 misleading `moot:`/`stale:` comments on unrelated audit trails that then had to be individually corrected. Re-run against the mapped `job_id`s, the same sweep closed exactly the intended 23 and the count moved 127 → 104. I had also mis-diagnosed the first failure as WAL read-lag in the helper; the helper was correct throughout.

**Next instance:** any tool pair where a *listing* surface and an *action* surface use different id namespaces that happen to overlap numerically — a queue viewer vs. a queue admin CLI, a dashboard row-id vs. an API resource-id. The tell is an action that reports success while the listing is unchanged; treat that as an identifier-namespace mismatch, not a caching artifact, and verify against the store before repeating the action in bulk.

**Change:** No change to the parent — recording recurrence, and one sharpening: the trap survives because the staged rule lives here while the sweep is driven from the `roborev` skill's backlog-sweep section, which still presents the helper's `#<id>` output next to `close <id>` examples with no mapping step. ## [removes-handback] A memory recording a user's one-off override is CONDITIONAL on its trigger — never let it decay into "ask them each time"
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` (near § Take the Steps): a stored memory of the form "when the user says X, do Y" authorizes Y **only when X is present in the current session, about the current artifact**. It is not standing permission to consult them. Before letting any recalled override suppress a default action, check that its triggering condition actually fired *this* session; absent that, the default fires silently. The failure shape is a memory quietly inverting from "here's what to do when they say X" into "check whether they want X" — which converts a rule that was written to *remove* a round-trip into one that manufactures one. Applies to any recorded override, not just this one.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — after `gh pr create` I ended the turn asking whether to run the babysit loop, despite `CLAUDE.md § Branch Workflow` step 4 explicitly saying to invoke it on the same turn and not ask. I talked myself out of the rule with a prior-session memory that the user had once said they'd babysit a PR themselves. unblock — the user said to babysit it and pointed out the ask "wasted some clock time"; the PR then converged over three review rounds with zero further input. The rule already existed and was unambiguous — what defeated it was a conditional memory applied unconditionally, which is why the fence belongs on memory-recall rather than on the babysit rule. (Session: 2026-08-04-plow3-1157-runtime-bounce)

## [removes-handback] A `[blocking] [security]` finding → enumerate what the actor ALREADY holds before designing any remedy — and test the destination CLASS, not one named target
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md § Broken-Glass Test` (step 4's neighborhood): before proposing or applying a security remedy, establish the actor's existing access — mounts, credentials, tool surface — and ask whether the finding grants anything new. Verify by running the check, not by reasoning about the config. If nothing is gained, the finding is **invalid**, not YAGNI: decline with that evidence and skip the remedy entirely. The second half is the trap: having established that one named target is already reachable, do **not** generalize to the class. Enumerate the destinations the mechanism can actually reach — a *relative* path resolves against a different root on each side of a bind mount, so "the agent already has `~/.hermes`" says nothing about `~/.ssh`. Check the class, then rule.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — on srosro/sams-str-hermes-agent#99 a bot flagged a host-side `cp -a` following symlinks an agent could plant in its own writable vault. I reproduced the symlink-follow, drafted a three-mount read-only restructure, and handed the choice back to the operator ("the restructure, or the 5-line guard?"). The unblock — the operator asked whether this was over-engineering for a one-user POC. One command answered it: the container already mounts the operator's state dir read-write, so it could already write that file directly; the escalation did not exist and both remedies defended nothing. But the very next round showed the other half — the same mechanism with a *relative* link reached `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, which no mount exposes, and I had wrongly declined it on the strength of the one target I had checked. Next instance: any reviewer finding labelled security in a different repo, where the remedy would add a guard, a mount, or a branch.

## Pre-PMF with one operator, a step the human will do by hand stays manual — don't design the scheduler around it
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Lean Less Conservative (Pre-PMF)`: when the operating point is a proof of concept with a single user, a step the operator is willing to perform by hand should stay manual. Don't propose a cron job, systemd timer, or nightly automation around it, and don't propose a second mechanism when one already covers the need. Scheduled automation is a second owner of the data, a new failure mode that fails silently, and a thing to maintain — and it tends to arrive with its own branch/state/reconciliation concepts. Lead with the manual design; mention automation as a later option, not as part of the recommendation.
**Why (autonomy):** A quality steer rather than a hard stop, recorded because it was an explicit operator directive. Designing where an agent's extracted-knowledge vault should live, I proposed a nightly job committing snapshots to a backup branch alongside a manual promote step. The operator cut it as over-engineering for one user and said he was content to commit by hand. Collapsing backup and promotion into the single manual step he already performed removed a whole branch/reconciliation concept from the design. Next instance: any single-operator project where I am about to propose a scheduled job for something the operator does occasionally and by hand.

### +1 — before building the mechanism, split the job into "a manual pass covers this" and "only code can do this", and ship only the second half
Same operating-point logic applied one step earlier — at *whether to write code at all*, not just whether to schedule it. Fixing `plow-pbc/plow#1148` (a root rename stranded ~21 installs' agent memory/skills at the old path, silently), I shipped a detector at +244/−11: its own module, a frozen dataclass, byte accounting, a bounded walk, 121 lines of tests. The operator's steer was to ask why code was needed at all when the population is bounded and a manual migration would do — and whether a couple of LOC of loud failure plus a comment would cover it. The useful split: a human can sweep the installs they can reach, but **cannot inspect a disk they have no access to**, and that residue — reporting which of the ~19 unreachable installs are affected — is the only part that earns code. Cut to +104/−11 with the module deleted, a 13-line inline check at an existing seam, and the guard against the *next* rename as a comment at the site that caused it rather than a mechanism. Next instance: any bounded-population data/state defect where I'm about to write a detector or migrator — name what a one-time manual pass covers first, and let only the remainder become code. (Session: 2026-08-04-plow-stranded-roots)

## [removes-handback] Repetitive lifecycle work at fleet scale → design a pacer + workers fan-out, don't report the volume as a limit
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps`: when a repetitive per-item lifecycle (babysit N PRs, triage N findings, migrate N repos) exceeds what one loop can drive, the answer is a fan-out design, not a status report saying so. Split it: **one pacer** owns the waiting (a single Monitor on the event source that emits one event per completion, zero polling), and **short-lived workers** own the per-item work (one bounded subagent per event that returns rather than looping). Do NOT give each item its own self-paced agent — subagents can't `ScheduleWakeup`, so N agents would each poll, and N concurrent pollers throttle the very service you're waiting on. Size the fan-out to the *downstream* concurrency (reviewer workers, CI slots), not the item count. Also split the work by whether it needs judgment: items whose answer is already known get handled in-loop by a paced script; only genuinely ambiguous ones justify a subagent's context cost.
**Why (autonomy):** the stop — with 32 migration PRs open I told the operator "32 PRs is more babysitting than one session can drive" and handed the volume back as a constraint. the unblock — the operator asked "can't you dispatch 32 subagents?", which reframed it from a capacity limit to a design problem. The right shape turned out to be neither 1 nor 32 agents: one persistent log-tail Monitor emitting a wake per landed review, plus ~3 concurrent bounded agents, plus a paced in-loop script for the items whose finding was already known. Next instance: any "N items each needing a review/CI/deploy round-trip" where I'm about to describe the count as the blocker.

## [removes-handback] Cleaning up a defect class you introduced across a fleet is inside the original mandate, not a scope extension
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps`: when a batch change you shipped turns out to carry the same defect in repos already merged, sweeping those repos is part of the task you were given — not new work requiring fresh approval. Ask instead whether the *remedy* is in-scope-shaped (net-neutral, same class, no new capability); if yes, do it and report. Reserve the check-in for a genuinely different concern or an additive remedy. A hand-back here costs a round-trip to authorize work the operator already believes is done.
**Why (autonomy):** the stop — after the reviewer surfaced a stale hardcoded count in two open PRs, I found the identical claim in 5 already-merged repos, fixed only the open ones, and asked "Want me to sweep them?" instead of sweeping. the unblock — "great please sweep all 5", one round-trip to authorize a one-line-per-repo fix to a defect my own migration had activated. Next instance: any fleet-wide change where a post-merge review reveals the same flaw in already-landed siblings.

## [removes-handback] Before deleting a copy because "the shared layer owns it", prove the shared layer reaches the same consumers
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md § DRY`: the justification for deleting a duplicated block is always "the canonical layer already says this" — verify that against the *rendered artifact the consumer sees*, not the canonical file's existence. Two things must hold: the canonical layer contains it, AND it reaches every consumer the deleted copy reached. A shared prelude prepended to only some call sites, or a default that applies only when no per-entity override exists, silently drops the guidance for the rest. Deletion is the irreversible half of a consolidation; when the delivery path is conditional in a way the copy wasn't, the copy wasn't redundant.
**Why (autonomy):** the stop — consolidating reviewer policy, I deleted each repo's operating-point statement on the reasoning that the org default supplied it, and shipped that to 3 merged repos. the unblock — the operator's steer to "make sure we don't lose track of" the pre-PMF posture prompted me to check the resolver, which is either/or: the org default fires *only* when a repo commits no policy file, so committing one switched it off and left no anchor at all. The voice posture genuinely was duplication (prepended unconditionally to every agent); the operating point was not. Next instance: any consolidation where a per-entity file and a global default are read by the same consumer.

### +1 — 2026-09-18 · memory:moving-ownership-needs-a-new-owner · the moved-responsibility form: prove the NEW owner does it, not that the old one stopped
**Change:** Extend the parent from deleted copies to moved responsibilities (sequencing, install, lifecycle). After the move, state the new owner's entry point in one sentence and test that one command through it produces the whole outcome, never the old owner's absence. If docs grew steps or a caller now sequences things, ownership moved to the human, and that is the regression.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — asked to make a shared CLI own deployment, I moved a domain script's deploy steps into documentation (three chained operator commands) and wrote a test asserting the script no longer orchestrated; it passed while the system got worse. Prior authority — the ask named the intended owner. Unblock — the operator read the resulting docs and asked why deployment was being taken away from the tool meant to own it.
**Next instance:** moving any install or migration step out of a service's entrypoint into an orchestrator, base image or shared CLI.

  ### +1 — 2026-10-06 · memory:dedupe-fix-the-assembly-seam-first · a shared prelude may only restrict
  **Change (extends):** When the fix for duplicated rules is a shared prelude prepended to every consumer, every sentence in it must be a restriction or shared judgment: never a grant ("you may read any file") and never an output directive ("state X in your output"). Consumers differ in envelope width and output contract, so a grant widens the narrowest one's fence and a directive breaks any consumer whose output is strictly validated. Fix the assembly seam in the same change that deletes the copies, and report the ownership table (N homes → 1) rather than a LOC target, since relocation-heavy consolidation is usually LOC-neutral.
  **Why (autonomy):** Stop — a reviewer-prompt consolidation put a grant in the shared prelude and it reached a consumer whose fence was narrower; the operator caught the widened fence. Prior authority — the parent's "prove it reaches the same consumers" check, which proves reach but not that reach is safe. Unblock — the operator's ruling that a prelude restricts only.
  **Next instance:** a shared system-prompt prefix for several agent roles in plow or hermes, where one role is read-only and another writes files.

## [removes-handback] In a multi-repo batch, read every varying value from that repo's own artifact — corpus-wide substitution produces silent per-repo falsehoods
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md` (§ DRY / § Verify neighborhood): when applying one edit across N repos, any value that could differ per repo — a heading name, a path, a count, a stance, a capability claim — must be read from that repo's authoritative file, not assumed uniform and pattern-substituted. The failure is silent and looks like success: the edit applies cleanly, the diff is tiny and identical, each file is internally coherent, and it is wrong only relative to a file the transform never opened. Where no faithful per-repo value exists, **delete the claim** rather than guess one — a rule reviewers can't evaluate manufactures false findings. Corollary: a spec's claim *about* its own implementation ("run this script, exit 0 = done") is itself a claim to verify, not a fact to inherit; the gap between the two is exactly the prose↔implementation drift such specs exist to catch.
**Why (autonomy):** four recurrences in one 32-repo migration, each caught by the reviewer rather than by me: (1) substituted the org-default "specs are sketches" over each repo's own spec-rigidity stance, inverting it in 27 SEED repos whose prose IS the contract; (2) cited `## Verification` in 5 repos whose heading is `## Verify`; (3) generalized "some probes are manual" from one repo to four where it was false; (4) claimed a script "implements the authoritative prompts" by quoting the spec's own framing without reading the script — which asserted materially less (any nonempty array vs a required topic set; `|| true` suppressing sync failure; a search assertion that always passes). Next instance: any templated change across repos/services/environments where the template contains a value that is per-entity by nature.

## [removes-handback] Once you've requested human approval, STOP pushing — an approval attests to the exact commit they saw
**Change:** Treat a posted approval request (a review request, any "ready for your look") as a push freeze on that branch. A human approval is bound to a specific `commit_id`; pushing after it silently decouples the approval from the head, and merging on the still-`APPROVED` `reviewDecision` would ship unreviewed code. If a genuine `[blocking]` correctness issue forces a push anyway, the prior approval is void — say so and re-request only once the new head is confirmed clean, so the human approves a converged commit rather than being re-pinged mid-churn. At merge time verify the latest `APPROVED` review's `commit_id == headRefOid` and treat a mismatch as fail-closed (re-arm, never merge). Companion: before declaring a bot review converged, scan **every** probe class the reviewer uses — an `[open]` probe with no severity tag still gates, so grepping only `[blocking]`/`[medium]`/`[low]` reads as converged when it isn't.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — I posted the approval tag on a PR I'd miscounted as converged (grepped severity tags only, missed an `[open]` `[bug]`: a Gmail search omitting `max_results`, silently dropping mail past the default page). The unblock — the human approved a commit, then my fix moved the head past it, and the merge gate correctly flagged the approval as stale; clearing it required re-pinging the same person for a second approval on work they'd already reviewed. Both halves are hand-backs I caused: one avoidable by counting probe classes properly, the other by not pushing after asking. (Promoted from a plow4 feedback memory.)

## macOS agent shell has no `timeout`, and one non-zero sibling cancels a whole parallel Bash batch — run fail-prone commands one per message
**Change:** Two environment facts worth stating where the agent will read them before batching. (1) There is no `timeout` binary in the macOS agent shell (exit 127) — for SSH use `-o ConnectTimeout=` / `ServerAliveInterval`; a *server-side* `timeout` inside a command that runs on a Linux host is fine. (2) When several Bash calls are issued in one assistant message, a single non-zero sibling cancels the rest of the batch and they return empty — which reads exactly like a degraded tool channel. So: send fail-prone commands (a `grep` that may not match, `ssh`, `git` checks) **one per message**, or neutralize the exit (`|| true`, `; echo DONE_$?`, `set +e` inside heredocs). An empty result immediately after a parallel batch is not evidence of broken tooling — re-run the one command alone before concluding anything about the harness.
**Why (autonomy):** Burned many turns reading batch-cancellation empties as harness failure and adding defensive backoff scheduling, when the real cause was a trailing non-matching `grep` (exit 1) or a `timeout …` (exit 127) sitting first in the batch. Quality-grade rather than a removed hand-back — no operator round-trip — but it stalls autonomous progress for multiple turns and recurs on every mac session. Related environment note: the Bash tool's cwd resets per call, so prefer absolute paths over relying on a prior `cd`. (Promoted from a plow4 feedback memory.)

## Open work by naming the business goal it serves — and let it outrank the spec on conflicts

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` (near § Delivering work): before implementing a handed-down spec or plan, state in one or two sentences the **user-facing business goal** the work serves, in the language of whoever benefits — then justify each non-trivial call against it, and say so explicitly when following the goal means departing from the spec. Specs are usually written in mechanical terms (sections to collapse, LOC targets, file layouts); optimizing the mechanics can satisfy every stated requirement while missing the point, and the goal is also the tiebreaker when the spec turns out to be wrong on a detail.
**Why (autonomy):** The human amended a running autonomous goal mid-flight to add that my *first* step should be to identify the business goal — framed for that project as wanting the agent to behave as if it were an employee. That framing immediately did real work: it reframed a policy change from "collapse three sections into one" into "an employee remembers who to call", which is what exposed that the existing rule made the standing cleaning/maintenance crew unwritable — the actual defect, invisible from the spec's mechanical description. It later settled two design calls the spec had gotten wrong. Next instance: any repo where a prior session hands over a design doc — leading with who benefits and how surfaces the defects the doc's own framing hides.

  ### +1 — 2026-08-07 · ltmm-poc1-memeval-goal
  **Change:** Extend it to the *absence* case, and to orientation rather than only implementation: when asked what a repo is for — or when orienting in an unfamiliar one — check whether its docs name the **decision** the work feeds, and treat "they describe only the machinery or the artifact" as the finding to report, not as the intent to adopt. Then offer to write the goal down where it was missing.
  **Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged, per the tag-bar rule) — asked to characterize a benchmark repo's "spirit", I read its README, REVIEW.md and CLAUDE.md and confidently reported a measurement-rigor project, then offered to build *more* of that rigor. The operator's correction named the real goal — decide which tools to install so an agent knows him better than anyone, they have to ingest passively, and no scientifically rigorous study is wanted — and asked whether that was clear in the repo. It wasn't, anywhere: the docs stated the artifact ("which of my memory systems retrieves best?") and never the decision, so two of the three selection criteria lived only in the operator's head and every session had been grading work against the wrong bar. Next instance: any unfamiliar repo whose goal section describes its pipeline or output rather than the decision someone acts on — say the goal isn't stated instead of inferring it from the machinery.


## [removes-handback] A silent failure earns an issue with BOTH a runnable repro and a non-destructive detector — the repro proves it, the detector tells existing installs whether they are already hit
**Change:** Add to `PR_LIFECYCLE.md § Issue hygiene` (which today owns search-first, severity, the close bar, and the transport — but says nothing about issue *content*): when the defect produces **no signal** — silent data loss, a dropped scheduled job, a config that empties itself — the issue body carries two artifacts, not one. (1) A **runnable repro**: if the real trigger is expensive or unsafe to induce, reproduce its *effect* instead (the wipe was a directory rename, so `mv <state> <state>.migrated` + restart reproduces it in three commands without inducing an auth failure) — and say which you did. (2) A **non-destructive detector**: a read-only command that answers "has this already happened on my install?", because a silent bug's whole cost is the installs sitting in the failed state right now with nobody looking. Also state explicitly what you *ruled out* (here: not a schema migration — both DBs same `schema_version`/table count; and the host was demonstrably up during the silent window), since for a no-signal bug the obvious mundane explanations are the first thing a reader reaches for. Next instance: any repo where you find a fail-quiet — a cron that stopped, a queue that drains to nowhere, a cache that silently resets — and are about to open an issue for it.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — after root-causing a fail-quiet on plow-pbc/plow (a gateway state re-provision silently emptying the cron store; three jobs dead for 21 days, ~24 missed deliveries, nothing logged anywhere), I closed the turn by *offering* — "worth an issue if you want me to write it up" — instead of filing it. unblock — the operator both authorized and specified the bar in one line: write it up, we want fail loud, include all info needed to repro. Filing it myself with a repro by default removes that round-trip entirely; the detector half is what the "already hit?" question needs and no existing proposal covers it (`§ Issue hygiene` governs *whether/where* to file, the silent-failure-fix proposal governs the *fix shape*, and #831 governs filing self-originated defers — none govern what a fail-quiet issue must contain). Landed as plow-pbc/plow#1171. (Session: 2026-08-04-plow9-ld-cron-restore)

### +1 — 2026-08-12 · plow1-model-preference-storm · "runnable" means literal commands + a baseline + a CONTROL + the expected output — a prose description of the action is not a repro
**Change:** Sharpens the parent's *repro* half into a shape check you apply before posting, whenever the issue exists so that **someone else executes it** (another operator, another machine, a future agent). Four parts, all of them: (1) **literal commands**, copy-pasteable — "kill the daemon" is a description, `pkill -f 'plowd.main:app'` is a repro; (2) a **baseline** to measure against, captured before you start (the pre-existing count, the current state) so the reader can tell a new occurrence from the existing one; (3) a **control run** that should produce *nothing*, because a positive with no negative doesn't isolate the cause; (4) the **expected output** — the literal log lines or values that constitute a confirmed repro, plus what a non-repro looks like and what it would mean. Add an explicit note when a step writes real prod state, so the executor knows the cost before running it. The tell you're about to get this wrong: a numbered step whose verb is a paraphrase ("restart the runtime", "trigger the job", "make it fail") with no command under it.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer with a real round-trip (untagged — no automation halted, but the operator had to spend a message auditing my work). Having root-caused a prod anomaly on plow-pbc/plow and filed plow-pbc/plow#1205 for another machine to reproduce, my "Repro plan" section read as prose — step 2 was literally "Kill plowd (or restart the runtime)" with no command, no baseline, no control, and no statement of what a confirmed repro looks like. The operator, who had already said he'd have a second machine attempt it, came back with a one-line audit — did the repro steps actually get in there clearly? Rewriting it produced the four parts above and, in the process, surfaced two things the prose version had hidden: the control case is what makes the result mean anything (the same box had 138 restarts and one POST, so "it fired" proves nothing without "and it didn't fire when Settings was closed"), and one variant writes real billing state that has to be reverted. Both belonged in the issue, and neither would have existed without the rewrite. Next instance: any repo where you file an issue, write a runbook, or hand an agent a brief that another party is expected to *run* rather than read.

## Polling a log to confirm your own action: anchor the match to your nonce/timestamp — an OR-grep plus a presence test happily matches the PREVIOUS run
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`: when a verification loop polls a log/journal for "did my action land", the success pattern must be anchored to *this* invocation — the nonce you sent, or a `--since` clamped to the moment you sent it. The failure shape is a two-alternative grep (`grep -E "$NONCE|phase=sent"`) followed by a presence test on one alternative (`grep -q "phase=sent"`): the window still holds the previous run's success line, the test fires on it, and the loop reports VERIFIED before your action has produced anything. A wall-clock `--since` is not the fix by itself — the journal's clock may be a different timezone than the timestamps inside the log lines, so a UTC value silently reads as future-local and returns "No entries", which looks like a clean failure rather than a broken query.
**Why (autonomy):** Self-caught, and recorded because it nearly published a false claim: driving a filesystem-touching probe through a real install, my poll printed VERIFIED on a `phase=sent` line emitted 38 seconds *before* the probe was even sent — the prior turn's reply, still inside a 4-minute window. Re-checking with the send time as the floor showed the real delivery had not landed yet; it arrived 38s later. The skill I was following had even warned that `phase=sent` alone can fire from an unrelated action, and the OR-grep defeated the warning. Next instance: any "wait for my thing to appear in the log" loop — CI, journald, a queue's audit table — where the log also carries other actors' success lines.


### +1 — 2026-08-25 · str2-plow-plugin-upstream-138 · the same trap fires on a NEGATIVE predicate, when the string you exclude appears in the thing you are waiting for
**Change (extends):** Anchoring applies to exclusions too, and there the failure is silent in the other direction — you wait forever instead of matching early. Build a wake/health predicate from a **positive marker unique to the event** (the bot's own HTML comment, a nonce you emitted, a run id), never from "everything except <string>": the string you are filtering out is routinely present in the very artifact you are waiting for, because bots document their own trigger commands in their footers. Same rule on the presence side: a count over a log that is never truncated says nothing about *this* boot — compare the newest match against the process start time, and treat a non-zero count as necessary, not sufficient. **Next instance:** any watcher keyed on another system's output — a CI log tail, a deploy watcher, a queue consumer filtering its own echoes.
**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — twice in one session the operator had to ask ("did you see the new review?", "there's another review?") because an armed Monitor could never fire: its filter excluded any comment containing `/srosro-update-review`, and the reviewer's own footer documents that command on every review it posts. *The unblock* — the operator's prompt, both times; the fix was to require the reviewer's `auto-post` marker instead of excluding text. The presence-side half bit the same session in a deployed skill: a smoke step counted `websocket connected` in a never-truncated log, so it stayed non-zero from a boot **17 hours** before the container started, on a gateway that was healthy — the count passed and only the timestamp comparison exposed it.

## [removes-handback] When the ideal deliverable is blocked, enumerate what IS runnable before reporting blocked
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps`: on hitting a blocker, do not report "blocked" in terms of what the deliverable *should* be. List the deliverable's inputs, mark each ready / partial / blocked, and ask what a **complete subset** produces — then ship that subset with its caveats stated in the same breath (which rows are degraded and why, what sample it rests on, which number is uninformative by construction). Withholding everything is correct only when no honest subset exists, which is rarer than it feels. The tell that you are about to get this wrong: your blocker sentence describes the ideal artifact rather than enumerating the inputs. Next instance: a deploy blocked on one environment's credentials — enumerate which environments *are* deployable and ship those; a migration blocked on one table; a report blocked on one data source.
**Why (autonomy):** hard stop, twice. Asked to run a benchmark comparison, I reported it unrunnable — one system's retrieval path was broken and the other's ingest was ~50% done — and framed the refusal as principled ("I'd rather hand you a blocked-and-documented comparison than a table built on a system that can't do dense retrieval"). ## An intentional opt-out and a real limitation print the SAME error — read the governing config before asserting a capability limit
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`, next to the existing "It can't run here" bullet: when a runtime reports a capability as unavailable, inspect the local config that could have disabled it *on purpose* (a per-model/per-service parameter, a unit drop-in, an env override, a feature flag) before concluding the platform or build lacks the capability. Ask "would a deliberate opt-out look identical to this?" — if yes, the check is mandatory. Test the override **non-destructively** (a per-request parameter, a one-shot env var, a shadow copy) rather than editing the operator's stored config. If the opt-out turns out deliberate, surface it and confirm intent before routing work around it — the setting is usually protecting a resource for something else. Related but distinct from the enforcer rule (§ "A self-healing enforcer on wrong-looking state means intentional"): there is no reconciler here to grep for, just a static parameter. Next instance: any "unsupported / not available / can't run here" signal from a service you don't administer — a driver capability, a disabled API surface, a build flag, a quota that is actually a configured cap.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged — no round-trip was halted, but a wrong published conclusion shipped and cost hours). Benchmarking local embedding models on a GPU host, three of four loaded on CPU while the card sat idle, logging `no usable GPU found, --gpu-layers option will be ignored`. I read that as the build lacking a CUDA path for embedding models, published a comparison table showing the one unpinned model as "10× faster", and wrote it into a reference memory. The operator asked whether the CPU placement had been configured manually — every one of those models carried an explicit `num_gpu 0` in its local model definition. Re-measured fairly (per-request override, no stored config touched), the real gap was 1.4×, not 10×. The wrong conclusion then drove a multi-hour rebuild on a model that measured *worse* and had to be reverted. The generalized move — read the governing config before asserting the limit — is what makes the next such call self-serviceable. Promoted from the `check-deliberate-config-before-inferring-capability` feedback memory. (Session: 2026-08-04-msgvault-vector-search)

## [removes-handback] A component the user NAMES in a cleanup/DRY ask earns a decision you deliver in the same turn, not a question handed back

What this rule forbids is the third option: returning the analysis with the named target silently left out and waiting. ## Accepting a "delete this guard" probe: write down what the guard SELECTS first — an optimization framing makes a correctness guard look free
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md` § Anti-Bloat (as the counterweight to "prefer the subtractive remedy"): before applying a reviewer probe that deletes a conditional, state in one sentence which *case* the guard selects, then ask what the guarded statement means in the other case. If the answer is "nothing to do", the guard is structural and the deletion changes behavior — decline and record why. If it is genuinely "the same thing, just redundant", delete it. The tell that you're about to get this wrong is your own justification being about **cost** ("saves an idempotent call", "avoids a redundant write") rather than about **which case reaches the line**. A green suite is not the check: the case a guard selects is exactly the case least likely to already have a test.
**Why (autonomy):** Not a hard stop — a reviewer round-trip, recorded because it nearly shipped a user-visible regression and the failure was in my reasoning, not the bot's. On `plow-pbc/plow#1177` a `[simplification]` probe asked to drop a same-side billing guard on a rollback path; I applied it and wrote the rationale myself as "the notify is idempotent and a restart failure is rare, so a redundant restore beats a special-case branch." That framing is what made it look free. It wasn't an optimization: a compensating call only *exists* when the preference actually moved, so firing it unconditionally let a same-side switch fail on a call that had nothing to undo — skipping the config rollback below it and stranding the status surface on a model the runtime wasn't serving, the exact defect the PR existed to fix. The next review asked for the guard back; restoring it with the correct rationale (and a matrix row that goes red on removal, mutation-verified) converged the round. Distinct from "re-run the first mutation after the cut" (verification *after*) and from "revert a new guard and confirm the test goes red" (proving a guard you just wrote) — this one fires at the moment you decide to accept the deletion. Next instance: any repo where a bot files a `[simplification]` probe against an `if` on an error/compensation path and the diff looks purely subtractive. (Session: 2026-08-04-plow-stranded-roots)

## [removes-handback] The record already answers it → apply and cite; deferring on YOUR uncertainty is not an operator decision
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps`: before routing a decision to the operator as "their call", check whether the record already settles it — the repo's README/spec/posture file, a ruling recorded when closing an issue or PR, or a comment in the code stating the rule. If it does, derive the consequence, apply it, and cite the source in the change. Reserve the hand-back for a record that is genuinely silent, or two documented principles that actually conflict. **The discriminator is whose uncertainty you're acting on:** if your stated reason for deferring is about *your* confidence — "I've misread this ruling before", "I don't want to overstep on user-facing copy" — that's over-gating, not deference. A prior error of yours in restating a ruling's *mechanism details* is not evidence its *core principle* is unclear; those are different things, and conflating them turns your own error into a reason to slow the operator down. Distinct from the "chain the obvious authorized next step" rule above, which keys on the operator having already said yes; this one keys on the answer being *written down* whether or not anyone said anything.
**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — a `[blocking]` reviewer probe found a README section contradicting a ruling the operator had recorded months earlier when closing an issue. I filed a *new* issue for it and declined the fix in-PR, arguing that rewriting a user-facing claim about measurement validity was an operator judgment — and named my own two earlier misquotes of that same ruling as the reason to defer. *The unblock* — the operator quoted his own ruling back and asked whether it wasn't already a clear-enough point in the docs to act on without his POV. It was: applying it took one commit, and the issue I'd filed closed the same session having added no information. Second instance in the same session, same root: after he had answered a framing question in conversation, I re-raised it in three consecutive turn-final summaries until he replied that he was confused about what I was even asking. Next instance: any repo where a doc, spec, or closed-issue ruling already implies the change and the temptation is to file-and-defer because the edit is user-facing. (Session: 2026-08-04-memeval3-review-posture)

## [removes-handback] A least-privilege improvement you spot mid-task is not a precondition — reuse the existing credential when blast radius is unchanged, and narrow at the boundary change
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Lean Less Conservative: when wiring a new consumer (repo, service, job) to an existing credential, and you notice the credential is broader than the new consumer strictly needs, do NOT convert that observation into a blocker ("first mint a narrowed service account, then…"). Ask what the change does to **blast radius**: if the new consumer sits inside the same trust boundary as the existing ones — same org, same operators, same push access — reusing the credential adds no reachable principal, so reuse it now and file the narrowing. Bind the narrowing to the moment the boundary *actually* moves (the repo going public, an outside collaborator gaining write, the credential crossing an org edge) — that is when the calculus changes and the work has a real trigger instead of a vague "we should." Stating a hardening as a gate you impose on yourself is the same over-conservatism as absorbing a reviewer's YAGNI guard; it just wears a security costume.
**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — handing back the plow-mac extraction, I wrote that the new repo should get a *newly minted, narrowed* 1Password service account rather than the existing one, and listed it as a thing the operator had to do. *The unblock* — "why have a new token?" The honest answer was that it changed nothing: the repo was private, only org members could dispatch its workflows, and every one of them already held the same token through the source monorepo. The narrowing is real work, but its trigger is the public flip, not this task. Reused the existing token, set it myself, and noted the narrowing against the visibility change instead.

## [removes-handback] Root cause established + remedy mechanical, reversible, and already backed up → apply it and report; the confirm is the hand-back

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps`: once (a) root cause is established, (b) the remedy is mechanical and verifiable by an existing check, and (c) a recovery path already exists (backup taken, state committed/pushed), **apply it** — then report what changed and the verification result. Do not end the turn on "want me to apply the repair?". Under a standing autonomous mandate this confirm is not caution, it is the hand-back the mandate exists to remove: the human must re-engage to say yes to work you have already fully specified and de-risked. Reserve the confirm for a remedy that is *irreversible*, *not yet root-caused*, or *ambiguous between two defensible outcomes* — none of which survive (a)–(c).
**Why (autonomy):** stop — having root-caused a corpus defect and established the fix was a lossless mechanical move verifiable by an existing test suite, with a filesystem backup and the prior state pushed to a remote, I still ended the turn asking permission to apply it. unblock — the human's next message was "is it repaired? are we done?", and they had already applied and merged the repair themselves. The whole round-trip was avoidable: every input to the decision was already in hand. Next instance: any repo where debugging converges on a scripted, test-verifiable fix and a backup already exists — apply, verify, report; the report is where the human exercises judgement, not a pre-approval gate.

## [removes-handback] A closing issue is not a handoff surface — move its cross-cutting decisions out before it closes

If so, **re-post that decision on the surviving owner issue** (the umbrella/epic, or the issue that consumes it) before closing. A closed issue's comments are not a handoff surface: they are off the default issue list, and the next agent picking up the parent will not find them. The test is not "is this issue done" but "would someone starting from the parent issue tomorrow have everything they need?"
