## [removes-handback] A bug report is a user ACTION that failed — trace that action's path before designing the fix, not the adjacent path you happen to be reading
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`: when the report is "I did X and it didn't work", identify the code path **X actually traverses** and confirm your fix sits on it, before writing the fix. Reading the code first inverts this: you find the path you can see, generalize the failure from *that* path's shape, and ship a change that is correct, tested, reviewed, and on the wrong branch of the system. The check is one question — *"which line does the user's own action reach?"* — and it costs nothing next to a merged PR that does not address the report. Especially load-bearing when the failing artifact could have been produced two ways (by the agent vs by the human), because the artifact itself does not record which.
**Why (autonomy):** the stop — asked why a message in a new group thread went unanswered, I traced the thread to an agent-initiated creation path, built the fix there (subscribe the chat id that path's own send returns), took it through two review rounds to convergence, and handed it off as done. It was merged. the unblock — the operator asked, in substance, *"so every time I start a thread I have to edit config and restart? sending that message in a new group would not enable it automatically?"* — which surfaced that his actual action (starting a thread from his handset) never passes through the path I had fixed at all. A whole PR's authoring + review budget spent on the narrower half of the problem. The real fix was a deletion in a different place, found in one API probe once the right path was named. **Next instance:** "clicking Save doesn't persist" — drive the button and watch which handler runs, rather than fixing the API endpoint you were already reading.

## [removes-handback] Establish POC-vs-product at brainstorming time — it sets the review budget, not just the LOC target
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Answer Shape` (or brainstorming's context step): before writing a plan, ask — or state and let the operator correct — whether the thing is a **proof of concept** or a **product**. It is one sentence and it prices everything downstream: the LOC target, the test depth, and above all **how many review rounds are worth running**. On a POC the correct answer to a structural review finding is usually "decline on the operating point and merge", because the code may not survive the week; rewriting working, verified code to satisfy a shape argument is most expensive exactly when it is least likely to last. Corollary for the review loop: an autonomous reviewer has no natural stopping point and will produce findings indefinitely, so *someone* must decide when it stops paying — watch for the treadmill tell, where round N's findings are mostly defects introduced fixing round N-1's, and say so plainly rather than continuing.
**Why (autonomy):** the stop — built a house-hunting skill, opened a PR, and babysat it through **eight** review rounds. From about round four the loop was net-negative: rounds 5-8 were largely fixing bugs I had introduced in rounds 4-7 (an SSRF guard, then an IPv6 spelling bypass in that guard, then a DNS-rebinding window in the fix for that). Across those rounds I ended turn after turn handing back the same unanswered question — "split into three PRs, or keep iterating?" — because the bot kept firing a size/stall trigger and I treated the scope call as the operator's. **the unblock** — the operator said, in substance, *"honestly this is a poc — what's your recommendation?"*. That single frame flipped the answer to every open structural question from "apply" to "decline and merge", and the PR merged in the next turn. Nothing about the code changed; only the price of rigor did. **Next instance:** a throwaway data-migration script gets a reviewer finding about missing retry/backoff — POC framing means decline it, run the migration, delete the script.

## [removes-handback] On a personal-scale tool, lead with the zero-infra option even when the user named a branded one
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Default to the Simplifying Option`: when a *personal* tool's request names a branded dependency ("a Google map", "put it in Postgres") **and** also signals low operational appetite ("ideally no server", "keep it simple"), surface the no-key/no-account/no-deploy substitute as the leading option with its capability cost named — don't silently honor the brand and don't present the two as equal-weight. The brand is usually shorthand for the capability, not a requirement. This is a scoped **refinement** of that section's carve-out (simplification must never shed runtime capability): on personal tools the operator will trade a modest capability loss to remove infrastructure. It does not extend to product or fleet work, where the carve-out stands.
**Why (autonomy):** the stop — asked to build a map of properties with "ideally no server", I surfaced a three-option menu whose recommended pick was Google Maps on a `file://` page with an unrestricted API key, and ended the turn asking which way to go. the unblock — the operator replied that OpenStreetMap was fine, *especially* if it meant no server. Leaflet + OSM needs no key, no account, and no quota, and the capability delta (satellite imagery) was irrelevant to the actual use. The whole round-trip existed because I ranked brand fidelity above the constraint the operator had already stated in the same sentence. **Next instance:** "a Slack notifier, but I don't want to run anything" → lead with an incoming-webhook URL over a bot app with OAuth and a hosted callback.

## Never `cd` inside a Bash tool call — the next call inherits it; use the tool's own path flag or a subshell
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Which machine you're on (or a new § Tool Use): the Bash tool's working directory **persists across calls**, so a `cd sub/dir && <cmd>` silently relocates every later call in the session. Reach for the command's own path flag instead — `git -C <dir>`, `uv run --project <dir>`, `pytest <path>`, `npm --prefix <dir>`, `make -C <dir>`, `cargo --manifest-path` — or, when a tool genuinely has none, scope the move with a subshell: `( cd <dir> && <cmd> )`. The tell that you've already drifted is an error naming a doubled or truncated path (`app/plowd/app/plowd/tests/…`, `no such file or directory: app/plowd`) or a build tool insisting a recipe doesn't exist when it plainly does — read those as "wrong cwd", not "wrong path argument", and re-anchor rather than editing the path. Next instance: any repo with a nested package — `cd frontend && npm test` followed by a `git add src/…` that resolves against `frontend/`, or a monorepo where the second call lands in a sibling service's tree and edits the wrong file.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged) — no operator round-trip; each failure was self-caught and re-run. Recorded because it was the single largest source of wasted calls in the session and it is purely mechanical: six failed Bash invocations across one PR-babysitting session, every one the same root cause. After `cd app/plowd && uv run pytest …`, the following calls tried `just lint` (→ `Justfile does not contain recipe 'lint'`), `git add app/plowd/tests/test_release_scripts.py` (→ `could not open directory 'app/plowd/app/plowd/tests/'`, then `fatal: ambiguous argument … not in the working tree`), and `sed -n '42,66p' app/scripts/upload-runtime-artifacts.sh` (→ `No such file or directory`). Two of those aborted a `git commit` that had to be re-issued. The harness even prints the rule in the Bash tool description; knowing it is not the same as never `cd`-ing. Worth noting the sharper edge the session didn't hit: the drifted call *failing* is the lucky case — a path that happens to resolve in the wrong tree succeeds silently against the wrong files. (Session: 2026-08-18 · plow3-oss-licenses-and-partial-bump)

### +1 — 2026-08-21 · plow4-drop-browser-container · the drift silently retargeted a *skill's own* helper script, not just a shell command

**Change:** Add the shape this instance adds: the drifted cwd doesn't only break the command you typed — it silently reparameterizes tooling that *derives* a path from cwd. `/cleanup`'s `mine-transcript.py` resolves the transcript directory from the working directory, so after an earlier `cd app/plowd && uv run pytest`, it aborted with `no *.jsonl transcript under …-Users-so-Hacking-plow4-app-plowd` — a project directory that has never existed. Same session also produced the doubled-path tell twice (`could not open directory 'app/plowd/app/plowd/tests/'` and `…/app/plowd/plowd/`). The generalization: after any `cd`, treat every *cwd-derived* value as suspect, not just relative path arguments — and prefer `uv run --project <dir>` / `pytest <path>` so the drift never happens. **Next instance:** any harness or skill helper that keys state off cwd — a session-scoped cache dir, a `.env` discovery walk, a monorepo tool that infers the package from where it was invoked.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged) — self-caught and re-run, no operator round-trip. Recorded because it is the second session in a row where the same mechanical error cost real calls, and because this instance shows the failure reaching *past* the shell into skill tooling, where the error message names a path the operator has never seen and reads like a broken script rather than a wrong cwd.

## "This is covered by a test" is a claim — prove it by mutation before asserting it, especially when arguing to KEEP something
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`: before writing "this is covered" / "this is load-bearing" / "this test pins X" — in a commit message, a review reply, or a code comment — **delete or invert the thing and watch a named test fail**. If nothing fails, the claim is false and the coverage does not exist. This is the test-coverage case of the section's existing rule that an absence claim carries the same burden as a positive one. It bites hardest when arguing to *retain* something a reviewer wants deleted: that is precisely when the claim decides the outcome and nobody else will check it. When the mutation refutes you, delete and say so — do not reshape the artifact to manufacture the coverage after the fact.
**Why (autonomy):** the stop — twice in one session a coverage claim of mine survived only because nothing checked it. First, a regression test written to pin a newly-required field asserted on an error message that an *earlier-checked* field also produced, so deleting the rule it existed to protect left it green; the reviewer caught that it "passes for the wrong reason". Then, arguing that two captured-fixture nodes were load-bearing coverage — reasoning from key ordering and traversal logic read out of the source — and the reviewer showed the search reaches the target node first regardless, so neither was ever exercised. **the unblock** — in both cases the reviewer supplied the mechanism I had not tested; deleting each node in turn confirmed 54 tests passed either way, and both came out. **Next instance:** before telling a reviewer "that guard is covered by `test_retry_on_timeout`", comment the guard out and confirm that exact test goes red.

## [removes-handback] Declining a blocking finding because a guardrail bars the remedy? Verify the remedy would even WORK, and whether it covers the whole surface, before handing it back
**Change:** When a reviewer's blocking finding proposes a remedy your guardrails forbid (force-push, prod write, destructive migration), the hand-back is not "I can't do X" — that hands the operator unverified work. Before declining, run two checks you *can* run: (a) **efficacy** — would X actually achieve the stated goal? and (b) **scope** — does X cover the whole affected surface, or only the slice this PR touches? Either check failing changes the deliverable from "please do X for me" into a filed decision with the real options. Next instance: a reviewer asks for a destructive prod backfill you're not authorized to run — measure whether the backfill fixes the rows it claims to, and whether the same corruption exists outside its WHERE clause, before escalating.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — a security probe demanded rewriting a PR's commits to scrub archive-derived identities; the babysit loop bars force-push, so I declined it and handed the rewrite to the operator as a to-do. unblock — the operator asked what I actually thought of the probe, and investigating produced the two findings that mattered: fetching the commit by SHA showed a force-push does **not** unpublish it (GitHub serves pushed objects by SHA regardless of branch state), and the same identities sat on `main` independently, so the rewrite would have closed the thread while the larger exposure stayed. That turned a bare hand-back into a filed repo-level decision with a surface table splitting editable-in-place from genuinely-unfixable. The efficacy check is what the operator's question extracted, and it is runnable without any of the barred permissions. (Session: 2026-08-18-ltmm-poc2-windowing)

## [removes-handback] Open the PR at the first shippable increment, not the last — don't accumulate rounds of commits on an unpushed branch
**Change:** Treat "push the branch and open a PR" as firing at the first coherent, tested increment, not when the whole feature is done. Until the PR exists there is nothing to link, nothing for CI to run, and no way for the operator to see progress except by asking. Local-only commits also strand the per-commit review findings behind a push gate that then gets exercised all at once at the end, so a blocked push is discovered late instead of immediately. When reporting status mid-stream and no PR exists yet, say so explicitly rather than describing commits as though they were visible somewhere. Next instance: a multi-day refactor in any repo — open the PR after the first passing slice and keep pushing to it, rather than presenting eleven commits at the end.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — the operator asked "do you have the pr url?" after I had landed eleven commits on a branch that had never been pushed; the answer was that no PR existed, which is a round-trip that only happened because I was hoarding. unblock — that question is what got the branch pushed and the PR opened, after which every later round had a durable surface to report against. (Session: 2026-08-18-ltmm-poc2-windowing)

### +1 — 2026-08-11 · kwr-session-1acdbf64 · the local pre-push review gate is what makes the unpushed loop unbounded
**Change:** Treat a local pre-push review gate as a reason to push sooner, not a bar to clear before pushing. Push once the work is coherent and the suite is green, even with local findings still open, and list them in the PR body. Reserve pre-push rounds for defects that would make the PR misleading to read, such as a broken build or a false claim in the body. A finding in another file or subsystem means file it and push, not widen the local loop.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — on a knightwatch-reviewer PR I ran several local fix → roborev → fix cycles before the branch was ever pushed, and the operator had to ask "do you have the pr url?". Prior authority — `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps` already chains build → PR → babysit as one authorized flow. Unblock — the operator's question, which got the branch pushed and the PR opened.
**Next instance:** a solo feature in any roborev-gated repo where each fix commit enqueues a fresh local review — open the PR after the first round, not after the gate goes quiet.

## A long unattended job whose work is RESUMABLE should be launched under a bounded retry supervisor, not bare
**Change:** Before backgrounding a multi-hour job (a seed, a batch, a sweep), ask whether its work is *resumable* — does it checkpoint, and does re-invoking pick up where it stopped? When yes, launch it under a bounded shell supervisor that re-invokes on non-zero exit (capped attempts, logged per attempt) rather than bare. A single transient network blip otherwise kills the run and it then sits dead until someone happens to look; the resumability that makes the retry safe is usually already built and already tested. Bounded, so a genuinely-down dependency still stops. This is an *operational wrapper around a job you are running*, not shipped retry machinery in the product — it composes with, rather than contradicts, "ship fail-loud, not retry machinery" (which governs the product fix and asks for evidence the fault recovers; a supervisor is how you gather that evidence). Next instance: a long CI-driven data migration or an overnight index rebuild that writes progress rows — wrap the invocation, don't just `nohup` it.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — a 387-window seed died twice on one un-retried HTTP timeout and sat dead for **3 hours** before I noticed while checking status for an unrelated question; the same fault later killed a judge run outright. unblock — checking the host showed it healthy (HTTP 200 in 5 ms, generating normally) and the store already resumable (`369 windows to process (18 already done)` with prior facts intact), so a six-line supervisor recovered the run and it completed. The evidence the supervisor gathered — three occurrences, healthy host, graceful resumption — is also what justified the durable in-product fix as a filed issue rather than a guess. (Session: 2026-08-18-ltmm-poc2-windowing)

## [removes-handback] Independent paths failing IDENTICALLY indict the shared input — decode your own fixture before blaming a provider or dependency
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`: when two independent consumers (two providers, two routes, two versions) fail the *same* way on the same artifact, that is evidence about what they SHARE — usually the input you generated — not corroboration that both are broken. Before filing a defect against a provider, dependency, or account entitlement, decode the fixture the way the consumer will (pixel/byte level, not a preview or a viewer) and assert the property you're relying on. Convenience viewers normalize; consumers don't. Corollary: a cross-consumer *disagreement* about one artifact is also a statement about the artifact — investigate it before the consumer, because a provider defect is the less likely explanation. Next instance: any repo where a generated fixture — a synthetic PDF, an encoded audio clip, a fabricated JSON payload, a screenshot — underwrites a conclusion about third-party behavior.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — plow-pbc/plow#1260 / #1261. I generated an OCR probe image with a tool whose output I never inspected structurally; it had a transparent background, which one provider composites onto black, so it read as a blank page. I took two "no text" results through different routes as convergent evidence of an upstream defect, filed an issue against the provider, used the false conclusion as a load-bearing argument against a design change the operator had asked for, and handed back a blocker that did not exist ("OCR still fails; needs a top-up or the upstream fix"). unblock — the operator decoded the PNG, found every pixel was RGB(0,0,0) with an alpha-0 background, re-ran the probe flattened onto white through all three configurations, and closed the issue as invalid. The tell I walked past: the same file rendered fine in my own terminal, because that composites onto white. Promoted from the `suspect-the-fixture-before-the-dependency` feedback memory. (Session: 2026-08-14-plow1-ocr-billing-fallback)

## [removes-handback] You flagged an assumption as unverified — that is a deploy gate, not a caveat to carry into production
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`: when you have written down that a change rests on an assumption you could not verify, that sentence **blocks the deploy**, not just the claim of doneness. Merge may proceed on the code's merits; shipping it to a running system may not, until the assumption is settled or the blast radius of it being false is known and acceptable. The tell that you are about to violate this: a deploy step whose own PR description contains the words "unverified", "pending", "still open", or a stated fallback plan of *closing* the PR. Reviewing your own hedge and shipping anyway converts an honest caveat into an outage with a paper trail proving you saw it coming — and the paper trail is worse than no note at all, because it establishes the failure was foreseen and overridden. If the assumption can only be settled in production, deploy behind something reversible in one step and verify *first*, before declaring the deploy complete.
**Why (autonomy):** the stop — I wrote in a PR that a websocket delivery contract was unverified and that if it proved false "this PR should be closed, not patched." It merged; I then deployed it, and it made a live agent deaf on every conversation including the operator's own, because the untested socket delivered frames with no payload. The operator lost message reception until I noticed and rolled back. the unblock — his pointer to the vendor's own documentation, which had stated the answer the whole time; nothing about the failure required production to discover. **Next instance:** a migration whose PR says "assumes no rows have NULL in this column, not checked against prod" — run the count before the deploy, not after the constraint fails. Related: the probe-property `+1` above, on how to settle the assumption once you have stopped.

## A warning states consequences, not remedies — and a remedy smuggled back in usually turns out to be false
**Change:** When writing a warning (a README banner, a runbook caution, a destructive-command notice), include only what happens, what it costs, and whether it can be undone. Leave out remediation — "the safe way to do this", a pre-flight checklist, "the routes that work". Preparing a safe version is a different task on a different day; guessing at it inside the warning makes it longer, less pointed, and frequently wrong, because implying an action helps requires an efficacy claim a pure consequence statement never has to make. Irreversibility *is* a consequence, so keep it and verify it. Reread the draft sentence by sentence asking "is this what happens, or what someone should do about it?" and cut the second kind; if a fact only matters because it implies an action, it belongs in an issue. Next instance: a runbook caution for a destructive migration in another repo — say it drops the table and cannot be rolled back, don't inline a backup procedure that may not match how that database is actually snapshotted.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged) — no hand-back; the operator redirected a README warning with "we don't need to suggest a fix, just make the consequences clear", trimming a two-route safe-publication procedure I had written into it. What earns the entry is what happened *after* the trim: across the next four rounds I reintroduced remedies three separate times, each disguised as a consequence, and **each one was factually wrong precisely because it was prescriptive** — a "still editable right up until it happens" framing of identifiers that were already in git history (so editing recovered nothing), a surface list that read as a pre-flight checklist, and a trailing claim about what had been done to the history that took three narrowing rounds before deletion turned out to be the fix. The reviewer caught the first two; the third I only resolved by deleting rather than rewording. A single trim did not generalize on its own, which is what makes it corpus material rather than a one-off correction. (Session: 2026-08-19-ltmm-poc2-warning)


## [removes-handback] An external capability is a claim too — a request shape being ACCEPTED is not evidence the behaviour exists

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`, as the inverse of the external-blocker family: when a design rests on how a third-party API *behaves*, read the vendor docs for that endpoint and capture one real payload before building on it. A `201`, a socket that connects and holds, and an optional field the schema accepts are all statements about the *request*, not the response you need. The discriminating experiment is a side-by-side: run the mode you trust and the mode you're assuming next to each other against one real event, because a single unproven channel seeing nothing is indistinguishable from "nothing happened". When the fact needs a human action you can't perform, ask for it as one explicit line rather than inferring and proceeding.

**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — a change shipped on "the endpoint returns 201 for a body with the chat id omitted", which read as an account-wide subscribe mode. It connected, stayed open for minutes, and delivered frames carrying no type and no payload; the gateway went deaf on **every** chat including the operator's own DM, in production. The docs never described that mode — the field is merely optional. *The unblock* — the operator's steer to go read the vendor docs, which settled it in one page; later in the same effort a second unverifiable field was settled by capturing one live frame, which then deleted a whole caching layer built to work around not knowing. Next instance: any undocumented parameter, assumed webhook, or "this field will be there" on a third-party payload.

## [removes-handback] A reversal of your OWN endorsed recommendation needs an explicit yes — announcing the flip is not ratification
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps`: when you recommended an approach, the operator engaged with it, and later evidence makes you want to reverse that recommendation, stating the reversal in passing does not ratify it. Stop and get an explicit yes on the flipped decision before anything downstream depends on it — most sharply when the reversal moves a security boundary, changes where code executes, or lands the work in a different repo than the one the operator agreed to. The correct shape is not to halt: do every part that does not depend on the flip, ship the rest under an explicitly stated assumption, and name the unratified decision as its own line in the hand-off.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — promoted from this project's feedback ledger, and it fired live this session: I recommended a fix, investigation then showed that fix could only land in a third-party repo, and the temptation was to quietly build something else in its place under the operator's original "write a PR". unblock — the operator's standing directive is that a flip gets an explicit yes first; following it produced a PR that shipped the achievable half with the trade-off stated, instead of a silent substitution the operator would have discovered at merge time. Next instance: any session where a design you already sold the operator on is invalidated mid-implementation — a different repo, a different subsystem.

## [removes-handback] A bounded job that overruns its stated window isn't dead — widen the wait before declaring it orphaned and handing back
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`: when a process with a documented duration (a review bot's "20–40 min", a CI job's typical runtime, a deploy, a migration) overruns, do NOT convert "past the window" into "it's dead" and end the loop with a hand-back. The stated range is a p50/p90, not a ceiling. Widen the wait at least once; reserve the orphaned/hung call for *positive* evidence that the runner is gone (no container, released lock, exited process, absent run dir), never for elapsed time alone. This is the section's own negative-claim burden applied to time — "it's dead" is an absence claim and owes the same proof as "it isn't in the database". The asymmetry is what makes it worth a rule: one more wait cycle costs a wake, while a wrong death-call ends the loop and costs an operator round-trip that only they can restart.
**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — on `plow-pbc/plow#1303` knightwatch's `👀 reviewing` placeholder had been up 59 min against its documented 20–40 min window. I declared the run orphaned, stopped the babysit loop, and handed back three paths I claimed were all blocked (push gated by the in-flight hook, re-trigger forbidden by a standing owner instruction, waiting pointless because nothing was running). *The unblock* — nothing was needed: the review landed at ~60 min on its own, and the entire hand-back was moot. I had also asserted "no reviewer run is alive" from a `pgrep` that only showed an unrelated tmux session — checking the reviewer's own run state was the available positive evidence and I skipped it. Next instance: a CI job documented at ~10 min sitting at 18, or a deploy past its usual window — widen once before calling it hung.

## [removes-handback] The pre-PR roborev drain has no stall lens — the rule that supplies one lives inside `babysit-pr`, which hasn't started yet
**Change:** `babysit-pr` § Step 6.6 already states the rule: roborev "reviews each commit's diff in isolation — no PR-intent fence, no cumulative-LOC trigger, no cross-commit stall lens — so it is a leaf-fix generator by construction", and the driver must supply the same-class-stall test (§ 6.5) and the cumulative-LOC ledger (§ 6.8) it structurally can't. But that text only fires once the babysit loop is running — i.e. after `gh pr create`. The drain that happens *before* the first push, the one `CLAUDE.md § Commit Frequently` mandates at every commit, has no such lens: every finding is correct in isolation, each one clears the pre-push gate, and nothing asks whether the class has stopped converging. Mirror the two checks into the `roborev` skill's own triage contract so they apply from the first commit rather than from the first PR.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — srosro/ltmm-poc#40 ran ~15 roborev rounds and eleven doc-only commits *before the PR was ever opened*, and the pre-push gate denied three separate times, each denial sending me into another round rather than prompting a class-level question. Every individual finding was correct; I cleared each as a gate to satisfy. unblock — knightwatch, on round 2 of the PR that finally existed, firing its LOC-growth callout. That was the first moment anything applied a whole-PR lens, ~15 rounds too late, and the `CLAUDE.md § Concise Code` churn tells (add-then-cut, findings concentrating in one subsystem) had all been present since round 5. Next instance: any repo with roborev installed where an agent builds a branch to review-ready before opening a PR — the leaf-fix generator runs unsupervised for the whole pre-PR phase.

### +1 — 2026-08-26 · claude-config6-slot-lane-rules · the finding-count RATIO against the PR reviewer is a sharper stall tell than same-class-3-rounds

**Change:** Add a mechanical tell alongside the class-recurrence one: when the cheap per-commit reviewer's finding count on a single artifact exceeds the expensive whole-PR reviewer's by an order of magnitude, the *artifact* is the defect — not any individual finding. It needs no class judgment and fires earlier than "same class 3 rounds", because each finding can be a genuinely different and correct defect while the ratio still holds. The remedy is the § Concise Code structural move aimed at the artifact: cut it back to the rule and stop specifying, rather than answering facet N+1. **Next instance:** any repo with both reviewers installed where one function or one paragraph keeps drawing local findings while the PR reviewer has moved on.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged) — self-caught, no operator round-trip spent. Recorded because the numbers were stark and available in real time: across `srosro/claude-config#176`, knightwatch raised **2 probes total over 3 reviews** (both real, both applied), while roborev produced roughly **40 findings across ~35 rounds**, about 30 of them on a single paragraph of one bullet, and the pre-push gate denied 9 separate times. Every roborev finding was correct about the text in front of it; the sequence — add a clause, be told to cut it, be told the cut left a gap — is what the ratio exposes and no single finding does. Two structural cuts of that paragraph (drop the embedded shell procedure; drop the local-anchor preservation step) each converged the local reviewer to "No issues found" immediately, which is the confirmation that the artifact rather than the findings was the problem.

## A reviewer's "delete X until real assets exist" judges the CONTENT, not the mechanism — keep the scaffold and ask the owner
**Change:** Add to `REVIEW_PRACTICES.md` (bot-findings neighborhood, near `CODING_STANDARDS.md § Broken-Glass`): when a reviewer's remedy is to DELETE a working section/component because its current *content* is placeholder — stub art, sample data, lorem copy, wrong-product imagery — split the finding in two before acting. Is the **mechanism** wrong, or is the **content** temporary? Only the first justifies deletion. A reviewer sees the repo and nothing else: it cannot know a designer is reshooting the art or that copy is in review, so placeholder content reads to it as permanent. Default to keeping the scaffold, replying that the placeholder is tracked, and asking the owner. Repeatedly flagging the placeholder without a reply is not consent to delete it. Corollary when you keep it: if the placeholder assets are **shared with another page**, decouple them onto their own filenames first — otherwise the eventual replacement silently mutates that other page too.
**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — on `plow-pbc/plow#1303` knightwatch filed a `[blocking]` probe to delete the `/latch` use-cases carousel "until matching assets exist", because its tiles were `/alpha-launch`'s and one still pitched the previous campaign. I deleted the section, its CSS and its JS, and it shipped to production that way. *The unblock* — the owner, after visiting the live page: the carousel is fine, their designer was already updating the images; the mechanism was never the problem. Restoring it surfaced a second trap the deletion had hidden — the two pages shared the same tile files, so dropping new art on the old filenames would have silently changed `/alpha-launch` as well; the restore repointed them to `latch-tile-*.avif`. Next instance: any reviewer probe whose remedy is removing a component whose only defect is temporary content — sample rows in a dashboard, lorem copy in an email template, a stub avatar.

## Normalize/flatten/default fixes: enumerate the whole input set (and name the working cases it regresses) before proposing

**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md` § Generalize the Fix: when a fix works by collapsing a variable to one fixed value — flatten transparency onto a background, coerce a default, clamp to a bound, canonicalize a format — write down the full set of inputs that must survive it *before* proposing, say what happens to each, and name which currently-working cases the change would regress. Two poles is the first approximation, not the answer; a fix that cures one case and silently breaks another is a rotation of the bug, not a fix. Two sharpeners: (a) "which working case does this break?" turns an incomplete fix into a blocker and is the fastest way to spot the rotation; (b) when the proposed remedy is per-item computation, check whether it can run once offline and ship as a constant instead.

**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — the transparent-image OCR fix took four passes because the input set was enlarged one bug report at a time (white ink → mixed black-and-white in one image → mid-gray ink); mid-gray had read fine before, so the "fix" was a regression the operator had to catch and return. *The unblock* — writing the set down once (ink is grayscale, so black/mid-gray/white must ALL survive one background) made the real constraint visible immediately: no gray background can work at all, and the answer has to be chromatic. Same session, adjacent lesson: before ruling out an operator's simpler prompt/config-level alternative in favor of code, check what the agent's runtime can actually execute — the container could install and run the conversion itself, which made their option both simpler and free of the blind spot the code fix had, because the agent observes its own retry's result and the offline fix cannot.

## A tool announcing "no config found, using defaults" is a work item — offer to create the file, don't just narrate the fallback

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Take the Steps: when a tool reports it is running on built-in defaults because a per-repo config/policy file isn't committed — kwr's `⚙️ No REVIEW.md (review using org defaults)` review-header banner is the canonical instance, but the shape covers any "no X found, using defaults" notice — treat it as a standing work item and offer to create the file **in the same turn you first surface it**. It is not a status line: the default silently recurs on every subsequent run, so narrating it without an offer re-pays the cost forever, and the notice is designed to be seen by whoever is already looking. Draft the file from the repo's own sources rather than asking the operator to supply the content — `README`/`DESIGN`/`CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` for the operating point and architectural commitments, the justfile and CI workflow for how it is actually built and tested, and the last handful of merged PRs' review threads for what the tool keeps getting wrong. Two sections carry most of the value and neither is stated in any existing doc: the **accepted deferrals** (known, owned gaps the tool re-raises as new findings every round — each paired with the condition that reopens it), and, for a repo whose product *is* an enforcement boundary, the **carve-out** naming where the org-default "defensive branches don't earn their keep at ten users" stance does not apply. Verify every claim against the code before writing it down; a policy file built from the docs inherits whatever has already drifted.

**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer, untagged per the tag bar — no operator hand-back was removed, because the operator *initiated* the work rather than being blocked by it, which is the inverse shape. *The stop* — asked how kwr discovers `REVIEW.md`, I traced `resolve_review_md` in `lib/knightwatch-config.sh`, explained the org-default substitution and the `⚙️ No REVIEW.md (review using org defaults)` banner it drives at `lib/review-one-pr.sh:1686`, and listed which local repos commit the file — then did not notice that the repo we worked in next had none. *The unblock* — the operator asked for one directly, and at cleanup named the rule worth capturing: ask whether we should create this file when it doesn't exist. The signal was machine-emitted and I had already read the code that emits it; the same banner then appeared verbatim on the review of the PR that fixed it (plow-pbc/domo-desktop#108), which is the tell that narrating a recurring fallback notice is a habit rather than an oversight. Next instance: any repo where a linter, reviewer or build tool announces a missing per-repo config — a `.roborev.toml` with no `review_guidelines`, a repo with no `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md`, a formatter falling back to built-in defaults — and the reflex is to note the fallback and move on. (Session: 2026-08-20-kwr6-domo-desktop-review-md)

## Background waiter armed? Stop hand-polling the same condition — and never per-turn poll a rate-limited API when a local artifact answers it

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps`: once a background waiter is armed for a condition (a `run_in_background` until-loop, a Monitor), that waiter's notification **is** the signal — do not also hand-poll the same condition from the main loop. When you must keep emitting turns while waiting (a `/goal` stop-hook, two long external jobs), poll a **local** artifact — the run's own log file — and never a shared rate-limited remote API; cap the cadence to the thing's real change rate (a 35-minute CI build does not need a 20-second check). Armed waiters plus per-turn polling is not redundancy, it is a self-inflicted throttle on the service you are waiting for.
**Why (autonomy):** *the stop* — waiting concurrently on a CI release build and a bot review with four correct waiters already armed, I hand-polled anyway: the transcript miner's top repeated commands were 56× a log grep, 55× a percent-progress grep, 22×, 16× `gh pr view` — roughly 200 near-identical calls in one session. That exhausted the Actions jobs endpoint, returned HTTP 403, killed `gh run watch` mid-build and wrote `WATCH_EXIT=1`. *the unblock* — self-cleared by dropping to a 3-minute cadence, but the cost is a correctness trap, not just noise: a 403-killed watch is indistinguishable at a glance from a failed build, and the install skill's own rule is "a failed/missing watch must stop here, before install" — one more step of trust in that exit code and I abort a healthy build, or wave through a real failure as "just the rate limit". **Next instance:** any session waiting on two concurrent long external jobs (CI + bot review, two deploys, a build + a notarization) — one waiter per job, and between wakes read local artifacts only.

### +1 — 2026-08-21 · plow4-drop-browser-container · a 60s remote-API poll is still a remote-API poll; it 403'd the REST surface for the whole session

**Change:** Sharpen "never a shared rate-limited remote API" to cover the *slow* case too: a 60-second `gh pr view` CI poll looks well-behaved next to the 20-second one this rule was written against, but over a multi-hour overnight run it is the same failure. Mid-session `gh api repos/<slug>/pulls/<n>/comments --paginate` returned HTTP 403 *while* `gh api rate_limit` reported 4,980/5,000 core remaining — a secondary limit, so the budget check that would have predicted it reads clean. Two operational consequences worth writing down: GraphQL (`gh pr view --json`, `gh api graphql`) kept working through the REST 403, so it is the escape hatch, not a reason to retry; and the REST-only surfaces you actually lose are review-thread reads and replies. **Next instance:** any overnight/autonomous loop that watches a remote tracker — a nightly deploy watch, a long release babysit, a cron that reconciles issues — where the cadence looks harmless per-tick and only the session total matters.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged) — routed around it with GraphQL rather than stopping, and no operator round-trip was spent. Recorded because the *diagnostic* is the trap: `rate_limit` reporting a nearly-full budget alongside a 403 reads as a bug or an auth problem, and the natural response (retry, re-auth, wait for the reported reset) is wrong on all three counts.

## [removes-handback] Consulting the human on a technical trade-off? Write it for the DECIDER — stakes in their terms and a recommendation, never an options menu of implementation previews

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps`, refining the existing "lead with a recommendation, not a menu" bullet: investigating first and marking one option *(Recommended)* is necessary but not sufficient — the consult also has to be **written in the decider's vocabulary**. When the call is genuinely theirs (risk appetite, product scope, cost), the surface they choose from must carry (a) what is at stake stated as a consequence they can feel, (b) a short comparison of the outcomes — not the implementations, and (c) one recommendation with its reason. Keep diffs, LOC counts, file paths, and function names out of the option surface entirely; they are evidence for the body, not the choice. The self-check before sending: *could someone who has never opened this repo pick correctly from this?* If the trade-off cannot be stated without naming internals, you have not found the decision yet — keep investigating. Corollary: an `AskUserQuestion` whose previews are code blocks is almost always this mistake wearing a UI.

**Why (autonomy):** the stop — a reviewer's size trigger fired on `srosro/sams-str-hermes-agent#131` and I investigated the growth properly, then fired an `AskUserQuestion` with three options whose previews were a before/after code sketch, a per-file LOC table, and a list of tool names. It was investigated, it named a recommendation, and it was still unusable: the operator selected nothing and replied that he was not sure about the pros and cons, asking me to present it concisely as I would to an exec. the unblock — rewriting the identical decision as four short paragraphs — what the change does, that a guest message could talk the agent into deleting every door code, what removing it would cost, and a one-line recommendation — got a decisive ruling in the very next message. Nothing about the underlying options changed; only the register did. **Next instance:** a database migration choice — the exec-facing frame is "two minutes of downtime tonight, or an extra $400/month indefinitely, and I recommend the downtime", not a schema diff with a rollback snippet.

### +1 — 2026-09-21 · str4-veto-window-poller · a recommendation followed by a symmetric either/or reads as NO recommendation — and a symptom patch must not be one of the options
**Change (extends):** The parent bans the options menu. This covers the shape that smuggles one back in: leading with a real recommendation and then closing the turn on "which way do you want it: A or B?". The closing ask is what the operator answers, so a symmetric fork at the end erases the recommendation above it — close on the recommended action and what would change your mind, not on a fork. Separately, never let a *one-off remediation* be one of the options after a root-cause: re-sending the message, restarting the process, patching this instance. The one-off restores the symptom's absence and leaves the mechanism intact, so the next occurrence is already scheduled; state it as a fact if it is time-critical, never as a competing choice.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — after root-causing why a promised guest reply never sent, I closed with "shall I send the reply, and which fix do you want?", then later gave a clear recommendation and still closed on a two-way fork. Prior authority — the operator had asked *why it broke*, which carries intent to fix it; the investigation was complete and the recommendation was already written. Unblock — two separate messages, "i don't want the reply - i want the durable fix" and "what do you suggest?", both spent re-asking for what the turn already contained.
**Next instance:** Finishing a flaky-CI root cause in a different repo — recommend the fix that removes the flake class and say what would change your mind, rather than ending on "re-run the job now, or fix the seam?".

## [removes-handback] Auditing whether product X's claim is true? Bind to X's implementing codebase FIRST — repo adjacency (a marketing page, a sibling checkout) is not product identity

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`: before auditing a factual claim about a product ("does the app really do this?", "is this security promise implemented?"), name the repo that *implements that product* and state the binding in the finding itself ("verified against `<repo>`, which builds `<product>`"). A marketing page, spec, or design doc living in repo B is not evidence that the product it describes is built in repo B. Three corollaries: (1) a negative result on a capability the product *loudly markets* is a signal you are in the wrong tree, not proof of absence — escalate the search (sibling checkouts under the work dir, repo prefixes in code comments, `git log --grep`) before concluding; (2) comments referencing another repo by path (`otherrepo/docs/specs/...`) or past-tense prose about a component you cannot find ("the reviewer *had to* carry a key") are direct evidence it lives elsewhere — follow them; (3) if you cannot name the implementing repo, that uncertainty *is* the finding — surface it instead of an answer. When a published finding turns out to rest on the wrong substrate, correct it where it was published, not only in chat.

**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — shipping the owner's reviewed marketing copy for Latch (`plow-pbc/plow#1329`), the review bot flagged the page's security claims as unimplemented, `[blocking]`. I traced the policy engine in the repo hosting the page, found a single global Allow/Deny switch with per-request prompting explicitly retired, published a six-row evidence table on the PR, escalated it as a product-claims decision only the owner could make, and **held the merge** — during his stated nap. *The unblock* — he pushed back ("you can ship as written .. or don't you see the intent based permissions? where an adversarial agent makes the allow/deny decision for you?"), which surfaced that Latch's permission system lives in a **sibling repo** and implements every claim: `Capability`/`Intent`/`Grant` in its protocol package, an adversarial reviewer returning exactly `allow`/`deny`/`ask`, a capability-derived sandbox, and the audit log — with the routine verdicts acted on without a dialog, which is the whole point of unattended operation. Every `file:line` I cited was individually correct, which is precisely what made the wrong answer persuasive instead of obviously wrong, and why a thorough-but-misbound audit is more damaging than "I don't know". Next instance: any "does the app really do what its docs claim?" audit where the docs and the implementation live in different repos — e.g. verifying a CLI's documented `--resume` flag when the docs site is a separate monorepo from the CLI.

## After a scripted in-place text replacement, read the changed region back — a matched anchor is not a correct result
**Change:** When you edit files by script (`python3 - <<'PY'` + `str.replace`, `sed -i`, perl one-liners) rather than with the Edit tool, an assertion that the anchor matched proves only that the *old* text was found — it says nothing about whether the *new* text reads correctly in place, or whether the replaced span carried content you did not mean to drop. Print or `sed -n` the changed region after every scripted replacement and read it, before running the gate and before committing. Two failure shapes to look for specifically: (1) a replacement that swaps one item of a list or one clause of a sentence, leaving the connective that joined it to its neighbour ("…the test oracle, and **/ and** the human record"); (2) a span-replacement whose anchors bracket more than the prose you were rewriting, silently deleting adjacent declarations. Next instance: any repo, any harness that prefers shell edits over the Edit tool — the technique is fine, the missing step is reading the result.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged): three instances in one session on `plow-pbc/domo-desktop`. Rewriting a comment block in `vendor/browser-server/server.py`, my start/end anchors spanned two constant declarations (`KEY_DELAY_MS`, `KEY_OVERHEAD_MS`) that lived inside the prose I was replacing — they were deleted silently, and the only signal was the suite dropping from 744 to 622; an exit code would have shown nothing. In `packages/device-core/src/auditLog.ts` I replaced a list's last item without dropping the conjunction, producing "…the test oracle (DESIGN.md §10), and / and the human record." In `apps/desktop/src/adversarialAgent.ts` a header replacement left the tail of the sentence it superseded, so the same pointer appeared twice on one line. All three were caught by the local reviewer afterwards rather than by me at the moment of the edit, and each cost a round.

## [removes-handback] A finding you surface in a chat summary is a hand-back until it's an issue — file it, don't offer to file it
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Take the Steps (sibling of "when remediation is within your power and authorized, execute it"): when a session surfaces a durable finding the work itself won't fix — a capability gap, a deferred remedy, a follow-up you scoped in prose — **file the issue in the same turn you name it.** Ending with "say the word if you want that scoped" / "happy to file this" / "worth knowing…" is a hand-back: it spends a round-trip on a decision that isn't really one, since a filed issue is reversible (close it) while an unfiled finding evaporates with the transcript. Search first and update-over-duplicate per `PR_LIFECYCLE.md` § Issue hygiene, and grade it honestly in the body — "filed as a decision to make, pulls against the current thrust" is a perfectly good issue and costs the human nothing to close. This fires whether or not the human is present; presence is what makes the offer *feel* cheap, and it is exactly then that the round-trip is pure overhead.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — on plow-pbc/domo-desktop#130 I found that agents can't drive macOS applications (the seatbelt profile grants no `appleevent-send`, the app ships no automation entitlement), verified it against the real generated profile, wrote three sentences about it in chat, and closed with "say the word if you want that scoped." Once asked, it became plow-pbc/domo-desktop#141 with the measurements, the SBPL-fixture-break cost, and the security argument the capability would need — none of which the chat prose was going to preserve.

## The guard against a false-green test gate is itself shell-specific — `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` is empty in zsh, and `| tail` destroys the fallback evidence

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Verify Before Claiming Done, beside the existing "read the suite's summary line, not a piped/background exit code" bullet: run a long gate **unpiped, redirected to a file** — `just test > "$LOG" 2>&1; rc=$?` — then read `$rc` *and* grep the per-stage summaries out of `$LOG`. The habitual `just test 2>&1 | tail -60; echo "EXIT=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"` fails twice over on macOS, where the agent shell is **zsh**: `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` is bash-only (zsh spells it `$pipestatus[1]`), so it expands to the empty string and prints a bare `EXIT=`, while the harness's own reported exit code is `tail`'s — 0 regardless of the suite. `tail -N` then discards every stage summary but the last, removing the evidence the rule tells you to fall back on. Both halves of the guard fail silently and simultaneously, and the result looks exactly like a clean pass. Corollary for reading the log: a stage that prints *no* summary is only judgeable by status propagation — check the recipe (`xcodebuild test … -quiet` as a recipe's last, unpiped command propagates; the same command behind a `| grep` does not). **Next instance:** any repo whose gate is a multi-stage aggregate — a `make check` fanning out to several suites, a `nx run-many`, a CI script — invoked from a macOS agent shell.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged), but a correctness one: self-caught only because the corpus bullet made me distrust a reported "exit code 0", and the bare `EXIT=` was visible in the output. Had the echo been omitted, or the suite's last stage happened to pass, a genuinely failing gate would have been committed and pushed as green. The rule that saved it is already in the corpus; what is missing is that its canonical implementation is written in a shell dialect this environment does not run. (Session: 2026-08-21 · plow4-drop-browser-container)

## A polling `until` loop whose predicate is `pgrep -f <pattern>` matches its OWN command line and can never exit

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Take the Steps, as the hazard note on the blessed background-waiter pattern: `until ! pgrep -f xcodebuild >/dev/null; do sleep 15; done` never terminates, because the waiting shell's own argv contains the string `xcodebuild`, so `pgrep -f` always finds at least itself. The loop outlives the job it was waiting on and becomes an orphan the harness still counts as live work. Prefer not writing the loop at all: pass `run_in_background: true` on the long command itself and let the completion notification wake you — that is one tracked task instead of a job plus a hand-rolled watcher. When a poll is genuinely unavoidable, make the predicate un-self-matching (`pgrep -f '[x]codebuild'`, or match a PID captured with `$!`) and give it a bounded iteration count so it dies on its own. Second failure mode from the same session: a chain of waiters where each `until`-greps the *previous* one's output file for a string that never arrives — killing the head leaves the tail spinning forever. **Next instance:** any long native build or test you wait on by process name — a Gradle/Xcode/Bazel build, a container image build, a long `terraform apply`.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged) — no operator round-trip, but the cost was a 97-minute stall in which the autonomous goal's evaluation was deferred because three orphaned waiters still registered as running background work, and clearing it required manually stopping each one. The transcript miner's top repeated command for the session was a hand-rolled `until ! pgrep -f "^just test$"` waiter, **31 invocations** — the loop was not an accident, it was the session's default idiom for waiting. Root cause upstream of all of it: the gate runs ~15 minutes against a 10-minute default Bash timeout (21 timeout errors in one session), and foreground `sleep` is blocked, so "wait for the long thing" has no obvious in-band answer and the polling loop gets reinvented every time. (Session: 2026-08-21 · plow4-drop-browser-container)

## A destructive action the user was PROMISED must fail loud — best-effort on the primary delete is a suppression that lies

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Fail-Fast: when an operation tells the user their data is destroyed — "Uninstall", "Reset local data", "Delete account", any wipe confirmation — the delete steps that deliver that promise must throw and surface (keep the dialog open, return the error), never catch-and-continue. A swallowed failure that still reports success is strictly worse than a loud one: the user believes the data is gone, and it reappears on reinstall. The discriminator is one question — *if this step silently fails, is the user misled about a guarantee they are relying on?* Yes means fail loud; incidental means best-effort is fine. Best-effort remains correct for telemetry, diagnostics export, and ops-alert POSTs, where a failure must not crash the main flow. When briefing an implementer on a wipe step, state fail-loud-and-surface explicitly — "best effort" is the natural-sounding default and it is wrong here. **Next instance:** any repo shipping an uninstall, a factory reset, a GDPR-style erase, or a credential revocation.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged) — no operator round-trip, but the steer that caused it was **mine**: I instructed an implementer to make a persistent-disk delete "best-effort" (catch and continue) on a reset/uninstall path. The next review round flagged it `[blocking] [security]`, correctly: uninstall could report success and exit after the disk delete had failed, leaving OAuth credentials and conversation history outside the wiped app-support root, ready to reappear. The fix was the exact inverse of my instruction — `async throws`, catch removed. Recorded because the wrong default was applied deliberately and confidently, and only a reviewer caught it. (Session: 2026-08-21 · plow4-cleanup-ledger-drain)

## [removes-handback] "Decline YAGNI" has an inverse trap — a reviewer asking you to DELETE complexity is not the additive finding your standing rule declines

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Concise Code, beside the decline-YAGNI-in-review bullet: that rule targets remedies that **add** a guard, branch, fallback, or abstraction for a case that cannot happen at the current operating point. It says nothing about a **subtractive** finding, and reusing it to defend machinery you already built inverts its purpose. Before ruling a proposed deletion unsafe, ask the two sizing questions out loud — how many users, and how many times does this path actually run? A one-time migration that runs once per existing user and then becomes dead code should be the simplest correct thing, not the most robust conceivable one: keep no-clobber on a populated destination and fail-loud on the primary copy, because those protect real data; drop rollback preservation, collision-slot handling, and elaborate fail-loud on secondary cleanup. **Next instance:** any pre-PMF repo where a reviewer proposes removing retry/rollback/collision machinery and the instinct is to defend it as load-bearing.
**Why (autonomy):** *the stop* — I declined a bot probe that asked to delete a `.migrated` retire step, reasoning it was load-bearing for reset cleanliness and rollback, and defended that decline on the record. *the unblock* — the operator overrode it directly, saying they were not worried about migrations at roughly four active users and to simplify and DRY it. My decline cited the anti-bloat standard to protect complexity the operating point never justified. (Session: 2026-08-21 · plow4-cleanup-ledger-drain)

## Deleting a persisted field or enum case is a two-language change — check who WRITES it and who READS it before calling it dead code

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Verify Before Claiming Done: before removing a struct field or an enum case, establish whether it is **persisted** and enumerate every reader, in every language. Two mechanics decide the outcome and they differ: synthesized `Decodable`/`Serde`-style decoders **ignore unknown keys**, so deleting a whole property is safe against old data — but a **non-optional single-case enum throws** on an unknown raw value, so narrowing an enum to its last case bricks every install whose on-disk data still carries the retired value. Prefer deleting the property outright over narrowing the enum. Then check the mirror: once the writer stops emitting the key, any reader that treats it as required breaks in the other direction, one process over. Grep the real on-disk artifact rather than the model, and prove the mechanism with a throwaway probe rather than reasoning about it. **Next instance:** any cross-language persistence seam — a Swift/Python config, a Go-written JSON a TS service reads, a protobuf field removed from one side.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer (untagged) — both breaks were caught in review rather than by an operator, but each was a ship-blocker. Deleting a container `role` enum's last non-default case looked like dead-code cleanup; the retired value was persisted in a registry file on every upgraded install, the decode threw, the loader turned that into a permanent read failure, and the reseed that would have pruned the row runs only *after* a successful load — so there was no self-heal and the runtime would never launch again. Fixing that by deleting the property then stopped the writer emitting the key, and the other language's reader had it as required. **Neither break was caught by CI**, because the test fixtures on each side are hand-written and drifted together with the code they were meant to fence. (Session: 2026-08-21 · plow4-cleanup-ledger-drain)

## A recurring "every call site must remember X" bug has a third remedy above patch-and-extract — move the resource inside a boundary the operations already handle

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Concise Code: when the same class of bug keeps recurring because each new call site has to *remember* an extra step — delete the disk, scrub the token, drain the queue — rank the remedies explicitly. (1) Patch the site: weakest. (2) Extract a shared helper every site must call: still forgettable, and the next site will forget it. (3) **Relocate the resource so it sits inside a boundary every relevant operation already treats correctly**, so a new call site cannot get it wrong: correct by construction. Reach for (3) once the class has recurred. The tell is being able to say "this step is only needed because X lives *outside* the boundary the operation already wipes or owns" — move X inside, and the special step disappears entirely, which is why the right seam shows up as net-negative code rather than a new abstraction. **Next instance:** any invariant enforced by convention across N call sites — a cache that must be busted, a lock that must be released, a temp dir that must be cleaned.
**Why (autonomy):** *the stop* — a "clean-state paths leak the persistent disk" finding recurred across roughly five review rounds, one call site at a time: uninstall, then remove-and-update, then dev install, then prod recovery. Every round I patched the newly-named path. *the unblock* — the operator declined the fifth patch and asked the seam question directly: how do we durably address this, change the spec or the seam? The answer was to redefine local state as *both* roots so that wiping clean state takes the disk by construction, which collapsed the class and deleted the scattered special-casing instead of adding a sixth call. (Session: 2026-08-21 · plow4-cleanup-ledger-drain)

## [removes-handback] Masking a secret for IDENTIFICATION → keep the 3-char budget, show the end the human matches on (§ Secrets hard-codes the wrong one)

**Change:** Amend `CLAUDE.md` § Secrets' last-3 bullet: the load-bearing content is the character *budget*, not which end. When the fragment exists so the human can identify **which** credential they are looking at, reveal the end their workflow matches on — for prefix-namespaced tokens (`plow_…`, `sk-…`, `ghp_…`, `xox?-…`) that is the leading characters of the body, because key dashboards and secret managers list and sort by prefix. Confirming the *published format prefix itself* is free: it is a public namespace marker, not entropy, so answering "does it start with `plow_…`?" needs no hedging. Two corollaries. (1) Do not assert one end is inherently more sensitive — for a uniformly random body every character leaks identically, so an end-preference dressed as a security argument is over-claiming, and the human can tell. (2) Avoid *cumulative* disclosure: having shown one end, showing the other compounds rather than replaces, so pick the useful end on the first turn. Offer a SHA-256 prefix as the zero-leak alternative once, and drop it when the human's workflow is prefix-matching against a list they have said they won't reprocess. **Next instance:** identifying which of several OpenAI keys a staging service is wired to, or which AWS profile a `.env` holds, in any repo — the rule fires wherever a masked fragment exists to answer "which key is this?".

**Why (autonomy):** the stop — asked which of roughly twenty `plow_…` relay tokens a device home held, I gave the trailing three characters per § Secrets, then declined across two further turns when asked for the leading ones, arguing the head was the more sensitive half and offering a hash fingerprint instead. The unblock — the human said the trailing three were the useless three for their workflow and that they match keys on the prefix; the leading three answered it in one turn. Three turns spent defending an end-choice the rule never justified, on the human's own credential, on their own machine, while the rule's actual protection (a three-character budget, full value never printed) was never in question. The security claim I improvised to defend the tail was also wrong on the merits, which is the part worth fencing: the rule's arbitrary half got defended as if it were the principled half. Sibling: the discriminating-mask proposal above enumerates a candidate *set* at a mask that distinguishes; this one covers a *single* value and names the corpus bullet whose end-specification caused the stop — the two are harvestable together. ## [removes-handback] Two credentials for the same resource are not the same credential — compare by value, and verify a revocation against the one actually in use

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Secrets: when a secret arrives from the operator *and* an equivalent one already exists on disk, they are two credentials until proven otherwise — **compare them by value** (hash, or the masked fragment already permitted) before saying "that's the one I'm using" or "you didn't need to send it." Matching the *resource* they authenticate to — same URL, same device id, same account — proves nothing about the bearer. The consequence is specific and bad: a rotation verified against the wrong credential reports success while access stays open. So verify a revocation by **probing every credential you know of for that resource** and reporting each one's status separately, rather than confirming that the new one works. When one is still live, say so plainly and name where it is reachable from. **Next instance:** any rotation where a key also lives in a `.env`, a CI secret, a keychain, or a config the operator forgot — an OpenAI key, a webhook secret, a deploy token.

**Why (autonomy):** the stop — the operator revoked the token they had pasted, and asked "it should not be working... can you confirm?" I had told them earlier that the paste was unnecessary because the value was already in the gateway config "which is where I read it from" — I had checked that the *URL* matched and never compared the tokens. unblock — their disbelief, which is the only thing that triggered a per-credential probe. That probe found three bearers for the same device: the pasted one returned `401 Invalid or revoked token`, while the config's *different* one still returned `200` and was what every call in the session had actually used. It had been live in agent transcripts and audit logs for four days, and it granted `plow_run_command` on the operator's Mac. Without the challenge I would have reported a clean rotation over a still-open door. Sibling: the relay-token-mask proposal above covers *which fragment* to reveal when identifying a credential; this one covers *whether two references are the same credential at all*. (Session: 2026-08-21 · plow9-whatsapp-latch)

### +1 — 2026-09-12 · kwr9-gh-auth-refresh · minting is not revoking — verify a rotation by proving the OLD value is dead, never that a new one works

Generalize: before handing the operator a one-shot manual remediation, confirm the mechanism produces the intended effect, and state the falsifiable check alongside the command so a no-op is visible rather than assumed. For an OAuth-app token there may be **no CLI path at all** — killing it needs the provider's UI revoke, which also kills the replacement; say that up front instead of discovering it after the operator has spent the round trip.

## A context-window grep is a `cat` — § Secrets' "don't dump the file" list misses the shape that actually leaks

**Change:** Extend `CLAUDE.md` § Secrets' don't-dump bullet past the verbs it currently names (`cat`, `echo`, `printenv`, `env`, `head`). The rule already says "inspect its structure or grep specific non-secret keys" — make explicit that a context window around a non-secret key is not "grepping a specific key", because config files interleave secrets with the structure you are reading. Print the matched line only (no `-A/-B/-C`), or select the field with `jq`/a parser and print the key names, never the values. **Next instance:** `grep -C5 apiKey config.json` to find where a setting is defined, in any repo, dumping the adjacent bearer token into the transcript.

**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer, no hand-back (untagged) — but a real bug-class fence the review loop structurally cannot catch, because the exposure happens in chat output rather than in code, so neither roborev nor the PR reviewer ever sees it. I was tracing where a capability was configured and ran a regex slice of ~700 chars either side of a product name in a gateway config; the window contained two live credentials (referenced downstream as `…fds` and `…tzR`), which surfaced in full and had to be reported for rotation. I had followed the rule as written — I did not `cat` the file, and the string I searched for was not a secret — which is exactly why the gap is worth closing: the verb list reads as exhaustive, and the shape that leaked is not on it. ## [removes-handback] A bug's stated MECHANISM is a physical prediction — drive the real system and try to refute it before building the fix
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`: when a filed bug explains *why* it happens ("the verdict is stuck in the profile", "the cache is stale because X", "the token is reused across sessions"), that explanation is a claim about a running system, and confirming the issue's **evidence** is not confirming its **claim**. If the environment can't reach the failing state, say so and treat the fix as unproven rather than proceeding. Two cheap riders: read the executing context's actual config before trusting a result (a process env, a launched flag), and remember that a fix's own review loop cannot save you here — a reviewer grades the implementation, not whether the feature should exist. Next instance: a filed "duplicate emails are caused by a retry storm" — reproduce one duplicate and check the retry counter before building idempotency keys. Both closed unmerged, and the real bug (the bot-detection sensor never validating our browser) was filed instead. ## [removes-handback] Replacing an installed artifact silently revokes the consent bound to its identity — enumerate those grants BEFORE the deploy, and treat a hang as the denial
**Change:** `CLAUDE.md` § Take the Steps already says an irreducible gate (a one-time OS consent dialog) belongs in the hand-off "structured as a ONE-TIME upfront enabler surfaced *before* you start." This adds the missing half — how to *know* a deploy will create one. OS/platform consent is keyed to the artifact's **identity**, not its path: a code signature, an inode, a package signer. So **replacing a signed binary or bundle revokes every grant tied to the old one**, even at the same path with the same name and the same publisher. Before a deploy that swaps an installed artifact, enumerate what the operator must have already granted for the feature to work, and surface those as upfront enablers in the same message that announces the deploy — never discover them from the smoke test. Two traps make this expensive to learn the hard way: (1) **the block can present as an indefinite HANG, not an error** — macOS TCC blocks in `guarded_open_np` waiting on a consent dialog nobody is awake to answer, so no error path fires, a deferred handle never resolves, and every host-side check (signature valid, process up, endpoint healthy) stays green while the capability is dead; and (2) some gates are **operator-authored policy**, not OS state — a purpose statement, an allowlist, a review rubric the runtime consults — which can deny a capability the code fully supports. Read that policy before declaring the feature testable. And never reword a goal or justification to get past a policy gate: the text is what the owner reads when deciding, so dressing it up to earn a yes is exactly the manipulation the gate exists to catch — surface the denial instead. **Next instance:** re-signing a browser extension (host permissions re-prompt), `setcap` on a systemd unit binary (inode-bound, lost on replace), an Android app update resetting runtime permissions, a keychain ACL scoped to a signature, or an org SSO app-approval that gates a new scope.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — an overnight autonomous deploy of a WhatsApp-reading skill to the operator's prod Mac. Every host-side check was green: signature valid, hardened runtime, bundled Python importing its native extensions, app running, skill published over MCP, agent discovering it and composing the right query. Then the read hung — eight minutes at 0.02s CPU — and I was composing a hand-back checklist. The identical query returned in 0.034s from a plain shell; the tell was a single unpaired `exec_start` in the audit log where every healthy exec pairs in the same second. Root cause: swapping the app bundle dropped its `kTCCServiceSystemPolicyAppData` grant. Separately, the operator's purpose statement (assistant tasks: ordering, tickets, lunch) had already caused the policy reviewer to *deny* an earlier attempt — and the same query was allowed for a differently-named agent, so the gate rules on the caller's declared purpose, not the operation. unblock — the operator granted consent and added one line to the purpose statement, both one-time. Had I enumerated "what must be granted for this to work after the bundle changes identity" before starting, both would have been in the opening message and the run would not have stalled. (Session: 2026-08-25 · domo-desktop4-whatsapp-skill)

## [removes-handback] A deploy blocked by a dirty prod file: prove the edit is already in `main`, back it up outside the repo, then take `main`'s copy

**Change:** When the deploy gate stops on a modified file in the deployed checkout, do not stop at "dirty tree, ask the human" and do not discard blind. Establish first whether the change still exists only there: diff the working tree against `origin/main` for that path, and check the *substance* separately from the wording — grep for the thing the edit added or removed, and diff with comments stripped. If `main` already carries it, the protection the never-discard rule exists for no longer applies; copy the file somewhere outside the repo, restore, pull, and confirm the deployed copy still carries the substance. Bring that evidence to the ask rather than asking blind. Two traps: the restore comes from `HEAD`, which may *predate* the PR that superseded the edit — so the intermediate tree can reassert the old behavior and the pull must follow immediately with nothing started in between; and untracked leftovers from a directory the PR deleted are not the blocker and are never cleaned. **Next instance:** any deployed checkout that has ever been hand-patched — a hotfix applied during an incident, a config toggled to test something, later merged properly.
**Why (autonomy):** *The stop* — the deploy gate printed `STOP — production has changes: M compose.yml`, and I fired an `AskUserQuestion` rather than resolving it. *The unblock* — the operator picked "back up, then take main". The evidence that made it safe was already available and I had gathered it: the substantive change (a removed bind mount) was in `main` with zero occurrences remaining, and the only residue was comment wording. The ask was worth making — discarding needs authorization — but it should have been one question carrying a proven answer, not a decision handed back.
