## Prefer INTERPRETING a recoverable agent argv over REFUSING it on a read path — refuse only the genuinely ambiguous residue
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Default to the Simplifying Option (the capability-vs-shape bullet's neighborhood): when an agent-facing gate (argv planner, tool-argument validator, provider front) meets a wrong-shaped but intent-recoverable request on a READ path, do what the agent meant — don't refuse with a correction. A refusal sheds capability (one call becomes N, and the agent must learn the correction) to buy a few LOC; the interpreting shape usually costs a branch and preserves the call. Reserve refusals for shapes that are genuinely ambiguous (a calendar id with no owning account under a fan-out) or unsafe (a flag that disarms the belt). Companion to the "extend the wrapped tool's own flag" +1 above: interpret *inside* the tool's grammar, not by overloading it.
**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer grade (untagged): plow-pbc/latch#229 r1 refused `--calendars` under a plow-gog fan-out and converged clean; the operator's "why do we have to do this? refuse calendars for reads?" reversed it. I'd have shipped the refusal. Next different instance: a Plow tool-argument validator rejecting a slightly-off but unambiguous date/ID shape instead of normalising it.

## [removes-handback] A genuinely-blocked step hands off as a runbook + the validation goal — never an options menu
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Take the Steps (beside "Reserve hand-offs for the genuinely-blocked parts"): once a blocker is real and on the operator's side (a GUI flow you can't drive over SSH, a credential you don't hold), lead with the exact commands/steps to run AND one line naming what the run validates — never an `AskUserQuestion` about whether/how to proceed. The menu burns turns after the decision is already forced; the operator wants the artifact.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — on plow-pbc/plow#722 I fired two rounds of option menus about a dev-install E2E the operator had to run. The unblock — "give me the instructions — what are you validating?" Promoted from the `handoff-blocked-step-give-runbook-not-options` feedback memory. Next instance: any repo where verification needs the operator's hardware/GUI (a phone test, a smart-home device, a signed build). (2026-08-28-plow9-named-lines-drain)

## Review probes demanding hermetic "the agent calls tool X with arg Y" tests → counter-propose the data/policy split
**Change:** Add to `TESTING.md` (behavior-over-implementation neighborhood): for LLM tool-use coverage, the data layer (tool forwards args; search returns rows) is hermetically testable; the policy layer (the LLM *decides* to call the tool with that arg) is only exercised by a real agent. A stubbed-LLM "tool-call recorder" harness asserts the mock args the stub was fed — the implementation-test the standards already reject. Counter-propose: unit/integration tests on the data layer + a real-agent scenario (or accepted manual E2E) for the policy assertion.
**Why (autonomy):** Owner ruling on plow-pbc/plow#722: "I'm fine without the hermetic test" the reviewer wanted. Quality-steer grade (untagged). Promoted from the `defer-llm-behavior-tests-to-e2e` feedback memory. Next instance: any agent repo's review loop demanding a mocked-agent behavior test. (2026-08-28-plow9-named-lines-drain)

## Declining a config-validation guard as YAGNI? Land a one-line doc example of the correct format instead
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md` § Anti-Bloat neighborhood: when you decline a malformed-config guard (e.g. rejecting the string `"false"` for a JSON boolean), don't stop at the decline — add a literal correctly-formatted example to the field's documentation (in SKILL/README prose; a strict-JSON example file can't carry comments). Prevents the typo at its source (the human editing the config) with zero runtime branches.
**Why (autonomy):** Owner ruling on plow-pbc/plow#769: "just decline and maybe give a one-line example in the config file for what a properly formatted false looks like." Promoted from the `decline-config-guard-add-doc-example` feedback memory. Next instance: any hand-edited config field with a plausible wrong shape, in any repo. (2026-08-28-plow9-named-lines-drain)

## A defense-in-depth bound that ripples into error semantics: scope it per-caller or delete it — never plumb a tri-state around it
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md` § Broken-Glass neighborhood: when a timeout/guard's failure path collapses through a boolean probe into a wrong state decision downstream, the additive fix (tri-state "unknown" contract + plumbing) is the wrong shape. Enumerate ALL callers of the seam first, then: bound only the callers on the *observed* freeze surface (where a hang is the real symptom and a timeout just fails loud), and drop the bound where it feeds the rippling semantic. Corollary: never present a scope fork to the operator without naming the load-bearing caller in the option text — an understated cost produces a decision you'll have to walk back.
**Why (autonomy):** plow-pbc/plow#784 — a `runLimactl list` timeout collapsed through `instanceExists()` into a mis-planned runtime digest; the suggested fix was +20 LOC of tri-state plumbing. Owner chose subtractive, later refined to per-caller scoping (bound `waitForReady`/`stop` — the literal #778 freeze; leave `instanceExists` unbounded) — and my initial fork omitted `waitForReady`, forcing the decision to be revisited. Promoted from the `defense-in-depth-bound-rippling-prefer-deletion` feedback memory. Next instance: any subprocess timeout or fallback whose error path feeds a state probe. (2026-08-28-plow9-named-lines-drain)

## Automerge armed (or PR already merged) with a review still in flight → valid late findings go to a NEW follow-up PR
**Change:** Add to `PR_LIFECYCLE.md` / `babysit-pr`: never race-push onto a branch that can merge or vanish at any moment. Monitor for the late review; a valid finding lands as a follow-up PR off updated main, with its own babysit loop.
**Why (autonomy):** Promoted from the `late-review-under-automerge-followup-pr` feedback memory: racing the automerge either loses the fix (merges before the push) or churns a branch about to disappear. Next instance: any repo with automerge or a fast human merger where a bot review lands post-merge. (2026-08-28-plow9-named-lines-drain)

## Disabling a behavior? Prefer DRY-to-a-toggle over ripping the code path out
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md` § DRY neighborhood: when the ask is "stop doing X on surface Y", the preferred shape is refactoring so on/off is a config flag or one-line change at a single control point — not a removal PR. A +50/−120 rip-out is a smell that the policy decision is wired through producers and restated across docs rather than centralized; it also destroys the ability to flip it back without another PR.
**Why (autonomy):** Owner declined the rip-out on plow-pbc/plow#766 and asked for a DRY + config toggle so a non-engineer could flip kiosk posting herself. Promoted from the `prefer-config-toggle-over-feature-rip-out` feedback memory. Next instance: any "turn off the notifications/banner/report" request in any repo. (2026-08-28-plow9-named-lines-drain)

## [removes-handback] Mask secrets by regex substitution over whole values — never a startswith/equality check

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Secrets: when dumping any config/JSON/env for inspection, redact by regex substitution applied to every string value (token-prefix patterns like `plow_[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`, `sk-\S+`, `ghp_\S+`, plus the generic `Bearer \S+`) before anything prints — never a `startswith`/equality test on the whole value. Secrets routinely live *inside* larger strings (Authorization headers, URLs, connection strings), so prefix checks on the value are the wrong shape. Prefer printing key paths only, extracting prefixes with a targeted `grep -oE`, which structurally cannot leak the remainder.

**Why (autonomy):** An ad-hoc masking script inspecting a dropped MCP config used `value.startswith("plow_")`; the credential was inside `"Bearer plow_…"`, fell through, and printed in full — forcing a hand-back to the operator ("please revoke this just-minted token and drop a replacement") that a substring mask would have removed entirely. Promoted from the `mask-secrets-by-substring` feedback memory. Next instance: any session that inspects an unfamiliar config file, HTTP header set, or `.env` on any host with a quick masking one-liner. (2026-08-28-latch6-credential-audit)

## Before polishing/re-homing/documenting a component, confirm its strategic direction — "is this surface being kept?" is part of the zoom-out

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Take the Steps (or the zoom-out skill): before investing review-loop rounds in fixing, re-homing, or documenting a component, confirm the component's strategic direction — from the operator, a roadmap/REVIEW.md thrust line, or recent deprecation signals in git history (a "moved to X" commit, a successor path). A surface being retired gets the minimal truthful fix plus a deprecation pointer to the successor, with the real investment going to the successor surface; only a kept surface earns polish.

**Why (autonomy):** After an incident-driven doc fix, I re-homed and iterated the legacy `plow-connectors` REST skill through 3 review rounds (plow-pbc/plow#1479) before the operator redirected: that surface is retiring, and the actual goal lived on the successor (latch/plow-gog — landed as plow-pbc/latch#234 in ~1 round once aimed right). A one-line direction check at zoom-out would have re-aimed the whole effort before the first PR. The eventual shape (minimal fix + "retiring, use X" note on the legacy surface, real fix on the successor) is what the rule produces up front. Next instance: any repo where a bug report lands on a module with a newer sibling — e.g. improving tests or docs for a code path a recent PR's message says was replaced. (2026-08-28-agent-mgr7-default-account)

## [removes-handback] Widening an agent's reach onto a chat/source with pre-existing history → pin its consumption cursor to "now" BEFORE restarting the consumer
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Verify Before Claiming Done (or an ops standard): when a grant/scope
widening (a line grant, an un-soft-delete, a new channel subscription) makes *pre-existing history*
newly visible to a backfill-style consumer, pin that source's checkpoint/cursor to the newest item
before restarting — an empty/default cursor replays months of history as live turns, and for an
agent with outbound reach that means unsolicited messages to real people. Next different instance:
adding an old Slack channel to a bot with a catch-up loop, or pointing a queue consumer at an
existing topic.
**Why (autonomy):** After I restored a soft-deleted chat into an agent's line grant and restarted
(hermes-plow-chat, str agent, 2026-08-29), the agent 👋'd a real cleaners' thread and announced it
would "respond shortly" to 2-day-old messages; the operator had to interrupt ("can we stop aspen…")
and apologize in-thread. The unblock: stop the container, write each newly-adopted chat's
checkpoint file to the newest message uid, restart, verify quiet. Filed as
hermes-plow-chat#38 for the code-level fix; the rule above is the operator-side fence that
prevents the incident regardless of consumer.


### +1 — 2026-09-03 · plow8-line-move-and-pin-chain · second instance, and the parent's own predicted trigger: a LINE GRANT, not a restored chat

**Change:** Sharpen the parent — the widening operation itself is the trigger, not the restart: an API that
moves an agent's grant (`PUT /v1/agents/cloud/{uid}/line`) reboots the consumer as part of the move, so there
is no post-move window to pin cursors in. Enumerate what the NEW grant covers *before* issuing the widening
call, and treat any covered source with pre-existing history as requiring a cursor pin (or an explicit
operator decision) as a precondition of the move.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — the operator interrupted mid-turn ("oh wait you're creating group threads?") after
a line move put their assistant into a two-week-old four-way test group; it backfilled 24 messages and posted
three replies to Aug-28 messages, one of them to another real person, who then engaged. Prior authority — I
had already listed every chat the target line carried (the group was in that very query's output) and had DB
+ code read access; the blast radius was one query away and I ran it without reading it as a blast radius.
Unblock — the operator's interrupt. Filed plow-pbc/plow#1727 (backfill replays acquired history) and #1728
(no per-chat exclusion).
**Next instance:** adding an existing Slack channel to a bot with a catch-up loop, or any grant-widening API
call whose server side restarts the consumer for you.

## [removes-handback] A teammate's competing PR is context to cross-link, not a reason to self-supersede — push ours and let review reconcile

**Change:** On discovering another person's open PR covering the same bug mid-task, do not park your own implementation as "superseded" on your own judgment. Push yours, open the PR, cross-reference the overlap in the body (differences named factually), and let the review loop / the humans reconcile which lands. Withdraw only on an explicit operator call.

**Why (autonomy):** The stop: with the fix implemented and committed, I ledgered the task "complete-by-supersession" (a teammate's PR covered the same adapter bug, mid-review) and left our branch unpushed — the deliverable halted. The unblock: the operator's direct redirect — open our PR, don't worry about the other one. Follow-on evidence the deference would have shipped the weaker fix: our PR's review rounds then surfaced data-integrity bugs (checkpoint-ordering first-turn loss, dropped greeting, restart windows) absent from the competing branch (hermes-plow-chat#35 vs #33, 2026-08-29). Next different instance: any repo where a mid-task `gh pr list`/review reveals an overlapping open PR from another engineer or agent session.

## A capability that must exist in two repos gets mutual cross-pointers and convergence-biased shape — in the same change that creates the twin

**Change:** When the same capability necessarily lands in two codebases (different runtimes, delivery mechanisms, or fleets), add a short header comment at BOTH sites in the same PR(s) that create the twin: each names the other (repo + path + the pin/mechanism that ships it) and states the convergence rules that keep the copies mergeable (env-only config, paths relative to the artifact's own directory, stdlib-only — whatever keeps one source serving both). Prefer shape changes that make the sources byte-identical over per-side variants, so the twin can eventually be one pinned artifact.

**Why (autonomy):** After porting a skill from plow's hosted-agent image to the agent-mgr Docker fleet (plow-pbc/plow#1475/#1487 + plow-pbc/agent-mgr#74, 2026-08-29), the operator directed: "we need to leave comments in both code bases pointing to each other and encouraging convergence over time" — a whole extra instruction round that a standing rule makes automatic. Two undocumented copies drift invisibly; the pointer biases every future editor toward extracting/sharing instead of patching one side. Next different instance: a config schema or client stub that must exist in both a server repo and an SDK repo, or a review-bot rubric mirrored between kwr and roborev. (2026-08-29-life-assistant3-06bfe47f)

## Work resting on a flagged-unverified platform capability → scope to verify-and-report, defer the dependent work to its own issue

**Change:** When an issue or plan touches work that depends on an unverified platform behavior (an API delivering a payload shape, a runtime supporting a feature), don't silently include the dependent work OR leave the dependency unchecked: add a small "verify the capability + comment the verdict on the issue" task to the current plan, and defer the dependent port/feature to its own issue/PR. Converts "unverified" into a known fact without inflating the current scope; a lost capability gets said plainly instead of tracked as forever-pending.

**Why (autonomy):** During a migration design (life-assistant issue #9, 2026-08-28), a skill port depended on plow_chat delivering inbound image parts — unverified. The operator's scoping steer: verify cheaply now, report on the issue, port later. Next different instance: any repo where a planned feature rests on an unconfirmed dependency behavior — e.g. a CI feature depending on an unverified runner capability, or a bot feature depending on an API field the docs don't guarantee. ## [removes-handback] "Converged / ready for your merge decision" includes the checks board — read `gh pr checks` before the banner

**Change:** Before emitting a CONVERGED banner or any "ready for your merge decision" hand-off, run `gh pr checks <PR#>` and account for every red row — resolve it, diff-scope it as pre-existing, or name it in the hand-off with its disposition. A review-comment loop (knightwatch/babysit) never surfaces scanner checks (CodeQL, deploy gates), so a clean review round is not a clean board. Corollary mechanics when the red is a code-scanning alert already ruled by-design: dismiss the alert with a documented reason (280-char cap), and since default-setup CodeQL can't be re-run and the check-run rerequest API 404s on it, retrigger with an empty commit.

## [removes-handback] A dead session's work is finished here, not reported recoverable — adopt the branch and drive its loop to done

**Change:** When asked to look at a crashed/limit-killed/orphaned agent session (another host, a subagent, a killed loop), the deliverable is the *completed work*, not a recovery report: back up its commits to the remote, extract its pending state from the transcript (unapplied review findings, undispatched fixes, unopened PRs), then adopt the branch in your own lane and run the remaining loop to merge-ready in the current session. Hand back only what is genuinely blocked (the dead account's rate limit does not bind your session — test by proceeding, don't assume).

## Setup answers a later unattended run needs get persisted at collection time — the unattended consumer recovers-or-asks-by-name, never guesses

**Change:** When designing (or RCA-ing) any agent/cron product where setup collects answers in conversation (a host, a login, a device id, a feed URL), give every answer a durable home at collection time (config/dotenv beside its siblings), make the unattended path recover it from there, and when it is missing make the refusal NAME the one answer only the owner can supply — the consumer messages the owner that question and stops; it never fabricates a plausible default. A guessed value that reaches an operator instruction (a wrong `ssh-copy-id user@host`) is worse than a stop. Corollary: coupled identity values (a host and its login) converge in ONE atomic write, or a crash re-creates the wrong pairing.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — the life-dashboard weekly digest cron failed for the owner with a wrong hand-off (`ssh-copy-id pi@…` when the Pi's login was `so`): the setup skill had collected `pi_user` in conversation and deliberately kept it out of config, so the unattended resume guessed. Prior authority — the owner's directive to fix the product holistically ("maybe it's just a simple fix to where the credential is stored") and the dotenv already durably holding the sibling value (the endpoint). Unblock — PRs #59 (life-assistant-hermes-agent) persisting `DASHBOARD_PI_USER`, making `{}` a full-state resume, and refusing by name. Promoted from the life-assistant2 feedback ledger (`holistic-fix-preference`).

**Next instance:** any repo whose onboarding interview feeds a scheduled job — a deploy target collected in chat that a nightly release cron later needs, a webhook URL a digest bot re-derives — same rule: persist at collection, recover-or-ask-by-name, never guess.


## An "update X" ask scopes to the named layer — adjacent version pins need their own explicit ask
**Change:** When the operator asks to "update <thing>", update exactly the layer that phrase names in their workflow (content, skills, app-level pins, restart) and leave adjacent version pins — base/runtime images, engine versions, OS-level deps — untouched unless explicitly asked. When an adjacent bump looks genuinely due, surface it as a one-line offer in the report, don't fold it into the update.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — an "update my assistant" ask got an adjacent runtime image pin bumped along with the intended skills+pins+restart, requiring an operator correction defining the scope. Prior authority — the ask named the assistant layer only; nothing authorized the runtime bump. Unblock — the operator's correction enumerating what "update my assistant" means.
**Next instance:** "update the dashboard" / "update the kiosk" in any repo — sync its app code and config; don't bump its container base image or runtime engine pin without a separate ask.

## [removes-handback] A converged stacked PR whose base just merged → proactively merge-resolve and re-verify, don't park on CONFLICTING

**Change:** When a stacked PR you're driving reaches converged/awaiting-merge and its parent PR then merges (base auto-retargets to main, state flips to CONFLICTING), treat that as a wake condition: merge the new base in, resolve (adopting main's canonical versions where the parent's squash duplicated your commits), rerun the full gate, and push — so the PR is sitting merge-ready when the human returns. The babysit loop's terminal exit on convergence should re-arm (or hand a note to the main loop) whenever the PR's base branch is another open PR.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — plow-pbc/plow#1544 sat CONFLICTING after #1542's squash-merge until the operator asked "can you resolve merge conflicts on this and then merge?". Prior authority — the babysit skill already directs autonomous merge-conflict resolution mid-loop, and the stacking (base = the sibling PR's branch) was my own recorded decision. Unblock — the operator's message restating exactly that resolution request.
**Next instance:** Any repo where a follow-up PR is opened against a feature branch: the moment the parent lands (squash or merge), the child needs the same resolve-retarget pass before the human looks at it.

**Change:** Extends to the base branch that merged WITHOUT being deleted: GitHub only auto-retargets a stacked PR when the base branch disappears, so the moment the parent PR merges, `gh pr edit <child> --base main` (or confirm the branch was deleted) before handing the child off — and after any human "merged" report on a stacked PR, verify with `git merge-base --is-ancestor <merge-sha> origin/main` before pulling main.

Unblock — I caught it only on the ancestor check and relanded it as #288; the operator merged twice.
**Next instance:** Any two-PR stack in plow-pbc/plow where the parent is merged with "delete branch" unchecked — the child needs its base flipped to main before its "converged" hand-off, or its merge is a no-op.

## [removes-handback] A design question whose recommended answer is reversible and evidence-backed isn't a question — take it, note the assumption

**Change:** Before issuing an `AskUserQuestion` during brainstorming/design, run two checks: (1) is the answer discoverable from reachable state (a host you can ssh to, a vault/config/live container the user already pointed you at)? — investigate first and only ask about what remains; (2) is your own "(Recommended)" option both reversible and backed by the evidence you just gathered? — take it, record the assumption in the design doc's decisions section, and let the user override at spec review instead of blocking mid-interview.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — during the checkin-watch design interview (str-hermes-agent#6 session, 2026-08-31), two of four AskUserQuestions were avoidable round-trips: the "what counts as cleaner started" ask was answered by the user pointing at state I could reach ("ssh <user>@wakeup and look — hermes figured it out today"), and the "which properties" scope ask was answered with the Recommended option verbatim. Prior authority — ssh access to the host, the vault/skill files holding the attribution mechanism, and the standing investigate-before-consult rule. Unblock — the user redirected me to evidence for one and rubber-stamped the recommendation for the other.
**Next instance:** Designing a backup-rotation feature in a different repo: instead of asking "which hosts should this cover?", enumerate the fleet from the tailscale host map, cover all reachable hosts, and note the assumption in the spec — the user edits the list at spec review if they want fewer.

### +1 (plow9 marketing-consolidation, 2026-09-01)
**Change:** Extends past design interviews: a reviewer's [blocking] fact-claim about an external/live system ("this redirect breaks agent installs") is also researchable, not operator-gated — curl the live paths, query the prod DB/logs for actual usage, `gh search code` across the org, then bring the operator only the residual intent call.

Unblock — operator: "can't you do research to figure it out?"; the research fully resolved the blocker in minutes.
**Next instance:** A reviewer claims "this API endpoint is still used by mobile clients" on a deprecation PR — query prod access logs and search the org's client repos before asking the operator whether to keep it.

### +1 (life-assistant7 plow-chat RCA, 2026-09-01)
**Change:** Extends past `AskUserQuestion` to the prose offer. An offer you make in a turn's closing line ("want me to file these?") that the human's next message doesn't answer is NOT a decline — it is an item you dropped. When the offered action is cheap and reversible (filing an issue, adding a comment, capturing evidence), just do it and report it in one line; reserve the offer for actions that are irreversible or outward-facing.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — during an RCA I offered three times across three turns to file two runtime bugs I had already fully evidenced, and only filed them when the operator finally said to. Prior authority — the operator had already said "file the issue" and "yes file that as well" for the sibling findings from the same investigation, filing is reversible, and the evidence (state DB rows, source line numbers) was already in hand. Unblock — the operator had to spend a turn saying "file the bugs".

**Change:** Extends the closing-line-offer case to an anomaly *you* surfaced. ## Never route a credential-store's contents through stdout, even "masked" — enumerate keys from the consumer's source instead

**Change:** To learn an unfamiliar secret-bearing file's structure (auth.json, .env, token pools), read the CODE that consumes it for key names/env vars, or print top-level key names only; never pipe values through an ad-hoc recursive masker (one unhandled container type — a list of dicts — fails open and dumps raw secrets). Prior authority — CLAUDE.md § Secrets already forbids echoing secret-bearing files; the masker was an end-run that felt compliant. Unblock — n/a (self-inflicted; the rule prevents the class).
**Next instance:** Inspecting any service's credential file on any host — a Slack token store, a k8s secret dump, a browser profile — where the "safe summary" impulse produces a value-walking script.

## [removes-handback] Arm a poll loop only after its probe succeeds once in the foreground — and make the loop distinguish "condition false" from "probe errored"

Silence must mean "condition not yet true", never "probe can't run here".

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — an ECS rollout watcher (`aws ecs describe-services … 2>/dev/null` in an until-loop) spun silently forever because this machine had no such AWS profile; the deploy's verification stalled until the human prodded "great please verify". **Next instance:** Watching a `kubectl rollout status` / `gh run watch` / `terraform apply` poll from a machine that lacks the cluster kubeconfig or gh auth — the foreground pre-flight fails fast and reroutes the watch to the host that holds the credential.

## Never chain a destructive command with its safety check in one invocation — the check gates nothing there

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Git Safety` (or a new shared-state bullet beside it): any command that deletes or overwrites shared state (docker `rm`/`volume rm`, DB drops, file/dir deletion, lock clearing) runs in its OWN tool invocation, issued only after the previous invocation's safety-check output has been read and judged clear. `check; destroy` in one call executes the destruction regardless of what the check prints — the check becomes decoration. Corollary for multi-agent hosts: shared docker volumes/DBs serve every numbered lane, so "my checkout's test infra" is usually not mine alone — `pgrep -fl pytest` (or the equivalent liveness probe) is part of the check, and any hit is a stop.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — none (self-caught, but the blast was real): recreating a wedged plow test-db, `pgrep -fl pytest` + `docker rm -f && docker volume rm` ran as one invocation; the pgrep output showed a parallel lane's live test runs — after the volume was already gone, failing their in-flight suites. Prior authority — CLAUDE.md's before-re-trigger rule already requires confirming the owner is dead before clearing state; the ordering error made the confirmation unreadable until too late. Unblock — recreated the DB immediately; the parallel session's next run recovered.

**Next instance:** Clearing a "stale" flock/pidfile, dropping a dev database, pruning a shared docker network or builder cache on any multi-lane machine — the liveness check lands in one call, the destructive command only in the next.

### +1 — 2026-09-12 · kwr6-403-denial-278 · the same shape when the CHECK is a PreToolUse hook — a gate fires once per command string, so anything chained ahead of it is invisible to it
**Change:** Extend beyond destructive+check to any command whose *gate* reads state that an earlier command in the same invocation changes. Harness hooks (`roborev-pre-push-gate`, the knightwatch in-flight push gate) evaluate once, before the whole Bash string runs — so `clear-the-gate && gated-command` is the same decoration as `check; destroy`, with the failure inverted: the gate blocks on state the very same invocation was about to clear. Issue the state change, read its result, then issue the gated command.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — none (self-caught, one wasted round-trip): I ran `roborev comment … && roborev close <id> && git push` as one call. The pre-push gate evaluated before any of it and refused, citing the still-open verdict the same string was two commands from closing. Prior authority — `CLAUDE.md` § Commit Frequently already spells this out for `git commit && git push` and names the once-per-string mechanism; I applied it to commit/push and not to close/push. Unblock — re-issued `close` and `push` as separate calls; the push went through unchanged.
**Next instance:** any gated action preceded by its own unblock — clearing a lock then acquiring it, dismissing a review then pushing, writing a config the next command's hook validates. The rule is one invocation per gate-visible state transition, in any repo.

## [removes-handback] A tool's non-interactive confirmation gate on a side effect INHERENT to the user's explicit request → use the documented ack and proceed
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps` (sibling of the autonomy-mandate hard-gate bullet): when a CLI refuses non-interactively but names its own acknowledgment mechanism (an env var like `AGENT_TRANSITION_ACK=1`, a `--yes`/`--confirm` flag), and the gated side effect is *inherent* to the operation the user just asked for — not incidental to it — set the ack and proceed, reporting the side effect in the summary. The gate exists to stop *unattended* invocations; a user-requested operation whose completion requires the gated step is already authorized. Still stop when the side effect is incidental (a restart the ask didn't imply), irreversible beyond the ask's scope, or the gate names a consequence the user plausibly doesn't know about.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — renaming a live agent per the user's explicit request, `agent-mgr down` refused non-interactively ("AGENT_LIVE=1, a restart messages its person"), and I fired an `AskUserQuestion`. Prior authority — the rename cannot happen without the restart, so the request already implied it; the tool documented the exact ack env var in its refusal. Unblock — the user picked "Yes, proceed (Recommended)", adding nothing the context didn't already hold; the very next operation (shutting the old agent down) used the ack without asking and drew no objection. **Next instance:** any gated CLI during a user-requested operation — a deploy tool's `--confirm`, terraform's `-auto-approve` on a plan the user asked to apply, a migration runner's "type YES" prompt with a documented non-interactive flag.

Read the feed itself — the `latest-mac.yml` / appcast / manifest the installed app actually polls — and compare it against the fix commit; a merged-and-tagged fix that never got promoted is invisible to every repo-side check. The remedy then is a **promote**, never a PR.

(b) **Before either check, bind the product name to the repo that actually builds it** — by searching the org for a string from the wire (`gh api "search/code?q=org:<org>+<field>"`), not by matching the product's name against repo names. ## [removes-handback] Asked to review a themed multi-issue plan? Audit the shared PREMISE before any per-issue mechanics or sequencing
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Take the Steps. When the operator hands over a batch of issues/PRs filed under one organizing thesis ("make X and Y one thing", "converge these", a migration roadmap) and asks for review, the batch's **premise** is the highest-leverage thing to audit and it is invisible from inside any single item — every issue reads as sound because each was filed *assuming* the premise. Audit it explicitly and first: name the thesis in one sentence, ask what it would cost if it were wrong, and check whether the two sides it wants to converge differ for a *reason* (a product difference, a distinct operating point) rather than by omission. That was the real review, and it went unasked for a full round-trip. When I did audit the premise it did not hold as written: the fleet's mutable bind-mounted home *is* agent-mgr's product, so converging it to the cloud's baked-image shape would have deleted the tool's reason to exist — a conclusion no per-issue review could reach.

## [removes-handback] Operator confusion about your approach is a STOP signal — re-derive the options, don't explain and continue

When the operator questions the *approach* mid-execution — "I'm confused why you're messing with X", "wait, that's not shipped, right?", "why does Y matter?" — treat it as a stop-and-re-examine signal, not a prompt to justify and keep going. They are usually surfacing a flaw you have talked yourself past, and the tell is that they are questioning the *premise* rather than the mechanics. Sequence: (1) pause the in-flight work — no further push, commit, or build; (2) re-derive the options from scratch, explicitly including the smaller, more-conservative one you skipped; (3) check what is actually **shipped** versus in-flight, and prefer a fix that keeps the build on known-good components over one that introduces an unshipped jump; (4) answer their question plainly — yes or no first — then present the real fork with a recommendation. A pick you made *earlier in the same thread* on incomplete information does not survive a later, better-informed confusion signal: don't cite the stale decision to justify continuing.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — mid-way through an autonomous durable-fix push for a message-delivery regression, I was bumping a third-party engine two major versions to "match" an in-repo change's new contract. The operator asked twice why I was touching a version that isn't shipped; the second ask is the avoidable round-trip. Prior authority — the conservative option (make the in-repo change work against the shipped engine, or revert it) was fully available and cheaper, and I had already recorded that the engine was unshipped. Unblock — the operator's repeated question; he was right, and I nearly pushed the riskier path having rationalized it as "fix-forward". (drained from the plow4 feedback ledger)
**Next instance:** Any autonomous session where the operator asks a skeptical one-liner about a dependency bump, a migration, or a rewrite you are mid-way through — in any repo. The signal is a question about *why this approach*, not about the code.

## [removes-handback] "The tooling doesn't do that yet" — check for the affordance in every SHAPE, not just the one you grepped for
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Verify Before Claiming Done, as a sibling of the "It can't run here" bullet. Before asserting that a convention, runner, or framework *doesn't* handle something — "there's no one-shot for X", "you'll have to do that manually", "nobody built the wrapper yet" — read its canonical source and check for the capability in **any** shape: a CLI, a library call, a git hook, a task-runner recipe, or an agent skill the installing agent executes. The failure mode is not reading nothing; it is reading for one shape (a shell script under `bin/`) and concluding absence when the capability ships as another (a `SKILL.md`). Enumerate the shapes before the assertion, not the filenames. Distinct from the opt-out rule above, which is about a *deliberate local config* making a present capability report as absent; this one is about looking in the wrong place for a capability that was never disabled.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — I told the operator a convention's dependency-install runner "isn't deployed" and handed him a manual sequence, which is precisely the sequencing that convention exists to automate. Prior authority — one `gh api repos/<org>/<convention>/contents` would have surfaced the install skill; nothing gated that read. Unblock — the operator pushed back that he thought the umbrella installed its own dependencies. He was right. (drained from the plow4 feedback ledger)
**Next instance:** Any "the tooling doesn't support that yet" claim about a framework the operator uses — a monorepo task runner, a CI convention, a deploy wrapper — where you checked one directory rather than enumerating the capability's possible shapes.

## A docstring or PR body's behavioral claim is not evidence — trace the mechanism's lifecycle before relaying it as fact

**Change:** When answering "how does X behave at runtime" (an indicator, a retry loop, a cache TTL), treat comments, docstrings, and PR descriptions as claims by a past author, not evidence: trace who sets the state, who clears it, and any timeout/refresh before asserting the behavior — and when comment and code disagree, surface the mismatch as its own finding. Kin to the corpus's tool-log-over-summary and diagnosis-from-both-ends rules, but those bind during debugging/verification; this binds during *explanation*, where no checker ever runs and a wrong relay ships with full confidence.

**Why (autonomy):** quality-steer with a real round-trip, promoted from a captured `feedback` memory. Asked whether quiet-mode message-dropping was compensated by the typing indicator, I relayed an adapter docstring's "the typing indicator already runs for the whole turn" as fact; the operator observed it was not continuous and had to bounce me back with a systematic-debugging directive. The trace showed the docstring wrong on day one — any mid-turn send permanently killed the indicator loop — and produced both the correction and the follow-on feature PR. **Next instance:** any repo where a "does it back off / retry / expire?" question tempts an answer from a code comment or an old PR body instead of the state-transition code itself. (Session: 2026-09-02 · plow2-typing-indicator)


## [removes-handback] A background task reported "killed" is a harness signal, not an operator interrupt — classify it before you stand down

**Change:** When a background task returns `status: killed` / "was stopped", do not treat it as the operator interrupting you. Read the evidence first: **exit 143 is SIGTERM** (a deadline), where a genuine failure exits 1; check how far the log actually got; and check your own `timeout` against the tool's cap — the Bash tool clamps `timeout` to **600000 ms**, so a larger value is silently shortened and a long gate dies at 10 minutes looking like a stop. Only after none of those explain it should you consider it a human stop, and even then re-read the standing authority before re-asking for it.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — three times in one session I read a killed background task as an interrupt. The worst instance: a killed CI-wait made me pause before a merge and ask for authorization the operator had already given in the same session, costing a full round-trip on a PR that was green. Prior authority — the notification itself carried the discriminator (exit 143, 56% through the suite), and the transcript carried an explicit "and then merge". Unblock — "great /babysit-pr to convergence and then merge." I later diagnosed the real cause: I had passed `timeout: 900000`, above the documented 600000 cap, so lint + suite crossed a 10-minute deadline I did not know I had set.

**Next instance:** any long-running gate (a full test suite, a CI poll, a deploy wait) backgrounded in any repo — the same clamp and the same 143 apply, and the same instinct to read the kill as disapproval. (Session: 2026-09-02 · plow9-vip-teardown)

## Enumerate EVERY path to an effect before a frequency or rarity claim — "the one X that does Y" comments are file-scoped, not global
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` beside the "benign/rare is a claim too" bullet: before telling the human how often something fires ("rebuilds are rare", "only on user action"), grep the effect itself across the whole area (`recreate|delete.*instance|force|digest|rebuild`), not the one subsystem you are reading; treat a local "this is the one op routed through Y" comment as scoped to that file. A frequency claim that feeds a design decision is load-bearing evidence; if it later proves wrong, lead the next message with the correction, and when the corrected number resolves a decision you had deferred, say so and proceed.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — asked how often the agent VM is recreated (load-bearing for the persistence design on plow#1025/#1028), I answered "rare, not per-update" from one Swift file's comment; a separate digest-change path recreates it on every app update, which flipped the decision from accept-loss to a dedicated persistent disk. Prior authority — the existing "it's benign / expected is a claim too" bullet. Unblock — a whole-area grep for the destructive effect.
**Next instance:** "how often does the cache get invalidated / the container restart / the token rotate?" asked before a persistence or retry design in any repo.

## Whole-directory migrations: `dotglob` for hidden entries, and trace each entry's writer/resolver before relocating it
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md` (Migrations or Fail-Fast family): a shell sweep of `"$dir"/*` is incomplete by construction without `shopt -s dotglob`; and "every directory is state, every file is config" is an assumption to verify per entry — a file the host rewrites on every start and that the consumer resolves relative to the moved dir is host-authored and must be re-delivered, never relocated (moving it freezes a stale snapshot and starves a fresh install). Rename the legacy tree to `<name>.migrated` rather than `rm -rf` so a rollback build still finds the data.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — plow#1032's migration loop skipped hidden state dirs and would have moved a per-start host-written `node.json` onto a VM-local disk the host can't write; the human's forensic supersession (#1036) caught both. Prior authority — § Git Safety's "verify before deleting a replaced deployment" and the ownership-census top rule. Unblock — per-entry writer/resolver trace plus `dotglob`.
**Next instance:** relocating any app's config/state directory onto a new volume or new path — a dotfiles installer, a container volume split, a cache dir move.

## A negative claim about a planning/design artifact must sweep the surfaces that artifact class is EXPECTED to live on off-tree
**Change:** Extend the absence-claim bullet in `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`: before asserting "no plan / design note / spec was ever written", check the gitignored workspaces the tooling deliberately uses (`.superpowers/sdd/`, `docs/superpowers/plans/`, session scratch dirs) and the PR/issue comment threads where durable copies get posted — repo policy (§ Don't Commit Plans) makes "not on any branch" the expected state for an artifact that WAS written.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — I told the human the execution plan for the plow #1067/#1107 durable-state work was never written; it was a full SDD plan in `.superpowers/sdd/` and reproduced verbatim as a comment on plow#1071, and the human had to correct me. Prior authority — the absence-claim bullet plus a project memory naming the SDD plan location. Unblock — the human pointing at the comment.
**Next instance:** any repo using superpowers/SDD or a gitignored plans dir, when asked "did we ever plan X?" or "where is the design for Y?".

## [removes-handback] Establish POC-vs-product at brainstorm time — on a POC, merge and use it rather than converging the review bot
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Concise Code` (beside "When iteration isn't converging"): ask "POC or product?" during brainstorming, before the PR opens, because the answer sets the LOC target, test depth, and how many review rounds are worth running. On a POC, decline shape/structure findings on the operating point (concede the argument, record the ruling on the PR), still fix security / data-loss / false user-facing claims, and recommend merge + real usage over another round. The treadmill tell — round N's findings are mostly bugs introduced fixing round N−1 — means the loop stopped paying; say so and stop.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — a side project ran ~8 automated review rounds before the human said "honestly this is a POC", which flipped every remaining structural finding from apply to decline-and-merge. Prior authority — the operating point was knowable at brainstorm time; nothing in the review loop asks it. Unblock — the human's framing, after the rounds were already spent.
**Next instance:** any repo where `/babysit-pr` or a bot review loop runs on a prototype, spike, or personal tool — a hermes agent skill, a kiosk seed, a one-off dashboard.

## Guard a wrapped CLI by the argument's VALUE shape, never by reconstructing which subcommand argv is running
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md § Fail-Fast` (or a security-guard sibling): when a wrapper must refuse hostile arguments, write the predicate over the dangerous property of the value (absolute path, `..` segment, file-reading flag by prefix/suffix rule) with no command names in it. Reconstructing the wrapped tool's command resolution from argv fails open — global flags sit before and between command words, every command has aliases — and a mismatched security guard silently stops applying rather than erroring. Mutation-verify every predicate change (revert it, name the test row that goes red), and check a candidate rule against real traffic before adopting it ("refuse any slash" would have broken every URL-bearing message).
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — a wrapper guard went through repeated review rounds, each moving the positional match one step (index 0 → subsequence → token membership) and each defeated by the parser; twice the new tests passed under the old implementation, pinning nothing. Prior authority — the danger was a property of the value all along. Unblock — the human's steer to guard the value, not the command.
**Next instance:** any PreToolUse hook, MCP tool wrapper, or agent-side allowlist that filters `gh`, `git`, `aws`, `docker`, or a vendor CLI's arguments.

## During a long build/install wait, pre-validate the external chain by hand so the install leaves exactly one unknown
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` (next to the executing-context bullet): when a 30–45 min build is the only delivery path for an integration, don't poll — fetch the same pinned artifact, verify its digest, stage it into the real runtime at a scratch path, and drive the chain with the real credential from inside the executing context (a read proves auth, a `--dry-run` write proves command shape). Remove the scratch copies afterward. A blind post-install test conflates credential, scope, reachability, command grammar, missing binary, and model routing; pre-validating collapses that to the one variable the install actually delivers.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — a 16-minute RC build was being waited out with polling while the integration's credential, endpoint, allowlist flags, and command shape were all testable without it. Prior authority — the pinned artifact and VM access were in hand. Unblock — the human's steer to stage it by hand during the wait; the install then had one open question, and it passed.
**Next instance:** any repo whose delivery path is a slow CI → package → install loop — a Mac app DMG, a container image pushed to a tenant, a firmware bundle — with an external API on the far side.

### +1 — 2026-09-04 · agent-mgr1-course-qa-hermes · a blocked ambient track is wait time to re-validate the goal's own acceptance evidence

**Change:** Extends the parent from a build wait to any wait on a shared resource you do not control — a review-bot fleet, a CI runner pool, a release train. While the ambient track is starved, re-run the acceptance evidence the goal is actually judged on against the current head, rather than reporting the queue position. File the starvation as an issue on the shared resource, then keep producing evidence.

**Why (autonomy):** Idle, not a hard stop (per the tag rule). Across roughly three hours the reviewer fleet's alphabetical queue starved a PR behind another org's, and I reported 'waiting, the watch will wake me' while three config and skill deploys went un-revalidated by any real run. Prior authority — the goal named the acceptance evidence itself (the container tests multiple course screens), which was runnable the whole time. Unblock — the operator asked how it was going and said to continue.

**Next instance:** any repo where the merge path is gated on a shared bot or runner pool — a busy monorepo's CI, a self-hosted reviewer, a staging environment with one slot — while a local acceptance run is available.

## [removes-handback] Before a session restart, hand off to the trackers — one self-contained comment per affected PR/issue, not a chat summary
**Change:** Add to `PR_LIFECYCLE.md § Issue hygiene` (or `CLAUDE.md § Answer Shape`): when the human says they're restarting or spinning up new agents, write the point of view into every affected durable surface — the plan issue (what expired and why), the defect issue (current authoritative state), the successor PR (actionable brief), your own PR (carry forward vs skip) — each timestamped, naming the ref measured against, with a runnable re-derivation block, and marking unverified claims as unverified. Prefer authoritative surfaces (a compare API) over convenient ones (local remote-tracking refs).
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — a session-end summary lived only in chat; a plan-of-record issue's premise had already expired (a squash-merge meant the fix never landed on `main`) and the next agent would have trusted the stale plan. Prior authority — the trackers were writable and the findings were in hand. Unblock — the human asked for the hand-off to go to the tickets.
**Next instance:** any multi-PR program in any repo where the operator says "I'm going to restart / kick off fresh agents" — a rollout, a migration, an incident.

### +1 — 2026-09-11 · plow8-invite-email-rollout · the same hand-off is owed at the END of a rollout, unprompted — "what I need from you" in chat is the stale-plan shape

**Change:** The trigger isn't only a restart. Any turn that ends a rollout with residue — validation nobody has run, a step blocked on a credential only the operator holds, an image that shipped but has never booted — writes that residue into the tracker as it reports: one issue per separable concern, each carrying how to validate it and when to close it, labelled so the operator can find them (`needs-testing`). The chat summary then points at issues instead of *being* the record. Closing asks in chat evaporate when the session does, which is the same failure as the stale plan-of-record, arriving from the other end.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — I closed a multi-repo rollout with a three-item "what I need from you" list in chat, and the operator had to ask for issues to be filed across the repos I had touched. Prior authority — `PR_LIFECYCLE.md` § Issue hygiene plus a captured project memory saying a self-named follow-up gets filed in the same pass, not left as prose. Unblock — the operator asking for an issue per touched repo, with steps to validate and close.

**Next instance:** the end of any deploy, migration, or incident where something shipped unvalidated or a step is blocked on the operator — file it, label it, then point at it in the summary.

## Judge an upstream dependency's changelog item by whether the product INHERITS or REPLACED the component it touches
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` (a sibling of "Does it ship?"): before claiming an upstream release item does or doesn't reach users, grep the repo for what the product replaced or brokered (custom channels/providers, proxy base URLs, forked extensions) and map the item onto inherited-core vs replaced-component. Expect a population split, not a binary: the default brokered path and a user-connected native provider path can differ for the same item. Core agent-loop items are usually inherited; channel-ingress and provider-tier items are usually replaced.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — in one session I called upstream iMessage-delivery fixes a product win (the product ships its own iMessage channel, so they were inert) and dismissed a new model as irrelevant (a native connect path made it live); the human corrected both. Prior authority — the replaced-component boundary was one grep away. Unblock — the human's corrections.
**Next instance:** any product embedding a forked or partially-bypassed framework — an agent runtime, a browser bundle, an ORM with custom drivers — when a release-notes digest or "should we upgrade?" question comes in.

## Team-owned skills stay in the product repo; a personal config repo gets same-named pointer skills, never copies or link plumbing

**Change:** Before relocating a repo-scoped skill (or any team-facing doc) to make it reachable from another checkout, ask who else consumes it. `srosro/code-config` is one operator's harness — other developers of the product repo don't have it — so a team asset moved there vanishes for them. Keep it canonical in the product repo; give a sibling repo reach with a same-named pointer skill (same `name`/`description` trigger phrases, body: "lives in `<owner>/<repo>` at `.claude/skills/<name>`; read it from a checkout on `main`"). Fixes found while a file is temporarily copied elsewhere land in the canonical copy.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — the operator had to catch "code-config is my personal repo, not all devs have it" after two PRs were already open moving the four `plow-prod-*` skills out of `plow-pbc/plow` into code-config (plow#1673 closed unmerged; code-config#209 reworked twice; the port-back landed as plow#1678; pointers as latch#289). Prior authority — the repo's README says code-config is the operator's own config; `just install` links it into `~/.claude` per host, not per team. Unblock — the operator named both the ownership rule and the pointer-skill shape.
**Next instance:** a latch or hermes-agent skill that a plow session wants; or a repo-scoped hook/runbook that "would be handy from anywhere" — same question, same answer.


### +1 — 2026-09-11 · plow4-qa-latch-smoke

**Change:** Same rule, two repos later: the QA smoke skills (`/plow-message`, `/plow-smoke`) and their `plow-say` CLI were built in code-config with PRs that DELETED the copies from `plow-pbc/plow` and `plow-pbc/plow-mac`. Before opening a PR that moves or deletes a repo-scoped skill, name who loses it; a personal harness reaches one operator's fleet, never the team.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — the operator caught it at hand-off time ("you just took this skill away from all of my coworkers"), after three PRs were open (code-config#218, plow#1894, plow-mac#12, all closed unmerged and re-homed as plow#1903). Prior authority — the same rule is already this proposal, from the `plow-prod-*` episode; I re-derived the wrong shape anyway. Unblock — the operator named the reach problem and chose the product repo.
**Next instance:** Any hermes-plugin-plow or life-assistant skill a plow session wants; or a hook/runbook that feels "handy from anywhere".

## [removes-handback] A UI PR hand-off carries its Vercel preview URL and a rendered screenshot

**Change:** When the PR changes anything a visitor sees and the repo deploys per-branch previews (Vercel comment on the PR, `vercel ls`), the `gh pr create` hand-off includes the preview URL as raw text and a screenshot of the changed surface — the rendered page is the artifact, not the diff.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — after handing off a one-line CSS fix (aiworthusing #22) with tests + a local screenshot, the operator's next message was a request for the preview URL. Prior authority — the Vercel bot had already posted the preview on the PR; `CLAUDE.md` § Verify Before Claiming Done already says a UI deploy is verified by its rendered page. Unblock — the operator asked; one `gh pr view --json comments | grep vercel.app` answered it.

**Next instance:** any static or Next.js site on Vercel/Netlify (plow dashboard, builder index) where a style or layout PR is opened.
### +1 — 2026-09-04 · plow-latch-preview

A claude.ai artifact is not the preview: it loses the site's routes, analytics, and asset behaviour.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — after opening plow-pbc/plow#1723 with local screenshots, the operator asked "can i get a preview?"; I published an artifact copy and *offered* a Vercel deploy as a question; the operator's next message was "give me the vercel preview" — two round-trips for one URL. Prior authority — `vercel` CLI was authenticated, `vercel project ls` listed the `plow` project, and the memory `project-plow100-served-from-api-deploy` already recorded that plow.co surfaces ship on their own pipeline. Unblock — the operator asked twice; the deploy took one link + one deploy command and the URL was verified through `vercel curl` in under a minute.

**Change:** Invert the 2026-09-04 +1's fallback order. The preview URL in a UI hand-off must (a) render the changed page and (b) open with no login. Verify both before handing it over: `curl -sI <url>/<path>` must return 200, not a 302 to an SSO page. When the repo's Vercel bot comment belongs to a sibling project, or the preview sits behind deployment protection, do NOT deploy a manual Vercel preview or publish an Artifact: serve the checkout locally (`nohup python3 -m http.server <port>` in the changed dir, leave it running for the session) and hand back `http://localhost:<port>/<path>` as raw text, with your own screenshot as verification. Prior authority — I had already served the page on localhost:8765 to screenshot it, then killed the server; `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` already says verify against the live surface. Unblock — restarting the local server and pasting the localhost URL; the operator then said going forward to skip the Vercel/claude login entirely and just render locally.
**Next instance:** a latch portal or agent-mgr dashboard CSS PR where the Vercel preview is protected; a docs-site change in a repo whose PR check belongs to the API app; any static-site edit on a machine where the operator is present and a localhost URL works.
### +1 — 2026-09-17 · plow3-build-page-iteration · the no-login ruling didn't fire, and the preview has to survive the session
**Change:** Three facets past the 2026-09-10 ruling. (1) Present-not-firing: I curled the Vercel preview, saw the redirect to a login page, and still offered it as a second option. Once curl shows a login redirect, drop the hosted URL from the hand-off entirely. (2) The operator's preview must outlive the harness: a `run_in_background` `http.server` was killed twice by the harness's low-memory reaper (the host had 80 GB available; brief pressure spikes) while the operator iterated against it for hours. Start it from the first hand-off as `systemd-run --user --unit=<name> --property=RuntimeMaxSec=8h`, tailnet-bound per the tailnet-bind proposal. Serve it with `Cache-Control: no-store` so stale copies don't mask edits, and with extensionless-path → `.html` mapping so clean-URL nav links work. Put the URL at the top of every reply that changes what it shows. (3) A plain-http tailnet URL is not a secure context (`navigator.clipboard` is undefined there): verify copy-button changes on localhost or https, and give the operator the localhost/tunnel URL to test them.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — across plow-pbc/plow#2044 and #2048 the operator asked for a local preview URL three times: after I paired the local URL with a login-gated Vercel link, after the URL scrolled below a status report, and again later. The server also died twice without notice. Prior authority — this proposal's 2026-09-10 ruling already said login-free localhost; keeping my own server alive needed no one. Unblock — re-pasting a working URL and restarting the server as a user unit.
**Next instance:** a Storybook or Vite dev server previewed from another tailnet device during a multi-hour copy/layout iteration in a different repo — transient user unit with a TTL, no-store caching, and the URL leading each reply.

**Change:** Widen the preview rule from PR hand-offs to design work: any mockup, screen flow or diagram shown to the operator mid-design goes through the superpowers brainstorming visual companion (a local server bound tailnet-reachable, per the tailnet-binding proposal), never the Artifact tool — even where that tool's own guidance says to publish.

In one session it printed no run dir for five PRs across three repos, including two with a review demonstrably running at that moment; the skill then treats a queued trigger as "latch CLOSED" and held a push for a full 30-min tick on a trigger aimed at a head already superseded. ## [removes-handback] "A works on host B" against your fleet-wide broken verdict → diff B's USED tools against the tools each agent is OFFERED before restating
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` (a sibling of the absence-claim bullet): when the operator says a sibling deployment does the thing you just declared broken everywhere, do not re-run your probe on the sibling and reassert. Pull the sibling's *mechanism* from its own record — the tool-call names in its session store — and fetch the tool list each agent is actually offered with that agent's own credential (an MCP `tools/list`, a plugin registry), then diff used-vs-offered across the two. "No agent used tool T" and "tool T is not offered" are different surfaces; a verdict built on the first is an absence claim from the wrong layer. Same family: before editing a seed/config directory that looks like the deploy source, confirm the deploy workflow actually builds from it (`agents.json`-style pins to external repos leave dead mirror trees in the monorepo).

## [removes-handback] A doc that has been wrong once this session is no longer a source of truth — re-verify its other claims against the system before acting on them
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`, as the trust-decay sibling of "'Does it ship?' → check the built artifact, not what the docs say *should* ship": once a file has asserted something about its own infrastructure that you have *demonstrated false*, stop treating that file as authoritative for anything else in it. Re-verify each remaining claim you are about to act on against the running system — the registry, the CI config, the deployed artifact. A doc's claims fail together far more often than independently, because they were written at one moment and the system moved underneath all of them at once. Especially: never build a work item (issue, ticket, hand-off) out of a doc's claim about a manual process without first checking whether automation already does it.
**Why (autonomy):** *the stop* — I told the operator three separate times that publishing a base image was manual and needed their ECR credentials, opened a tracking issue instructing them to run `docker buildx --push` by hand, and answered "where do I go to publish?" and "okay how do I publish?" with command blocks. Publishing was fully automated: a `.exe.hermes.revision` bump in a sibling repo triggers `build-agent-image.yml`, which built and pushed within four seconds of the merge. *prior authority* — the same README had already been proven wrong **twice** in that session: it named an ECR repository holding zero tags (I fixed it), and it asserted "agent-mgr runs this base image" when the manifest pinned upstream directly (I fixed that too). I had also *observed* the automation's fingerprint — bases appearing ~30 min after each merge, four workflow runs that day — and attributed it to a diligent human. Two demonstrated errors in one file plus visible contrary behaviour, and I still trusted its third infrastructure claim. *the unblock* — the operator pasted a PR link whose body said "merging this is what publishes". **Next instance:** any repo whose README documents a release/deploy/publish step as manual — checking `.github/workflows/` and the registry's recent push timestamps before writing a runbook or a hand-off ticket that duplicates CI.

## [removes-handback] Before removing or lowering a guard, floor, cap or timeout, find why it was added — the rationale often inverts the change
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`): when a change deletes, lowers, or overrides an existing limit someone else chose — a floor, cap, timeout, retry count, default — read the comment and blame around it and search the issue number it cites *before* writing the diff. State in the PR body what the original intent was and why the change is still right. If no rationale exists, say so; absence of a reason is itself a finding. This applies equally to a value your own earlier change introduced.
**Why (autonomy):** *the stop* — I had approval in hand to delete an inert `timeout` key across five repos and was starting the work. *prior authority* — the rationale was one `sed` away in the same file I had already read twice. *the unblock* — the operator interrupted with "before you start, can you find the PR? work to understand why it was implemented." The floor existed precisely to stop compression being cut short: a reasoning model summarising a large history legitimately exceeds the old default, and truncating it degrades compaction to a deterministic marker. So a value low enough to *bite* would have re-introduced the exact bug the floor was added to fix — my "reach the fallback faster" framing was backwards. The same read surfaced a second mechanism I had missed entirely: a separate 60s no-progress timeout already caught dead streams, so the tuning aimed at a case that was handled elsewhere. That one question turned a cleanup of a no-op into the removal of a latent regression. **Next instance:** any PR that lowers a retry limit, shortens a lock timeout, or removes a defensive clamp in a service someone else tuned — where the constant's comment names the incident it came from.

## [removes-handback] Before building a multi-repo pin/publish chain, trace what the DEPLOYED consumer actually resolves — its resolution code + one live artifact — not what the docs/summary claim
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` as the build-time face of the executing-context rule: when a fix ships by bumping a pinned ref through a chain of PRs (plugin pin → base image → variant `FROM` → registry/revision pin, or any lockfile/module-ref cascade), verify FIRST that the running consumer resolves the artifact your chain publishes — read the resolution end-to-end (which registry, which ref, from which source of truth) and confirm against one live deployed artifact — BEFORE opening PR #1. Two chains can coexist and stale docs routinely name the wrong one; building on an assumed delivery path risks N merged PRs that never reach the target.
**Why (autonomy):** stop — I opened and drove all four PRs of a cloud-agent pin chain, and only traced the resolver (`exe.py`: `{registry}:base-{revision}`, registry from terraform `ecr.tf`, revision from `agents.json`) plus a live `cloud_agents` DB row when the operator handed me a two-supply-chain summary and asked "does this change your POV?". prior authority — full code access to the resolver + terraform and a queryable live DB row, all available before PR #1; the summary I was handed even carried a stale claim (that provisioning reads the old registry) that the code + row refuted. unblock — the operator's own investigation and POV-check, which is exactly the trace I could have run proactively; the chain happened to be correct, so this was a near-miss, not a recovered loss — the preventable part is that the verification was the operator's to prompt.
**Next instance:** any cross-repo version bump where a deployed service resolves the artifact indirectly — a shared library pinned in a lockfile a running service loads, a Terraform module ref, a base-image tag another image builds `FROM` — confirm the deployed consumer resolves the exact ref you're about to publish (its resolution code + one live artifact) before opening the PR chain, not after it merges.

## Debugging against the operator's real sensitive data file → answer from metadata only, never contents

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Secrets: when the input to a bug is one of the operator's own sensitive files (a password-manager export, a bank CSV, a vault dump, a message archive), work from metadata — `stat`, `unzip -l`/`tar -t`, entry sizes and counts, magic bytes — and never `cat`, `unzip -p`, parse, or grep its contents; don't echo attachment filenames either. Unblock — the root cause (a 200 MB whole-file cap vs. a 277 MB export that was 276 MB of unread attachments) came entirely from `unzip -l` sizes, proving the fence costs nothing.
**Next instance:** A Plow or msgvault import bug reproduced against the operator's real WhatsApp/iMessage archive or a real bank statement export, in any repo — tempting to `jq` the file to "see the shape".

## A dev twin that serves what the real API refuses makes the whole suite pass on a fiction — check the vendor's machine-readable contract

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Verify Before Claiming Done: when code calls a third-party API through a local twin/emulator/fake, verify the request shape against the **vendor's own machine-readable contract**, never against the twin. Most large APIs publish one — Google's discovery document (`curl 'https://<api>.googleapis.com/$discovery/rest?version=v1'`) gives every method's parameter enums in a single call. Two rules follow: the twin must **refuse what the vendor refuses**, with the same status code, so an impossible request fails in the dev stack exactly where it fails in production; and no test may assert a URL or payload the vendor would reject. A twin serving *more* than the real API is the same bug class as one serving less, and it is the more dangerous half because everything stays green.

**Why (autonomy):** No operator hand-back — a reviewer caught it — but the failure mode is worth a fence. A merged-and-deploying email feature fetched Gmail threads with `users.threads.get?format=raw`. That format does not exist: `raw` is a `users.messages.get` format, and `threads.get` accepts only `full|metadata|minimal`, per Google's discovery doc. The read path could not have worked in production for a single thread. Nothing caught it because the fiction was pinned twice — the dev twin had been taught to serve thread-`raw`, *and* a provider test asserted that exact invalid URL — so a green suite was evidence of nothing. One `curl` of the discovery document settled it; the fix was `minimal` for the outline plus a per-message `raw` fetch, and the twin now answers `400` on the unsupported format.

**Next instance:** any vendor API reached through a local double — a Stripe fake, an S3 emulator, a hand-rolled webhook stub. Before adding or changing a call, read that method's schema from the vendor, and make the double reject what the vendor rejects.

## Post GitHub bodies from a file — an inline `--body "…"` lets the shell execute and silently delete backticked text

**Change:** Add to `PR_LIFECYCLE.md` § Issue hygiene (which already mandates the `Write`-file + `jq --rawfile` transport for issues) and generalize it to **every** authored body: PR descriptions, PR comments, review replies, issue bodies. Write the text to a file with a quoted heredoc (`<<'MD'`) or the `Write` tool and pass `--body-file`; to edit an existing comment, build the JSON in Python and `gh api --method PATCH … --input <file>`. Never an inline double-quoted `--body`. After posting anything long, read it back and confirm the text survived.

**Why (autonomy):** No hand-back, but it silently corrupts published work. In a double-quoted shell string backticks are command substitution, and technical writing is full of backticked identifiers. Posting a correction to a filed issue, a `` `Dockerfile:86` `` reference was executed ("command not found") and **removed from the published comment** — the sentence went out missing the file reference its argument depended on, and the only reason it was caught was reading the comment back. It looked safe for many earlier posts purely because unbalanced triple-backtick fences happened to absorb most pairs, which is luck, not a boundary.

**Next instance:** any `gh`/`glab`/`curl` call carrying prose you authored — a release note, a PR body, a status comment on someone else's issue. File in, `--body-file` out, then read it back.

**Next instance:** any repo vendoring a service or CLI that ships its own admin/config UI (a Postgres admin, a Grafana, a vault server), where a reviewer probe asks to delete the app-side duplicate of that UI.

## A native binary bundled into a distributable → inspect the link set of the artifact INSIDE the built bundle before calling it shippable
**Change:** For any compiled payload added to a package (vendored server, helper binary, Rust/Go tool), run `otool -L` (macOS) / `ldd` (Linux) on the binary *inside the built bundle*, not the intermediate build output, before claiming it ships; prefer the dependency's static/vendored feature (`vendored_openssl`-style) over whatever the build machine has; and make the build assert the invariant so it fails at build time — including on the cached path, since a stamp keyed on the upstream commit happily reuses a binary built before the fix. This is `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`'s "check the built artifact, not the recipe" in the one shape where the artifact is a binary you compiled rather than a bundle you can grep.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — on the Latch vault PR (Aug 2026) the vendored vault server compiled cleanly, passed every test and review, and was handed off as shippable while linking a Homebrew `libssl.3.dylib` path no user has — the feature would have failed on arrival for everyone without Homebrew. Prior authority — the build log and `otool -L` were available on the packaging machine the whole time. Unblock — the link set was inspected after the hand-off and the vendored-OpenSSL feature plus a build-time assertion landed.
**Next instance:** a compiled helper (a Swift or Rust tool, a Python wheel with native extensions) added to the Plow desktop bundle or a runtime tarball built on mbp and installed on a family machine.


## [removes-handback] "There's no way to do X" is a claim — enumerate the primitives you actually hold before telling the operator a capability is missing

**Change:** Extend `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`'s "'It can't run here' is a claim too" bullet from
*command execution* to *product capability*. Before reporting that something cannot be done — no migration
path, no way to change this, the only option is destroy-and-recreate — write down the primitives you actually
hold (root shell, a DB row, an API verb, files on a persistent disk) and test the cheapest one. A product
surface lacking a feature is not the same as the substrate lacking it: an "immutable image" is still files on
a disk you have root on, and a "non-deletable" record still has an ownership resolver you can read.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — three times in one session I told the operator something was impossible and was
corrected each time. (1) "There is no in-place upgrade; the only way is delete and re-provision" → "isn't this
even simpler? just a new pin?" — the fix was a 90-line file swap that became the session's whole spine. (2) A
yes/no question answered with an unresolved ambiguity → "so does that mean elm is verbose or not?" — the
resolution was one call I already had access to. (3) "You can't deactivate that thread from Plow's side" →
"but if he messages it, the routing re-creates linked to him, right?" — correct, and one function read away.
Prior authority — in all three I already held root SSH, DB read, and the source; nothing was gated.
Unblock — the operator supplied the better hypothesis each time.
**Next instance:** "this SaaS has no export API" before checking whether its web app's own XHR endpoints are
callable, or "this dependency can't be pinned" before reading its resolver.

### +1 — 2026-09-10 · plow9-elm-reconnect · "no API can target that line" when a random assignment can be re-drawn

**Change:** Before reporting that a specific target is unreachable, check whether a random/pooled assignment can simply be re-drawn: a create call that returns its assignment before anything is spent (no auth, nothing consumed until redemption) is a primitive you hold — loop it until it lands on the target, then spend only the winning draw.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — told the operator their agent could not be put back on a specific line with the current code, and ended the turn asking whether to open an API PR. Prior authority — I had already read the activation endpoint: unauthenticated, picks the line at random, and returns the line in the response before redemption. Unblock — operator: "Are you sure?"; the second draw landed on the target, one text, no code change (the durable fix filed as plow-pbc/plow#1870).
**Next instance:** a cloud API that assigns a random zone/IP/port from a pool when you need a specific one, or a queue that hands out a random worker slot — re-request before filing a feature request.
