## Before calling a capability unsupported, read the user's live data — not just the repo

**Change:** "X isn't supported" is a claim about three separable things: the *data* (does the user's own file/config already carry the field?), the *code* (can it write that field?), and the *policy* (is a rule blocking it, and in which phase?). Check all three and report the narrowest one that is actually false. When the user says a restriction looks out of date, answer it as a vintage question — `git log -S "<the rule>"` and `--diff-filter=A` dates — rather than re-asserting the current file.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — asked whether a monitor could keep a "suggested next step" current, I read the repo and answered that no such concept existed, which sent the conversation toward "build the feature". Prior authority — the user's live file was one Latch read away, and the restriction's age was one `git log -S` away. Unblock — the user pushed back that support had been added; reading his actual sheet showed the column already there, the real gap was ~3 constants in a helper, and the restriction I cited was the *newest* line in the repo rather than a stale one.

**Next instance:** any repo where a user asks "can it do X?" about a feature that operates on data they own — a config file, a spreadsheet, a vault, a dashboard — and the answer is being drafted from source code alone. (Session: 2026-09-18 · founder-agent-wiki-pipeline)


## Another agent's judgment is its inference, not your finding — attribute it or verify it, never lead with it

**Change:** The corpus rule to verify an agent's *state* claims against the tool log extends to its *conclusions* ("this is a spoof", "this is blocked", "this is unrelated"). Before relaying one, ask what that agent structurally could not know — relationships, history, intent — and weight its confidence down by that gap. Say "X flagged it" rather than asserting it, until the underlying artifact is checked yourself. Never promote an unverified agent conclusion to the lede of a report.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — a monitored agent flagged an investor's reply as a probable spoofed lookalike domain, citing a DKIM error and different mail infrastructure. I led my report with it as a security finding and added emphasis. Prior authority — the raw headers were fetchable, and the agent had no way to know the relationship. Unblock — the user, who did have that context, said it was almost certainly just a different address; the "evidence" was never independently checked. Amplifying made a weak inference look verified on a topic with real social cost if wrong.

**Next instance:** any session co-driving an agent or tool that emits judgments — a reviewer bot's severity, a monitor's alert classification, a scanner's "malicious" verdict — where the temptation is to forward the verdict rather than its evidence. (Session: 2026-09-18 · founder-agent-wiki-pipeline)


## A teardown request ends at torn down — do not provision the successor

**Change:** Deactivate / de-register / retire / tear down means stop when it is down. Do not mint a replacement credential, claim a line or number, recreate a volume, or start a successor — even when the stated motive is "so I can spin up a fresh one", which explains why they want it gone rather than adding a second task. Split the request at the verb: do the destructive half (after backing up what it destroys and naming where the backup is), hand back the constructive half.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — asked to de-register an agent so a fresh one could be tested, I revoked it and then also minted a new credential on the freed line, deleted the home volume and started a replacement. Prior authority — none for any of that; the request named one verb. Unblock — the user interrupted a tool call mid-verification and said to just tear the old one down. Undoing it cost a second revoke and deleting a volume that should never have existed.

**Next instance:** any decommission ask — a container, a cloud resource, a DNS record, a bot registration — where the motive sentence mentions a replacement and every credential needed to build it is already in hand. (Session: 2026-09-18 · founder-agent-wiki-pipeline)

## What belongs in a shared/base repo is decided by instance count, never by how thin or fat a consumer looks
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md § DRY`: when drawing a shared-repo boundary, count instances per candidate item first. Rule-of-2+ (strongest with drift) moves; rule-of-1 stays with its consumer however small that consumer is. A rule-of-1 item moved at the user's explicit ask is labelled built-to-ask, not extracted. A shared skeleton inside per-consumer files becomes a shared contract test, not a merged file (merging needs a template step, the complexity the DRY was meant to avoid).
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — I proposed a boundary by consumer size ("config-only agents live in the shared repo; the one with an application layer keeps its own"), and the operator had to correct the heuristic in review. Prior authority — § DRY already keys on duplication, and the instance counts were readable from the repos. Unblock — the operator's correction: the domain layer isn't shared because it isn't duplicated, whatever the consumer's size.
**Next instance:** splitting a fleet into base + per-product repos, e.g. deciding which Hermes skills belong in a base image versus each agent repo, or which CI steps go into a shared workflow.
## [removes-handback] Choosing a model, provider or dependency? Gather published evidence BEFORE recommending — your own measurement answers cost, never capability
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Verify Before Claiming Done: a selection decision between models, providers or third-party dependencies needs *two* evidence sources before a recommendation goes to the operator — your own measurement (cost, latency, does-it-work-here) and the published record (benchmark scores, the vendor's own technical report, community reports of real use). Local measurement is authoritative for price and integration; it says nothing about capability, and capability is usually what the operator is actually choosing on. Name both, and say which number is measured and which is claimed.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — recommended a model on measured cost and cache behaviour alone, and the operator had to send *two* separate messages asking for the missing half ("which one is better based on community feedback on the internet? published test scores?", then "do some research"). Prior authority — the research tools were available and already used earlier in the same session. Unblock — the operator's instruction to go look; the published scores then reversed the recommendation outright (the cheaper model scored 23 on Artificial Analysis against 34, and roughly half on agentic benchmarks), which no amount of local cost measurement would have surfaced.
**Next instance:** picking an embedding model, a vector store, a queue, or an OCR provider — the local spike proves it integrates and what it costs per call; the published record is what says whether it is any good at the job.

### +1 — 2026-09-18 · plow-hermes-agent6-glm-fleet · the same gap on a THRESHOLD, and the instrument can be wrong too
**Change (extends):** The same two-source rule governs a *number* you pick — a timeout, a context ceiling, a batch size. State the provenance in the same breath: measured here, inherited from a vendor's published figure, or a judgement on a continuous trade-off with no knee. And check that your instrument measures the thing being decided: a needle-in-haystack probe is the task long-context models pass at ~99% while real performance collapses, so passing it is not evidence a ceiling is safe.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — picked a compaction ceiling from the spend distribution and presented it as if it were a capability finding; the operator asked "why that number?" twice before the answer admitted it was a cost curve, not a quality one. Prior authority — the published long-context research (Chroma's context-rot study, Adobe's NoLiMa) was one search away and, once read, moved the number. Unblock — the operator's repeated challenge. Promoted from the `context-window-is-not-usable-capacity` feedback memory.
**Next instance:** any "what should we set this to?" — a rate limit, a retry budget, a chunk size — where the round number looks measured but was inherited from a benchmark's tick mark or a billing curve.

### +1 — 2026-10-20 · plow2-blessed-base-image · normalize by exposure, and strip incumbency, before the first recommendation
**Change (extends):** When choosing between two options we have *invested in unequally* (two agent runtimes, two vendors, two internal libraries), label each signal *intrinsic* or *incumbent* before recommending. Intrinsic signals: upstream health, outside-developer choice, measured per-unit reliability, retention and cost, and limits of the architecture. Incumbent signals: our LOC, our fixes, our own first-party agents. Normalize every adoption or outcome number by exposure (event attendance, time on market, engineering PRs per option), and mine the data already on hand before ending on a question: prod DB, event pages, registries.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — the first recommendation (Hermes) leaned on our own maturity and incident counts. The second ended on "should I run a bake-off?". The operator had to send two messages: first that this was just the option we'd worked on longer, then to expand with data, given unequal investment and hackathons with different attendance. Prior authority — `CLAUDE.md` § Take the Steps "investigate before you consult" and "ground tradeoffs in reality"; the prod DB, Luma pages and agent index were all readable. Unblock — the operator's two prompts. The normalized analysis (turn-level reply rate, per-registrant developer conversion, investment per PR) flipped the recommendation to OpenClaw and shrank an apparent 2:1 developer preference to 1.6×.
**Next instance:** choosing between two payment providers when one has two years of our integration fixes; picking which of two SDKs to standardize on when one had a launch campaign behind it.

## [removes-handback] Issue-tracker scaffolding and WIP specs don't belong in the repo — reject the CATEGORY at triage, don't rank the variants
**Change:** Extend `CODING_STANDARDS.md` § Don't Commit Plans past plan docs to **issue-tracker scaffolding** (`.beads/`, `bd init` output, any in-repo tracker) and any committed WIP spec. At PR triage, when a cluster of PRs adds this, the finding is the *category*: recommend closing all of them with one note naming the policy, and close their dependents too (a PR that files issues into the tracker dies with it). Do not spend the round ranking them by completeness and proposing a keeper.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — nine near-duplicate tracker PRs (83–100% pairwise file overlap, five of them created within 60 seconds of each other by a parallel agent fan-out, none declaring itself a successor) had sat open ~3 weeks. I measured the overlap, built a comparison table, and recommended *keeping the cleanest one* — which would have merged tracker scaffolding into a public repo. Prior authority — `CODING_STANDARDS.md` § Don't Commit Plans already states the principle for plan artifacts, and I was independently stripping committed `PRD/*.md` from three separate PRs in the same session while failing to generalize it. Unblock — the operator ruled "close all of them, we don't have WIP specs / issue trackers in the codebase", which closed ten PRs and 7,504 additions in one pass.
**Next instance:** Any repo where a PR adds a self-hosted tracker, a `docs/plans/` directory, or a committed design doc alongside code — including when the PR is otherwise well-built and approved.

## Before drafting any text that quotes a size ledger, fetch the authoritative numbers first — sequencing is what makes the rule hold
**Change:** When a reply, summary, or status will quote a LOC/size ledger, run the authoritative query (`gh pr view <N> --json additions,deletions`) *before* writing the prose, in the same call that gathers the round's state — not as a check afterwards. `babysit-pr` § Step 6.8 already says to measure the PR rather than the working tree; what it doesn't say is *when*, and the ordering is the whole control.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — posted a wrong ledger twice in one session on two different PRs, each time drafting from `git diff` arithmetic and only querying the PR afterwards, which meant the error was already public and needed an in-place `PATCH` to fix. Prior authority — § Step 6.8 states the correct source explicitly, and I could quote it; knowing the rule did not prevent either instance because the draft was written first. Unblock — self-caught both times, but only after posting, so it cost two edits and two corrections in chat.
**Next instance:** Any round-based loop where a number gathered from local state gets quoted into a durable artifact — a coverage percentage into a PR body, a row count into an issue comment, a benchmark delta into a release note.


## [removes-handback] A replacement isn't shipped until the thing it replaces is swept org-wide — delete the dead readers now, file the live ones with their blocker
**Change:** When a change introduces X to replace Y (the design or issue says "absorb", "replace", "one reader", "move here"), treat Y's retirement as part of the same work graph, not a follow-up the operator has to raise. Before asking for the merge, enumerate Y's readers and consumers across every repo the org owns: `gh search code --owner <org>`, then `git grep` on `origin/<default>` in sibling checkouts. Sort each hit: **delete now** (no live consumer — open the deletion PR in that repo), **blocked** (file or update an issue naming the live consumer and what must happen first), or **keep** (a different purpose, say which). The merge hand-off leads with the org-wide net LOC (X's additions minus every deletion, landed or filed), not only the repo where the local copy shrank.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — plow-pbc/latch#455 plus the new plow-pbc/plow-messages repo shipped a "one reader for chat.db" CLI. I deleted Latch's own SQL read recipes (−169), reported that, and asked for both merges. Prior authority — latch#167's design said the CLI *absorbs* plow-cli's `plow imessage` reader, and `CLAUDE.md` § Boy-Scout says to delete dead code whenever it's net-negative. Both the reader and its dead status were findable with one `git grep`. Unblock — after merging, the operator had to say he was worried we weren't deprecating old code. The sweep then found plow's `cli/` copy dead (deleted in plow-pbc/plow#2096, −1,153), plowd's ~5,450-line stack live for 9 accounts (filed plow-pbc/plow-mac#13), and a raw-SQL copy in a Life agent skill (tracked in life-assistant-hermes-agent#20). The org-wide net went from a reported −169 (really +1,020) to about −130.
**Next instance:** Moving an API-side capability from a monolith into a hosted MCP server in a different repo: before the MCP PR merges, grep the monolith and every agent repo for the old endpoint and CLI subcommand, delete what nothing calls, and file the rest against its live caller.

## An incident-born issue gets the full forensic body on first filing — timeline, environment, invocation chain, evidence, confidence-labeled mechanism, ranked fixes

The thin "summary + repro + one suggestion" shape discards context you uniquely hold at filing time and forces a "can you add more details?" round-trip; the forensic detail is also what lets the next engineer (or agent) falsify your theory cheaply.

## A recovery that worked is evidence about its WHOLE delta — bisect which difference mattered before naming the cause or recommending the fix
**[Recovered 2026-09-19 — written 2026-06-12 by a `/cleanup` on mba `~/Hacking/code-config0`, stranded on that checkout's local `main` (the class srosro/code-config#249 fixes) until now; text unedited.]**

## [removes-handback] A failure reproduced in YOUR shell is not a repro of the app — diff the execution context before naming a mechanism

**Change:** Extend `CLAUDE.md` § Verify Before Claiming Done's executing-context bullet to the *negative* direction, and widen its scheduled-job sibling. Both currently point outward — "done" needs the artifact produced BY the owning runtime, and a cron/systemd job must be verified under its timer. The missing direction is that **your own interactive shell is often the odd one out**, so a failure you reproduce in it is evidence about your shell until proven otherwise. Before naming a mechanism for a failure, reproduce it where the failing behavior lives. And when the operator calls the failure intermittent while yours is deterministic, that mismatch IS the finding: the difference between the two contexts is the variable, not the mechanism you can already see. On macOS the cheapest discriminator is `launchctl managername` — a Claude Code shell under tmux is `Background`, a Finder-launched app is `Aqua`, and a GUI app inherits the launchd domain of whatever opened it, so `open -a` from tmux silently puts the whole app in the wrong one. The general form: read the context identity on both sides and diff it before theorising.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — handed back a confident root cause for a silently-failing `say` ("no seatbelt profile can let speech synthesis work; the sandbox is the cause"), built entirely on a repro in my own tmux shell, and ended the turn on it. It was wrong: the app's own generated profile speaks fine in the desktop session, and the real variable was that the app had been `open`ed from tmux and inherited the `Background` domain — seatbelt AND that domain together, neither alone. Prior authority — the installed app was running on the same Mac, its MCP credential was already on disk, and the repo's own smoke skill drives one real call through the live app; nothing about the decisive experiment needed the operator. Unblock — the operator said it sometimes works and asked for a comparison across both of their Macs, which is what forced the context matrix that found it.

**Next instance:** a systemd/cron unit whose command "works when I run it by hand" — reproduce under the timer before blaming the command; equally a container vs its host, a CI runner vs a laptop, or a daemon vs a login shell. Any time the report is "intermittent" and your repro is not, diff the contexts first.

## [removes-handback] A hardcoded model / version pin you read in passing is a claim about currency — check it against the available set before you move on
**Change:** When work puts a pinned model id, image tag, or dependency version in front of you — even incidentally, even when the pin is not what you were sent to change — check it against what is actually available before moving on. Reading a pin and not questioning it is implicitly endorsing it, and the next person to touch it inherits your silence as a decision. The check is cheap and has two halves: what does the platform's allowlist / registry / model table offer now, and does the newer option cost *less* (newer tiers routinely undercut the one they replace). Where a pin looks stale, say so in the same turn you report the work you were sent to do — a one-line "this is pinned to X; Y is current and cheaper, want it as its own PR?" — rather than filing it silently or saying nothing. Do **not** widen the current PR to carry the bump: it is separable work and gets its own branch.

Prior authority — the model id was in my own context; the standing preference for best-in-class models is recorded; and the platform's allowlist naming the newer model sat in a sibling repo in the same lane. The unblock — the operator noticing it for me. The bump turned out to be strictly better on both axes (more capable *and* $2/$10 per MTok against $3/$15) and carried a real trap the review then confirmed: the newer model rejects the old thinking parameter outright, and on a fail-closed reviewer an opaque provider 400 denies every operation.
**Next instance:** any repo where a `FROM` tag, a `runtime:` version, a pinned SDK, or an embedding-model constant passes under your eyes while you are fixing something adjacent — the question "is this still the right one?" costs one lookup and the answer is load-bearing surprisingly often.

When such a skill exists but its description keys on a different ref type than the operator used — it triggers on a *user* ref while they named the *instance* — that mismatch is the CSO bug to fix in the same pass, not a reason to hand-search.

Asked what was wrong with "my spruce", I searched the local agent home, `docker ps` on two hosts, `~/services`, the cloud provider's VM list, and four fleet hosts over SSH before reaching `plow-prod-agent-ops` — the plow-repo skill whose entire stated purpose is mapping a person or agent to their cloud-agent VM and shelling into it, which then answered in one call. Its description triggers on "a Plow user by phone, name, or id", so an *agent* name never matched it, even though the CLI it wraps accepts an agent uid directly. No operator round-trip — nobody had to intervene, which is why it would have kept recurring silently.

**Next instance:** locating which host a named knightwatch reviewer worker, a named customer agent, or a named container runs on, in any repo that ships an ops skill.

## [removes-handback] Having stated a recommendation on a design fork, commit to it — don't close the same turn with a pick-one menu

**Change:** In a design conversation, once the analysis is done and a recommendation is stated with reasoning, that recommendation IS the decision: name the runner-up and what would change your mind, then proceed on it. Do not append "so, A or B?" to a turn that already argued for A — a menu stacked on top of a recommendation makes the operator decide twice and reads as hedging. Reserve a genuine question for forks your own analysis cannot resolve: product intent, priority, an observed failure mode. This is the trailing half of the existing "lead with a recommendation, not a menu" rule — leading with one and then re-asking satisfies its letter while losing its point.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — a brainstorm on messaging-send approval granularity: recommended per-recipient with full reasoning (blast radius, one approval per thread, matches how the owner would say it), then closed the turn asking the operator to choose between per-recipient and per-app anyway. Prior authority — the analysis was complete and the code already traced (the rule-eligibility constraint and the read-prefix precedent were both read that turn); `CLAUDE.md` § Take the Steps already says lead with a recommendation, not symmetric neutral options. Unblock — the operator spent a turn bouncing it back ("what do you think?"), after which the same recommendation was restated verbatim as the decision and accepted unchanged. Promoted from the `recommend-then-decide` feedback memory.

**Next instance:** any repo, any tool — recommending a rollout strategy for a deploy, a migration ordering, or which of two libraries to adopt: state the recommendation, name the runner-up, and proceed, rather than ending on a two-option pick.

## [removes-handback] A number that drives a recommendation goes in a table or on its own line — prose buries it and the operator re-asks
**Change:** When a recommendation turns on a quantitative comparison — price, latency, size, LOC, token cost — the comparison is the decision input, so give it a structure the eye lands on: a two-row table, or its own line with both values side by side. Never leave it inside a paragraph, and never leave it inside a paragraph whose *first* clause is about something else. This is `CLAUDE.md` § Answer Shape's "lead with the result" applied at sub-message granularity: the section already says a ledger beats prose for batch work and that a buried ask costs a round-trip, but a single decisive number is neither a ledger nor an ask, so nothing currently catches it. The tell that you are about to do it: you are writing the number as a subordinate clause in a sentence whose subject is your reasoning ("meanwhile X is cheaper — $2/$10 against $3/$15") rather than as the sentence's whole point. A corollary for the *same* number later: when the operator asks about something you already told them, do not open by saying you already answered — answer it in the format that works and move on; the re-ask is evidence about your formatting, not about their attention.
**Why (autonomy):** The stop — the operator asked whether the newer model was more expensive, one turn after I had told them it was cheaper, with both price pairs correct. Prior authority — nothing was missing; the comparison was already in my message and in the PR body. The unblock — them asking again, which cost a full round-trip on a fact already delivered. The cause was placement: the numbers sat mid-paragraph in a reply that opened with dependency-adapter archaeology, so the paragraph read as justification rather than as the answer. Re-sent as a two-row table, the same two numbers landed with no follow-up.
**Next instance:** any "should we switch to X?" where the case rests on a measured delta — a cheaper instance type, a faster library, a smaller image, a model bump. Put the two numbers adjacent and scannable before writing a word of the reasoning that follows from them.

## [removes-handback] Handing over a link to something you published → state its access boundary in the same message

**Change:** When you give the operator a URL to something you just stood up — a tailnet-served report page, a preview deploy, an unlisted token page, a dashboard, a shared doc — name in the same message **who can reach it and who cannot**. One clause is enough ("tailnet-only, so the four of you; nobody off it can reach the port"). The operator's next question after receiving a link is almost always "can I send this to someone?", and they cannot answer it from the URL alone: reach is a property of the binding, the ACL and the sharing model, all of which you chose and they did not watch you choose. Verify the claim rather than asserting it from the deploy recipe — read the actual listening address, check for a public-exposure config (`tailscale serve`/`funnel`, a project's protection setting), and load it once from a second host — then state the boundary and, when you know a limit you did not check, name that too.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — a production capacity report was published to the operator's tailnet pages host and handed over as a bare URL with no statement of its audience; the operator had to come back and ask whether their coworkers could view it. Prior authority — `CLAUDE.md`'s rule that operator-facing pages are hosted on the operator's own infrastructure already fixes the mechanism and even names loading it from a second tailnet host before handing it over, so the reach was fully knowable at publish time; the answer took one `ss -ltnp` and one `tailscale serve status`. Unblock — the operator's direct question, which cost a round-trip on a page that was already correct and already shareable. **Next instance:** any turn that ends by handing over a URL the agent created — a Vercel preview whose deployment protection decides whether a reviewer can open it, an unlisted `plow.co/i/<token>` page for an investor, a kiosk page on a Pi, or a Claude doc — state the boundary beside the link. (session: plow1-capacity-review)

## [removes-handback] Grade an exposure against the operating point BEFORE the red banner — a non-incident escalation costs a round-trip and dilutes the real ones

**Change:** When you discover data of the operator's in a place it should not be — a public repo, a log, a transcript — establish its sensitivity *at this company's operating point* before choosing the response. Read what the project already says about itself: a `REVIEW.md` operating-point line, a public-company-context source the agent's own config names, a build-in-public posture. A figure the company broadcasts on its own stream is a **cleanup** — remove it, say you did, carry on in the same turn. Reserve the red BLOCKED banner and the hand-off for exposures that are actually irreversible or actually sensitive: credentials, third parties' data, contact identifiers. Removing the data is right either way; the grading decides whether a human has to be woken for it.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — found the operator's monthly burn figure in a public repo's commit history, remediated it (clean branch, PR closed, contaminated branch deleted), then raised a red BLOCKED banner and handed back a GitHub Support purge request as the only remaining step. Prior authority — the agent's own resource catalog in that very session named the company's public build-in-public site as standing context, and the repo's `REVIEW.md` states a pre-PMF handful-of-installs operating point; both were already read. Unblock — the operator's ruling that a livestreamed company's burn is fine to expose, followed by two bare "continue"s to restart work that had stopped on it.

**Next instance:** an API base URL or a staging hostname committed to a public repo — check whether it is already in public docs before escalating; a customer name in a log line — that one keeps its weight, because it is a third party's, not the operator's. The discriminator is whose data it is and whether they already publish it, not whether the surface is public.

## Assert infrastructure topology from the account, never from the repo's own prose

**Change:** Before stating which line, host, tenant, channel or instance something runs on, query the surface that owns that fact — the provider CLI, the account API, the deployment's own config — and say that is where it came from. A persona file, a docstring or a README describes intent *inside* the repo; it is not evidence about the world outside it. In particular, a "do not present yourself as X" instruction says nothing about whether X is the thing you are running on. Where the only available evidence is prose in the repo, mark the claim unverified rather than stating it.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — asked whether to reply to a named assistant to answer the paper's questions, answered "no, that is a different assistant" on the strength of a persona line telling the agent not to introduce itself under that name. Prior authority — the account's own CLI lists the operator's lines in one call, and a second call showed the named line's thread carries the delivered PDFs. Unblock — the operator pushing back twice and pointing at their account; both my assertions were wrong, and both were about topology inferred from prose.

**Next instance:** "which cluster is this cron running on?" answered from a comment in the repo rather than from the scheduler; "that bucket is not ours" from a naming convention rather than from the cloud account listing. Any claim of the form "X is/isn't the thing that runs this" is an account question wearing a code-reading disguise.
