## [removes-handback] Probe every assumed blocker reversibly before handing it back — most dissolve
**Change:** When preparing an autonomous-run handoff, every step you are about to name as needing the human gets a **reversible probe first**. Hand back only what survives the probe. Probe writes with a throwaway value you immediately delete; read the service's own API for a setting before believing a CLI's silence means dashboard-only — absence of a CLI subcommand is not absence of the capability. A gate survives only when the capability genuinely does not exist (UI-only credential minting, a physical action), not when it is merely unverified. Surface survivors as a ONE-TIME upfront enabler with the exact command, before the run starts.
**Why (autonomy):** *the stop* — I was about to hand the operator a three-item blocker checklist before an overnight run. *prior authority* — all three were testable with credentials already in hand. *the unblock* — probing dissolved two of three: Route53 write on the production zone was proven by UPSERT-then-DELETE of a throwaway TXT record, and "Vercel deployment protection is dashboard-only" was simply false — the project API showed `ssoProtection.deploymentType = all_except_custom_domains`, so attaching the custom domain made it public with no setting change. Only the PAT survived, because GitHub has no API that mints one. A three-item handback became a one-line ask. **Next instance:** any overnight or autonomous handoff whose checklist names DNS, a cloud console setting, an IAM change, or a "you'll have to do this in the UI" step — in any repo, on any provider.

## [removes-handback] Projecting an internal tracker onto a public surface: gate on an explicit opt-in tag, never a broad existing filter
**Change:** When a public surface renders content sourced from an internal or private tracker — a public roadmap, changelog, status page — gate publication on an **explicit opt-in tag applied per item**, not on a broad existing filter that happens to select roughly the right set. Lead with opt-in and state the leak count out loud: enumerate what the broad filter would have published. Offer the blanket filter as the named alternative with its cost.
**Why (autonomy):** *the stop* — asked to surface user feature requests publicly, my first instinct was `label:enhancement`, which on the private monorepo selected 56 open issues of which ~50 were internal engineering chores (preview-deploy gaps, DB pool exhaustion, visual redline work) and 5 were the actual user asks. *prior authority* — the blast-radius asymmetry was computable before asking anyone; I had the counts. *the unblock* — putting the enumeration in front of the operator made the choice obvious in one round instead of shipping the leak and retracting it. Opt-in inverts the failure mode: forgetting to tag hides an item, which costs a round trip; forgetting to exclude publishes internal work, which cannot be undone. **Next instance:** any private→public projection in any repo — a docs site built from internal notes, a metrics dashboard shared with investors, an agent transcript surfaced to end users.

## [removes-handback] Before declaring BLOCKED on a capability, list the CALLER REPO's own `.claude/skills/` — the escalation path is usually a repo-owned skill, not a global one
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Verify Before Claiming Done: "it can't run here / I don't hold that
credential" is a claim with the same burden as any other. Before handing it back, enumerate the
capability surface — `ls <caller-repo>/.claude/skills/` and read any skill whose name touches the blocked
verb (`*-write`, `*-ops`, `*-admin`, `*-deploy`) — not just the global `~/.claude/skills/` list the
session prompt already showed you. A read-only tool's `--help` proves that tool is read-only; it proves
nothing about whether a *different, documented* path exists.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — emitted a red BLOCKED banner asking the operator to mint an admin API key.
Prior authority — they had already authorized the re-pin, and the caller repo shipped
`.claude/skills/plow-prod-db-write/SKILL.md`, whose first section says `plow-ops` is read-only and the
write goes through a *different AWS profile* + ECS exec. Unblock — the operator asked why an admin key
was needed at all; that path then did the whole job in one call, and incidentally closed a verification
gap I'd also handed back. I had checked `plow-ops --help`, seen "read-only", and stopped there.
**Next instance:** a `latch` session concluding a device-credential rotation needs something I don't
hold — check that repo's `.claude/skills/` for an ops/admin skill before saying so.

## Policy text for a repo doc stays at ruling + test + precedent — one rule per bullet
**Change:** Add to `AUTHORING.md`: when drafting policy text that lands in a repo doc (`REVIEW.md`
posture bullets, `AGENTS.md` carve-outs), cap each bullet at ~3–5 sentences carrying the ruling, the
concrete test, and the precedent. Cut consumer lists, restated rationale, and examples the precedent
already implies. These files are re-read by a bot on every review, so a long bullet dilutes the one rule
it carries.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — a drafted posture bullet came back for a second pass. Prior authority — the
corpus already treats prose accretion as the failure mode. Unblock — the operator asked for it shorter.
**Next instance:** drafting a `REVIEW.md` posture bullet for `hermes-plugin-plow` — write the ruling and
its test, not the full rationale, on the first pass.
## [removes-handback] The operator names the SCOPE of an outward action → do that scope and offer the broader one; never hand back the broader command

**Change:** When the ask names its own blast radius ("install it on *this mbp*", "roll it to *wakeup*") and the standing mechanism for that kind of action is broader (publish → whole fleet auto-updates; deploy → all five hosts), perform the **scoped** action autonomously and offer the broader one in a line. Do not stop and hand back the broader command because the documented mechanism is broader than the ask — the named scope IS the authorization, and it is the reversible half.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — operator asked to build via CI and install on this Mac; I built, verified the artifact, then handed back a `gh release edit --draft=false` command instead of installing, because the standing preference (verify via the real update flow) publishes to the whole fleet and I treated that as the only sanctioned path. Prior authority — the ask already named the machine, the artifact was already built and verified (notarized, correct version, both PRs present in `app.asar`), and a bundle swap on one Mac is reversible. Unblock — operator had to ask a second time, "can you install it on my mbp?", after which I did exactly the scoped install with no new information.

**Next instance:** A different repo and mechanism — operator says "put this build on rpi5" while the project's documented path is a fleet-wide `/deploy` across five hosts. Install on rpi5, verify it there, and offer the fleet rollout in one line, rather than replying with the fleet command and waiting.

## [removes-handback] Asked for a goal statement, write a definition of done — verifiable conditions, not an aspiration

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Take the Steps`: when the operator asks for a goal statement, the deliverable is a **definition of done** — a checklist a third party could verify without trusting the agent's narration. Name the artifact, where it lands, who produced it, and what "zero errors" means concretely. Prefer conditions that prove the *mechanism* rather than the outcome: for a scheduled job, require it to fire from the real scheduler on a modified schedule time, so the cron path itself is exercised instead of bypassed by a manual invocation. An aspiration ("get it working", "in a way that's best for everyone") is not a goal — it lets the agent declare victory on a partial fix.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — the operator asked for a goal statement, rejected the one produced, asked again, rejected the second, and finally wrote it himself. Two round-trips and the authoring work handed back. Prior authority — he had already said he was going to sleep and wanted autonomous work overnight; the whole point of the goal was to stand in for his judgment while he was unavailable, which is exactly what an unfalsifiable goal cannot do. Unblock — he wrote the definition of done himself, including the modified-cron-time condition the agent had not thought to require.
**Next instance:** any overnight or multi-day autonomous run that opens with "here's what I want, write me the goal" — a fleet migration, a release train, an unattended data backfill. The moment the operator will be asleep or away is the moment the DoD has to be checkable without them.

## [removes-handback] Announce a verification artifact BEFORE it reaches the operator's physical or social space

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`: when a verification step will emit something outside the transcript — a printed page, a sent message, a delivered file, a calendar invite — say so in advance: what will appear, where, and that it is a test artifact rather than a real deliverable. Prefer the least intrusive proof that still settles the question (a queue listing, a dry run, a status read) and escalate to the real emission only when absence of evidence is genuinely ambiguous. If it has already landed, say plainly that the artifact is the agent's and can be discarded.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — a print-leg verification put a real page in the operator's tray; because it rendered a deliberately degraded test edition, he picked it up and asked why the layout looked wrong, and the answer took a full round-trip of diffing three editions to establish the page was a test artifact and the template was fine. Prior authority — the verification itself was in scope and correct; nothing required it to be a surprise, and a queue listing (which was run afterwards, and answered the same question) would have been the cheaper first probe. Unblock — the operator asking what he was looking at.
**Next instance:** any check whose signal lives outside the terminal — sending a test notification through a real channel, writing a row a dashboard will display, triggering a build that posts to a shared thread. The surprise is the cost, not the action.

## [removes-handback] A reviewer's `[blocking]` rates the bug, not the scope — an out-of-intent bug is still filed and declined

**Change:** Before applying any review probe, ask the intent question first and the severity question second: *would this change exist if the PR's stated goal vanished?* If no, file the issue, reply with the link, and say plainly that severity is not scope — **including when the probe is marked `[blocking]`**. Watch the tell that the finding lives in files the PR only touched incidentally (a config flag the PR enabled made a dormant bug path live, which pulled its whole subsystem into review). If several such probes were already absorbed, offer the split without being asked.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — the operator opened the PR and immediately said it was a huge diff for what looked like a pin change, a round-trip spent on scope I should have policed. Prior authority — the file-and-decline rule for out-of-intent findings was already in `babysit-pr` § Step 5 and in `CLAUDE.md` § Concise Code; the stated ask was "make Watson one-click deployable". Unblock — the operator's own read of the diff size. `[blocking]` reads as an instruction to fix it *here*, so the file-and-decline rule quietly stops firing exactly when scope discipline matters most: on `srosro/watson-triage#1`, four rounds and ~281 of 1,214 insertions went to pre-existing checkpoint-sequencing bugs in upstream code, unrelated to deployability.

**Next instance:** A `/babysit-pr` loop on a different repo where the bot marks `[blocking]` a race in a module the PR only imports — file it, decline it, and keep the PR the size of its ask.

## Proving a test is load-bearing requires the gate's own command — a bare `FAILED` can be a collection error, not a test

**Change:** To show a test catches the bug it was written for, break the fix and re-run **the gate's exact command** (`just test`, `unittest discover -s tests`, whatever CI runs), then read the *assertion message* — its text, its file, its line — not just the `FAILED` line. If the failure text isn't your own assertion, the experiment failed, not the code.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — none; the bot reviewer caught this, not the operator, so it is graded as a near-miss rather than a removed hand-back. Prior authority — `CLAUDE.md` § Verify Before Claiming Done already says to read the suite's summary line rather than an exit code. Unblock — roborev flagged that the test passed with the fix deleted. Running one test by dotted path is a *different command with a different `sys.path`*: the `FAILED` was a `ModuleNotFoundError` at collection and the test never executed. That reads exactly like success at proving a point — you wanted red, you got red — and the claim was published in two PR replies before it was caught.

**Next instance:** Proving a new lint rule or schema guard actually rejects bad input in any repo — revert the guard, run the project's own gate recipe, and confirm the output names the guard's own error.

## Capture a commit SHA after committing — never write one into a reply before the commit exists

**Change:** Draft any message citing a commit with a literal placeholder that cannot be mistaken for a SHA (`<SHA>`), run the commit, then `git log --oneline -1` and substitute. Same discipline for every identifier quoted as evidence: PR numbers, issue numbers, image digests, tags.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — none; self-caught both times by re-reading the posted text. Prior authority — `CLAUDE.md` § Verify Before Claiming Done's re-fetch-before-asserting rule. Unblock — self-correction, twice, each costing a `gh api -X PATCH` repair on `srosro/watson-triage` PRs #1 and #3. A SHA reads as a verifiable citation, so nobody double-checks it; a wrong one sends a reader to a commit that does not exist, in a message whose whole purpose is letting them check the work.

**Next instance:** Any deploy report or status update naming the artifact digest it claims to have shipped.

## Recommend from the surface the operator named, not its backing API

**Change:** When the operator links a page and asks you to choose from it, the candidate set is that page's **rendered list**, not whatever its backing API returns. Fetch the API for detail if you like, but intersect it with the UI's own visibility gate before ranking, and say which surface you ranked from.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — the operator had to redirect a recommendation drawn from a catalog's API rather than the page they linked. Prior authority — the operator's message named the page. Unblock — their correction. An API commonly exposes rows the page filters out (unpublished, unlisted, deprecated), so a ranking built on it recommends things the operator cannot see and did not mean.

**Next instance:** Asked to pick from a Vercel project list, a dashboard's visible deploys, or an app-store listing page — rank what the page shows, not what the endpoint returns.


## A scheduled job pins the model/config it resolved at creation — changing the global default does not move it

**Change:** After changing a deployment-wide default that already-registered background work resolves against — the model a scheduler infers with, a pinned image tag, a cached credential profile — re-point the existing jobs explicitly and verify one of them reports the new value, before reporting the change as live. "The config says X and the process restarted" is not evidence that tomorrow's scheduled run uses X. Look for the scheduler's own re-resolve verb (`hermes cron resnap --all` is one; a queue's re-enqueue or a warm pool's drain are others) and treat its existence in `--help` as the tell that snapshots are being kept.
**Why (autonomy):** self-caught, untagged — but it was one command from silently invalidating a whole night's work. After a merged PR moved a paper agent's default model and the container was rebuilt and restarted, the live config read the new model correctly. The registered cron job still carried `model_snapshot: <previous model>`; unpinned, but snapped at creation. The scheduled run would have executed on the old model while every surface I had checked — the config file, the running container, the deploy SHA — said otherwise, and I would have reported a model comparison that never happened. The same trap fired a second time the same night after the next pin change, and a third after the revert; each needed its own re-point.
**Next instance:** a CI runner image tag changed while queued workflows hold the old digest; a feature flag default flipped while warm serverless instances keep the old resolution; a cron'd backup pointed at a credential profile that was rotated after the job was registered.

## A stopgap only counts as removed when the code that reads it is gone AND the state it left is swept

**Change:** When a hand-applied workaround is superseded by a real fix, closing it out has two halves, and the second is routinely skipped: prove the shipped code no longer *reads* the workaround (grep the deployed artifact for a runtime read, not just the repo for a mention), then sweep the *state* the workaround left behind — the backup files, the copied credentials, the archived config. Enumerate residue by asking which paths the product itself creates: anything else in that tree is session residue and gets removed, and a backup holding a superseded credential is the highest-priority one, since it is a secret nobody is rotating any more.
**Why (autonomy):** promoted from the `operator-hand-pokes-must-become-dead-code` feedback memory, and load-bearing again this session. The operator's definition of done named it directly: the credential file must be gone *because the code no longer reads it*, not because someone deleted two lines. Verifying the first half in the deployed container (zero runtime reads; only a docstring mention) is what made the removal safe. The sweep then found three residue files outside the product's own backup directory — including one still holding the revoked static credential whose revocation had been the original outage — none of which any product code creates. Distinguishing product-managed state from session residue was the whole difficulty: the product's own backup directory looked identical to mine until three image scripts were found referencing it.
**Next instance:** a temporary `/etc` drop-in added to unblock a deploy and later fixed properly in the image; a hand-copied token used to bridge an auth migration; a feature flag forced on locally while the real default shipped.

## [removes-handback] An unanswered closing ask is asked once — automated wakes report the delta, not the ask again

**Change:** When a message ends with an ask the operator hasn't answered yet (merge consent, a deploy decision), later turns driven only by background events (Monitor expiries, subagent completions, spent-monitor notices) report what changed in one line and do **not** repeat the ask. Re-surface it only when the answer becomes load-bearing (the work it gates is otherwise complete) or the operator returns. A no-op wake with nothing new needs no reply beyond re-arming. The `Links` block and final-line ask rules in `CLAUDE.md` § Answer Shape govern replies to the operator, not every background wake.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — across a long multi-PR babysit loop (the-plow-times-hermes-agent #96–#111), the same "should I redeploy wakeup?" ask ended ~20 consecutive monitor-wake replies and was never answered; the operator eventually asked for the deploy in their own words, and a separate "is it converged? are there merge conflicts?" showed the real status had been buried under the repeated ask. Prior authority — § Answer Shape already says "Say it once; do not re-ask something already answered", but its final-line-ask and every-message `Links` rules read as mandatory on each background wake. Unblock — the operator's own later message.
**Next instance:** a CI-watch loop re-asking "want me to promote the release?" on every job completion; a deploy Monitor re-asking for a sudo password on every health-check tick.

## [removes-handback] A backgrounded long job needs a liveness check, not only a completion notification
**Change:** When a remote or long command outlives its timeout and moves to the background, arm a watcher in the same turn that also reports liveness: progress, such as an output line count or a row counter, plus CPU/load or `/proc/<pid>/wchan`. It emits when progress stalls, not only when the job exits. A job with flat progress and load near 0 is hung. Find where it is blocked and fix that; don't keep waiting.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — a full-filesystem `sha1sum -c` on a 1-CPU agent VM was left running in the background with only a completion notification. It blocked for ~16h reading `/dev/console` (the image manifest had a placeholder file at that path), and the operator had to ask "how's it going?" to restart the work. Prior authority — the upgrade was already authorized, and a single `ps` / `wchan` check would have shown load 0.00 and a blocked read within minutes. Unblock — the operator's status question; the first liveness probe then found the block immediately.
**Next instance:** a `pg_dump`, `rsync`, or image build on another fleet host that stalls on a lock, a FIFO, or a network read. Its completion notification never fires, and the session idles until the human checks in.


## Read a number from its source as you write it — never from memory, never from arithmetic you did in your head
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done`, beside the test-summary-line bullet: every quantity that goes into a PR comment, issue or report is read from its source in the same breath as writing it — `gh pr view --json additions,deletions`, the suite's printed `Ran N`, the actual diff stat. Never recalled from earlier in the session, and never computed by summing two other figures: overlapping edits mean slices rarely add up. Draft with a placeholder, run the read, substitute. A wrong figure already posted is corrected in place, not stacked under a correction — and the endpoint is surface-specific: `issues/comments/<id>` for a top-level comment, `pulls/<n>/reviews/<review_id>` for a review body, `pulls/comments/<id>` for an inline review-thread comment, `issues/<n>` for an issue or PR body.
**Why (autonomy):** Bug-class fence, self-caught, so untagged. Three wrong LOC figures in one session — `+593/−20` that was `+600/−16`, `+580/−18` that was `+582/−17`, `+11/−1` that was `+9/−1` — each caught only by re-reading my own posted text and each costing a `PATCH`. A number is the one part of a message nobody re-derives: it reads as a citation, so it is believed. The cause was identical every time — the figure was true at an earlier commit and the round moved it. Generalizes the existing SHA rule from identifiers to quantities.
**Next instance:** a migration report quoting row counts; a deploy summary quoting image sizes; any "N of M done" in a fleet sweep.

## [removes-handback] Align on the goal in plain words before writing or rewriting any spec
**Change:** Before drafting or revising a spec, even one fixing an earlier mistake, restate the goal in 2–3 plain sentences and get a yes. Mechanisms, file names and pipeline steps come only after.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — an advisor-feature spec was rewritten ~10 times (271→150→…→247 lines), each round ending on "approve?" while the goal was unsettled; next session I started rewriting it again. Prior authority — `superpowers:brainstorming`'s one-question-at-a-time flow. Unblock — the operator interrupting to align on the goal first.
**Next instance:** designing a new CLI subcommand or dashboard page from a vague ask in any repo.

## [removes-handback] Something described as missing: check whether it ever existed before reconstructing it
**Change:** `git log -S '<marker>' --all` first. If it never existed, say so and return to the decision; don't rebuild it from leftovers to show what it would have looked like.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — asked to preview a visual before choosing which duplicate block to cut, I started reconstructing markup that had never been written from orphaned CSS; the operator stopped the render. Prior authority — git history. Unblock — the operator halting the preview.
**Next instance:** an "unwired" config flag or a dead route handler in any codebase.

## A daily job's overnight proof run carries the morning's date
**Change:** Prove a once-a-day job before midnight, or clear its date-keyed history and locks after the proof, so the real morning run doesn't read the proof as "today".
**Why (autonomy):** Bug-class fence, untagged — a 01:27 proof of a 07:00 paper wrote a same-date history entry; the morning run dropped its YESTERDAY line and an earlier proof stood down on a same-day sentinel.
**Next instance:** a nightly report or backup job proven at 1am in any repo with date-keyed dedupe.

## [removes-handback] A missed done-criterion on a scheduled job: fix it and force a real run now
**Change:** Lead with fix + force a real run today and verify the artifact; "watch the next natural run" is only the fallback.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — after the morning paper missed a line, I offered "watch tomorrow's" as an equal option. Prior authority — the fix was merged and a manual run was available. Unblock — the operator: "definitely want a re-run… work until this thing prints".
**Next instance:** a cron-driven email digest or a CI nightly whose fix you can trigger by hand.

## An overnight /goal ends in a printed morning report
**Change:** Render the morning ledger (PR URLs, evidence, what's unverified) to a PDF and print it on the operator's LaserJet through Latch after the morning paper, confirmed by the `lp` job ID — never overnight.
**Why (autonomy):** Operator preference, untagged — they start the day from paper, so a terminal-only report gets missed.
**Next instance:** any overnight autonomous run in any repo.

## A component that keeps moving between homes should be deleted
**Change:** Three homes across three rounds is the tell: stop re-siting it and ask whether the feature needs it at all; collapse to the smallest delta and record what was discarded.
**Why (autonomy):** Quality steer, untagged — a durable-facts store moved from `pt/facts.json` to Hermes `USER.md` to the wiki; the operator's "we're overcomplicating this" cut it entirely and halved the spec.
**Next instance:** a cache layer re-sited from app to proxy to DB across design rounds.

## A bad value with one source gets fixed at the source, not stripped at the shared chokepoint
**Change:** Prove the source is singular (grep callers, check prod failure paths), fix the caller in one line, and stop; a proxy-level strip is YAGNI until a second caller exists.
**Why (autonomy):** Quality steer, untagged — a one-line `temperature: 0` removal became a 4-file proxy strip + schema + test; the steer was "this should be a one-line change".
**Next instance:** a malformed header from one client breaking a shared gateway.

## Re-surface a scoped-down fix when evidence shows it is unsafe or marginal
**Change:** If review or capacity math shows the minimal fix the operator chose is unsafe or barely helps, stop and re-surface the trade-off with options; don't ship it on the strength of the earlier "minimal".
**Why (autonomy):** Untagged — on a DB-pool fix the minimal bump turned out to inflate other pools toward RDS limits; re-surfacing led the operator to pick the root fix.
**Next instance:** a quick rate-limit bump that review shows would starve a sibling service.

## Single-replica services gate the load balancer on liveness, not a DB-backed readiness check
**Change:** With one task there's nowhere to route on DB-down, so a DB-backed LB check only turns app errors into LB-wide 503s; point the LB at a no-DB `/healthz` until there are ≥2 replicas.
**Why (autonomy):** Quality ruling, untagged — a DB-backed `/health` on a desired=1 service created a 503 cascade and an endless review fight about protecting the probe.
**Next instance:** any single-instance service behind an ALB or k8s readiness probe.

## [removes-handback] Under a merge mandate, one addressed review round is the bar
**Change:** When the operator authorizes merge and goes offline, address the valid findings of one knightwatch round, decline the rest with rules cited, push and merge; don't hold for a second clean round.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — I was about to park a finished low-risk PR overnight waiting for a verification round. Prior authority — explicit merge authorization. Unblock — the operator's "merge aggressively once anything valid is addressed".
**Next instance:** an overnight docs or marketing PR in any repo with merge authority granted.

## [removes-handback] Bound every network call with a timeout; a background wait has a deadline you check, not a notification you trust

**Change:** Wrap remote git/gh/ssh calls in `timeout <N>` (fetch/push ~120s, `gh api` ~60s), fan out per-target work in parallel, and when a backgrounded job runs past its expected time, inspect it (`ps -o etime`, a direct connectivity probe) and recover — kill the hung call, retry over a different transport, or source objects locally (`git fetch <sibling-checkout>`) — instead of ending the turn to await its completion notification.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — repointing ten slot checkouts, one `git fetch` over SSH hung 27 minutes with no timeout while the turn ended waiting on the background loop; the operator had to ask "how's it going?" before the hang was noticed. Prior authority — the repoint was already authorized and every recovery (kill, HTTPS probe, local fetch from `ft0`) was a reversible, in-lane step. Unblock — the status question; the fix then took one minute.
**Next instance:** A fleet-wide `ssh` sweep across tailnet hosts where one host's sshd half-answers, or a `docker pull` in a deploy script on a flaky registry — any batch of remote calls where one silent hang blocks the rest.

## [removes-handback] A missing value only the human holds blocks that value, not the deliverable — ship it with marked placeholders as a draft PR

**Change:** When a deliverable is complete except for values only the operator holds (phone numbers, an account ID, a price, a domain), don't end the turn asking for them. Fill obviously fake, inert placeholders (e.g. the reserved `555-01xx` range), mark the spots in code, open the PR as a **draft** with a fill-in table naming every placeholder site, babysit it, and *then* ask for the values. The draft status is what keeps it from merging with fakes.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — asked to add new line personas with vCards, I built the generator, then ended the turn with "send me the numbers" (I couldn't read the Linq key). Prior authority — the operator had already asked for the cards, and a draft PR is reversible and in scope. Unblock — the operator had to ask "can you open this as a PR with placeholder numbers?" so they could hand it to eng (plow-pbc/plow#2261, 2026-10-05).
**Next instance:** A Terraform PR that needs a not-yet-issued AWS account ID or ACM cert ARN, or a pricing-page PR waiting on a final price — ship it as a draft with marked placeholders instead of stopping.

## [removes-handback] Replacing prior art? Its TEST NAMES are a list of bugs it already fixed — re-assert each or they reopen in the new implementation
**Change:** Add to `CODING_STANDARDS.md` § Incremental Improvement (and reference from `CLAUDE.md` § Take the Steps' prior-art bullet): when new code *replaces* existing code — a CLI superseding prose recipes, a v2 superseding a v1, a rewrite superseding a module — the thing being deleted is a capability **plus every bug fix its history accumulated**. Before deleting a test alongside the code it covered, classify each test: is it asserting a *fix*, or just asserting behavior? Grep the old test names for fix, regression, over-disclosure, leak, never, only, and any issue numbers in their comments. Fixes get ported and re-asserted against the replacement in the same PR; plain behavior tests may go with the code. Corollary: an existing test that FAILS after the port may itself have been asserting the buggy shape — correct it, don't work around it.
**Why (autonomy):** Promoted from this project's feedback ledger (captured 2026-09-15). Stop — shipped a CLI replacing SQL read recipes in which `thread --handle H` resolved a handle to every chat that handle had spoken in, groups included, returning all their rows; asking for one person's thread would have handed the agent every other participant's messages from every group that person was in. The deleted recipe carried exactly that fix, under a test named "reads ONLY the named contact's chat, never every chat (over-disclosure fix)". Prior authority — the fix and its name were in the git history of the very file being deleted in the same diff. Unblock — a reviewer caught it as blocking; a second instance of the same class (group-vs-direct guessed from an identifier prefix, misreading 193 of 2,413 group chats on a real store) shipped undetected in my version and was only caught when the work was re-landed by someone else.
**Next instance:** Replacing a hand-rolled retry wrapper with a library's built-in retry — read the wrapper's tests for the jitter/thundering-herd fix someone added after an incident, and re-assert it against the library's config, rather than assuming the library's defaults cover it.

## [removes-handback] A size/altitude bar is cleared by changing the diff, never by documenting the overshoot in the PR body
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Concise Code, beside the altitude-check bullet: when the pre-open check trips (>20 files / >600 additions for one ask), the only outcomes are **split, cut scope, or name why it is genuinely atomic**. Writing the overshoot honestly into the PR body is not a fourth outcome — the bar exists to prevent the review rounds, and a candid paragraph prevents none of them. Two concrete tests at the check: (1) compute **deletions alongside additions** — a change that adds a capability the repo already has in another form is an *addition that should have been a replacement*, and retiring the old path is what makes the size legitimate; (2) distrust a one-line "this can't be split" justification, which is the shape a rationalization takes — verify it against what the diff adds versus removes.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — computed +1,598/−187 across 19 files for a single-capability ask, wrote exactly those numbers into the PR body as an honest overshoot with a "a provider is not usable split" justification, and opened it. Prior authority — § Concise Code's altitude bar, which I had read and quoted in the same session. Unblock — the operator replied that the PR was huge and they worried the infra would be brittle; investigation then confirmed the real defect was that it added a second reader of a data store without removing the first, and that only ~33 of 605 new lines were irreducible.
**Next instance:** A migration PR hits 700 additions because it ships both the new schema path and a compatibility shim — at the check, notice the shim means the old path survives, and either retire it in the same PR or split the shim out, rather than opening with a note explaining the size.

## [removes-handback] Redeploying a bot that sits in third-party threads: trace and suppress every outbound the redeploy triggers there (intros, contact cards), and verify through logs, not a test message
**Change:** Before a retire-and-recreate (or reinstall) of an agent or bot that is a member of real conversations with outside people, trace what the platform sends into existing threads when the agent or its chats are re-created: welcome text, contact or vCard follow-ups, "I'm back" pings. Pick the path that sends nothing — e.g. restore the archived chat rows so inbound resolves to the existing chat instead of auto-creating one, then verify the swap through the agent's logs, its checkpoint state and the message table (zero new outbound in those threads). Never prove it with a smoke message in a real thread.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — the operator had to add "don't message the group threads, i don't want a bunch of contact cards in them" to the go-ahead (2026-10-05, plow4 Meetly swap). Code read afterwards showed the default retire-and-recreate *would* have posted a vCard into each of 3 groups on their next message (named-line chat auto-create, `deliver_line_card`). Prior authority — the operator's original question was "still maintain the group threads?"; the outbound paths were readable in the API before acting. Unblock — the explicit constraint; I then restored the chats 2 seconds after the delete, and nothing was sent.
**Next instance:** reinstalling a Slack or Discord bot that posts a join message into every channel it re-enters; re-provisioning a support bot whose recreated conversations re-send a greeting to customers.


## [removes-handback] "How come X isn't Y?" about the operator's own tooling asks for Y — do the reversible fix, don't seek sign-off on a boundary that only reads public content

**Change:** When the operator asks why their own system lacks something ("how come these aren't indexed / backed up / mirrored?"), take the question as a request for that thing. Trace the cause, then apply the reversible fix and report it, naming the boundary you crossed in the report. Ask first only when the fix runs or executes the untrusted content, or can't be undone.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — knightwatch-reviewer status page, 2026-10-06. Asked why six outside-contributor repos showed "not indexed", I traced it to a split between the host and container repo lists, then asked whether to clone and index those public repos on the reviewer host. Prior authority — the question itself implied "index them". The change was a gitignored config edit plus clones (reversible: delete them). Indexing only computes embeddings and runs none of the repos' code, and the reviewer already reads the same code in its containers. `CLAUDE.md` § Lean Less Conservative says to lead with the looser option. Unblock — a bare "yes you can".

**Next instance:** In a different tool, the operator asks "why isn't repo X in the search index / backup set / mirror list?". Add it, sync it, and report what was added, instead of asking whether you may.

## Recurring resource-limit failures ship the fix plus a visibility surface, not another point patch
**Change:** When a quota, rate-limit or exhaustion failure recurs (the operator calls it whack-a-mole), the deliverable is the fix plus one durable measurement that makes the next occurrence self-diagnosing. That can be an attribution log naming the endpoint or caller that tripped the limit, a usage counter, or an early warning before the limit is hit. Ask "when this happens again, which single line would name the cause?" and ship that line in the same PR.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — knightwatch-reviewer's GitHub secondary-rate-limit trips kept recurring across several point fixes. Each recurrence restarted a forensic dig that correlated logs across containers and hosts by timestamp, until the operator pushed back on the whack-a-mole. Prior authority — the recurrence itself was the evidence that the gap was visibility, not another leaf patch. Unblock — a previously added attribution log naming the tripping endpoint collapsed hours of correlation into one grep.
**Next instance:** A different service keeps hitting an LLM provider's 429s or a database connection-pool limit. Ship the fix together with a per-caller counter or log line, so the next trip names its top consumer without an investigation.


## [removes-handback] A merge you perform runs its whole sequel — "/cleanup not run" in a done report is a hand-back, not a status line
**Change:** When you merge a PR yourself (outside `/babysit-pr`'s Step 7 merge action, e.g. a hand-run `gh pr merge` after an explicit "merge it"), run the whole merge sequel that Step 7 owns before reporting done: `/cleanup` always, plus any deploy the ask named. The final report lists the sequel as done, never as "not run". Shape fix rather than a new rule: Step 7 already states this, but only inside its merge action, which a hand-run merge never enters. Name the sequel where merges happen, for example as a line in `PR_LIFECYCLE.md` § Merge.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — on knightwatch-reviewer#305 the agent merged and deployed after "merge once fixed and deploy", then reported "Not run: the post-merge `/cleanup`". Prior authority — babysit-pr Step 7 says the sequel follows every merge, whoever performs it. Unblock — the operator replied "please /cleanup".
**Next instance:** In a different repo, the operator says "merge it" on a converged plow PR and the agent runs `gh pr merge` directly. The `/cleanup` sequel should run in that same turn, not wait for a follow-up message.

## [removes-handback] The operator's stated purpose is the PII waiver — never mask the field the task exists to deliver
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Secrets` a sibling of the length-aware mask bullet: the mask convention binds **secrets** (keys, tokens, passwords) unconditionally; **PII about the operator's own users** (phone, email, address) is masked only in *intermediate* output nobody acts on. When the operator states a purpose that requires a field — "I want to reach out to them", "who should I call", "send them X" — that request is the waiver for that field: print it unmasked in the deliverable, the same turn. Masking the one field the task exists to produce returns the work half-done.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — asked for "as much info as possible" on three Plow users because the operator wanted to reach out, I ran my PII-masking sed over the whole dump and delivered area codes only; the operator had to come back with "what's scottie's phone number?". Prior authority — the stated purpose (outreach), the analytics skill's own rule ("resolve identity when the answer turns on who someone is"), and a project memory recording that the operator waives PII masking for their own users. Unblock — the operator asked for the number directly.
**Next instance:** a different repo's customer/guest lookup — a short-term-rental guest the operator wants to text, a CRM contact for a sales follow-up, an investor's email for a data-room send — where the deliverable *is* the contact field; print it in full, keep secrets masked.

## Pre-launch, take the root-cause fix — "users feel the gap now" is the only justification for the patch, and there are no users

**Change:** on a system with no live users, when weighing "patch the symptom now, fix the cause later", take the cause; say the visible gap persists until the root fix lands and treat that as acceptable rather than working around it.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — I recommended hand-restoring operational facts a regeneration had dropped, so an agent would have them "today"; the operator corrected it (no users, no today), and the hand-restore would have left the extraction bug in place to drop them again. Prior authority — the pre-PMF operating point and the fix-the-generator proposal. Unblock — the operator's one-line steer. (Session: 2026-08-02-str-wiki-regeneration)
**Next instance:** a staging-only billing service double-counts a usage event — fix the dedupe key rather than hand-correcting the ledger rows.

## [removes-handback] An app-layer gate (PIN, login, admin token) on data you need → read the backing store over host access you already hold before asking
**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md` § Take the Steps, beside "Investigate before you consult": when a UI or API gate hides state you need (a PIN-gated plan, an admin-only endpoint), check whether you already hold read access to the store behind it — SSH to the host, a read-only DB open, the deploy clone — and read it there (read-only, secrets unprinted) instead of telling the operator you can't see it or asking them for the value.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — math-practice, 2026-10-19: asked which lessons a kid had queued, I said the plan was behind the grown-ups PIN and asked the operator to supply the order. Prior authority — passwordless SSH to the Pi was in the host map and the README named the DB path. Unblock — the operator replied "can't you ssh into the rpi5 to determine?"; a one-line read-only query answered it.
**Next instance:** a different repo's admin dashboard needs a login to show a feature-flag value, while the flag table sits in a Postgres reachable over the operator's tailnet — query the table read-only instead of asking for credentials or the value.

## [removes-handback] A result that lives at a URL leads the done-summary with that URL — not only PRs and issues
**Change:** extend CLAUDE.md § Answer Shape's raw-URL rule from PRs/issues to any deliverable the operator will open: a listing page, a deployed site, a dashboard, a published release. Put its raw URL on the summary's first line.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — plow3, 2026-10-19: I reported an Agent Index listing as up to date and one-click deployable without its URL, and the operator had to ask "can you give me the url?". Prior authority — the URL was in the operator's own request, and the raw-URL rule already existed for PRs. Unblock — the bare request for the link.
**Next instance:** a different repo's Vercel preview or a tailnet report page finishes deploying; the summary opens with the page URL, not "deployed ✓".


## [removes-handback] A "deployed / live / ready to use" report carries the place the human goes to use it, as a raw link

**Change:** Any message that claims something is live, published, deployed, or ready names the URL (or path/command) the human uses to reach it, raw and clickable, in that same message — even when it is unchanged from before, and in addition to the PR/issue `Links` block.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — after an overnight merge+deploy of srosro/math-practice#16 the final report carried the PR and issue links but not the site, and the operator's first message was "what's the url?". Prior authority — `CLAUDE.md` § Answer Shape already requires every PR/issue to carry its raw URL; the deliverable here was the site, not the PR. Unblock — the operator asked for the link.
**Next instance:** a kwr/plow-api `/deploy` or a Vercel promote: the report names the dashboard or service URL the operator will open, not only the merged PR.

### +1 — 2026-10-26 · odio-dev-ai-consult-tracking · the merge sequel's report must restate the ship state, since it is the message the operator actually reads last
**Change:** When a merge sequel (`/cleanup`, `/deploy`, a post-merge verify) runs in the same turn-chain as the ship, its report leads with one line restating the ship state and the live raw URL ("live: https://<site>/<page>, verified in-browser") before its own ledger. The ship banner two messages up is not what the operator sees when they return.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — srosro/odio-dev#32 merged, Vercel auto-deployed, and production was driven in a real browser; the MERGED banner said "live on odio.dev/ai-consult" but carried no clickable `https://` link, and the `/cleanup` readiness report that followed became the last message. The operator came back and asked "did you deploy?" — a completion question for a deploy that was already done and verified. Prior authority — the merge+deploy mandate and the verification evidence were both in hand. Unblock — the operator's completion question.
**Next instance:** a plow `/deploy` whose `/cleanup` sequel prints a workspace-readiness report last: that report opens with "deployed: <host> @ <sha>, <url> verified" rather than only the readiness table.

## A review probe asking "is this edge-case branch contractual / worth a test?" is a cut signal — answer with a completeness guard that removes the branch, not a test that pins it
**Change:** When you added a branch for a rare edge case and a reviewer asks whether its plumbing is contractual enough to deserve its own endpoint test, first ask whether a completeness/fallback guard (rich path only when provably complete, else the plainer complete path) deletes the branch. Prefer removing branch + param + test over pinning all three.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — plow#866: an `extra_target` branch threaded through the endpoint drew a probe about testing it; I started designing the test. Prior authority — `CODING_STANDARDS.md` § Anti-Bloat and REVIEW.md's cut-LOC posture already rank deletion above a guard. Unblock — the operator asked "what is this for, can we cut it?" and a one-line guard replaced branch, param and test.
**Next instance:** a different repo's API handler grows an optional parameter for a double edge case and the bot asks for a parametrized test on it; the answer is the guard that makes the parameter unnecessary.

## Per-PR "one review then merge" authorization: the auto-review on open IS the round — fix anything real, merge pinned to head, trigger nothing further
**Change:** When the operator authorizes "one knightwatch review then merge" for a small low-risk PR, treat the review that auto-posts on open as that round: apply real findings, reply, then merge with `--match-head-commit`; do not post `/srosro-update-review` unless the round found a blocking bug. Per-PR, never standing.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — plow#2200 (a one-file route restore) was headed into the full iterate-to-convergence loop. Prior authority — the operator's explicit per-PR grant. Unblock — "one kwr review then merge."
**Next instance:** a kwr or code-config pointer-only restore PR the operator waves through with the same phrase; the loop ends after the opening review.

## A blocking startup-ordering probe on a feature's headline contract gets the real reorder plus a supervised boot, not a documented gap
**Change:** When a reviewer escalates "side effect X can fire before dependency Y is live" to blocking on the feature's headline promise, lead with reordering so the side-effect-capable work starts only after the dependency binds, and verify with a real boot/run of the changed path. A code read never validates a boot reorder.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — plow#747: offered (a) reorder + supervised dev boot vs (b) accept the cold-boot gap and downgrade; the operator picked (a). Prior authority — `CLAUDE.md` § Lean Less Conservative already says lead with the action-oriented option. Unblock — the operator's pick confirmed the instinct; the consult was a round-trip the rule already answered.
**Next instance:** a different daemon's alert relay that can emit before its transport is registered; move the registration ahead of the first emit and boot it once to prove the order.

## Bumping a hardcoded option id that users' persisted selection references: keep the old id statically listed beside the new one
**Change:** A picker whose options come from a server/catalog but whose selection is persisted client-side renders blank when the persisted id is missing from the catalog. When bumping such an id, list both the old and the new entry statically; do not inject the active selection dynamically.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — plow#821 bumped a model id and upgraded users got a blank picker while silently running the old model; I proposed injecting `active_model` into the catalog if missing. Prior authority — § Default to the Simplifying Option. Unblock — the operator rejected the dynamic injection for the static pair.
**Next instance:** a different app's region or plan dropdown backed by a server list; a renamed default must keep the prior entry until no persisted state references it.

## Cross-repo boundary docs give the system's shape and one example per boundary — mechanism choices are deferred to the PR that needs them
**Change:** When asked for "what lives where" / README / REVIEW.md ownership text across sibling repos, deliver orientation: the repos, what each owns, a one-line "is this mine?" test, one concrete example per boundary. Don't force design decisions into the doc or ask the operator to make them.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — a boundary-doc task turned into a settings-manifest transport design and a question for the operator. Prior authority — the stated purpose was "an agent in the wrong repo should notice." Unblock — the operator said the doc gives shape, not decisions.
**Next instance:** a monorepo split into app/infra/plugins repos; the README map names owners and the test, not the RPC schema the plugin will use.

## Marketing copy for the operator: at most 2–3 plain, understated options; exact words supplied are implemented verbatim
**Change:** For landing/marketing copy, skip tiered option menus and em-dash, imperative-urgency phrasing; offer two or three short plain lines, and when the operator hands over wording, ship it unchanged.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — a six-option tone-tiered banner pitch was called out as reading LLM-generated, and the operator wrote the understated line himself. Prior authority — his prior copy on the same site already set the voice. Unblock — "implement my words."
**Next instance:** a different product's launch banner or CTA; two restrained options, no survey.

## Building durable shared-resource test infra does not require holding that shared resource — a parallel session using it is not a collision
**Change:** Separate the deliverable (the mechanism: route, credential convention, runbook) from the operational last mile (claiming a specific shared line/account right now). Treat state moving under you as a contested-checkout alarm only in your own lane's checkout, never on a shared account resource another session legitimately uses.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — plow#1995: another session provisioned an agent on the shared test line and I stopped as if my workspace were contested. Prior authority — § Workspace Isolation's alarm is scoped to the checkout. Unblock — the operator clarified the two efforts were independent.
**Next instance:** a different repo's staging Slack workspace or shared test phone number in use by a teammate while you build the smoke harness that will use it.

## [removes-handback] A page or UI change ships with its preview URL in the first report — serve it before the review loop, from a no-store server
**Change:** The moment a user-visible page/UI change exists on disk, stand up the tailnet preview (bound per the "binds tailnet-reachable" proposal, with `Cache-Control: no-store` so a plain reload tracks the branch) and lead the report that first mentions the change with its raw URL — before `gh pr create` and before any review round. Screenshots in the agent's own context are verification, not a preview the operator can judge; a Vercel preview behind deployment protection does not count either.
**Why (autonomy):** Stop — plow#2554: the page was verified by Playwright and the PR opened, and the operator had to ask "can I get a preview?" and then "what's the preview? I'd like to see the URL" before seeing it; the design was then redesigned twice on sight (a text wall → /build's pattern → a separate quick-start page), after a review round had already been spent on the first shape. Prior authority — `CLAUDE.md` § Code Lives in ~/Hacking already says operator pages are hosted on the tailnet, and the operator's standing preference is to judge UI by looking at it. Unblock — the operator asked for the URL, twice.
**Next instance:** a Latch or dashboard UI change in another repo, or a docs-site page: serve the branch on the tailnet with no-store headers and put the URL at the top of the first message that says the change exists, so the shape gets judged before knightwatch burns a round on it.

## [removes-handback] When the dispatcher says they'll re-ticket you on the merge, the merge-watch is theirs — stop yours, and an empty tick never messages

**Change:** Resolve the conflict with the merge-watch proposals above ("A converged PR with a promised post-merge rollout gets a merge-watch", "watch merge state at 1–2 min") by an ownership census of the merge-wake: when the operator or a dispatching agent states that *they* own the merge signal ("I'll ticket you if he says merge"), `TaskStop` the babysit Monitor at convergence and say the loop is parked until re-ticketed — two watchers of one event is the finding, and the human-facing one wins. Separately, in every live loop a wake that observes no state change (no new comment, review, CI result, merge or close) emits nothing — not a re-arm notice, not a "still waiting" line — because in a dispatched session every wake reaches the operator.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — on plow-pbc/str-hermes-agent#114 (2026-10-28, str-hermes-agent2 cook session) the converged PR's watcher kept re-arming and each wake reported; the dispatcher first asked for state-change-only reports, then had to ask again to stop the watcher entirely because silent wakes still pinged them. Prior authority — the PR was converged and labeled, the merge was stated to be the human's, and the dispatcher had already said they would relay the merge. Unblock — two operator messages ("only report on a real state change", "stop the watcher entirely").

**Next instance:** A sous-dispatched cook babysits a code-config or plow PR to convergence; the sous says the merge will come as a new ticket. The cook stops its Monitor at convergence instead of ticking every 30 min, and the merge sequel (`/cleanup`, deploy) runs when the ticket arrives — as it did here (#114 merged → re-ticketed → deploy + `/cleanup`).

## [removes-handback] A host/tool failing is not "unreachable" until you've re-scanned the capabilities that surfaced mid-session

**Change:** Add to `CLAUDE.md § Verify Before Claiming Done` ("It can't run here" bullet): when a tool call fails with an unreachable/not-connected error, re-check the current skill and tool list — skills and deferred tools can appear mid-session in system reminders — for another path to the same host before telling the operator it's offline or asking them to fix it.

**Why (autonomy):** Stop — the Plow Latch MCP returned "mba is not connected", and I told the operator their Mac was offline and asked them to bring it online. Prior authority — a `latch` skill (the CLI that replaced the MCP, `--host mba`) had been surfaced in a system reminder earlier that session. Unblock — the operator asked whether I'd noticed the move from the MCP to the CLI; the CLI worked on the first call.

**Next instance:** any integration migrated from an MCP server to a CLI or skill (a Google Workspace connector, a browser driver, a deploy tool) where the old tool still answers with a connectivity error in long-lived sessions.
